title: Roadworks on Manchester Road Old Section to begin on 25 October 2026
excerpt: Temporary closure of part of Manchester Road Old Section in Rochdale from 25 October 2026 due to roadworks.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks will commence on the Old Section of Manchester Road from 25 October 2026. The work is expected to last until 30 October 2026, or until completion if sooner.

The affected area will see a temporary closure starting 1 metre north of the junction with Castle Avenue, extending 10 metres further north. This closure will impact traffic flow, particularly for those using this section of the road.

Motorists and local residents should plan their journeys accordingly, as diversions may be necessary during the roadworks. The council has provided a map of the roadworks and restrictions on their website for those seeking further details.

This development is significant for local commuters and residents, as it may affect access to nearby businesses and homes. For the latest updates and to view the roadworks map, visit the Rochdale Borough Council website.

title: Rochdale Council awards contract for Queen's Park SEND improvement project
excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to enhance the play area at Queen's Park, Heywood, focusing on inclusivity for children with special educational needs.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to MASSEY & HARRIS (ENGINEERING) LIMITED for the Queen's Park SEND and Improvement Project. This initiative aims to create a more inclusive play area at Queen's Park in Heywood, enhancing facilities for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

The project will involve several key improvements, including the extension of the existing play area, the installation of a dance arch, the creation of a sensory area surrounding the dance arch, and the addition of a wheelchair swing. These enhancements are designed to ensure that all children can enjoy the park's facilities, regardless of their physical abilities.

The decision to improve the play area reflects the council's commitment to inclusivity and accessibility in public spaces. By investing in these facilities, Rochdale Council aims to provide a safe and engaging environment for all children in the community, promoting social interaction and play.

The next steps will involve the commencement of construction works, with further updates expected as the project progresses. This development is significant for local families, particularly those with children who have SEND, as it will provide them with improved recreational opportunities in their community.

title: Does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall?
excerpt: The house on Clegg Hall Road is real and protected, the boggart story is old — but the medieval “tragedy” that feeds the legend is not supported by contemporary records.
summary: The house on Clegg Hall Road is real and protected, the boggart story is old — but the medieval “tragedy” that feeds the legend is not supported by contemporary records.
body:
Short answer: there is no documentary proof that Clegg Hall was the scene of a medieval massacre and therefore no factual basis to claim a still‑active, historically verified haunting. The house that people call Clegg Hall survives as a recognisable historic building and the boggart tale survives as folklore recorded by Victorian collectors; the two things sit side by side, not one inside the other. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

What we can say with confidence about place and period is plainly written in the records. The standing house on Clegg Hall Road is Grade II* on the National Heritage List for England and is described there as a house of about 1610, probably built for Theophilus Ashton; the list entry records its form, materials and a National Grid Reference (SD 92242 14490). The List entry is concerned with architecture and history, not ghost stories. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

The boggart story — the thing people mean when they talk about “Clegg Hall” in the way they might say “that place is haunted” — is a well‑attested piece of Lancashire folklore. It was written down and popularised in the nineteenth century by folklorists and local balladists. John Roby included an extended narrative about the “Clegg‑Hall Boggart” in his Traditions of Lancashire, and nineteenth‑century collectors and compilers (and later commentators) preserved variants that add striking motifs: murdered heirs, demons walking the house, an exorcist who bargains for “a body and a soul” and then produces “the body of a cock and the sole of a shoe” as a trick to lay the spirits. Those details recur across Roby, local ballads and later folklore anthologies. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

That still leaves a gap between colourful tale and verifiable fact. County historians who examined surviving deeds, visitations and surveys note that the estate’s documentary trail is ordinary land‑transaction history: the Clegg estates passed through Belfield, Howorth and other families, and the present house is likely a seventeenth‑century rebuild rather than a thirteenth‑ or fourteenth‑century timber manor in which a serial murder took place. The 1889 History of the Parish of Rochdale specifically warns that Roby’s dramatic narrative is “pure imagination” while acknowledging a living tradition of a ghost and even a local proverb, “As ill as Clegg Hall boggart,” meaning hard to get rid of. In short, land deeds and the Manor Survey (1626) document ownership and a substantial house; they do not record the alleged atrocity that underpins the legend. ([your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com](https://your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/04145039/chapter-xvii-old-houses-and-old-families-butterworth-pages337-389.pdf))

How historians and folklorists read that difference matters. Folklore scholars treat the Clegg Hall boggart as a regional example of a wider boggart tradition in Lancashire — mischievous, sometimes malevolent household spirits attached to particular places — and they trace how oral tale, ballad and antiquarian retelling built up the colourful episodes now associated with the site. Local‑history sources, by contrast, look for contemporary legal or parish records to corroborate dramatic claims and find none that support a medieval massacre. Both approaches are valid but answer different questions: one asks how people told and remembered the place, the other asks what can be proved from surviving documents. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

So does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall? If you mean “is there corroborated historical evidence of a medieval tragedy that left a ghost,” the answer is no. If you mean “does the story still haunt local memory and appear in collections and ballads?” the answer is yes — the tale is part of Rochdale‑area folklore and was repeatedly collected and retold in the nineteenth century and later. The difference is between living local tradition and verifiable historical fact. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

If you want to pursue the matter further: the National Heritage List entry is the authoritative source for the building’s architecture and dating; nineteenth‑century folkloric accounts (Roby and others) are the primary sources for the boggart narrative; and county histories and deed records (summarised in the parish history) are the place to check whether documentary evidence exists for any supposed crime. The List entry and county history are the best starting points for anyone who prefers deeds to apparitions. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

title: Two Rochdale men among ten charged in drugs supply investigation
excerpt: GMP says two Rochdale men are among ten people charged following a seven-month investigation. All ten have been remanded ahead of a Crown Court appearance.
content_html:
Two Rochdale men are among ten people charged following a seven-month investigation into the suspected supply and distribution of drugs across Greater Manchester and the West Midlands.

Greater Manchester Police named the local defendants as Jailil Ahmed, 53, of Twinegate, Rochdale, and Shakil Ahmed, 51, of Whittaker Lane, Rochdale.

In a statement issued on 27 October, the force said eight men, a woman and a 16-year-old boy had been charged with conspiracy to supply controlled drugs in classes A, B and C, and conspiracy to supply an unauthorised medicinal product.

The boy cannot be named for legal reasons. The other adult defendants are from Burnage and Wolverhampton, or have no fixed abode, according to the police statement.

GMP said its Serious and Organised Crime Group carried out the investigation into suspected large-scale supply and distribution in the two regions.

All ten have been remanded in custody ahead of a scheduled appearance at Manchester Crown Court on Friday 13 November 2026, the force said.

The charges are allegations. No finding of guilt should be inferred, and all defendants are presumed innocent unless and until convicted.

title: Middleton prepares for Christmas lights switch-on event
excerpt: Middleton is making final preparations for its Christmas lights switch-on event, scheduled for Saturday, November 14, in Middleton Gardens. The festive atmosphere is already taking shape with decorations appearing throughout the town, including a special red shoe outside Middleton Library in memory of Rochdale Council officer Lauren Mason, who passed away tw
content_html:
Middleton is making final preparations for its Christmas lights switch-on event, scheduled for Saturday, November 14, in Middleton Gardens. The festive atmosphere is already taking shape with decorations appearing throughout the town, including a special red shoe outside Middleton Library in memory of Rochdale Council officer Lauren Mason, who passed away two years ago.

The switch-on event will begin at 12pm and will feature a variety of attractions designed to engage the community and spread festive cheer. Attendees can look forward to food and drink stalls, fairground rides, and market stalls, including the Teenage Market, which supports local young entrepreneurs. Additionally, The Art House will host personalised Christmas card-making sessions and face painting for children.

As the day progresses, visitors will enjoy performances from local community groups, culminating in a performance by Middleton Brass Band at 4.30pm, which will help set the festive mood ahead of the lights being switched on.

This event not only marks the start of the Christmas season in Middleton but also provides an opportunity for local businesses and young entrepreneurs to showcase their offerings. Residents and visitors alike are encouraged to attend and participate in the festivities, making it a significant occasion for the community.

title: Sunderland held to a draw at Rochdale in League One clash
excerpt: Sunderland took the lead twice but were unable to secure a win against Rochdale, resulting in a frustrating draw in their League One fixture.
content_html:
In a League One match on 27 October 2020, Sunderland faced Rochdale at the Crown Oil Arena, where they were held to a 2-2 draw. Sunderland took the lead twice during the game but could not maintain their advantage, leaving them frustrated as they sought all three points.

The match saw Sunderland's hopes of climbing the league table thwarted, as they remained in seventh place following the draw. The result was disappointing for the visiting team, who had aimed to secure a win to improve their standing in the league.

Rochdale, on the other hand, managed to earn a valuable point at home, which could prove crucial as they aim to secure their position in League One. The draw reflects the competitive nature of the league, where every point counts.

This match highlights the unpredictability of football, where teams can struggle to convert leads into wins. Fans of both clubs will be looking ahead to their next fixtures, hoping for better outcomes. What are your thoughts on the match?

title: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing updates on Representative Body developments
excerpt: Andrew Johnson has been re-appointed as Chair of the RBH Representative Body, with Rachael Ray as Deputy Chair, as they work to improve services for residents.
content_html:
Andrew Johnson has been re-appointed as Chair of the Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) Representative Body during a meeting held last week. He welcomed Rachael Ray as the new Deputy Chair and acknowledged the contributions of outgoing Deputy Chair Rob Dyson. This update was shared on October 27, 2026, and highlights the ongoing commitment of the Representative Body to enhance services for residents.

During the meeting, the Representatives approved RBH's Annual Report to Customers, which is available on the RBH website. Johnson expressed satisfaction that the Representatives were able to provide additional oversight before the report's publication. The body also approved the findings of a recent scrutiny review aimed at improving customer feedback regarding the investment programme.

The scrutiny review resulted in six out of seven recommendations being accepted, including tailored approaches for gathering feedback from different customer groups. Johnson thanked the panel members and RBH staff for their efforts in this review, which aims to enhance how the organisation interacts with its customers and manages services.

Membership in RBH allows residents to have a voice in shaping the services that affect their homes and communities. Johnson encouraged those not yet members to sign up, emphasizing that their involvement strengthens the organisation and ensures it remains responsive to the needs of the community.

title: Heywood prepares for Remembrance Day services on 8 November 2026
excerpt: The borough of Rochdale will hold Remembrance Day services across various townships, inviting public participation to honour servicemen and women.
content_html:
The borough of Rochdale is set to hold Remembrance Day services on Sunday, 8 November 2026, across various townships, including Heywood. The council has extended an invitation to all members of the public to attend these commemorative events, which aim to honour the sacrifices made by servicemen and women, both past and present.

In a statement, the Mayor of Rochdale expressed the importance of community solidarity during this time of remembrance. The council is committed to supporting all members of the armed forces community, ensuring that their contributions are recognised and appreciated by the public.

Poppies, a symbol of remembrance, can be purchased at Number One Riverside in Rochdale and other designated locations. Additionally, they are available for purchase online through the Royal British Legion's website. The public is encouraged to wear poppies as a mark of respect and gratitude towards those who have served in the armed forces.

As the date approaches, residents are reminded of the significance of Remembrance Day and the opportunity it provides to reflect on the sacrifices made for peace and freedom. The council looks forward to seeing a strong turnout from the community to pay their respects.

title: Hopwood Hall College celebrates topping out of new Clegg Building
excerpt: A topping out ceremony at Hopwood Hall College marks a significant step in the construction of the new Clegg Building, set to enhance educational facilities in Rochdale.
content_html:
A topping out ceremony was held at Hopwood Hall College on October 26, 2026, marking a significant milestone in the construction of the new Clegg Building. This event celebrated the completion of the building's structure, which is being developed by Willmott Dixon and funded by the Department for Education, Rochdale Council, and the college itself.

The ceremony was attended by notable figures including Principal and CEO Julia Heap OBE, Rochdale MP Paul Waugh, and the Mayor and Mayoress of Rochdale, Faisal Rana and Iram Faisal. Family members of the late Robert Clegg OBE, after whom the building is named, were also present, highlighting the personal connection to the college. Robert Clegg served as Chair of the Corporation from 2007 to 2018 and made significant contributions during his tenure.

During the event, attendees were taken to the roof of the new building, which offers panoramic views of the borough, including landmarks such as Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Parish Church. Guests were invited to leave messages on the roof parapet, creating a lasting record of the occasion.

The Clegg Building is expected to provide a modern and inspiring learning environment for students at Hopwood Hall College, enhancing educational opportunities in the area. As construction progresses, the college community looks forward to the completion of this landmark development, which aims to foster a better learning experience for current and future students.

title: Man dies in three-vehicle crash on Rochdale Road in Edenfield
excerpt: A man has died following a serious three-vehicle collision on Rochdale Road in Edenfield, which remains closed as emergency services respond to the incident.
content_html:
A man has died following a serious three-vehicle collision on Rochdale Road in Edenfield. Emergency services were alerted to the incident at 11.24am on October 26, 2026, after the North West Ambulance Service contacted Lancashire Police.

Upon arrival, emergency services found that three vehicles had been involved in the crash. Tragically, a man was pronounced dead at the scene. The road remains closed while emergency services manage the situation, and it is expected to stay closed for some time as investigations continue.

Cllr Simon Holland, the ward councillor for Greenfield and Eden, reported a significant emergency service presence and noted the disruption caused in the village due to the incident. He described the scene as chaotic, with many residents affected by the road closure and the emergency response.

This tragic event highlights the ongoing concerns regarding road safety in the area. Local residents are advised to avoid Rochdale Road and seek alternative routes while the road remains closed. Updates will be provided as more information becomes available.

title: Littleborough defeat Trafford MV in ADM Lancs/Cheshire 2 clash
excerpt: Littleborough secured a victory against Trafford MV, maintaining their position at the top of ADM Lancs/Cheshire 2 despite challenging weather conditions.
content_html:
Littleborough Rugby Club faced Trafford MV in a challenging match in the ADM Lancs/Cheshire 2 league on Saturday, October 26, 2026. The match took place at Littleborough's home ground, where the team managed to secure a win despite adverse weather conditions, including heavy rain and strong winds.

Trafford MV entered the game with a number of key players unavailable due to injuries, which affected their performance. They initially took the lead with a try from Mica Dyos, making the score 5-0. However, Littleborough responded quickly, scoring a try and converting it to lead 7-5 at half-time.

In the second half, Littleborough capitalised on the weather and the slope of the pitch, scoring another try and a penalty to extend their lead to 15-7. They added a further try, bringing the score to 22-7, before Trafford MV managed to score again through Aaron Booth, who converted his own try, reducing the deficit to 22-12.

This victory keeps Littleborough at the top of the league, while Trafford MV slips further down the standings. The match highlights the challenges teams face during adverse weather conditions and the impact of player availability on performance.

title: Rochdale foster carers recognised for supporting over 1,000 children
excerpt: At an awards ceremony in Rochdale Town Hall, 34 foster families were honoured for their commitment to caring for vulnerable children, collectively fostering for 465 years.
content_html:
Thirty-four foster families were honoured at the annual Foster Carer Celebration Awards held at Rochdale Town Hall, recognising their dedication to providing safe and nurturing homes for vulnerable children. Collectively, these families have fostered for an impressive 465 years, supporting over 1,020 children and young people from newborns to 18 years old.

Among those celebrated were Michael and Marilyn, a couple from Milnrow, who have fostered for 50 years since 1976. They have cared for over 330 children, primarily focusing on newborns and siblings. Marilyn expressed her love for fostering, stating, "How long is a piece of string?" when asked how long they would continue. She reflected on the joy of seeing children grow up and receiving letters from adoptive parents thanking them for their influence.

The event highlighted the vital role foster families play in the community, providing stability and care to those in need. The awards serve not only to recognise the individual contributions of these families but also to raise awareness about the importance of fostering in Rochdale.

This recognition is significant as it underscores the ongoing need for foster carers in the area. With many children still in need of stable homes, the event aims to inspire others in the community to consider fostering. For those interested in becoming foster carers, further information can be obtained from the local authority's fostering service.

A total of 34 fostering families were honoured at the council’s recent annual Foster Carer Celebration Awards at Rochdale Town Hall in gratitude for their outstanding commitment to providing safe, stable and nurturing homes for some of the most vulnerable. Between all the carers, it is estimated they have supported more than 1,020 children and young people from newborn to 18, while working with the local authority. Among those celebrating their individual milestones was Michael, aged 79, and Marilyn, aged 75, who are marking 50 years. Predominantly caring for newborn babies and siblings since 1976, the married couple from Milnrow have cared for more than 330 children in that time and are still welcoming youngsters into their home. Marilyn said: “We’ve been to their weddings, adoption parties, christenings, 18th and 21st birthday parties. “It’s lovely when you think you started off with them as a baby and now, they’ve grown. Ian and Carole McLean celebrate 40 years of fostering with Rochdale Council “We’ve had letters from adoptive parents saying, ‘They’ve turned out like they have because of you’ which is nice.” Michael added: “We feel privileged and proud.” Another couple who have dedicated their lives to providing a safe and stable home to those who need it the most, is Carole, 65, and Ian 67. McLean from Rochdale, who are celebrating 40 years. Ian said: “When the children do go, they always take something with them of us because we give them that stability, assistance and support. “We even give them support when they’ve gone and we’ve got a number of former foster children that we class as family and they call us mum and dad, I’ve even given two of them away at their weddings.” READ MORE: New college building reaches construction milestone Among many more memorable moments they have shared as foster carers, Carole was also the birthing partner to another former foster child, an experience she simply described as being ‘brilliant’ to be a part of. In the four decades they have provided care, they have supported more than 200 children in total. Other special milestones celebrated during the event included Richard and Susan Shaw, who are retiring as foster carers after 25 years. Speaking after the recent celebration event, Cllr Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, said: “Our foster carers make an extraordinary difference to the lives of children and young people across our borough every single day and thank you simply isn’t a big enough expression for how grateful we are to them. Richard and Susan Shaw retire from fostering with Rochdale Council after 25 years “The dedication, compassion and commitment shown by these families is truly inspiring, and these awards are an opportunity to recognise and celebrate everything they do. “Whether they have been fostering for a few years or several decades, each and every one of them has helped provide the stability, care and support that children need to thrive. “On behalf of Rochdale Council, I would like to thank all our foster carers for the life-changing contribution they make to our communities.” Anyone over the age of 21 with a spare room in their home can become a foster carer and support those most in need. To accommodate various lifestyles and commitments, Rochdale Council, as part of Foster for Greater Manchester, also offers a number of different fostering arrangements from respite care to long-term fostering. People with the determination to make a positive impact in a young person’s life and who would like to find out more about fostering with Rochdale Borough Council, can visit the Foster for Greater Manchester website or call 0300 303 0321. title: Heywood school pupil wins competition to name new road after community figure
excerpt: Ava McEvoy, an eight-year-old from Our Lady and St Paul's RC Primary School, has won a competition to name a new road in Heywood, which will be called Murphy Close.

The competition was designed to engage the community and encourage local children to participate in the development process. Ava expressed her desire for the road to be named after Father Murphy, ensuring that his memory would be preserved in the area.

The new development, which is set to enhance the local infrastructure, is located in Heywood, although specific details about its exact location have not been disclosed. The project aims to provide improved facilities and housing options for local residents.

As the development progresses, it is expected to have a positive impact on the community, providing new opportunities and amenities. The next steps will involve the construction phase, with updates likely to follow as the project moves forward. This initiative highlights the importance of community involvement in local developments and the lasting impact of naming places after significant local figures.

Ava McEvoy put forward the name Murphy Close for the housing association’s 27-home Bury Old Road project in honour of a local Catholic priest. An eight-year-old school pupil has won a competition to name a road for a new £6.4 million First Choice Homes Development in Heywood. Ava McEvoy put forward the name Murphy Close for the housing association’s 27-home Bury Old Road project in honour of a local Catholic priest. A panel of judges decided the year 4 student’s suggestion will now take pride of place at the development's entrance. Father Morris Murphy founded a parish for the Darnhill Estate in the 1960s and was a respected community figure until his death in 2013. Ava, who goes to Our Lady and St Paul's RC Primary School, received a Samsung tablet for her winning name. "I'm really happy that my street name was chosen," she said. "I picked Murphy Close because Father Murphy did so much for the local community, and I wanted people to remember him." Headteacher of Ava’s school, Hollie Aspinall added: "We are incredibly proud of Ava and all the pupils who took part in the competition. “It has been a fantastic opportunity for our children to learn about local history and feel connected to a development that will become part of their community. Congratulations to Ava on her well-deserved win." FCHO project and partnerships officer Ghazalla Ibqal said: "This competition has given local children the opportunity to leave a lasting mark on the neighbourhood while learning about the people and stories that have helped shape Heywood. “We'd like to thank the school for working with us and congratulate Ava on her fantastic entry." The Bury Old Road project by Built Developments for FCHO comprises 12 two-bedroom and 15 three-bedroom properties. Nineteen are for social rent and eight rent-to-buy. Completion is scheduled for May next year. The judging panel was FCHO chief executive Mark Gifford, FCHO construction manager Jamie Smith, Ghazalla Iqbal, Hollie Aspinall and local councillors Stuart Crawford and Peter Joinson. title: Heywood nursery loses planning bid to keep caravan as outbuilding
excerpt: Little Oaks Nursery in Heywood has been denied permission to retain a caravan used as an outbuilding, following a planning decision by Rochdale Council.
content_html:
Little Oaks Nursery, located on Bamford Road in Heywood, has lost its bid to keep a caravan that replaced a temporary Portakabin in its yard. The nursery applied for retrospective planning permission for the caravan, which has been used as an outbuilding since the Portakabin was removed in 2024 after being granted temporary permission in 2022.

A report from a planning officer indicated that pre-application advice had been sought regarding the placement of a static caravan on the site. The advice stated that such a structure would not be visually appropriate and would be highly visible from both directions along Bamford Road. Despite this, the caravan was placed on the site without the necessary planning permission, prompting the nursery's application to regulate its presence.

The planning officer's report further noted that the caravan does not meet the high-quality design standards required for a permanent structure. It was concluded that the caravan does not offer any visual improvement over the temporary Portakabin it replaced, which was only accepted for a limited time due to its unsuitability for permanent retention.

This decision by Rochdale Council highlights ongoing concerns regarding planning regulations and the visual impact of structures within the area. Local residents and businesses may be affected by the enforcement of these regulations, as they aim to maintain the aesthetic integrity of the neighbourhood.

Little Oaks Nursery applied to Rochdale Council for retrospective planning permission for the caravan which is being used as an outbuilding at its site in Bamford Road, Heywood. It follows planning permission granted in 2022 for a temporary Portakabin classroom which was removed in 2024. A planning officer’s report said: “Simultaneously, pre-application advice was requested and given for the siting of a static caravan on the site. “The advice given was that such a structure would not be visually appropriate for the site and would be highly visible from both directions along Bamford Road. “Notwithstanding, it appears that a static caravan was nonetheless placed at the site without the benefit of planning permission and this application therefore seeks regulation of such. “The caravan does not provide the high-quality design that officers had previously stated would be required for a permanent structure. “In design terms, the caravan is of no visual improvement over the temporary Portakabin it replaces, which was accepted only for a temporary period on the basis that it was unacceptable for permanent retention. READ MORE: Remembrance Sunday services across the borough “The domestic, leisure-caravan character makes the structure even less suitable for permanent retention on the application site than a modular classroom would be. “Officers therefore consider that the visual harm that had been tolerated previously due to the transient and temporary nature of the development (being the Portakabin) is not acceptable in this instance where the structure would be of permanent nature.” Officers said that while the caravan is currently screened from view by fencing and a trellis, the trellis is a temporary measure and would require separate planning permission. The report added: “The unauthorised screening is insufficient to mitigate this harm, and the development is therefore contrary to policy.” Refusing the application, the council said: “The proposed development, by reason of its siting, massing, design, and temporary utilitarian appearance, would appear as an incongruous, poorly designed feature which would be readily visible from the surrounding street scene by virtue of its prominent location along Bamford Road. “The proposed development would fail to achieve high-quality design and would therefore be harmful to the visual amenities of the area. “The limited public benefits are insufficient to outweigh the harm caused and the proposed development is therefore contrary to Policies DM1 and P3 of the adopted Rochdale Core Strategy, Policy JP-P1 of the Places for Everyone Joint Development Plan, and the National Planning Policy Framework.” The nursery must remove the caravan or appeal the decision. title: GTAS weekly guide brings Halloween fun and a remembrance walk to Rochdale
excerpt: Get Together After Serving has shared its programme for 26 October to 1 November, including afternoon tea, a remembrance walk, Halloween activities and football.
content_html:
Get Together After Serving has shared its weekly programme for 26 October to 1 November 2026, with afternoon tea, a remembrance walk and Halloween activities at Denehurst Café, alongside football fixtures.

The community group is encouraging people to come along, get involved and support its activities. Here is the programme supplied by GTAS.

Monday 26 October: Afternoon tea at Denehurst Café runs from 12.30pm to 2.30pm. Booking is required, so contact GTAS to check availability before attending.

Wednesday 28 October: The Remembrance and Reflection Walk offers a gentle amble around the park, with time to chat and reflect. Meet at Denehurst Café at 12.15pm, ready for a 12.30pm start. GTAS men’s nine a side team is also in action; the supplied programme does not give a kick off time or venue.

Friday 30 October: Halloween activities at Denehurst Café include a movie night at 5pm and a spooky dog walk at 6pm.

Saturday 31 October: GTAS lists Port Vale v Rochdale with a 12.30pm kick off. Its programme also suggests parking up, meeting at Denehurst Café and walking to the ground. The fixture description and those walking arrangements need clarification, so confirm the match venue and meeting details with GTAS before travelling.

Sunday 1 November: GTAS Men’s Sunday League kicks off at 11am, with the venue still to be confirmed. GTAS Ladies are listed at Saddleworth 3Ds FC with a 3.30pm kick off.

The programme offers opportunities to spend time with others locally, whether over tea, on a walk or through sport. Check the GTAS page for updates, booking information and any changes before setting out. Prices, movie details and booking contact information were not included in the supplied guide.

Which activity would you like to join? Share your thoughts in the comments and pass the guide on to someone who might enjoy coming along.

title: Heights Lane roadworks to begin on 26 October 2026
excerpt: Roadworks on Heights Lane in Rochdale will result in temporary closures from 26 October to 1 November 2026, affecting local traffic.
content_html:
Heights Lane in Rochdale will undergo roadworks starting from Monday, 26 October 2026, until Sunday, 1 November 2026. The road will be temporarily closed from its junction with Knowsley Street to its junction with Mizzy Road during this period.

The roadworks are expected to take place daily from 8 am to 5 pm, which may cause disruptions for local residents and commuters. An alternative route will be available via Howard Street, Whitehall Street, and Quarry Street.

This initiative is part of ongoing efforts by Rochdale Borough Council to improve local infrastructure and ensure safer travel for all road users. Residents are encouraged to plan their journeys accordingly during the closure period.

For more information, residents can view a map of the roadworks on the Rochdale Borough Council website or check Google Maps for directions.

title: Free benefits checks at Littleborough and Wardle libraries on Monday and Tuesday
excerpt: Council advisers will offer free, no booking needed benefits checks at Littleborough Library on 26 October and Wardle Library on 27 October, from 10am to noon.
content_html:
Residents unsure whether they are receiving all the financial support available to them can speak to council advisers at two free library drop in sessions this week. The sessions are particularly relevant to pensioners, carers, disabled residents and people worried about household costs, but the council says they are open to adults generally.

The first is at Littleborough Library in Hare Hill Park, Littleborough OL15 9HE, on Monday 26 October 2026 from 10am until noon. The second takes place at Wardle Library, 448 Birch Road, Wardle OL12 9LH, on Tuesday 27 October, also from 10am until noon. No appointment is needed for either event.

The council says advisers can check potential entitlement to Pension Credit, explain Attendance Allowance, review Council Tax Support eligibility and give information about Winter Fuel Payments, Blue Badge applications and other cost of living assistance. They can also signpost residents to organisations offering further help, including Citizens Advice and Age UK. Attending does not guarantee entitlement to a benefit or an immediate payment: decisions depend on the relevant eligibility rules and application process.

Anyone attending is asked to bring details of their income, pensions, savings and benefits already received, so advisers can offer a more accurate check. Those visiting on behalf of a family member should bring relevant information if available. Take care with personal documents and give sensitive details only to the advisers at the official session.

Both sessions are advertised by Rochdale Borough Council as free and do not require booking. Anyone unable to attend can use the council's published events information to find its contact details and check for other advice sessions.

Official event details: Littleborough Library https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/1484/pension-credit-awareness-drop-in-event---littleborough-library and Wardle Library https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/1485/pension-credit-awareness-drop-in-event---wardle-library.

title: Rochdale Council Tax Direct Debits delayed by one day after system error
excerpt: Council Tax Direct Debits due on Monday 26 October will instead be collected on Tuesday 27 October, Rochdale Council says. The notice applies to the affected collection date.
content_html:
Residents whose Rochdale Council Tax Direct Debit was due to leave their account on Monday 26 October 2026 should expect it to be collected on Tuesday 27 October instead, following a system error at the council.

The authority has placed a notice across its official website explaining that payments scheduled for Monday 26 October will be taken one day later. It has not said in that notice how many accounts are affected, what caused the error or whether any other collection dates will change. The published change concerns this specific Monday collection date, not every Council Tax instalment.

For residents who budget closely around outgoing payments, the practical point is to leave enough money in the account for the revised Tuesday collection. A payment not showing as taken on Monday does not, by itself, mean the instalment has been cancelled. Residents should avoid making an additional manual payment simply because the usual Direct Debit has not yet appeared, without first checking their account or speaking to the council.

The council says residents can check their Council Tax balance through its MyAccount service. People who need help can contact the Council Tax team on 0300 303 8870. These are official council channels; no bank details should be supplied to an unsolicited caller or message claiming to be about the delay.

The notice was checked on Monday 26 October. It does not explain whether customers will receive individual notifications. Rochdale Daily will update this report if the council announces any further change.

Official information: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/counciltax. Council Tax account guidance: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax/council-tax-account-balance-enquiries. Council contact details: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/contactcentre.

title: Wednesday deadline to comment on parking changes in Rochdale, Littleborough and Milnrow
excerpt: Residents have until Wednesday 28 October to comment on three proposed parking orders affecting Mere Street, Wardle Street and the Butterworth Hall area.
content_html:
Drivers and residents have until Wednesday 28 October 2026 to object to or comment on three proposed parking restriction changes across Rochdale borough. The council has published notices of intent for Mere Street in Rochdale, Wardle Street in Littleborough and the Butterworth Hall and Royds Street area in Milnrow. These are proposals, not restrictions already in force.

On Mere Street, near Drake Street in the Milkstone and Deeplish ward, the proposal would shorten existing no waiting at any time restrictions on both sides of the road from 22 metres to 15 metres from the junction. That would release a small additional length for parking. The council says the change follows the introduction of one way working and pavement build outs, and is intended to improve local parking provision without compromising visibility. The order reference is H60/1456.

On Wardle Street in Littleborough, the council proposes new no waiting at any time restrictions on the north side for 10 metres from Whitelees Road, and on the south side between Whitelees Road and Frederick Street. Its stated reasons include junction visibility, narrow carriageway width and reports of vehicles parking on both sides or on the footway. The reference is H60/1457.

In Milnrow, the Butterworth Hall area proposal would introduce no waiting at any time restrictions on the south side of Butterworth Hall for 59 metres from Royds Street, and on the east side of Royds Street for 24 metres from Butterworth Hall. The council cites double parking and difficulties for refuse and other larger vehicles using the roads. The reference is H60/1459. The notice's heading labels the amendment as 2027, while its objection deadline is explicitly 28 October 2026; readers should use the council's order reference when asking for clarification.

Comments or objections must reach the council by 28 October. Residents can email trafficorders@rochdale.gov.uk or write to Network Management, Floor 2, Number One Riverside, Smith Street, Rochdale OL16 1XU, stating the relevant reference and the reasons for their objection. The council also accepts comments in support while the objection period is open.

The full notices, maps and reasons are available through the council's Traffic Regulation Orders page: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/roadworks-repairs-restrictions/proposed-permanent-restrictions-highways-traffic-regulation-orders.

title: New book showcases unseen 1930s photographs of Rochdale's Norden Riviera
excerpt: A new book featuring 600 unseen photographs captures the essence of 1930s Rochdale, including the lost Norden Riviera lido, highlighting the area's historical significance during a transformative decade.
content_html:
A new book titled "Britain in the 1930s" by Steven Brindle and Maureen Hill features 600 previously unseen photographs, including images of Rochdale's lost Norden Riviera lido. This collection captures the essence of Greater Manchester on the brink of World War II, showcasing the stark contrasts of the era.

The Norden Riviera, which opened in 1935, was a popular outdoor swimming pool located off Edenfield Road in Norden. It provided a seaside experience for local families who could not afford to travel far. The facility included diving boards, slides, and spectator stands, surrounded by gardens and sports fields, making it a cherished local attraction during the 1930s.

The book highlights the economic challenges faced by the north of England during this decade, with unemployment rates soaring due to the decline of traditional industries. However, it also reflects a time of joy and resilience, as communities sought leisure and enjoyment amidst the hardships of the Great Depression and the aftermath of World War I.

"Britain in the 1930s" is available for £50 and covers various regions, including parts of the old Lancashire, now Greater Manchester. The inclusion of Rochdale's Norden Riviera serves to illustrate the area's rich history and the importance of preserving local heritage.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Unseen pictures of 1930s from Manchester's Ritz to Rochdale 'Riviera' - Manchester Evening News ‌ ‌ Skip to main content Manchester Evening News: Number one for news, opinion, sport & celebrity news Unseen pictures of 1930s from Manchester's Ritz to Rochdale 'Riviera' From Rochdale's lost "Norden Riviera" lido to an almost deserted East Lancashire Road, a remarkable new book featuring 600 unseen 1930s archive photographs captures Greater Manchester on the brink of WWII. View 8 Images Cashier at the Ritz Dancing Hall. Manchester, on Boxing Day 1938 Add to preferred sources Comments News Neal Keeling Chief reporter 05:53, 26 Oct 2026 Storm clouds were gathering again globally. But on Boxing Day 1938 she captured, vivaciously, just one aspect of that decade. Crimson-lipped the cashier of the Ritz Dancing Hall in Manchester reflected the population's determination to find joy after the dark days of the First World War, the Great Depression, and unemployment. The 1930s led novelist and broadcaster JB Priestley to his famous vision of "three Englands" – the ancient country of cathedrals and villages, the blackened and scarred industrial Britain created by the Victorians, and the Americanised new consumer world of suburbs, cinemas and motorcars. He came to the conclusion after travelling the country with his suitcase and a typewriter to find material for his book "English Journey" published in 1934. ‌ Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter The decade in Britain saw a nation in transition. The north was hit hard by economic turmoil with unemployment levels soaring above the national average due to the collapse of industries like coal mining and shipbuilding. However, seaside cities became alive in the 1930s, thanks to the expansion of cheap rail travel and the emerging concept of paid holidays with thousands of working-class families flooding to the coast during their “Wakes Weeks” But the south and the midlands had seen a growth in new industries, notably car making, and electrical goods, and were able to withstand the economic fallout which the book says were distributed in a "grotesquely uneven way". ‌ A picture of a young, very well dressed couple, on Oxford Street, London, shows how affluence thrived in parts of the country while elsewhere, like the Lancashire George Orwell (pen name for Eric Blair) discovered in his travelogue "The Road to Wigan Pier" working class communities were decimated by the decline of traditional industries. View 8 Images A Wigan street decorated with washing, 1930s. The land as a place of marked contrasts is captured in a new book, Britain in the 1930s by Steven Brindle and Maureen Hill from Atlantic Publishing, price £50. It features 600 unseen black and white historic photographs of the UK. Counties covered by the book include parts of the old Lancashire, which are now in Greater Manchester, Cheshire, Yorkshire, Lancashire, and Northumberland. ‌ Images include an outdoor swimming pool in Rochdale in 1936 known as the Norden Riviera; soldiers clearing snow from the Manchester to Sheffield railway line; and a busy Deansgate in December 1930. A now lost Rochdale lido gave Mancunians a chance to enjoy a seaside experience without having to travel to the coast or abroad. The Norden Riviera opened in 1935 during when open air swimming was booming in Britaian. Located just off Edenfield Road in Norden, it was 'Rochdale by the sea' for many who could not afford a longer journey or who preferred something nearer to home. The pool was heated and came equipped with diving boards, slides and spectator stands. It was surrounded by attractive gardens, a cafe, a sports field with horse riding facilities, fences for show jumping, cricket pitches and areas for ball games. ‌ View 8 Images The "Rochdale Riviera" - the open air pool as it was at Norden in 1936. The Manchester Guardian newspaper on August 17, 1935. described the facility. It said: "The Norden pool, which measures 80ft by 40ft and is from 2ft 6in deep to 9ft deep is situated in the grounds of what, before the war, was Tenter House, just beyond the bleachworks at Norden, and the stables, where horses are kept for hire, belonged to this residence." "It is surrounded by green deckchairs and by an outdoor café, where one may have tea (or other meals) under green and yellow umbrellas. All around are delightful woods, beyond which one can see a shoulder of hill - but not the three factory chimneys lower down the valley. "A round paddling-pool satisfies the children too young to swim, and the conservatory of the old house has been turned into a ballroom. Next season, tennis courts, a gymnasium, a miniature golf course, and a children's playground will be added to the attractions of the Norden Riviera. ‌ View 8 Images A well-dressed couple in Oxford Street in 1932. "Bathing in the warmed water often continues till late by the light of powerful electric lamps." Other images in the book include Manchester's Cenotaph in St Peter's Square in 1935 in its original location before it was dismantled and reconstructed by Manchester City Council in 2014 at the northeast corner of the square next to the town hall to make way for the expansion of the Metrolink tram service. The memorial was first unveiled on July 12th 1924 by the Earl of Derby assisted by a Mrs Bingle, a local resident, whose three sons all died in the First World War. ‌ View 8 Images Manchester's Cenotaph in St Peter's Square pictured in 1935. A street in Wigan is pictured decorated with washing strung out across it. A Liverpool policeman directing traffic is seen standing in a protector box. These days the East Lancashire Road can be a notorious spot for traffic chaos. But a 1933 picture of the then "Liverpool to South East Lancashire Road" shows just eight vehicles over a half mile distance. The 27 mile highway was built at a cost of £3m. Britain was on the cusp of change in the 1930s. A world that would soon be transformed forever by the Second World War. ‌ Photographs in the book cover every county and city at that time, revealing a nation poised between tradition and modernity. View 8 Images A busy Deansgaate, Manchester in December 1930 The 1930s marked the golden age of the British seaside. Packed beaches, bustling promenades, pleasure piers and elegant hotels lured millions. Blackpool and Morecambe became synonymous with summer holidays. Camping, walking and boating holidays grew in popularity, while lidos, dance halls and pavilion theatres reflected a new culture of recreation and entertainment. ‌ Beyond the towns and cities, much of rural Britain appeared little changed from previous centuries. Medieval market squares, village greens and ancient churches dominated the landscape, while agricultural shows, livestock markets and seasonal fairs continued to shape everyday life. The decade was a world where horses and carts still shared roads with motorcars, and where quaint picturesque villages, market towns and centuries-old buildings remained at the heart of British identity. Co-author, Steven Brindle, is an historian and conservationist from Blackburn. He studied History at Oxford and spent almost forty years with English Heritage in a variety of roles as a historian and Inspector of Ancient Monuments. He has published extensively on architectural and engineering history. The photographs in the collection are from the archive of Associated Newspapers, plus contrbutions from many distinguished photographers. ‌ View 8 Images Holidaymakers on the sea front in Blackpool 1930s. They include: James Dixon-Scott, a photographer who wanted to record landscapes and ways of life that he felt were vanishing. He travelled around Britain taking pictures of buildings and rural scenes with exceptional compositions. Anthony Frank Kersting was a leading British architectural photographer. He was a Londoner who studied at Dulwich College where he developed his creative interests. His work featured a wide range of subjects from industrial landscapes to village life across the country. He was one of the leading architectural photographers of his generation and a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society. Will F Taylor was known for photographing sweeping panoramic landscapes across Britain from the end of the Victorian period right through the 1930s. His work has featured in many social history collections. ‌ The book is published on November 5th. View 8 Images The book Britain In The 1930s will be published on November 5th. title: New documentary explores the history of Hollingworth Lake
excerpt: A new YouTube documentary delves into the fascinating history of Hollingworth Lake, revealing its origins and significance to the local community.
content_html:
Hollingworth Lake, a popular recreational area for residents of Oldham, Rochdale, and surrounding regions, has been the subject of a new YouTube documentary that explores its intriguing history. Created by Malc Grimwood, a local history enthusiast, the documentary is part of his channel "Tales From Trails Around The Dales."

The lake, situated on the outskirts of Littleborough beneath the Pennine hills, is a man-made body of water that was established during the Industrial Revolution to support the extensive canal network. Grimwood highlights the lake's significance, stating, "Hollingworth Lake is one of Rochdale's most cherished and well-known beauty spots, offering an escape and a place to enjoy its open spaces and rural setting."

The documentary not only sheds light on the lake's origins but also aims to connect viewers with the natural beauty and historical context of the area. It showcases the surrounding countryside, wooded slopes, and moorland that contribute to the lake's charm and appeal.

For those interested in local history and the environment, the documentary serves as an engaging resource. It invites viewers to appreciate the rich heritage of Hollingworth Lake and encourages them to explore the area, fostering a deeper connection with this beloved landmark.

Published: 26 October 2026 Foster carers who, between them, have clocked up a total of 465 years supporting children and young people across the borough have been recognised by Rochdale Borough Council. A total of 34 fostering families were honoured at the council’s recent annual Foster Carer Celebration Awards at Rochdale Town Hall in gratitude for their outstanding commitment to providing safe, stable and nurturing homes for some of the most vulnerable. Between all the carers, it is estimated they have supported more than 1,020 children and young people from newborn to 18, while working with the local authority. Among those celebrating their individual milestones was Michael, aged 79, and Marilyn, aged 75, who are marking an incredible 50 years. Predominantly caring for newborn babies and siblings since 1976, the married couple from Milnrow have cared for more than 330 children in that time with no signs yet of them slowing down. “How long is a piece of string?” Marilyn joked when asked how long she will continue to foster for, before adding she would really miss fostering. "We’ve been to their weddings, adoption parties, christenings, 18th and 21st birthday parties. “It’s lovely when you think you started off with them as a baby and now, they’ve grown. “We’ve had letters from adoptive parents saying, ‘They’ve turned out like they have because of you’ which is nice.” Adding to their reflection as foster carers, Michael said: “We feel privileged and proud.” Ian (right) and Carole McLean (left) celebrate 40 years of fostering with Rochdale Borough Council. Another couple who have kindly dedicated their lives to providing a safe and stable home to those who need it the most, is Carole, aged (65) and Ian (67) McLean from Rochdale, who are celebrating 40 years. Looking back at their own experience as foster carers, Ian said: “When the children do go, they always take something with them of us because we give them that stability, assistance and support. “We even give them support when they’ve gone and we’ve got a number of former foster children that we class as family and they call us mum and dad, I’ve even given 2 of them away at their weddings.” Among many more memorable moments they have shared as foster carers, Carole was also the birthing partner to another former foster child, an experience she simply described as being ‘brilliant’ to be a part of. In the 4 decades they have provided care, they have supported more than 200 children in total. Richard (left) and Susan Shaw (right) retire from fostering with Rochdale Borough Council after 25 years. Other special milestones celebrated during the event included Richard and Susan Shaw, who are retiring as foster carers after 25 years. Speaking after the recent celebration event, Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, added: "Our foster carers make an extraordinary difference to the lives of children and young people across our borough every single day and ‘Thank you’ simply isn’t a big enough expression for how grateful we are to them. “The dedication, compassion and commitment shown by these families is truly inspiring, and these awards are an opportunity to recognise and celebrate everything they do. "Whether they have been fostering for a few years or several decades, each and every one of them has helped provide the stability, care and support that children need to thrive. “On behalf of Rochdale Borough Council, I would like to thank all our foster carers for the life-changing contribution they make to our communities." Anyone over the age of 21 with a spare room in their home can become a foster carer and support those most in need. To accommodate various lifestyles and commitments, Rochdale Borough Council, as part of Foster for Greater Manchester, also offers a number of different fostering arrangements from respite care to long-term fostering. People with the determination to make a positive impact in a young person’s life and who would like to find out more about fostering with Rochdale Borough Council, can visit the Foster for Greater Manchester website or call. title: Tree falls across the top of Belfield Road
excerpt: A large tree has come down at the top of Belfield Road in Rochdale, with its trunk and branches lying across the carriageway and pavement.
content_html:
A large tree has fallen at the top of Belfield Road in Rochdale.

A photograph sent to Rochdale Daily shows the trunk lying across the carriageway, with branches reaching to the front of a terraced house on the opposite side of the road. Debris covers the pavement, and part of a metal railing appears to have been knocked over.

It is not yet known when the tree came down or what caused it. There have been no reports of anyone being hurt.

With the trunk lying across the road, drivers and pedestrians are advised to avoid the area and use another route until the tree has been cleared.

A fallen tree blocking a public road can be reported to Rochdale Borough Council's highways team. If it has brought down power lines or poses an immediate danger, call 999 and keep well away.

Rochdale Daily will update this story when we know more about clearance and whether the road has reopened.

Were you affected, or did you see the tree come down? Tell us in the comments or email news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, said “Nothing fills me with greater pride in my role than hearing about the tremendous achievements of our cared for children and getting the opportunity to celebrate their individual successes during Our Big Day. “They are all exceptional young people and show phenomenal determination to be their very best and this doesn’t go unnoticed by those around them.” Children attended with their families and carers. Activities included trampolines, funfair rides, face painting and character appearances. The council hosted the event with support from local sponsors, including Matthew Moss High School, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, GFM and Rochdale Hornets. title: Traffic congestion on M62 near Rochdale following accident
excerpt: An accident on the M62 has caused significant traffic delays on the eastbound carriageway between junctions 21 and 22, affecting commuters and local drivers.
content_html:
Traffic congestion is building on the M62 this afternoon, October 25, following an accident on the motorway near Rochdale. The incident has resulted in partial blockage of the eastbound carriageway between junctions 21 (Milnrow) and 22 (Rishworth Moor).

According to traffic monitoring service Inrix, long queues have formed as a result of the accident, with motorists advised to expect delays. Motorway cameras show significant congestion in the area, impacting both local drivers and those travelling further afield.

Inrix later updated their report, indicating that the blockage is now attributed to a 'traffic problem' rather than a continuing accident. However, congestion remains on the eastbound carriageway, suggesting that the aftermath of the incident is still affecting traffic flow.

Motorists are encouraged to check current traffic conditions before travelling and to consider alternative routes if possible. The situation highlights the importance of staying informed about road conditions, especially during peak travel times.

title: Remembrance Sunday services planned across Rochdale borough
excerpt: Residents will gather on November 8 to honour those who served in the armed forces, with parades and services in multiple towns.
content_html:
Residents across the Rochdale borough are set to come together on Sunday, November 8, to pay their respects to those who have made sacrifices defending the country. Remembrance Day commemorations will feature a series of services and parades in towns including Rochdale, Castleton, Heywood, Littleborough, Middleton, Milnrow, Norden, and Wardle.

The events will see representatives from the Navy, Army, and Royal Air Force join veterans and civic dignitaries. Each service will include hymns, prayers, the Last Post, a two-minute silence, and the national anthem, ensuring a solemn tribute to those who served.

In Heywood, the parade will commence at 10.15am on Tower Street, proceeding to St James’ Street before arriving at Heywood Memorial Gardens for a service at 10.55am. Similarly, in Middleton, the parade will gather at 10.10am facing the Harbord Harbord pub, departing for Middleton Remembrance Gardens at 10.20am, with the service starting at 10.45am.

In Rochdale, participants will assemble outside The Flying Horse Hotel in Packer Street at 10.30am, where they will be joined by ward councillors and other civic guests. The parade will march to the Cenotaph for the service at 10.55am, followed by a march past before returning to The Flying Horse Hotel.

title: Rochdale mum diagnosed with breast cancer after routine NHS screening
excerpt: Sarah Hickman, 50, encourages women to attend NHS breast screenings after her cancer was detected early during a routine mammogram.
content_html:
A Rochdale mother, Sarah Hickman, has been diagnosed with breast cancer following a routine NHS screening, prompting her to urge other women to attend their appointments. At 50 years old, Sarah received her invitation for a mammogram and attended without any health concerns. However, just a day later, she was called back for further tests at the Breast Unit at Bolton NHS Foundation Trust.

After undergoing additional imaging, an ultrasound, and a biopsy, doctors confirmed that Sarah had a small breast cancer detected at a very early stage. Reflecting on her experience, she described it as a 'textbook case' and expressed gratitude for the NHS screening process, which allowed for early detection before any symptoms appeared.

Sarah's case highlights the importance of regular breast screenings, especially for women aged 50 and over, who are invited for routine mammograms every three years. Early detection can significantly improve treatment outcomes and survival rates, making it crucial for women to take these invitations seriously.

As Sarah continues her treatment, she hopes her story will encourage others to prioritise their health and attend NHS screenings. Women in Rochdale and beyond are reminded that these screenings can save lives, and they should not hesitate to book their appointments.

The road closures are part of the arrangements made by Rochdale Borough Council to facilitate the Remembrance Sunday events, which honour those who have served in the armed forces. For more information on the roadworks and to view a map of the affected areas, residents can visit the Rochdale Borough Council's official website.

title: Bridge Street in Heywood closed over building safety concerns
excerpt: GMFRS says firefighters attended for around two hours and 40 minutes after concerns about a building structure. The road's reopening remains unconfirmed.
content_html:
Firefighters attended concerns about a building structure near Bridge Street in Heywood for around two hours and 40 minutes on Saturday 24 October, according to an updated GMFRS statement reported by the Bury Times.

Update: 12.55pm GMT, Sunday 25 October 2026

The fire service said one engine from Heywood was called at about 6.30pm on Saturday. Crews inspected the building and made the area safe alongside Greater Manchester Police and Rochdale Council.

The Bury Times also reported that police attended to help manage the cordon. Emergency services have not confirmed that the storm caused the structural concerns.

The reports reviewed do not confirm when Bridge Street reopened or provide information about injuries. The precise building has not been identified. The end of firefighters' attendance does not establish that the road reopened.

Earlier update: 11.31pm BST, Saturday 24 October 2026

The Manchester Evening News reported concerns that strong winds could cause a derelict building to collapse. Its 9.20pm BST update said the area had been made safe, the building was still standing and firefighters remained at the scene when that report was issued.

Earlier report: 9.25pm BST, Saturday 24 October 2026

the source reported that Bridge Street was closed by emergency services. Its photographs showed a police cordon, a marked police car blocking access and a fire engine.

Anyone encountering restrictions should follow directions from emergency services. Further confirmed information about the road will be added to this article.

title: Rochdale Council encourages reporting of concerns regarding HMOs
excerpt: Residents are urged to report any issues with Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) to ensure tenant safety and compliance with regulations.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council is urging residents to report any concerns related to Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs). This initiative aims to protect tenants from inappropriate and illegal behaviour by landlords, ensuring that living conditions meet safety standards.

Residents can report issues through the council's dedicated webpage, which provides contact details and access to the licensing register for HMOs. The council has a legal obligation to address concerns and maintain housing standards in the borough.

The number of HMOs has been increasing in Rochdale, raising concerns about tenant safety and compliance with housing regulations. By reporting issues, residents can assist the council in taking appropriate action against non-compliant landlords.

For more information or to report a concern, residents can visit the Rochdale Borough Council's website or email housing.standards@rochdale.gov.uk.

title: Accrington Stanley thrash Rochdale 5-0 in League Two clash
excerpt: Accrington Stanley secured a dominant 5-0 victory over Rochdale, marking their biggest away win in Football League history and extending their unbeaten run to nine games.
content_html:
Accrington Stanley achieved a remarkable 5-0 victory against Rochdale in a League Two match on Saturday, October 24, 2026. This win marks the largest away victory in Accrington's Football League history, showcasing their dominance throughout the match.

The goals came from Josh Woods, Charlie Warren, Tyler Walton, who scored twice, and substitute Alex Henderson. The scoring began in the 14th minute when Woods capitalised on a mistake by Rochdale's goalkeeper, Sam Waller, to slot in a low shot from 20 yards. By half-time, Accrington had already secured a commanding lead with three goals, leaving Rochdale's players and fans frustrated. The second goal came in the 38th minute when Walton set up Warren, who lashed a low strike in off the post. Walton then added a third goal just before the break, arcing a shot over Waller in stoppage time.

Accrington's manager, John Doolan, expressed his satisfaction with the team's performance and set a target for the play-offs, highlighting their impressive unbeaten run of nine games across all competitions. Doolan noted that the team is now just one point off the play-off positions, a significant improvement from their previous season where they finished 16th. He described the performance as possibly the best of his tenure, urging his players to build on this momentum.

The defeat leaves Rochdale in a difficult position, having not won in their last five matches. The result is a stark reminder of the challenges they face as they look to turn their fortunes around in the coming weeks. Fans expressed their disappointment as the team was booed off the pitch after the match.

title: Weather warning issued for Rochdale as Storm Boelo approaches
excerpt: Residents in Rochdale are advised to prepare for potential disruption as Storm Boelo is expected to bring strong winds and heavy rain this weekend.
content_html:
Residents in Rochdale are being warned to prepare for disruption as Storm Boelo approaches the borough this afternoon. The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for wind, predicting strong gusts that could cause damage to buildings and trees, as well as affecting local rivers and roads.

Forecasters expect Storm Boelo to bring a very windy and wet spell this weekend, with strong winds spreading across northern parts of the UK on Saturday afternoon. Gusts of 55-65 mph are likely widely, with some coastal and exposed areas potentially experiencing gusts of 70-80 mph or more, particularly in Scotland and the far north of England.

The storm follows closely on the heels of Storm Austen, which recently impacted the south, south-west, and parts of Wales, with winds reaching up to 84 mph. Residents are encouraged to stay updated on weather conditions and take necessary precautions to ensure their safety during the storm's passage.

As Storm Boelo is expected to persist overnight and through much of Sunday, it is crucial for local residents to remain vigilant and prepared for possible disruptions. This weather event highlights the importance of being aware of severe weather warnings and taking proactive measures to protect homes and property.

title: Rochdale station regeneration scheme progresses with new homes and public square
excerpt: A significant regeneration project around Rochdale railway station is underway, featuring new homes and a public square, aimed at improving access to the town centre.
content_html:
A regeneration scheme aimed at transforming the area around Rochdale railway station is making significant strides, according to local officials. The project includes the construction of 81 new homes on vacant land adjacent to Rochdale’s Central Retail Park, part of a broader initiative to enhance connectivity between the train station and the town centre.

The development, named John Rennie Place in honour of the Scottish civil engineer who designed the Rochdale Canal, began in November 2026 and is expected to be completed by December 2027. The homes will consist of two, three, and four-bedroom properties and are being built as affordable net zero homes, marking a significant step in sustainable housing for the area.

In addition to the residential units, the regeneration plan includes the creation of a new public square in front of the station and 33 apartments on a brownfield site at the corner of Maclure Road and Station Road. This initiative is part of a larger effort to reconnect the station, which historically served as a hub for industrial transport, with the town centre, reflecting the changing needs of the community.

The project was made possible by a successful bid for £15 million from the government’s Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund, which has enabled the local authority to move forward after years of planning and investment challenges. The local council reports that the development is already benefiting the local economy and community, providing much-needed housing and improving public spaces.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The scheme to regenerate land around Rochdale station progressing | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The scheme to regenerate land around Rochdale station progressing George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 24, 2026 | 9:23 AM Print A scheme which would transform the gateway into Rochdale is making significant progress, town hall bosses say. Some 81 two, three-and four-bedroom homes are currently under construction on vacant land next to Rochdale’s Central Retail Park. This forms part of a wider scheme to create a connection between the train station and the town centre. The wider regeneration of the area around Rochdale railway station also involves the creation of a new public square in front of the station and 33 new apartments on a brownfield site on the corner of Maclure Road and Station Road. The train station in Rochdale was once a hub for industrial business generations ago, so the distance between the station and the town centre was purposeful separation. But as times changed, society changed and the station suddenly started transporting people, not goods. This is why there is an idea to improve access and avenues from the station and the main hub of the town. This 81-home development, known as John Rennie Place, in honour of the late Scottish Civil engineer who masterminded the Rochdale Canal, got under way in November last year, and is due for completion in December 2027. The project, approved years ago, was unlocked following a successful bid for £15m from the government’s Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund. The transformation has been on the cards for a long time, but the local authority struggled to get the investment until last year. The properties will be the first affordable net zero homes delivered as part of a housing scheme supported by the council. The local authority says the development is already delivering benefits to the local economy and community. Contractor Willmott Dixon, working on behalf of the council, has already spent £3.3m with local civil engineering firm, Hovington Ltd, and supported a total of 95 weeks of apprenticeship and T-Level training, including three T-Level placements from Hopwood Hall College. Seven local people are also employed on the project, including two people who were previously unemployed, with the council’s work and skills team supporting the recruitment. Tommy Patterson, 22, from Middleton, is one of the local people working on the new homes. He said: “I had been out of work for six months when the job centre arranged for me to get my CSCS card and that led to me securing a scaffolding apprenticeship here on site. I have always worked and had been let go, so getting this job was a lifeline. “I live on my own and I was struggling to pay my bills. It’s great to work here. Everyone is lovely; it’s a smashing team.” Daniel Fletcher, 17, is studying for a T Level in design, surveying and planning at Hopwood Hall College, said: “I really like it here. I’ve been talking to the different trades delivering this project, so I’ve been exposed to different parts of the job, and I have the freedom to go onto site on my own. It’s already changed massively since I started in the summer.” The project is being led by Rochdale Development Agency (RDA) on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council. Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for housing and regeneration at Rochdale Borough Council, said: ”We want local people and businesses to feel the benefit of local projects and it’s great to see that these benefits are already being felt on this development before a single house has even been completed. “By ensuring that social value is embedded in our procurement system, we’re making sure that local people are invested in the extensive regeneration which is taking place on their doorstep and are benefitting from the economic transformation we’re spearheading across the borough. That’s how it should be and how it will continue to be.” Work to create 142 apartments next to the new homes is ongoing, with the procurement of a delivery partner expected to get underway soon. title: Community efforts revive historic Lodge Mill after devastating fire
excerpt: Lodge Mill in Middleton, a historic site dating back to 1850, is seeing a revival thanks to community support following a fire that left it in ruins.
content_html:
Lodge Mill, one of the oldest mills in Middleton, is undergoing a revival after a devastating fire left the historic structure nearly destroyed. The fire, which occurred earlier this year, resulted in the loss of significant parts of the mill, including a children's dance studio and an ice cream parlour. Fortunately, no injuries were reported during the incident.

The mill, which dates back to around 1850, was deemed uninsurable following the fire, complicating efforts for its restoration. However, local residents and volunteers have rallied together to support the rebuilding efforts. A GoFundMe page was established, raising over £7,000 to aid in the restoration process, demonstrating the community's commitment to preserving this historic landmark.

Martin and Paula, who were actively working on renovating the three floors above Lodge Mill prior to the fire, are now at the forefront of the recovery efforts. Thanks to the dedication of volunteers, life is returning to Lodge Mill, with plans to restore it to its former glory.

The revival of Lodge Mill is significant not only for its historical value but also for the community spirit it embodies. As restoration efforts continue, the mill is set to become a focal point for local activities once again, highlighting the importance of community involvement in preserving local heritage.
