evidence_sources.captured_text: The potential return of Lodge Mill | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The potential return of Lodge Mill George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 24, 2026 | 2 hours ago Print Community effort to clear up rubble at Lodge Mill in Middleton Lodge Mill in Middleton was devastated by a fire six months ago. Now there is hope for its future thanks to some dedicated business owners, volunteers and one avid ice cream fan. In March, firefighters were called to the massive blaze that left businesses in tatters and left the historic mill a shell. Several businesses were based on the ground floor of the building, believed to be one of the oldest mills in Middleton. A children’s dance studio, an ice cream parlour, a tea room, a dog chiropractor business and the Engine House event space, which held weddings, functions and parties, were all lost in the fire. The former silk and cotton mill, on Townley Street, dates back to around 1850. It was bought by couple Martin Cove and Paula Hickey in 2019, who were working passionately to renovate the three floors above. The pair have since kickstarted a fundraising campaign to restore the building soon after the fire, because the mill was uninsurable. Martin and Paula said the blaze ’caused the almost total loss of the main mill structure’. “No one was injured, and for that we are incredibly thankful,” the couple said at the time of the fire. “But we are heartbroken at the loss of not only our beloved Lodge Mill, but also the homes of the many local businesses and the community space we had all built together. “The outpouring of love and compassion from the people of Middleton and the surrounding area has given us the strength to carry on.” The GoFundMe page has raised just over £7,000 since it was launched six months ago. Thanks to a group of keen volunteers, life has returned to the mill. Rubble has been moved from the old Engine Room and more than 120 pallets of full bricks, Yorkshire Stone and specialty bricks have been picked up by hand and stacked. The annual duck race was held at the site in May, the ice cream shop has reopened and there are upcoming events for Halloween and Christmas. There is a long-term vision to bring the mill back into proper use again, with businesses on the ground floor and new flats above. But before that can happen, the site needs to be cleared. One keen volunteer is Dawn Alker, she visited The Ice Cream Shop at Lodge around eight years ago. She has returned many times since, but most recently as a volunteer. She said: “I went there for ice cream about seven or eight years ago and fell in love with the place. When it burnt down they asked for volunteers to clean it up. “Everyone goes down and chips in and does what they can on the day. “I used to be a manager in the NHS and now I am making a monster for Halloween in a burnt down mill. “It’s really nice to be working collectively. It’s turned into a community support project in a way. “I have mental health issues and I had stopped going outside and stayed inside too much. I started helping, selfishly, because I wanted the ice cream place back open again. “My mental health started to improve as I got moving more and others have said the same. “In terms of the project we have got to clear the site because it was bulldozed. Then the end goal is to rebuild it. “Then we want small businesses with flats over the top of them. That is just a vision at the moment. “It is going to  be a long project but it is going to be brilliant.” Dawn went on to say that the managers of Lodge Mill, Martin and Paula, have already instructed architects and looked at the structural integrity of the remaining walls at the mill. The business owners are hoping to submit planning proposals to the council in the coming months. title: Upcoming services and events at st Luke’s Church, Deeplish
excerpt: St Luke’s Church in Deeplish is hosting several community events this week, including a Holy Communion service and a women’s breakfast.
content_html:
St Luke’s Church in Deeplish is set to hold a service of Holy Communion on October 25 at 10am, officiated by Revd Sylvia Barron. Following the service, attendees are invited to enjoy tea or coffee and engage in conversation, fostering a sense of community among participants.

Additionally, on October 28, the church will host a Bible study group at 10am, welcoming anyone interested in exploring the Bible in a friendly and informal setting. Later that day, at 11am, there will be a Morning Praise service led by Reader Sue Horobin, open to both regular members and newcomers.

This morning, the church is also hosting a women’s breakfast from 9am to 10:30am in the parish room. This event offers a chance for women to connect with friends and meet new people, with breakfast provided free of charge.

The main service on October 29 will begin at 10:30am, focusing on Matthew, chapter nine, verses 18 to 24. The church encourages anyone who hasn’t attended before to come as they are, with refreshments available after the service.

title: Decision on 450-home development in Bamford delayed again
excerpt: The planning committee has deferred a decision on a housing scheme in Bamford, citing insufficient drainage details and historical flooding issues.
content_html:
The Rochdale planning committee has once again delayed a decision on a proposed housing development in Bamford, which aims to build 45 homes as part of a larger 450-home project. The committee's latest meeting on October 22 revealed ongoing concerns about drainage and flooding on the site, which is located behind Greenvale.

In August, the committee had previously deferred the application from Wain Homes, expressing the need for more detailed plans to address historic drainage issues. Councillors noted that without a comprehensive masterplan for the entire development, they could not make an informed decision. The site, which was removed from green belt status under the Greater Manchester housing strategy, has been flagged for its seasonal flooding problems.

Objector Lisa Bailey highlighted the site's history of flooding, stating that the area is 'seasonally wet ground'. She urged the committee to ensure that infrastructure and access issues are adequately addressed before any development proceeds. Coun Stephen Anstee remarked on the unusually high number of conditions attached to the application, indicating that the proposal is not yet ready for approval.

Wain Homes' planning agent, Stephen Harris, argued that a flood risk management assessment was included in their application and that the other developers involved in the wider scheme had no objections. However, the committee decided to defer the application again, requesting a full report on drainage management from Wain Homes before proceeding.

title: Rochdale wins gold at Britain in Bloom awards, crowned champion
excerpt: Rochdale has been awarded gold at this year’s Britain in Bloom awards, securing the title of overall winner in the Town Centres and City Centres category.
content_html:
Rochdale has achieved a remarkable victory by winning gold at this year’s Britain in Bloom awards, being crowned the overall champion in the Town Centres and City Centres category. This accolade places Rochdale ahead of competitors such as Floral Godalming from the Southeast and Shaftesbury in Bloom from the South, as well as Sidcup Partners Limited from London.

The town's success in this prestigious competition is a continuation of its strong performance in recent years, having previously secured gold in 2018 and being named Best Small City in 2022. Last year, Middleton town centre held the title, making this win particularly significant as it keeps the award within the borough.

Judges praised Rochdale for its vibrant floral displays, which were provided by Bowlee Garden Nursery, as well as its recycling initiatives and exceptional cleanliness. They highlighted the pride, teamwork, and dedication of the community, along with the commitment to local biodiversity and strong partnerships that exceeded the gold standard in horticulture and environmental responsibility.

Rochdale's historic Baillie Street Quarter and the striking murals created during the 2025 Rochdale Common Walls Festival were also noted for showcasing the town's culture and civic pride. This recognition not only celebrates the town's beauty but also reflects the ongoing regeneration efforts supported by a multi-million-pound National Lottery Heritage Fund grant.

title: Rochdale Borough Council awards £1.1 million contract for young people's accommodation
excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract worth over £1 million to Stepping Stone Projects for a new supported accommodation service for young people at risk of homelessness.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract valued at £1,108,081 to Stepping Stone Projects for the Rochdale Team Around the Young Person Accommodation Model (TAYPAS). This initiative aims to provide supported accommodation for young people aged 18 to 25 who are at risk of or experiencing homelessness. The contract will run from November 2, 2026, to November 1, 2029.

The TAYPAS model will deliver specialist, psychologically informed support within a newly developed, purpose-built facility that will feature 28 self-contained units. The service will offer 24/7 support and management, ensuring that young residents receive the assistance they need to transition into independent living.

This development is significant for the local community as it addresses the pressing issue of youth homelessness in Rochdale. By providing a safe and supportive environment, the council aims to improve the life chances of vulnerable young people in the area, helping them to build skills and confidence.

The next steps involve the construction and operational setup of the accommodation, which is expected to be completed in the coming months. This initiative not only reflects the council's commitment to supporting young people but also highlights the importance of addressing homelessness in the borough.

title: £150 off energy bills: Rochdale households urged to watch for important letter
excerpt: Warm Home Discount confirmation letters are arriving for eligible households, with the £150 energy credit applied over the winter rather than paid to everyone at once.
content_html:
Rochdale residents who qualify for £150 off their energy bills are being urged to check their post as Warm Home Discount confirmation letters begin arriving.

The government started issuing letters on Thursday, 22 October, with correspondence continuing through to January 2027.

Around six million households across Britain are expected to benefit this winter. The letters will explain whether the discount will be applied automatically or whether the recipient needs to provide more information.

Anyone whose letter asks them to contact the Warm Home Discount helpline must do so before 26 February 2027.

The Warm Home Discount supports eligible households, including people receiving qualifying means tested benefits. Eligibility depends on the scheme’s rules, including benefit entitlement and the electricity account arrangements on the qualifying date.

For this winter, the qualifying date was 23 August 2026.

The £150 is normally applied directly to an eligible household’s electricity account. It is not a cash payment into a bank account, and there is no single payment day for everyone in Rochdale.

Eligible customers should receive their discount by 31 March 2027. Residents can check their supplier’s app, online account or bill for the credit.

The scheme is separate from the Winter Fuel Payment and Cold Weather Payments. Receiving the Warm Home Discount does not affect either entitlement.

For households watching every pound, the important step is to read the letter carefully and respond if action is requested.

Have you received your letter or seen the £150 appear on your energy account? Tell us your supplier and experience in the comments, keeping account numbers and personal details private.

Scheme information: https://www.gov.uk/the-warm-home-discount-scheme

Qualifying date and payment timetable: https://www.edfenergy.com/help-support/warm-home-discount

title: Rochdale projects £10.6 million spending on roads as repair programme targets borough streets
excerpt: Council figures project £10.63 million in carriageway maintenance spending for 2026/27, around 26 per cent more than the previous year.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council projects spending £10.63 million on carriageway maintenance this financial year, around £2.16 million more than the previous year.

The figures appear in the council’s Highways Maintenance Transparency Report, which sets out how it maintains the borough’s roads and where the money goes.

Projected carriageway spending for 2026/27 is approximately 26 per cent higher than the £8.47 million recorded for 2025/26. The total includes £1.357 million in Department for Transport incentive funding.

The £10.63 million covers carriageway maintenance across the borough, including wider repairs and resurfacing. It is a spending projection for the full financial year, rather than a sum already spent.

The council’s capital programme lists 6.01 kilometres of road resurfacing and a further 7.10 kilometres of preventative treatment.

Named resurfacing locations include Whitegates Road in Middleton, Wordsworth Way and Seymour Street in Heywood, Belfield Lane, Kiln Lane and sections of Edenfield Road.

The report also records 10,998 permanent repairs and 364 temporary repairs during 2025/26, illustrating the scale of ongoing maintenance. Those figures count repairs rather than individual streets.

For residents, the practical question is what improvement that spending will deliver on the roads they use every day.

Which street should be a priority, and have previous repairs lasted? Tell us the road name and nearest junction in the comments so we can investigate specific locations.

title: Roadworks on Elizabethan Way in Milnrow to begin on 23 October 2026
excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks will commence on Elizabethan Way in Milnrow from 9pm on Friday, 23 October 2026, until 6am on Saturday, 24 October 2026, or until the work is completed, whichever is sooner.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks will commence on Elizabethan Way in Milnrow from 9pm on Friday, 23 October 2026, until 6am on Saturday, 24 October 2026, or until the work is completed, whichever is sooner.

The roadworks will result in the temporary closure of part of Elizabethan Way, specifically between the roundabout junction and Newhey Road, covering a distance of approximately 418 metres. This closure will affect traffic in both directions, impacting local drivers and residents.

In addition to Elizabethan Way, nearby roads including Bridge Street, Dale Street, and Newhey Road may also experience disruptions during this period. Local residents and commuters are advised to plan their journeys accordingly and seek alternative routes where possible.

For further information and updates on the roadworks, residents can visit the Rochdale Borough Council website, where a map of the affected area is available.

title: From six modems to 580 staff: Rochdale’s Zen Internet puts people and planet alongside profit
excerpt: Rochdale’s Zen Internet grew from £5,000 and six dial-up modems into a national broadband provider. Its B Corp approach puts customers, staff and the environment alongside profit.
content_html:
A Rochdale broadband business that began with £5,000 and six dial-up modems is highlighting how its B Corp approach shapes decisions about customers, staff and the environment.

Zen Internet was founded in 1995 after a conversation over a couple of pints between brothers Richard and Daniel Tang. Today, the company employs 580 people and supplies connectivity to homes and businesses across the UK.

Alongside that growth, Zen has retained its independence. Founder and chief executive Richard Tang remains its sole shareholder and has pledged never to sell the company.

What does being a B Corp mean?

Zen became a Certified B Corporation in 2020, joining a movement of businesses assessed against B Lab’s standards of social and environmental performance, transparency and accountability.

For Zen, that means considering the impact of its decisions on employees, customers, communities and the environment alongside financial performance.

The company points to practical examples, including two paid volunteering days each year for every employee, a fully UK based customer service team and a Contract Price Promise offering no mid-contract price rises.

Its community support includes donations to charities chosen through staff votes, involvement in the Rochdale Ambassadors scheme to attract investment and support for Rochdale Circle, which helps older residents live independently.

Zen also says it reinvests profits in its network and services, uses 100% renewable energy and refurbishes routers to extend their working lives and reduce waste.

One sourcing decision involved choosing an alternative to planned solar panels after identifying modern slavery concerns in the supply chain, despite the additional cost.

A business built for the long term

Tang says the company’s independence gives it freedom to make decisions with lasting benefits.

“From the moment I started Zen, I wanted to build a company that made a positive difference to the wider world, not just the bottom line,” he said.

“Becoming a B Corp was a natural fit given our freedom to make long-term choices, like keeping our support team in the UK and never raising prices mid-contract, that a purely shareholder-first business might struggle to justify.”

For Rochdale, Zen’s story is also one of a locally founded company growing into a national provider while continuing to employ hundreds of people.

For customers, the practical questions are straightforward: how much will a service cost over the full contract, who will answer when something goes wrong, and what happens to equipment when it is replaced?

Zen’s approach puts those everyday concerns at the centre of its business story.

What matters most when you choose a broadband provider: price, reliability, customer service or its wider impact? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: The Healey Dell prophecy: Eleanor Byron, Mother Bagden and what the records actually show
excerpt: A short guide to the strange local tale that a Lady Eleanor was “maid, wife and widow in one day” — what early collectors wrote, what the Heritage Centre tells visitors, and what survives as documentary fact.
summary: A short guide to the strange local tale that a Lady Eleanor was “maid, wife and widow in one day” — what early collectors wrote, what the Heritage Centre tells visitors, and what survives as documentary fact.
body:
Healey Dell’s narrow gorge — the Thrutch — is one of Rochdale borough’s most durable story‑places. The best‑known version of the tale says a local noblewoman, usually called Lady Eleanor (later linked by tellings to the Byron family), visited a fortune‑teller named Mother Bagden; the woman predicted Eleanor would be a maid, a wife and a widow all in one day, and on her wedding night the bridegroom was killed. That dramatic sequence appears in the earliest printed collections of Lancashire lore and in the Dell’s modern visitor material, but the story’s status changes sharply once you separate nineteenth‑century collectors from contemporary medieval records. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

The oldest printed witness we can point to is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire, a book of collected oral tales published in the early 1800s; Roby preserves a long, romance‑style narrative set at Healey that includes a miller, a ‘Fairies’ Chapel’, a talisman and the fatal wedding night that fulfils the prophecy. Roby’s purpose was to record local storytelling rather than to provide documentary proof of medieval events, and his account reads as literary folklore rather than archival history. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Local antiquarians and guidebooks of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries amplified Roby’s version. The Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s trail guides and a short history leaflet reproduce the same outline: Ralph the miller, a messenger, Mother Bagden who claims intimate contact with a Fairy Queen, and the prediction that Eleanor will be “maid, wife and widow” in one day, followed by the death of her groom in a family feud. Those local guides attribute their narrative to older local histories such as William Robertson’s writings. The Heritage Centre presents the material as local myth and interpretation, alongside explanations of the Dell’s geology and industrial archaeology. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

What is demonstrably factual? Healey Dell is a managed nature reserve and visitor attraction at 121 Dell Road, with industrial archaeology (old mill sites, lodges) and a prominent Victorian railway viaduct that now forms part of a riverside trail. The viaduct is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those physical and administrative facts are public and documentable. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

What is folklore and what is missing from the archive? The supernatural elements — a Fairy Queen with prophetic power, spells that cause a bridegroom’s death, a named medieval Lady Eleanor whose wedding‑night fate is attested in contemporary court rolls or parish registers — lack contemporary documentary support. The story’s appearance in sources begins with nineteenth‑century collectors (Roby) and later local antiquarians (for example William Robertson as cited in modern guides); no contemporaneous medieval legal documents or parish entries confirming the prophecy or the precise characters named in the tale have been produced in those printed sources. In short: the prophecy belongs to the region’s oral and printed folklore tradition rather than to verified medieval record. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Why the story endures is straightforward: Healey Dell’s dramatic rock cleft, the Thrutch, looks for stories. A recess by the river invites the idea of a “Fairies’ Chapel”, and the valley’s history of mills, local rival families and visible ruins supplied the narrative scaffolding that collectors and guidebook writers later filled with characters and prophecy. The Heritage Centre explicitly treats the tale as part of the Dell’s storytelling — useful to visitors but not presented as archival fact. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

If you want to follow the trace yourself: read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the early printed narrative; consult the Healey Dell Heritage Centre material for the local retelling and references to later antiquarians; and visit the Dell to see the viaduct, the Thrutch and the mill remains that inspired the story. If you hope to find a medieval legal record proving the prophecy, those proving documents are not cited in the early printed collectors and have not been produced in the local guides that preserve the tale — which is why historians and the Heritage Centre treat it as legend, however rooted in local memory it may be. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Why the story endures is straightforward: Healey Dell’s dramatic rock cleft, the Thrutch, looks for stories. A recess by the river invites the idea of a “Fairies’ Chapel”, and the valley’s history of mills, local rival families and visible ruins supplied the narrative scaffolding that collectors and guidebook writers later filled with characters and prophecy. The Heritage Centre explicitly treats the tale as part of the Dell’s storytelling — useful to visitors but not presented as archival fact. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

If you want to follow the trace yourself: read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the early printed narrative; consult the Healey Dell Heritage Centre material for the local retelling and references to later antiquarians; and visit the Dell to see the viaduct, the Thrutch and the mill remains that inspired the story. If you hope to find a medieval legal record proving the prophecy, those proving documents are not cited in the early printed collectors and have not been produced in the local guides that preserve the tale — which is why historians and the Heritage Centre treat it as legend, however rooted in local memory it may be. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

The roadworks are part of ongoing efforts to improve infrastructure in Rochdale. For more details, visit the Rochdale Borough Council website.

title: Rochdale selected for £9.4m children’s mental health pilot
excerpt: Breaking: Rochdale will join Stockport and Tameside in Care Together, bringing NHS mental health professionals into children’s social care teams from early 2027.
content_html:
Rochdale has been selected for a new government mental health pilot designed to make support easier to access for children involved with social care and their families.

The Department of Health and Social Care has announced up to £9.4 million over three years for Care Together, which will operate across Rochdale, Stockport and Tameside.

Mental health professionals from existing NHS services will work within children's social care teams. The aim is to help families receive expert support earlier, with less difficulty navigating separate services.

NHS Greater Manchester Integrated Care Board will lead the programme alongside the three local authorities. It is expected to launch in early 2027 and run until 2029.

Who could benefit?

The department says up to 7,000 children and young people across the three participating boroughs could be covered, alongside their parents, carers and guardians. That figure covers all three boroughs combined. A separate allocation for Rochdale has not been provided in the announcement.

The groups identified include children in need, those on child protection plans, children in care, care leavers and adopted children.

Support could include family therapy and help for parents and primary caregivers, with services tailored to individual needs.

What will change for families?

Mental health professionals will work within social care settings, bringing expertise into the teams already supporting children and families.

The government hopes this will make it easier to identify needs and arrange appropriate help before problems reach crisis point. Faster access is an intended benefit of the pilot, with its effectiveness to be evaluated during the programme.

Dame Diana Johnson, Minister of State for Public Health and Patient Safety, said:

“For too long, fragmented mental health services have left young people in care, care leavers, parents, carers, and guardians not knowing where to turn for support.

“We are committed to change how we support young people, and this exciting and innovative pilot will see thousands more children across Greater Manchester get specialist mental health support based on their personal needs and in quicker time, before they reach crisis point.”

Children's Minister Josh MacAlister said children supported by social care can face severe mental health challenges because of trauma and adversity. He said the pilot forms part of wider efforts to support vulnerable young people as they move into adult life.

Professor Manisha Kumar, Chief Clinical Officer at NHS Greater Manchester, said the programme would help partners provide earlier support that takes account of children's experiences and wider family circumstances.

She said learning from the work in Rochdale, Stockport and Tameside would also help shape changes nationally.

When will Care Together start?

The pilot is expected to launch in early 2027 and run until 2029. An evaluation will assess whether the approach could be extended to other parts of the country.

The announcement does not yet specify how many Rochdale families will receive support, how referrals will work or which local teams will take part.

For local families, those practical details will matter: who can access help, how quickly it becomes available and whether bringing services together makes support easier to obtain.

What would make the biggest difference to mental health support for children and families in Rochdale? Share your thoughts in the comments, while protecting children's privacy and avoiding details that could identify them.

title: Planning approved for new £11.4 million special needs school in Rochdale
excerpt: Rochdale Council has received planning permission to build a new special needs school, set to open in 2028, aimed at supporting children with complex needs.
content_html:
Rochdale Council has been granted planning permission to construct a new special needs school, designed to accommodate pupils with complex educational needs. The £11.4 million project will be located on a site off Mayfield Street and will serve as a satellite for Redwood School, focusing on children with autism and social-emotional challenges related to autism.

The new school will provide 64 places for students aged 11 to 16 and is expected to open its doors on September 1, 2028. The development will include a part one, two, and three-storey split-level building, complete with parking, play areas, and landscaped grounds. The aim is to create a secure and therapeutically informed learning environment that supports vulnerable young people.

Seven Architecture, the firm behind the design, stated that the facility will enhance the quality of special educational needs (SEN) provision within the borough. The school will feature a café and spaces designed to foster personal development and effective behaviour management, ensuring that staff can deliver specialist teaching in a supportive setting.

Construction is set to begin next year, marking a significant step forward in expanding educational resources for children with special needs in Rochdale. This initiative is crucial for local families seeking tailored educational support for their children, reflecting the council's commitment to improving SEN services in the area.

title: Plans for 17-storey tower next to historic Marble Arch pub rejected
excerpt: Councillors have rejected a proposal for a 17-storey tower block beside the Grade II-listed Marble Arch pub in Manchester, citing concerns over its impact on the historic site.
content_html:
Plans for a 17-storey tower block next to the historic Marble Arch pub have been rejected by Manchester City Council's planning committee. The proposal, submitted by The McGoff Group, aimed to construct 153 flats adjacent to the Grade II-listed pub on Rochdale Road, which has been serving customers since 1888.

The pub's owners expressed concerns that the development would threaten its future, describing the proposed building as "overbearing and oppressive". Councillor Jon-Connor Lyons voiced his worries about the potential impact on "one of Manchester's distinctive and much-loved historic pubs", highlighting the importance of preserving the pub's setting.

In addition to the concerns raised about the Marble Arch, councillors noted the absence of affordable housing in the proposed development as a significant factor in their decision to refuse the application. The committee's rejection reflects a growing awareness of the need to balance urban development with the preservation of historical sites.

This decision is significant for local residents and businesses, as it underscores the importance of maintaining the character of the area while addressing housing needs. The Marble Arch pub remains a key landmark in the community, and its protection is seen as vital for preserving local heritage.

title: Rochdale Council generates nearly £3 million from parking fines over three years
excerpt: Rochdale Council has collected £2.88 million from parking fines since 2023, with funds reinvested into local road infrastructure.
content_html:
Rochdale Council has reported a total of £2.88 million generated from parking fines over the last three years, according to data obtained through a Freedom of Information request. This figure represents an average of just under £1 million per year from 2023 to 2026, with the highest earnings recorded in 2025, amounting to £990,256.

In total, the council issued 90,644 parking charge notices (PCNs) during this period. The overall value of these notices exceeded £5.6 million; however, the actual income is lower due to successful challenges against fines and the costs associated with enforcement. The council has stated that all revenue from PCNs is reinvested into the local road network, which may include repairs to potholes, repainting road markings, and funding larger infrastructure projects.

The council emphasised that PCNs are issued not only for revenue generation but also for safety reasons, such as ensuring adequate space for wheelchair users on pavements and preventing blind spots at junctions. The data also highlighted the busiest areas for parking fines, with Newgate, Yorkshire Street Central, and Oldham Road Central identified as the top hotspots for PCNs issued.

This financial strategy raises questions about the balance between enforcement and community needs, as residents may feel the impact of increased parking restrictions. As the council continues to reinvest these funds into local infrastructure, it remains to be seen how this will affect road safety and accessibility in Rochdale. Readers are encouraged to share their thoughts on parking regulations and their impact on the community.

title: Rochdale woman loses over 12 stone and reaches Slimming World semi-finals
excerpt: Vikki Gurney from Rochdale has lost 12 stone 3 pounds and reached the semi-finals of Slimming World’s Woman of the Year competition, meeting Olympic champion Nicola Adams in the process.
content_html:
A Rochdale woman has achieved a remarkable weight loss of 12 stone 3 pounds, leading her to the semi-finals of Slimming World’s Woman of the Year competition. Vikki Gurney, 39, was selected to represent her Cutgate group after her inspiring transformation from 22 stone 1 pound to 9 stone 12 pounds.

The semi-finals took place at Slimming World’s head office in Derbyshire, where Vikki had the opportunity to meet double Olympic boxing champion Nicola Adams. Vikki's journey began after she saw a photograph of herself at a friend's wedding, prompting her to join the Slimming World group.

Vikki credits her success to a supportive community and a sustainable eating plan that allowed her to enjoy her favourite foods without feeling deprived. She highlighted the importance of weekly meetings with her consultant, Alyson Hartley, and fellow members, which provided her with encouragement and new ideas for meal preparation.

This achievement not only reflects Vikki's personal commitment to health and well-being but also serves as an inspiration for others in the Rochdale community. Her story underscores the positive impact of support networks in weight loss journeys and the importance of finding a plan that fits one's lifestyle.

title: M6 Theatre receives £73,500 funding for 50th anniversary project
excerpt: M6 Theatre in Rochdale has been awarded £73,500 to support its 50th anniversary project, which will include community outreach and an interactive exhibition.
content_html:
M6 Theatre, a prominent institution in Rochdale, has been awarded £73,500 to fund its upcoming 50th anniversary project, set to take place in 2027. This funding will support a range of initiatives aimed at celebrating the theatre's rich history and its impact on the community over the past five decades.

The anniversary project will feature an interactive exhibition and a digital archive, allowing audiences to engage with the theatre's legacy. Additionally, M6 Theatre plans to conduct community outreach projects that will collect stories from individuals who have been involved with the theatre throughout its history. This initiative aims to highlight the journeys of both audiences and theatre professionals.

Founded in 1977, M6 Theatre has made a significant impact on the lives of over 500,000 children and young people through its touring theatre productions. The anniversary celebrations will include a new youth theatre show, a community gala, and the commissioning of a specially made film and poem, all designed to enhance public accessibility and involvement.

The project will unfold over the course of one year, culminating in a celebration of M6 Theatre's contributions to the arts and education in the region. This funding not only marks a significant investment in the arts but also underscores the importance of community engagement in preserving local cultural heritage.

The Rochdale company will create an oral history project, an interactive exhibition and a publicly accessible digital archive during a year-long programme. Founded in 1977, M6 specialises in touring theatre for children and young people. Its anniversary plans also include community outreach projects, a new youth theatre show, a community gala and a specially commissioned film and poem. Laura Rodwell, from M6 Theatre, said hundreds of local people would take part in the heritage activities. She said, “Hundreds of local people will participate in heritage activities and we will work with our communities to share and celebrate both M6’s journey over 50 years, and the journeys of our audiences, participants and theatre professionals past and present.” The project will collect stories and memories from people involved with the company over the past five decades. Helen Featherstone, director for England, North at The National Lottery Heritage Fund, said M6 had worked with more than 500,000 children and young people. She said, “We're thrilled to be supporting M6 Theatre Company in marking their 50th birthday, thanks to money raised by National Lottery players.” M6 also received the Cultural Legacy Award at this year’s Rochdale Culture Awards. title: Two drivers have vehicles seized for ignoring Heywood school crossing patrol
excerpt: Two vehicles were seized by police in Heywood after drivers ignored a school crossing patrol, highlighting ongoing concerns about road safety near schools.
content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

21:24 BST, 22 October 2026

Two vehicles were seized by police in Heywood after drivers ignored a school crossing patrol, highlighting ongoing concerns about road safety near schools.

Police in Heywood have seized two vehicles after drivers failed to stop for a school crossing patrol. The incident occurred when Mr. Jones, the crossing patrol officer, was already standing in the road as the vehicles approached. Fortunately, no injuries were reported during these incidents.

The vehicles seized included a moped and a silver Skoda. Police collected evidence, including witness statements, before taking action. This incident is part of a broader concern, as there have been 137 reported cases of vehicles failing to stop for school crossing patrols in the Rochdale area.

Councillor Williams expressed his dismay at the incidents, stating that such behaviour is unacceptable and poses a significant risk to children. In response to these ongoing safety issues, police have been using body-worn cameras in hotspot areas to deter dangerous driving.

The seizure of these vehicles underscores the need for increased vigilance and compliance with road safety regulations, particularly near schools. Local residents and parents are encouraged to remain alert and report any similar incidents to the authorities.

Published: 23 October 2026 2 irresponsible drivers who failed to stop for a school crossing patrol in Bury Old Road have had their vehicles seized by police. The incidents took place on Tuesday, 13 and Wednesday, 14 October 2026, with school crossing patrol, Barry, having to move out of the way to avoid the vehicles, a moped and a silver Skoda, even though he was already standing in the road. Fortunately, nobody was injured in the incident. The matter was reported to police, who used new powers under section 59 of the police reform act 2002, to seize the vehicles after collecting evidence, including witness statements. Cars and other vehicles failing to stop for school crossing patrols is a growing problem, with 137 fail to stops reported across Rochdale borough over the past 5 years. Body worn cameras are now being used in hotspot areas to try to deter dangerous driving and support prosecutions where needed. Councillor Dylan Williams, cabinet member for highways and facilities, said: “It beggars belief that somebody would see a school crossing patrol clearly standing in the middle of the road and continue to drive. Frankly I’m appalled. “We would like to thank GMP for their quick and decisive action and I think it’s a really good result. “We will not compromise on the safety of our schoolchildren, their parents and carers and our school crossing patrols. Being able to get to and from school safely and to be able to go about your job without fear is the very least anyone should have the right to expect. That’s why we will continue to report incidents to the police and to push for prosecutions wherever possible.” School crossing patrols across Rochdale borough have recently been issued with new coats which will make them even more visible as the nights start to draw in. Nicola Mcilvenney, the council’s school crossing patrol supervisor, said: “Our school crossing patrols do an extraordinary job and I’m relieved that nobody was hurt in these incidents. It could have easily been a tragedy. “We would like to remind drivers to be extra vigilant, particularly as it gets darker in the evenings. As soon as the school crossing patrol raises their stick, it’s time to stop. As we always say, slow and steady wins the race." Paul Clarke, traffic Police Community Support Officer (PCSO) team leader at Greater Manchester Police (GMP), said: “There are a number of offences related to failing to stop for a school crossing patrol, and, having considered all the circumstances here and looking at the evidence, we felt that seizure of the vehicles was appropriate. “School crossing patrol officers play a vital role in protecting children and other pedestrians and drivers are reminded that when a school crossing patrol officer displays the stop sign, all traffic must stop.” Related content Councillor Dylan Williams Council news from across the borough of Rochdale Road safety Was this page helpful? title: New HMO licensing requirements introduced by Rochdale Borough Council
excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced new licensing requirements for Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs), aimed at ensuring safety and compliance among landlords.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has introduced new licensing requirements for landlords operating Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) within the borough. This initiative is part of the council's ongoing efforts to ensure that all rental properties meet safety and compliance standards, thereby protecting tenants and the wider community.

Under the new regulations, landlords must obtain a specific HMO licence for each property they manage. The licence is valid for five years, with a fee of £1,011 plus an additional £53 inspection fee per habitable room. This means that landlords with multiple properties will need to apply for a separate licence for each one, ensuring that all HMOs are properly regulated.

The council will conduct thorough checks to determine if landlords are 'fit and proper persons' to manage these properties. This may include a Disclosure and Barring Service check if initial assessments raise concerns. The licensing process aims to enhance the safety and living conditions for tenants residing in HMOs across Rochdale.

These changes are significant for both landlords and tenants in the area. Landlords must ensure compliance with the new licensing requirements to avoid penalties, while tenants can expect improved safety standards in their living environments. For more information on the licensing process, landlords can visit the Rochdale Borough Council's official website.

How to apply To apply for an HMO licence: Complete an HMO licence - register fit and proper persons form. Complete an HMO licence - make an application form . Your licence is only valid for one property. If you have multiple properties you use as HMOs you need to apply for a licence for each property. How much it will cost A licence will normally last for 5 years but in certain circumstances a licence can be granted for a shorter period. The total fee for 5 years is £1,541 - this is the standard application fee plus the total inspection fee. This would work out at £308.20 per year. Conditions to meet We'll grant a licence if we’re satisfied that: The property meets the HMO space, facilities and amenities standards – Housing standards for Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMO) The person applying is a fit and proper person. They are the most appropriate person to hold the licence. Any manager involved is also a “fit and proper person.” The management arrangements are suitable. The person managing the property is competent. The financial arrangements for managing the property are appropriate. If we refuse to issue you a licence If your property doesn’t meet standards or you don’t pass the fit and proper person check, we may refuse to issue a licence. In that case, we can apply for an Interim Management Order to manage the property for up to a year. If there’s no improvement, we may apply for a Final Management Order, which can last up to 5 years. You will keep your rights as a property owner. How to appeal against our decision If we refuse you a licence contact us using the contact details on this page, initially to try and resolve the issue. The RPT is an expert independent tribunal that will act instead of the county court to either overturn or conﬁrm the council’s decision. title: East Lancashire Railway steam gala draws more than 2,000 passengers as numbers rise 21.4 per cent
excerpt: Four visiting engines, late trains and a tribute to preservation pioneer Richard Greenwood marked a busy autumn gala on the heritage railway serving Heywood.
content_html:
More than 2,000 passengers visited East Lancashire Railway's Autumn Steam Gala as four visiting locomotives helped deliver a 21.4 per cent increase in passenger numbers on last year's event, according to the railway.

The heritage line, which serves Heywood, held the gala from 16 to 18 October. Three of the four visiting engines were making their first appearances on the ELR, with autumn colours along the Irwell Valley providing the backdrop to a packed weekend of passenger trains, goods workings and late evening journeys.

A first visit from the Bluebell Railway

One of the headline visitors was South Eastern & Chatham Railway Class O1 No. 65, which travelled from the Bluebell Railway for what the ELR described as its furthest ever visit north.

Built at Ashford in 1896 and rebuilt into its present form in 1908, No. 65 appeared in ornate green SECR Wainwright goods livery. It joined resident Lancashire & Yorkshire engines 1300 and 752 in marking significant anniversaries connected with 1896.

Both resident engines received fresh paintwork in lined Lancashire & Yorkshire livery for the gala. No. 1300's finishing touches were completed the day before the event by the railway's resident Heritage Painters team.

Last chance to ride behind visiting pannier tank

Great Western pannier tank No. 7714 arrived from the Severn Valley Railway, courtesy of the SVR Pannier Tank Fund. Built in Stoke-on-Trent by Kerr, Stuart & Co. in 1930, the engine faced south during the gala, giving photographers a different view of the line.

Photographic run pasts with the railway's goods train at Burrs Country Park raised £493 in cash donations. The ELR says passengers have a final opportunity to travel behind No. 7714 on 24 and 25 October before it returns to the West Midlands.

LSWR S15 No. 30506, owned by the Urie Locomotive Society and visiting from the Mid Hants Railway, returned to the ELR for the first time since the 1993 Festival of Steam. It is due to haul scheduled steam services on 31 October and 1 November, as well as taking part in a photographic charter.

The fourth visitor, Hudswell Clarke No. 1208, also made its ELR debut. Usually based at the Embsay & Bolton Abbey Railway and owned by Stephen Middleton, the industrial tank engine worked shuttles to Ramsbottom and paired with No. 65. It carried names from different stages of its working life, including Harold, Illingworth and Mitchell.

Remembering a preservation pioneer

Resident engines City of Wells, Standard 4MT No. 80097 and Lancashire & Yorkshire Pug No. 11243 also featured during the weekend.

Friday included a tribute to preservation pioneer Richard Greenwood, who died earlier this year. Engines 752 and City of Wells, both associated with his preservation work, ran together while his family and friends travelled in the Lancashire & Yorkshire Directors Saloon. The railway said his ashes were scattered into the firebox as the train departed.

Saturday's programme continued after dark, with brake van journeys behind visiting Southern engines, a rare trip into Rawtenstall's bay platform and late passenger workings.

More than 250 volunteer turns

The ELR said more than 250 volunteer turns were needed to deliver the weekend.

General manager Lee Kenny said: “These are results that everyone involved can take pride in. They reflect a great deal of work before the first train runs, throughout the weekend and after the last visitors have gone home.”

He thanked the crews, station teams, stewards, cleaners, catering staff and those responsible for preparing and maintaining the railway, alongside the small team organising the event.

“The gala depends on people across the railway working together, and we are very grateful for the effort and commitment that went into this year's event,” he said.

The railway said the passenger increase helped raise funds for ongoing preservation. Transport for No. 65 was supported by the East Lancashire Railway Preservation Society and a private individual.

What is coming next?

The Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day on 14 November is due to feature engines 752 and 1300 together on the steam service. Pug No. 11243 is also expected to offer short driver experiences around Bury Bolton Street station limits for a small fee. The Directors Saloon is due to offer another opportunity to travel.

The ELR has also announced provisional enthusiast event dates for 2027, when it will mark 40 years since reopening between Bury and Ramsbottom:

6 February: Winter Warmer Diesel Running Day.

19 February: Roch Valley L&Y Pug Railtour Anniversary, with brake van specials planned to mark 60 years since the final Whitworth branch railtours.

20 February: Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day.

12 to 14 March: Spring Steam Gala.

10 April: Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day.

1 to 4 July: Summer Diesel Gala.

23 to 25 July: 40th Anniversary of the ELR Gala.

11 September: L&YR Running Day.

24 to 26 September: Autumn Diesel Gala.

15 to 17 October: Autumn Steam Gala.

6 November: L&YR Running Day.

These dates and locomotive appearances are provisional. Check the railway's latest information before travelling at https://www.eastlancsrailway.org.uk.

Anyone interested in volunteering can find details of departments and recruitment tours at https://www.elrps.co.uk/volunteering.

title: Urgent appeal to find woman after suspected human tissue discovered in Rochdale
excerpt: Police fear a woman who may have recently given birth needs urgent medical attention after a discovery near Watkins Street and Charter Street, off Kingsway.
content_html:
BREAKING NEWS | ONGOING AND DEVELOPING STORY. This report will be updated when further verified information becomes available.

Detectives are trying to find a woman who may need urgent medical attention after suspected human tissue was discovered off Kingsway in Rochdale.

Greater Manchester Police said evidence found near the junction of Watkins Street and Charter Street suggests a woman may have recently given birth. Officers were called shortly before 9am on Thursday 22 October.

Police have been examining the scene and carrying out enquiries. Their priority is to find the woman and make sure she is safe and well.

Detective Inspector Daniel Daly, from GMP's Rochdale CID, said: “She may be in need of urgent medical attention, and she is our absolute priority at the moment - that is why we are asking anyone with information to contact us.”

Anyone with information, or who may have seen a woman in distress, should call 101 and quote incident number 684 of 22/10/2026.

Information can also be reported online or through GMP's LiveChat service at https://www.gmp.police.uk. Alternatively, contact Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

DI Daly asked the public not to speculate: “We would ask that people don't speculate on the circumstances of this discovery as it hinders our investigation and is upsetting for those involved.”

The information in this report comes from Greater Manchester Police's appeal issued on 22 October 2026. Police have not confirmed further circumstances in that appeal.

title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
excerpt: The tale of Lady Eleanor, Mother Bagden and the Fairies’ Chapel at Healey Dell is well attested in local printed collectors — but it survives as folklore, not as a documented medieval event.
summary: The tale of Lady Eleanor, Mother Bagden and the Fairies’ Chapel at Healey Dell is well attested in local printed collectors — but it survives as folklore, not as a documented medieval event.
body:
Ask a local where the Fairies’ Chapel is and they’ll point you down the steps from Station Road, into the ravine by the River Spodden. Ask whether fairies live there and the practical answer is simple: no verifiable evidence supports the existence of fairies; what the records do show is a named rock formation, a cluster of old stories collected in the nineteenth century and a long history of people visiting the site because the place feels, to many, a little uncanny. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

Those are not trivial facts. Healey Dell is a designated Local Nature Reserve and an area of industrial archaeology that straddles borough boundaries; part of the valley was legally made a statutory LNR in April 1976. The most dramatic built feature is the Healey Dell Viaduct, a high, eight‑arched sandstone railway viaduct that is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those designations are documentary and can be checked. ([rossendale.gov.uk](https://www.rossendale.gov.uk/download/meetings/id/4148/e2_appendix_2))

The Dell’s historical record is everyday, material and useful. The valley contains the remains of nineteenth‑century mills and the disused Rochdale‑to‑Bacup railway line; archaeological and conservation surveys catalogue those features and guide how the reserve is managed for wildlife and visitors. Management is led locally by Rochdale (and neighbouring Rossendale) authorities and by volunteer groups; published ecological reports and neighbourhood plans reference Healey Dell when mapping green infrastructure for the area. That is the part of the story that affects readers’ lives—path repairs, parking signage, listed‑building consent for the viaduct—because those are things the council, landowners and statutory consultees can change. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

The Fairies’ Chapel and the Healey Dwarf belong to a different archive: folklore. Nineteenth‑century writers and local collectors, notably the county antiquarian tradition and later local compilers, set down tales about a natural recess in the rock that looked a little like an altar and could be called a chapel. Early print references—quoted in modern guides—describe a hidden pulpit‑like formation revealed when a flood washed away a covering ledge; later colourful retellings add a Fairy Queen, a Fairy King and a bewitched dwarf or witch‑figure, motifs common to British fairy lore. Those stories come from literary and folkloric sources rather than parish registers, court records or archaeological excavation reports; they are valuable for what they tell us about local imagination and nineteenth‑century reading habits, not as evidence of the supernatural. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

You can still see the place‑name on the ground. Local walking leaflets and heritage trails mark a route down to the feature and signposts to a ‘Fairy Chapel’ appear on nearby footpaths and at the steps off Station Road. Community events and the Tearooms’ heritage material reproduce the old legends for visitors, which keeps the stories alive. None of these modern references change the distinction: a name, an attractive rock formation and repeated storytelling are not proof of otherworldly residents. ([whitworth.gov.uk](https://www.whitworth.gov.uk/uploads/walkingdocuments/files/WALK%206%20Healey%20Dell%20-%20captioned%20viaduct.pdf))

What remains uncertain—and worth noting—is provenance. Some of the best‑known versions of the Healey tales were shaped by nineteenth‑century collectors and local storytellers; when folklore circulates in print, oral tradition and tourism literature it can harden into ‘local history’ in popular memory. Where claims involve specific historical persons, dates or events, they should be tested against archival material; in the case of the Fairies’ Chapel, the archive records the place and the stories about it, not supernatural events. If you want proof, visit the council‑maintained reserve, look up the Historic England listing for the viaduct and read the nineteenth‑century sources for yourself—then decide whether the place’s atmosphere does the rest. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))
content_html:
Healey Dell’s narrow gorge, the Thrutch, has long been a place that invites stories. Visitors still stand under the Victorian viaduct, follow the path to the small pool visitors call the Fairies’ Chapel, and hear the familiar local version: a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden prophesied that a noblewoman, usually named Lady Eleanor (later linked with the Byron family), would be a maiden, a wife and a widow in one day; on her wedding day the bridegroom was slain and the prophecy fulfilled.

That dramatic sequence is not a modern invention. The earliest printed form widely available to readers comes from the 19th century: John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire preserves a long, romance‑style account set at Healey that gives the tale its shape and characters. Later local antiquarians — notably William Robertson in his regional histories — recycled and amplified the narrative, and modern site interpretation at Healey Dell Heritage Centre follows that printed tradition when it tells visitors the Fairies’ Chapel story.

What is verifiable fact? Healey Dell is a named Local Nature Reserve and visitor attraction at Dell Road, with recognisable industrial archaeology (mill sites, lodges) and a prominent Grade II listed viaduct built for the Lancashire and Yorkshire extension railway in 1869–70. Those are public, documentable features you can still see. The Heritage Centre publishes its own guides that describe the gorge, the so‑called Fairies’ Chapel and the local legends; Rochdale Borough Council lists the reserve, its address, opening details and facilities. The viaduct is recorded on the National Heritage List for England. These are the things you can check on official records and by visiting.

What is folklore? The supernatural elements — a Fairy Queen who issues prophecies, a witch‑fortune‑teller who communes with her, or the idea that a named medieval Lady Eleanor’s fate is attested in contemporary legal or parish records — belong to oral tradition and antiquarian storytelling. Roby, Robertson and later guide‑book writers recorded what people were telling in their own times rather than producing medieval documents. Local interpretation today openly presents the story as legend rather than as archival history.

How the story changed over time is itself revealing. Roby’s early 19th‑century text gives a literary, sometimes florid narrative with named characters: a miller, a talisman, Oliver Chadwyke and a Lady Eleanor. Later retellings folded in local family names (Byron, Chadwick) and local topography (the Thrutch, the Fairies’ Chapel). The Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s material adapts those versions when it points visitors to the rock formation and to the flood of 1838 that altered the gorge and submerged some of the features said to be the ‘chapel’. That lineage — oral tale into printed folklore into heritage interpretation — is a common path for many English place legends.

What cannot be shown from surviving records is the medieval documentary backbone the story implies. I found no contemporary 15th‑century court rolls, parish registers or legal documents that confirm a wedding‑night killing, a named Lady Eleanor Byron of the period, or a recorded prophetic witch in Healey Dell. Where claims cannot be matched to contemporary archives, the careful historian treats them as tradition and story. The result is not dismissal but classification: good material for local imagination, caution for anyone treating it as proven history.

If you want to see the story’s sources for yourself: read John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the early printed tale, inspect the Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s guide for the way the tale is now presented on site, and consult Rochdale Borough Council and the National Heritage List for England for the reserve’s practical and architectural facts. The prophecy endures because place, geology and a few dramatic printed versions make for memorable storytelling. That is a valuable local inheritance — so long as readers keep legend and archive in separate pockets.

Practical details: Healey Dell Nature Reserve and the Heritage Centre are listed by Rochdale Borough Council (address Dell Road, Healey). The viaduct is Grade II listed on Historic England’s National Heritage List. For maps, opening times and the Heritage Centre’s explanatory leaflets, use the council and the centre’s published material.

title: Rochdale Council Rejects Takeaway Application on Health Grounds
excerpt: Plans for a new takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street in Rochdale have been rejected by the council due to concerns over public health and the existing number of fast-food outlets in the area.
content_html:
Rochdale Council has refused an application for a new takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street, citing health concerns related to the high number of existing fast-food establishments in the area. The proposal, submitted by Sheeraz Ahmed, aimed to convert the former Ria Money Transfer shop into a takeaway primarily focused on collection and delivery.

The application detailed plans for a business serving a variety of hot food products, including burgers, fried chicken, pizzas, kebabs, desserts, waffles, and milkshakes. It included internal alterations to create customer serving areas, food preparation spaces, and cooking facilities. The proposed opening hours were set from 11am to 11pm, and the establishment was expected to create four new jobs.

However, the council's planning officer raised concerns regarding the potential impact on local eating habits. The Public Health officer noted that the application would increase the availability of food high in fat, salt, and sugar. Furthermore, it was highlighted that a health impact assessment had not been conducted, leading to the recommendation that the development should not be approved.

This decision reflects ongoing efforts by Rochdale Council to manage the proliferation of fast-food outlets in the town centre, aiming to promote healthier eating habits among residents. The refusal of this application may influence future proposals for similar establishments in the area.

A doorman at Ko-Ko Lounge in Rochdale has raised concerns about the normalisation of racial abuse after witnessing a disturbing incident on Saturday night. Jawad Ali, 20, reported that a woman became aggressive and shouted racial slurs at a black security guard when asked to move away from an exit.

The incident, captured on video and shared widely online, shows the woman making derogatory gestures towards the guard. Ali, who was working for Protective One Security at the time, described the behaviour as "disgusting" and stated that he now expects such incidents during his shifts.

Greater Manchester Police confirmed they have received a report regarding the incident and are currently conducting inquiries. Ali alleged that the woman also directed racial abuse towards him before the video was recorded.

This incident raises significant concerns about the treatment of security staff and the prevalence of racial abuse in nightlife settings. As investigations continue, it highlights the need for greater awareness and action against such behaviour.

title: St Cuthbert’s RC High School closes following bomb threat
excerpt: St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was closed after a bomb threat, with all students and staff accounted for and safe. The school plans to reopen on Monday.
content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

01:33 BST, 22 October 2026

St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was closed after a bomb threat, with all students and staff accounted for and safe. The school plans to reopen on Monday.

St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was closed on Friday following a bomb threat that prompted an immediate response from Greater Manchester Police. Emergency services evacuated all school buildings as a precautionary measure, ensuring the safety of students and staff.

During the incident, all students and staff were accounted for, and the school confirmed that there was no actual threat or danger to anyone present. Parents were reassured about the situation, particularly in light of speculation circulating on social media regarding intruders or weapons.

The police responded swiftly to the threat, and after thorough checks, it was determined that there was no risk to the school community. The school administration has communicated with parents to clarify the situation and dispel any false rumors that may have arisen during the incident.

St Cuthbert’s RC High School is expected to reopen as usual on Monday, allowing students to return to their regular schedule. The incident highlights the importance of safety protocols in schools and the effective response of emergency services in such situations.

title: Rochdale Borough Council invites feedback on proposed Customer Access strategy
excerpt: Residents are encouraged to share their views on the proposed Customer Access & Experience Strategy, which aims to enhance how the public interacts with the Council over the next five years.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has launched a consultation inviting residents to provide feedback on its proposed Customer Access & Experience Strategy for the next five years. The strategy aims to simplify how residents contact the Council and ensure they receive consistent support, whether online, by phone, or in person.

The Council has identified six priorities for enhancing customer access and nine pledges detailing what residents can expect from the service. The aim is to create a seamless experience for users, allowing them to receive assistance without needing to navigate the Council's organisational structure. The Council emphasises the importance of making it easy for individuals to access the right help, especially during challenging times.

Residents can review the draft strategy and related documents, including the Equality Impact Assessment and Sustainability Impact Assessment, on the Council's consultation hub. The Council is keen to know if the proposed priorities resonate with the community and whether any aspects have been overlooked. The consultation documents are available for review and can be accessed through the Council's website.

The consultation is open now, and residents are encouraged to participate to help shape the final version of the strategy. Feedback can be submitted through the Council's website until the consultation period closes. This initiative represents an opportunity for the community to influence how the Council interacts with its residents over the coming years.

title: Martlet Kitchen in Rochdale wins prestigious international award
excerpt: The Martlet Kitchen, located in Rochdale Town Hall, has been awarded the Tripadvisor Travellers’ Choice Award for 2026, recognising its commitment to quality and customer satisfaction.
content_html:
The Martlet Kitchen, situated within the historic Rochdale Town Hall, has received the prestigious Tripadvisor Travellers’ Choice Award for 2026. This accolade is granted to establishments that consistently earn positive reviews from customers, placing them among the top 10 per cent of listings on the popular review platform.

Opened in 2024 and led by chef Darren Parkinson, who trained at Hopwood Hall College, the restaurant has quickly established a reputation for serving high-quality British cuisine. Parkinson, who has previously worked at notable venues such as Shibden Mill Inn in Halifax and the Fleece Inn in Ripponden, emphasised the importance of using local ingredients, sourcing supplies from nearby businesses like Jacksons Farm in Milnrow and Defiance Distillery at Spotland Mill.

Restaurant manager Sarah Crabtree highlighted the team's dedication to providing a consistent dining experience, noting that the menu is regularly updated while retaining classic dishes like fish and chips. The Martlet Kitchen offers breakfast and lunch services, along with a grill club on Fridays and fine dining on Saturday evenings. Additionally, private dining options are available in the Mayor’s reception room at the Grade I listed town hall.

This award not only recognises the hard work of the Martlet Kitchen team but also enhances the profile of Rochdale as a destination for quality dining. As the restaurant aims for further accolades in the future, local residents and visitors alike can look forward to enjoying a dining experience that prioritises excellent service and locally sourced ingredients.

Published: 22 October 2026 Rochdale Town Hall’s Martlet Kitchen has picked up the Trip Advisor Travellers’ Choice Award 2026, placing it among the top-rated restaurants in the world on the popular review site. The award honours businesses which consistently receive great reviews, with their scores placing them in the top 10 per cent of all establishments registered on the popular review site. With millions of businesses from around the globe listed on the site, the award is a huge accolade for the Martlet Kitchen, which recently celebrated its second birthday. It’s not the first time the restaurant, which specialises in traditional, high-quality British food, has been lauded. In his food column for The Guardian, legendary food critic Jay Rayner, described the Martlet Kitchen as a ‘victory of professionalism, good sense and, most of all, great taste and skill’ when he visited shortly after its opening in 2024. The Martlet Kitchen is helmed by multi award winning chef, Darren Parkinson, who trained at Hopwood Hall College before working at acclaimed establishments including Shibden Mill Inn in Halifax and the Fleece Inn in Ripponden, both of which boast 2 AA rosettes. Rooted in the community, its food and drink is sourced from the local area, including Milnrow’s Jacksons Farm, Defiance Distillery at Spotland Mill and Grandpa Greene’s in Oldham. Commenting on the win, Darren said: “This award is great news and we’re aiming for more accolades in the future. It’s about good old fashioned British grub, cooked to perfection, using top quality local ingredients, coupled with excellent service.” Restaurant Manager, Sarah Crabtree, said: “I’m so proud of what we’ve achieved. I think one of the keys to the Martlet’s success is that we change the menu regularly to keep it fresh and seasonal, but we also keep the old favourites that people particularly enjoy, like fish and chips. Everyone who works here takes huge pride in their job, so the experience for the customers is really consistent. You know you will get excellent service and food every time you come in.” As well as breakfast and lunch, the Martlet Kitchen offers a fine dining experience on Saturday nights and a Friday grill club. The venue’s unique setting in the Grade I-listed Rochdale Town Hall has also enabled it to offer unique experiences, with a recently launched private dining offer giving guests the chance to dine in the Mayor’s reception room. Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and culture, said: “When we spearheaded the restoration of the town hall, with the support for the National Lottery Heritage Fund, we wanted every part of its operation to live up to this building’s grandeur and The Martlet Kitchen has delivered this in spades. To have our visitors place it among the top restaurants in operation is incredibly special and long may people enjoy this wonderful place.” Related content Councillor Sue Smith Council news from across the borough of Rochdale The Martlet Kitchen Was this page helpful? title: Police appeal to find missing 22-year-old Sean in Rochdale
excerpt: Police are seeking help from the public to locate Sean, a 22-year-old man who went missing in Rochdale's Milkstone area on October 20. Family members describe his disappearance as unusual and urge anyone with information to come forward.
content_html:
Police in Rochdale have launched an urgent appeal for information regarding the whereabouts of a 22-year-old man named Sean, who has gone missing. He was last seen in the Milkstone area of Rochdale town centre at approximately 7am on October 20, 2026.

Sean is described as white, with a slim build, standing around 5ft 9in tall. He has dark hair and a thick moustache. At the time of his disappearance, he was wearing a distinctive black Moncler jacket made from shiny material, a black bodywarmer, and black trousers.

Family members have expressed their concern, stating that Sean's disappearance is unusual for him. They are pleading with the public to share the appeal widely in hopes of locating him quickly. They have not provided a last name for Sean, but they are urging anyone who may have seen him or has information about his whereabouts to come forward.

Anyone with information about Sean's whereabouts is urged to contact Greater Manchester Police by calling 0161 856 8643 and quoting log number 110-211026. The police are keen to hear from anyone who may have seen him or has any information that could assist in locating him.
legal_disclaimer: This article reports a police welfare appeal published on 21 October 2026.

corrections.note: An earlier version incorrectly combined this appeal with an unrelated missing-person appeal. The unrelated material has been removed and the original publication date corrected to 21 October 2026.

title: Road closures announced for Rochdale Bonfire and Firework Display on 4 November 2026
excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced temporary road closures for the Bonfire and Firework Display on 4 November 2026, affecting several key routes in the area.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has confirmed that several roads will be temporarily closed on 4 November 2026 due to the Bonfire and Firework Display. The closures are part of safety measures to manage the event effectively and ensure public safety.

The specific roads affected by the closures include those where no waiting or loading will be permitted at any time. Details on the exact roads have not been disclosed, but the council advises that there will be no alternative routes available for vehicles during the event.

Residents and visitors are encouraged to plan their journeys accordingly, as the closures may impact access to local businesses and residences. The council has not provided specific times for the closures, but they are expected to be in effect throughout the duration of the event.

For further information, including a map of the roadworks and any additional restrictions, residents can visit the Rochdale Borough Council website. It is advisable to check for updates closer to the event date.

title: Chris Cheap appointed managing director of Northern Gateway regeneration in Bury and Rochdale
excerpt: Chris Cheap has been appointed managing director of the development corporation overseeing the Northern Gateway regeneration programme, which aims to enhance infrastructure and housing in Bury and Rochdale.
content_html:
Chris Cheap has been appointed as the managing director of the development corporation responsible for the Northern Gateway regeneration programme, which spans Bury and Rochdale. This initiative aims to coordinate the development of new homes, employment spaces, and infrastructure improvements in the area.

Mr Cheap joins the Atom Valley Northern Gateway Mayoral Development Corporation after nearly 23 years at Avison Young, where he led the UK transactional team. His extensive experience in real estate is expected to be pivotal in driving the regeneration efforts forward. He stated that successful delivery will require collaboration between public and private sectors.

One of the key projects under the Northern Gateway programme includes enhancing road connections to the M66 and M60 motorways, which is intended to facilitate further development and improve traffic flow in the region. This project is part of a broader strategy to boost economic growth and infrastructure in the Atom Valley Mayoral Development Zone, which also includes areas of Oldham.

The appointment of Mr Cheap is seen as a significant step towards revitalising the local economy and improving living conditions in Bury and Rochdale. As the project progresses, local residents and businesses can expect updates on developments and opportunities arising from this regeneration initiative.
