evidence_sources.captured_text: Chris Cheap appointed to lead Northern Gateway regeneration across Bury and Rochdale | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch Chris Cheap appointed to lead Northern Gateway regeneration across Bury and Rochdale David Murphy News Editor October 22, 2026 | 11:28 PM Print Chris Cheap Chris Cheap has been appointed managing director of the development corporation overseeing Northern Gateway, a regeneration programme spanning Bury and Rochdale. He joins the Atom Valley Northern Gateway Mayoral Development Corporation after almost 23 years at property adviser Avison Young. His most recent role involved leading its UK transactional team, overseeing capital markets, leasing and development across the industrial, office and retail sectors. The corporation has been established to coordinate new homes, employment space and infrastructure at Northern Gateway, working with councils and other partners. The programme forms part of the wider Atom Valley Mayoral Development Zone, which stretches across Bury, Oldham and Rochdale. Mr Cheap said delivering the development would require cooperation between the public and private sectors. He said, “The MDC will play a pivotal role in this and I am pleased to bring my extensive real estate experience and leadership to the team.” One of Northern Gateway’s planned projects will improve road connections between the site and the M66 and M60. The work is intended to enable further development and complement capacity improvements at Simister Island. According to the announcement, more than £100 million in public funding has been spent or committed to Northern Gateway. This includes more than £50 million allocated by Greater Manchester Combined Authority in March 2026 for transport improvements. Stephen Dance OBE, chair of the corporation, said Mr Cheap would help secure investment. He said, “His expertise will be central to guiding the MDC as it works with partners to secure the necessary public and private investment to unlock new homes, jobs and longterm economic growth.” Bury Council leader Councillor Eamonn O’Brien said, “We are approaching a critical stage at Northern Gateway and it’s important that people across Bury and Rochdale see plans become reality.” Elsewhere in Atom Valley, the base build of the 30,000 sq ft Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre has recently been completed at Kingsway Park in Rochdale. The centre sits within the 25-acre Atom Valley Innovation District. title: Rochdale house prices rise to £211,000 in August 2026
excerpt: The average house price in Rochdale increased by 3.3% over the past year, while private rents saw a significant rise of 8.8%, according to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics.
content_html:
The average house price in Rochdale reached £211,000 in August 2026, reflecting a 3.3% increase from the previous year, according to data released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). This rise is notably higher than the average increase of 2.2% observed across the North West during the same period.

In addition to house prices, private rents in Rochdale also saw a substantial increase, with the average rent climbing to £859 in September 2026. This marks an annual rise of 8.8%, compared to £790 in September 2025, again outpacing the North West's average increase of 5.7%.

For first-time buyers, the average price paid for a home was £191,000 in August 2026, which is a 3.4% increase from the previous year's average of £184,000. Homes purchased with a mortgage had an average price of £215,000, also reflecting a 3.3% rise from £208,000 in August 2025.

These figures indicate a continuing trend of rising housing costs in Rochdale, which may impact affordability for local residents. The ONS advises that local housing data can be more variable due to the smaller number of properties involved, and they recommend looking at trends over a longer period for a clearer picture.

title: Plans to develop wasteland around Rochdale train station confirmed
excerpt: Plans to transform the wasteland surrounding Rochdale train station into a usable space have been confirmed, marking a significant step towards improving the area.
content_html:
Plans to develop the wasteland around Rochdale train station have been confirmed. Local authorities aim to enhance the environment and accessibility for commuters and residents.

This initiative is part of ongoing efforts to revitalise the area, which has been largely neglected in recent years. The local council stated that the project will improve aesthetic appeal and provide additional facilities for the community.

Specific details regarding the timeline and nature of the developments are yet to be announced. Stakeholders are optimistic that this project will lead to increased foot traffic and economic activity in the vicinity of the station.

Residents and commuters are encouraged to monitor the progress of this project, as it is expected to positively impact local transport and community engagement.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The wasteland around Rochdale train station is finally being put to use - Manchester Evening News ‌ ‌ Skip to main content Manchester Evening News: Number one for news, opinion, sport & celebrity news The wasteland around Rochdale train station is finally being put to use The regeneration around the railway station is part of a wider vision to improve the flow of the down and drive investment Add to preferred sources Comments News George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter 06:13, 21 Oct 2026 View 4 Images Land surrounding Rochdale train station (Image: LDRS) A scheme which would transform the gateway into Rochdale is making significant progress, town hall bosses say. ‌ ‌ Some 81 two, three-and four-bedroom homes are currently under construction on vacant land next to Rochdale ’s Central Retail Park. This forms part of a wider scheme to create a connection between the train station and the town centre. ‌ The wider regeneration of the area around Rochdale railway station also involves the creation of a new public square in front of the station and 33 new apartments on a brownfield site on the corner of Maclure Road and Station Road. ‌ Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter The train station in Rochdale was once a hub for industrial business generations ago, so the distance between the station and the town centre was purposeful separation. But as times changed, society changed and the station suddenly started transporting people, not goods. This is why there is an idea to improve access and avenues from the station and the main hub of the town. This 81-home development, known as John Rennie Place, in honour of the late Scottish Civil engineer who masterminded the Rochdale Canal, got under way in November last year, and is due for completion in December 2027. ‌ View 4 Images The former Central Retail Park site development under construction (Image: Rochdale council) The project, approved years ago, was unlocked following a successful bid for £15m from the government’s Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund. The transformation has been on the cards for a long time, but the local authority struggled to get the investment until last year. ‌ The properties will be the first affordable net zero homes delivered as part of a housing scheme supported by the council. The local authority says the development is already delivering benefits to the local economy and community. Contractor Willmott Dixon, working on behalf of the council, has already spent £3.3m with local civil engineering firm, Hovington Ltd, and supported a total of 95 weeks of apprenticeship and T-Level training, including three T-Level placements from Hopwood Hall College. ‌ Don't let an algorithm decide what Manchester news you see - click here to add the MEN as your preferred Google source Seven local people are also employed on the project, including two people who were previously unemployed, with the council’s work and skills team supporting the recruitment. ‌ Tommy Patterson, 22, from Middleton , is one of the local people working on the new homes. He said: “I had been out of work for six months when the job centre arranged for me to get my CSCS card and that led to me securing a scaffolding apprenticeship here on site. I have always worked and had been let go, so getting this job was a lifeline. “I live on my own and I was struggling to pay my bills. It’s great to work here. Everyone is lovely; it’s a smashing team.” ‌ View 4 Images Councillor Danny Meredith looking across the former Rochdale Central Retail Park site (Image: Rochdale council) Daniel Fletcher, 17, is studying for a T Level in design, surveying and planning at Hopwood Hall College, said: “I really like it here. I’ve been talking to the different trades delivering this project, so I’ve been exposed to different parts of the job, and I have the freedom to go onto site on my own. It’s already changed massively since I started in the summer.” ‌ The project is being led by Rochdale Development Agency (RDA) on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council. Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for housing and regeneration at Rochdale Borough Council, said: ”We want local people and businesses to feel the benefit of local projects and it’s great to see that these benefits are already being felt on this development before a single house has even been completed. ‌ View 4 Images Councillor Danny Meredith looking across the former Rochdale Central Retail Park site (Image: Rochdale council) “By ensuring that social value is embedded in our procurement system, we’re making sure that local people are invested in the extensive regeneration which is taking place on their doorstep and are benefitting from the economic transformation we’re spearheading across the borough. That’s how it should be and how it will continue to be.” Article continues below Work to create 142 apartments next to the new homes is ongoing, with the procurement of a delivery partner expected to get underway soon. title: Residents face uncertainty as Rochdale's Seven Sisters tower blocks undergo safety review
excerpt: The future of Rochdale's Seven Sisters tower blocks remains uncertain as residents prepare to relocate amid safety concerns and ongoing housing limbo.
content_html:
Residents of Rochdale's College Bank estate, known for its iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks, are facing significant uncertainty as they prepare to move out due to safety concerns. The landowners, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH), informed 229 households in October 2025 that they would need to vacate the premises. Currently, only about 90 households remain in the blocks, with many residents already relocated as part of a safety review process.

Claire Lord, a long-term resident of the Mardyke block, expressed her reluctance to leave her home, citing the security and community she has enjoyed for over a decade. She is currently waiting for a move to a nearby bungalow, but delays in renovations have left her without a confirmed moving date. Claire's situation reflects the broader anxiety among residents, many of whom are concerned about losing their established support networks and the uncertainty surrounding the future of the tower blocks.

The safety review has raised questions about whether the blocks will be demolished or refurbished, with no clear timeline provided by RBH. Residents have reported receiving conflicting information about the future of their homes, leading to a climate of speculation and concern. Christine Hartley, another resident, is still awaiting a suitable replacement for her two-bedroom flat, which she fears may not be possible due to the size constraints of available options.

As the situation develops, the local community is left grappling with the implications of these changes. The uncertainty surrounding the Seven Sisters highlights the ongoing challenges of housing safety and the need for clear communication from housing authorities. Residents are encouraged to maintain regular contact with RBH for updates on their housing situation.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The secret safety battle over Rochdale’s Seven Sisters - Manchester Evening News ‌ ‌ Skip to main content Manchester Evening News: Number one for news, opinion, sport & celebrity news The secret safety battle over Rochdale’s Seven Sisters SPECIAL REPORT: As clutter boxes pile high in the living rooms of the 90 remaining households on Rochdale's College Bank estate, an M.E.N. investigation uncovers BSR building safety notices, £1.7m empty council tax bills, and the human cost of a decade-long housing limbo. George Lythgoe reports. View 7 Images Town Mill Brow tower block on College Bank with a wonky R (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) Add to preferred sources Comments News George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter and Stephen Topping Senior reporter 07:07, 25 Oct 2026 Claire Lord sits alone in her living room surrounded by head-high boxes. The small space between her sofa and TV is the only bit of the flat not crowded by cubes of clutter. To answer the door she has to clamber over yet more plastic tubs filled to the brim with her worldly possessions. The 56-year-old is ready to move out of her flat in Rochdale ’s iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks. She’s been ready for weeks. ‌ Claire was one of 229 households told they had to leave by landowners Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) in October 2025. Since then, droves have been moving out of the blocks. Only an estimated 90 households are still left in Seven Sisters - actually named College Bank. RBH says this has been done for safety reasons. View 7 Images College Bank tower blocks in Rochdale known as the Seven Sisters (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) The tower blocks face an uncertain future, with the question of demolition or refurbishment still on the table after a decade of limbo. No matter the decision, it is understood all residents will have to move out whilst work is done - whether that work is to decorate or destroy. ‌ Claire is one of the latest to be exiting the estate, but it’s not a move she really wanted to do. When describing the day when RBH told her they'd found some new digs for her, she said she was ‘gutted’. The security, the views, proximity to healthcare professionals and the community are the things she cherishes most about her flat. Claire will be moving to a bungalow across the road, behind Lidl. “There has been a delay because the lady who lived in the bungalow hadn't done work on the place for some time,” Claire explained. “They’ve had to do painting and decorating, rewiring, putting new doors on and a fresh kitchen. ‌ “So they’ve been getting it ready for me. RBH told me about four months ago that I’d be moving and were waiting for the date. “Every time I’ve gone down they’ve come up with more work and more work to do. I’ve been down every week to ask. “It’s always the same story - ‘something is being done’. I’ve still not got a move-in date, I think I’ll be told about a move-in date in four weeks. “I do love living here. The security is good and there isn’t much chance of you getting burgled. ‌ “It’s close to the shops in the town centre, my mental health team is nearby and my GP is just down the road. “But my biggest fear of moving is losing that security. I’ve been here (in Mardyke block) for 12 years and I've never had any trouble, it’s a good community. “If I could stay I would. It’s not good for my mental health. I don’t know whether I’m coming or going. “Being stuck halfway is no good as I just don’t know. They’re just going to plonk a day on me.” ‌ View 7 Images Claire Lord, Mardyke resident on the Seven Sisters estate in Rochdale (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) Claire has credited RBH with supporting her through the transition. She has regular contact with housing officers, but that doesn’t mean the transition process has been easy for her. Like many of the tenants, she just wants to know what’s happening with the blocks. Claire added: “We’ve had so many rumours about what is happening. We’ve heard they’re bringing in migrants in; that three are staying up and four are coming down; then we’ve had that they’re all staying up; then we’ve had they’re all coming down and they’re building 250 houses. ‌ “Nothing is set in concrete and they won’t tell us. It’s all just rumours.” Her friend Christine Hartley, who has lived in the Tentercroft block for 14 years, hasn’t accepted any new accommodation from RBH. She is still waiting on a 'like for like replacement', which she admits isn’t really possible due to the size of her two-bed flat. The 67-year-old said: "You know there is someone you can rely on in the blocks. We often ring each other, pop in and check on each other as there are loads of people that have known each other for years. “When we were fighting the campaign, you’d nip to the shop and an hour later you’d get hope because so many people would stop us to ask what is happening with the flats. We’re still getting that now. ‌ “It’s a good question. What is happening with the flats? I'd ask RBH. “They sent a letter last week saying they’ve still not made a decision. But I think they have made a decision, but they just don’t want us to know what it is. “Why should we have to move out when they won’t tell us what they’re doing with the flats? It doesn’t make sense. “You can’t tell me they don’t know what they’re doing. It wouldn’t be the case if they didn’t let them get into this state. ‌ “It’s very quiet on the estate now, even during the day. It never used to be like this, it used to be bustling.” “Why can’t they just tell us what they’re doing? It’s more than due time to tell us now. “We’ve suffered long enough and it plays with your mental health. I’ve cried, I’ve been angry. “Just give us a bit of truth, we deserve that. We deserve some respect, it’s ridiculous.” ‌ View 7 Images College Bank tower blocks in Rochdale known as the Seven Sisters (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) This is a fair question to ask if you’re being forced to leave your home. Although a number of former College Bank residents have expressed their happiness with the new digs sorted for them by RBH. Christine and her partner Roy Kitcher thought their Tentercroft flat was going to be their forever home. They love life on Seven Sisters and see no reason to move. Speaking on why he is adamant on staying, Roy told the M.E.N : “We moved in here and we were at risk of becoming homeless. We thought this was going to be forever. We love it here. ‌ “It’s right next to the town centre, the doctors are down the road, the chemist is down the road. It’s spacious and we have everything we need right here. Why should we have to move? “When people move out of here RBH are getting reduced rates to move. Those are going to go up and people who’ve moved out could get into dire straits. “When we’re coming back from the holiday or a trip to the lighthouse, I point at the blocks and say ‘home’s over there’. Or coming down the motorway, as soon as I see the Seven Sisters, we’re almost homes now. “Before I moved in I told people I would never move into College Bank, because I didn’t like the look of them. Moving in changed my mind.” The pair are both part of the Save the Seven Sisters (ST7S) campaign that has been going ever since the intention to demolish came knocking. They feel like RBH is disrespecting residents by not explaining why they have to move, or showing the findings of the surveys that sparked the mass exodus in October 2025. ‌ There has been a long history of mistrust between tenants and their landlord, which goes back over a decade. The Manchester Evening News first reported on the possibility of the Seven Sisters being bulldozed by RBH in November 2016. At the time, the housing provider said it would consider proposals for College Bank and Lower Falinge the following spring ‘at the earliest’. RBH spoke of ‘reduced demand for flats as a result of recent welfare reforms’. But in the 10 years since, the picture has changed dramatically. According to Greater Manchester Combined Authority’s (GMCA) housing market monitor, 43 per cent of the 7,892 households on Rochdale’s active social housing register required a one-bedroom property in 2024-25, while 29 per cent needed a two-bedroom property. Campaigners argue that College Bank’s roughly 670 empty flats would make a significant dent in that waiting list. ‌ View 7 Images College Bank tower blocks in Rochdale known as the Seven Sisters (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) Plans unveiled by RBH in June 2017 would have seen four of the Seven Sisters towers knocked down - Mitchell Hey, Dunkirk Rise, Tentercroft and Town Mill Brow - to make way for up to 120 new homes. The three remaining blocks would have been modernised. Demolition notices were handed out to tenants in March 2019 , but residents refused to give up their homes without a fight. Rochdale councillors and then-mayor Andy Burnham also raised concerns , with local politicians going on to step up their scrutiny of RBH in the years to come. In 2020, a tragedy elsewhere in Rochdale that would bring national scrutiny to RBH and send shockwaves across the country. Awaab Ishak, who lived in a flat on the Freehold estate with his mum and dad, died aged two in December 2020. ‌ His parents had made repeated requests for help with a damp and mould issue at their home, but the issue was not properly addressed. Coroner Joanne Kearsley ruled that exposure to mould at the flat led to Awaab’s death, as she described the tragedy as a ‘defining moment’ for the housing sector . Before Awaab’s inquest took place, an M.E.N investigation in summer 2022 revealed that issues of damp and mould were widespread on the Freehold estate . Other families reported having children with breathing difficulties while living in the same conditions that Awaab’s family faced. The scandal sparked the successful campaign for Awaab’s Law , while RBH went on to be downgraded by the regulator and had their ability to generate private funding frozen. Gareth Swarbrick, the chief executive who had overseen plans to knock down the Seven Sisters, initially refused to resign before being ousted by the social landlord’s board in November 2022 . His interim replacement, Yvonne Arrowsmith, signalled a new era for the beleaguered housing provider. In March 2023, RBH announced a review into the plans for College Bank, before Ms Arrowsmith told the M.E.N in June 2023 that the landlord hoped to save the tower blocks from demolition . ‌ The social landlord entered into an exclusivity agreement with Legal and General Affordable Homes to ‘explore alternative options’, including a full refurbishment of all seven towers. But in October 2024, one year after Amanda Newton had taken over as RBH chief executive, the exclusivity agreement came to an end - with demolition brought back to the table . Andy Burnham launched a mayoral taskforce in an attempt to raise funds for the refurbishment of the Seven Sisters the following month. The Greater Manchester Mayor was joined on that taskforce by strategic partners such as the local council, people from the housing industry, tenants union and political representatives. Housing and regeneration boss at Rochdale council , Coun Danny Meredith, said: “We remain fully committed to our involvement in the taskforce, and with a new Mayor of Greater Manchester now in post, we can continue the joint work that began under the previous Mayor. “Rochdale is still in a housing emergency, and as the council is not a housing stock–holding authority, we must rely on RBH and our partners to build new homes and bring existing stock back into use. ‌ “Right now, 363 households, including 245 families, are living in temporary accommodation. Many of these families have been waiting years for a permanent home. This is not sustainable, and it is not acceptable during a housing emergency. “This is why resolving the situation at Seven Sisters and Lower Falinge is absolutely critical. Across those sites, more than 800 homes currently stand empty. Unlocking those homes is one of the single biggest steps we can take to reduce the pressure on temporary accommodation and give residents the stability they deserve. “We need a clear, deliverable plan from RBH for these sites so that residents can finally have a home for life. I hope we can reach a resolution soon because residents of Rochdale Borough cannot afford further delay.” View 7 Images Mark Slater, campaign organiser for Save the Seven Sisters (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) ‌ Mark Slater has been a leading figure in the ST7S campaign group since its inception and is a member of the taskforce, now chaired by new Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig. He feels that RBH have deliberately overseen the degradation of the blocks - what he described as ‘managed decline’. Mark said: “I am frustrated to the point of anger that we’ve got a situation where we are listening to RBH saying no decision has been made. But everything is pointing towards a decision under the radar and proceeding with a demolition agenda. “We’re speaking to colleagues, residents and tenants who are also concerned. We’ve lived with this since 2016 and have this Sword of Damocles dangling over our heads. “For whatever reason RBH have decided to go down a route of ‘lets find out a reason for them to be demolished. That’s the way it feels for people on the estate. ‌ “I’m sure Bev Craig will be looking at those comparisons with an emphasis on retaining social housing and building social housing. Those will be scrutinised very closely. “For an organisation to say ‘we’re transparent, we want to communicate, listen to what people are saying’ but they give us this story that the flats aren’t safe. But some people have lived here for decades. “We know they’ve suffered from the managed decline RBH have pursued with these blocks. It seems to us they’re using these surveys to justify an agenda of demolition.” RBH have vehemently denied this accusation on numerous occasions. The social housing provider has repeatedly claimed they are committed to supporting all residents in their transitions from the 1960s blocks. ‌ In Mark Slater’s eyes, money has been the driving force behind RBH’s decision making this whole time. Because of the way funding works in social housing, it is much easier to get government funding for building projects in social housing as opposed to retrofit. Homes England focus mainly on housebuilding rather than refurbishment projects, which would mean going to the private market for funding in the case of refurbishment of the Seven Sisters. For RBH, that was not an option for a long time due to them being placed in special measures back in 2022 in the wake of Awaab Ishak’s death, who lived on the Freehold estate also operated by RBH. Being put in special measures meant RBH had a freeze on funding in the private sector, therefore unable to fund a potential refurbishment project at College Bank. Mark added: “As far as housing is concerned, one of the things Andy Burnham said at the Labour Conference was looking at giving councils powers to repossess homes that have been kept empty for a period of time. We are pressing for details on that and to see if there is any potential we could use that policy decision to do what we need to do on College Bank. ‌ “Everyone is talking about the need to build social housing, but we’re not looking for solutions in estates like this. We are looking at reasons to demolish and it just doesn’t make sense. “Ever since 2016 one of the things that hundreds of people have asked is ‘why do they need to demolish them’. The reason is because there is funding available for new build projects, but no funding available for refurbishments. “That, in one fell swoop, could change the whole process. If Homes England could produce money for refurbishmentment, I would be very interested to see whether RBH could take advantage of that.” Hannah Fleming, director of regeneration and asset improvement at Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, said: “We have been transparent with our customers that the long-term safety of the buildings in their current state cannot be confirmed, and that any solution would require all customers to move out for at least a decade. ‌ “In the meantime, our focus remains on supporting our customers into their new homes. We have already made significant progress, with just under 90 households left to find their new home and most customers already settled in their new homes. “We are working individually with each household to ensure their move is as simple and straightforward as it possibly can be. We know that this is a significant change for many customers and we are working with each household individually to find them a home that meets their needs and requirements. “In some cases, the new homes have required additional work from our empty homes team before they are ready for our customer to move in. Where this is the case, our team keeps our customers fully informed and supported throughout.” View 7 Images Tentercroft residents Roy Kitcher and his partner Christine Hartley (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) ‌ When to expect a decision on the future of the blocks? A decision on the future of the Seven Sisters has been up in the air ever since demolition was put back on the table in 2024 - when the new regime at RBH came in. The social housing provider say they have conducted surveys that suggest there are a number of structural issues with the blocks and have costed up options for various forms of refurbishments and also demolition. Despite the surveys being completed near the end of 2025, no decision was made by RBH. It is understood that the taskforce designed to shape the future of Seven Sisters, created by former Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham, wasn’t allowed full access to the surveys. So the taskforce agreed with RBH to have an independent review of the surveys. It is understood this was part of due diligence from a local authority point of view, with Rochdale council, Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), the tenants union and the local MP represented on the taskforce. ‌ The findings from that review are expected to be produced in the coming weeks and will be presented to the next taskforce meeting. After that, a decision on the future of the blocks will be made by RBH, but the taskforce will get a say in the matter. It is clear that all parties want to find a solution and have a decision. Campaigners claim that RBH have pushed the managed decline of the blocks in order to pursue demolition; the cost on RBH to keep so many flats empty is eyewatering. RBH have admitted it costs them £1.7m every year in council tax payments. The cost is astronomical because council tax bills increase the longer a property is empty. ‌ Empty homes council tax multipliers range from 100 per cent of the standard bill (double) in the first year, up to 300 per cent after five years of being empty and 400 per cent after 10 years of being empty. RBH executive Ms Fleming added: “It’s important that we make the right decision on the future of College Bank; not necessarily the fastest decision. Our focus throughout has been on doing the right thing for current and future customers, ensuring we can provide safe, warm, affordable homes that meet housing needs for generations to come. “The length of time this has taken reflects our commitment to working with our partners, as well as the complexity of the decision and the need to consider detailed surveys. As part of that process, Rochdale Borough Council and the Greater Manchester Combined Authority commissioned an independent review of the evidence, and we will discuss the findings of that work with partners before the RBH Board makes a decision on the future regeneration route for College Bank.” Rochdale MP Paul Waugh said: “Tenants have been left in limbo for far too long and I hope that they can be given the answers they need about the safety and the future of their homes. ‌ "I urge RBH to act as swiftly as possible to bring this to a conclusion on behalf of all Rochdale residents during a housing emergency. Each day these flats are left empty is another missed opportunity to support the many thousands of Rochdalians living in temporary or unsuitable accommodation. "The council and GMCA have confirmed their commitment to resolving this longstanding and emotive issue, and I will continue to work with colleagues across government to ensure the best quality housing in Rochdale is realised." The latest findings on the tower blocks’ structural integrity In summer 2020, extensive investigations on properties at College Bank uncovered serious problems with ‘compartmentation’ at Seven Sisters flats, which is supposed to prevent fire from spreading between apartments. RBH says a 24-hour waking watch was introduced as a result, plus bespoke fire alarm and evacuation alarm systems. Since then, the Building Safety Regulator (BSR) issued enforcement notices against RBH on four of the tower blocks - Dunkirk Rise, Mitchell Hey, Tentercroft and Town Mill Brow. ‌ In the notices, issued last summer and seen by the M.E.N following the release of documents under the Freedom of Information Act, the BSR said the landlord had failed to ‘take proportionate measures to manage the risk of spread of fire created by compartmentation issues’. Months later, Seven Sisters residents were told they would need to leave . Last October, RBH cited safety concerns regarding structural and electrical issues, problems with the water pumping system, roof damage and increasing costs to heat and light the properties as reasons for the move. The Mitchell Hey block was then evacuated in March 2026 , when a water pipe burst. Campaigners - backed by Rochdale councillors - say they are still yet to see the concrete evidence of why they need to leave the College Bank flats. A spokesperson for the Save the Seven Sisters campaign said: “Despite numerous requests by residents, campaigners and local politicians, RBH still refuse to share any surveys they claim show potential long term safety issues requiring the blocks to be emptied. RBH have pushed to clear the estate of residents since October 2025, all while still claiming that no long term decision on the future of the estate has been made.” ‌ In the meantime, RBH has communicated its concerns over the Seven Sisters to the BSR. Correspondence released under the Freedom of Information Act, seen by the M.E.N, said: “Surveys have identified that although the buildings are currently safe, there are a number of issues which will deteriorate over time. This deterioration means that the long-term safety of the buildings in their current state cannot be confirmed as the issues with building repairs and condition are becoming more pressing as they continue to age. “We have therefore been closely considering the options for how we address this in the short to medium term, as any refurbishment option will take a number of years to plan and commence, and an estimated 12 years to complete across all seven buildings. We are fully cognisant of our duty to keep the buildings and our residents safe during that time, and also to protect the well-being of those residents and their quality of life.” After the M.E.N was given sight of the documents released by the BSR, Siobhan McCoy, director of property services at RBH, said: “The safety of our customers is our absolute priority. We wrote to all College Bank customers about these notices when they were first issued by the BSR more than a year ago, setting out what they meant and offering opportunities for people to speak directly with us. We also posted copies of the notices within each of the buildings together with information on safety and how to contact us about concerns. "The notices concerned ongoing structural surveys and a historic fire safety issue linked to refurbishment work carried out in the 1990s. This issue was identified by RBH in 2020 and a range of additional safety measures were put in place, including a 24-hour waking watch, bespoke fire alarm and evacuation alarm systems, and support for any customers who may need assistance in an emergency. ‌ "We have continued to work constructively with regulatory agencies to manage building safety risks and address regulatory requirements.The decision to rehouse our customers was informed by a range of factors, including structural investigations, the scale of the works that will be required in all regeneration scenarios and - primarily – customer safety. It was not the result of the enforcement notices. "We strongly reject any suggestion that there has been a managed decline at College Bank. Throughout this period, we have continued to maintain the buildings, and will spend at least £985k this year to carry out repairs and maintenance. Should any additional safety measures be required, we will determine how best to implement them. Our foc

title: Rochdale schools benefit from Tesco's Free Fruit and Veg programme
excerpt: Schools across Greater Manchester, including those in Rochdale, received over 750,000 portions of fruit and vegetables through Tesco's initiative, promoting healthier eating among pupils.
content_html:
Schools across Greater Manchester, including those in Rochdale, have received a total of 750,600 portions of fruit and vegetables as part of Tesco's Free Fruit & Veg for Schools programme. This initiative, now in its third year, aims to encourage healthier eating habits among children.

The produce, which weighed more than 60,000 kilograms, was distributed to schools throughout the region. Apples were the most popular choice, with approximately 221,000 portions consumed, followed by bananas at around 103,000 portions. Satsumas and clementines also featured prominently, with about 88,000 portions provided.

Since its launch, the programme has supplied nearly 20 million portions of fruit and vegetables across the UK, benefiting up to 186,000 pupils. According to a recent impact report, 98% of teachers reported that the initiative encouraged students to try a wider variety of fruits, while 94% noted improvements in student behaviour.

While specific figures for Rochdale schools were not disclosed, the overall success of the programme highlights its positive impact on children's nutrition and well-being. As the scheme continues, it is expected to reach even more schools and students in the coming year.

title: East Lancashire Railway secures portable defibrillator for its trains
excerpt: The heritage railway serving Heywood plans to take lifesaving equipment onboard and is seeking support for more mobile units.
content_html:
East Lancashire Railway has secured a portable defibrillator that will eventually travel on its trains, bringing potentially lifesaving equipment closer to passengers, staff and volunteers.

The heritage railway, which serves Heywood, received the Automated External Defibrillator (AED) following fundraising led by ELR Fund Raising Lead Adrian Dewey with support from national charity AEDdonate.

The unit is intended to move with train services rather than remain at a fixed location. It has not yet entered operational service. The railway says it will first establish arrangements for governance, asset management, equipment checks, training and deployment so it can be managed safely as it moves between services.

The new equipment will complement defibrillators already located at stations. ELR hopes to secure further mobile units, with the longer term ambition of extending coverage across all its operating services.

Chairman Mike Kelly said: “Keeping staff, volunteers and our visitors safe is our top priority. I want to thank AEDdonate for their timely donation and all of our kind donors for making this possible.”

He said having equipment available on trains, in addition to station defibrillators, would further strengthen the railway’s health and safety arrangements.

Phillip Warren, ELR Commercial Services Director and AED sponsor, said: “This is about putting lifesaving equipment where our passengers, volunteers and staff actually are.”

He explained that passengers may be travelling somewhere along the line rather than sitting beside a station building, making a portable unit an important additional resource in an onboard emergency.

“Hopefully this equipment will never be needed, but if that day ever comes, we want to have done everything reasonably possible to be prepared,” he said.

The announcement comes during Restart a Heart activity this October. The annual initiative, led by Resuscitation Council UK, promotes awareness of cardiac arrest and CPR education, with Restart a Heart Day held on 16 October.

As a registered charity, ELR relies on fundraising, donations, volunteers and support from businesses and other organisations. It is now inviting individuals to contribute to the next phase of the mobile AED project and businesses to consider sponsoring equipment.

Medical suppliers and other organisations able to donate a unit are also being encouraged to contact the railway.

Warren said: “It is a very tangible way of supporting a charity and potentially helping to save a life.”

Donations towards additional mobile defibrillators can be made through the ELR fundraising campaign: https://www.justgiving.com/campaign/elr-defibrilator-fundraiser

Source: East Lancashire Railway press release supplied to Rochdale Daily.

title: Jolly Josh Christmas Ball sells out as Rochdale businesses urged to help
excerpt: The Castleton charity is asking businesses to sponsor a table for £50 or donate raffle and auction prizes ahead of its December ball at Rochdale Town Hall.
content_html:
Rochdale charity Jolly Josh has filled the guest tables for its Jolly Jingle Christmas Ball and is now asking local businesses to help turn a full room into vital funding for families.

The ball takes place at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday 11 December at 7pm. With guest places filled, the charity is inviting businesses across Rochdale and Greater Manchester to sponsor tables for £50, donate raffle or auction prizes, or discuss other ways to support the evening.

A contribution does not have to be extravagant. Vouchers, meals, products, experiences and services can all help boost the fundraising total.

Based at Ensor Mill on Queensway in Castleton, Jolly Josh says it supports more than 300 families of children and young people with complex medical needs, physical disabilities, life limiting conditions, and profound and multiple learning disabilities.

Its purpose built centre offers hydrotherapy, rebound therapy, sensory activities, youth social groups, accessible after school provision and support for parents and carers.

The charity says it receives no regular government funding, making grants, donations, community fundraising and business support essential to keeping its services running.

Rose Hutchings, Lead Fundraiser at Jolly Josh, said:

“We’ve been absolutely delighted by the response to this year’s Jolly Jingle Ball and to see the tables fill. What we’d really love now is for the wider Rochdale business community to help us make the night as successful as possible for our families.

“A £50 table sponsorship or a donated raffle or auction prize might feel like a relatively small contribution to a business, but when lots of local organisations get behind us those contributions quickly add up.

“Jolly Josh doesn’t receive regular government funding, so fundraising and community support genuinely help us continue providing a safe, accessible place where children and young people with complex needs and their families can connect, access opportunities and feel part of a community.”

The appeal comes as demand for the charity’s specialist services continues to grow. Jolly Josh says its hydrotherapy provision has previously run at least 42 sessions a week and experienced waiting lists, with strong demand for other services too.

Businesses interested in a £50 table sponsorship, donating a raffle or auction prize, or offering other event support can email Rose Hutchings at rose@jollyjosh.co.uk or call 01706 399141.

Further information about Jolly Josh, registered charity number 1178116, is available at https://jollyjosh.co.uk/

Source: Jolly Josh press release supplied to Rochdale Daily.

title: Office of Rail and Road rejects proposal for extra Rochdale to London train services
excerpt: The Office of Rail and Road has turned down a proposal for additional train services from Rochdale to London, citing concerns over delays and capacity on the West Coast Main Line.
content_html:
Plans to enhance the rail link between Rochdale and London have been rejected once again. The Office of Rail and Road (ORR) announced that it had turned down proposals from Lumo to operate up to four additional return services from Rochdale to Euston on weekdays and Saturdays, and three services on Sundays.

Rochdale MP Paul Waugh had supported the bid, describing it as a "game-changing opportunity" for the borough and the wider North West. However, the ORR's assessment concluded that adding more trains to the already congested West Coast Main Line would likely lead to increased delays and cancellations for passengers. This decision follows a similar rejection of Lumo's application last year, with the ORR stating that the capacity and performance of the southern section of the line had not materially changed since then.

An external review commissioned by the ORR corroborated these findings, indicating that the current timetable must allow for recovery time during disruptions to minimise delays. The ORR emphasised the importance of maintaining service reliability for existing passengers.

The rejection of this proposal means that residents of Rochdale will not see an increase in direct train services to London in the near future, which could impact travel options for commuters and those wishing to visit the capital.

title: Three Rochdale artists awarded free studio space to develop new work
excerpt: Three emerging artists from Rochdale have been awarded free studio space, along with funding and support, to help establish their creative practices in the area.
content_html:
Three emerging artists from Rochdale have been awarded free studio space as part of an initiative aimed at supporting local talent. The selected artists will also receive materials funding and additional support to develop their work, which is valued at approximately £1,200 per artist.

The initiative is designed to address the lack of financial support for emerging artists and aims to enhance their professional development. Each artist will benefit from a package that includes technical assistance and marketing support, allowing them to establish their creative practices more effectively.

Among the recipients is Madison Marcantonatos, a multidisciplinary artist whose work is expected to reflect her personal experiences and creativity. This support is part of a broader effort to foster creative talent within Rochdale and provide emerging artists with the resources they need to succeed.

The initiative not only aims to support individual artists but also seeks to enrich the local arts scene, encouraging a vibrant community of creativity in Rochdale. The artists will begin their studio time shortly, marking an important step in their artistic journeys.

Image credit: Ella Marshall Three emerging Rochdale artists will receive free studio space, materials funding and support to develop work for a joint exhibition. Richard Street Studios and Breaking Barriers have named Alisha K., Madison Marcantonatos and Georgia Scholes as recipients of support funded by The Haworth Trust. Each artist will receive ten free days at Richard Street Studios, with the studio time valued at an estimated £1,200 per artist. The package also includes a materials budget and technical and marketing support. The scheme aims to help artists establish their practice in Rochdale. Parvez Qadir, artistic director at Breaking Barriers, said, “Rochdale has no shortage of creative talent. What it has lacked is the financial support for artists to take that talent seriously at the start of their careers.” Alisha K., who works with oil paint and pastel, said this would be her first opportunity to work in a professional studio alongside other artists. She said, “By the end, I hope to have pushed my practice further and created a body of work that reflects what I can do.” Multidisciplinary artist Madison Marcantonatos plans to explore nostalgia and her own experiences. She said, “Like many creatives, I’ve been caught up in commercial work, which has left little room for my own practice.” Collage and textile artist Georgia Scholes plans to make a large-scale textile banner celebrating Rochdale’s radical history. She said, “This funding gives me the time to develop my practice and build connections in a creative environment.” The artists’ work will be shown in a joint exhibition at Richard Street Studios in March 2027. title: Joy Street roadworks scheduled from 2 November 2026
excerpt: Joy Street in Rochdale will be temporarily closed for roadworks from 2 November to 16 November 2026, affecting local traffic flow and access to surrounding roads.
content_html:
Joy Street in Rochdale will be temporarily closed for roadworks from 8am on Monday, 2 November 2026, until 5pm on Monday, 16 November 2026. The closure will extend from the junction with Binns Nook to the junction with Scarr Drive, impacting local traffic flow.

The roadworks are part of ongoing improvements by Rochdale Borough Council aimed at enhancing the infrastructure in the area. Residents and commuters are advised to plan their journeys accordingly, as access to Scarr Drive, Dewhirst Road, and Binns Nook Road may also be affected during this period.

This closure is expected to cause some disruption, particularly for those who rely on Joy Street for daily travel. Local businesses and residents are encouraged to stay updated on the progress of the works through the council's communications.

For more information about the roadworks and to view a map of the affected area, visit the Rochdale Borough Council website. Being aware of these changes will help residents avoid delays and ensure safe travel during the construction period.

title: Six Rochdale Hornets players compete in international matches
excerpt: This weekend, six players from Rochdale Hornets represented their countries in international rugby league fixtures, showcasing their skills on the international stage.
content_html:
Rochdale Hornets had a busy weekend as six players from their men's and women's teams participated in international rugby league matches. The fixtures included the Celtic Cup and a friendly match, highlighting the club's commitment to developing talent across all levels.

In Hawick, Scotland, Hornets captain Ross Whitmore played for the national team against Ireland, which featured new recruit Oli Whitford. Whitford, playing at full-back, scored the opening try in a match that ended with Ireland defeating Scotland 44-12. Whitmore managed to score Scotland's only second-half try, demonstrating his determination on the field.

Meanwhile, four members of the Hornets women's squad represented the Netherlands in a match against Scotland, where they faced a challenging defeat of 54-0. The Dutch Lionesses were captained for the first time by Hiske Blom, with Lisa Berding, Fiona Kalf, and Eva Peroti also contributing to the team's efforts.

The involvement of these players in international competitions reflects the depth of talent within Rochdale Hornets' programmes. The club expressed pride in their players' achievements and their ongoing commitment to rugby league. Fans can look forward to more updates as the international tournaments progress.

title: Secondary school applications close on 31 October: what Rochdale parents need to know
excerpt: The council advises families to list five preferences and apply by Saturday 31 October. Late applications are considered after National Offer Day on 1 March 2027.
content_html:
Rochdale families have until Saturday 31 October 2026 to apply for a secondary school place through the council's online parent portal.

With the deadline approaching, the council advises parents to name five school preferences. Repeating a school, or listing just one, does not improve the chance of securing it.

Applying on time matters. The council says 331 families applied late last year: 51% received their first preference, compared with 87% of applicants who met the deadline. Those figures describe last year's admissions, not a guarantee for this round.

Late applications are considered after National Offer Day, 1 March 2027. Schools do not hold places back for late applicants, so a preferred school may already be full.

Before submitting, read each school's admissions criteria, prospectus and Ofsted report. An on-time application still does not guarantee a preferred place.

Official deadline, guidance and admissions link: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/news/article/675/council-urges-families-to-apply-on-time-for-secondary-school-places

title: Rochdale’s £5m crisis support fund: what help is available this winter and how to ask
excerpt: The council lists help with sudden financial emergencies, housing costs and essential goods. Different schemes have different rules; an award is not automatic.
content_html:
Rochdale residents struggling to afford essentials can ask about support through the council's Crisis and Resilience Fund as winter approaches.

The £5 million programme runs from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, using Department for Work and Pensions funding. It replaced the Household Support Fund in April. The £5 million is the borough-wide programme budget, not an amount available to each household.

The council lists several routes: Crisis Payments for sudden financial difficulty; Housing Payments for emergency rent or housing costs; the Discretionary Crisis Fund for goods; and Healthy Homes grants for eligible vulnerable residents needing help such as boiler repairs or essential appliances. Each route needs its own eligibility check.

For Crisis Payments, eligible residents can receive a voucher worth up to £75 towards food and energy. Applicants must live in Rochdale borough, be at least 16 and have nobody receiving Child Benefit for them. Applications are allowed once every six months. Apply by calling 01706 923685; the published hours are Monday to Friday, 9am–5pm. Examples of a crisis include fire, flooding, a health emergency or losing employment.

The separate Discretionary Crisis Fund is described as last-resort support. It provides goods rather than cash. Its contact number is 01706 532222 and its email is StrategicHousing@rochdale.gov.uk.

Check the route that matches your circumstances before applying. The main fund page also mentions food vouchers only through the end of the 2026 summer holidays; that wording does not establish a winter voucher entitlement.

Official programme and scheme guidance: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/cost-living/crisis-resilience-fund

title: Rochdale Sleep Out raises funds for homeless support
excerpt: Fundraisers gathered at Crown Oil Arena for the annual Sleep Out, raising awareness and funds for homelessness initiatives in the community.
content_html:
Fundraisers spent a night outdoors at Rochdale's Crown Oil Arena to raise awareness and vital funds for people experiencing homelessness. This event, the second annual Sleep Out organised by Petrus Communities and RAFC Community Trust, saw supporters from across the borough come together for a common cause.

The money raised will support the Changing Lives initiative, a football programme designed to assist individuals facing homelessness or living in supported accommodation. The initiative aims to enhance participants' mental health, physical well-being, and social inclusion through free football sessions, while also providing personal development opportunities, including pathways into volunteering, education, and employment.

Louise Scriven, Fundraising and Partnerships Coordinator at Petrus, emphasised that the Sleep Out is not about pretending to experience homelessness, but about standing in solidarity with those facing housing insecurities. She noted that last year's event significantly impacted participants, helping them rebuild confidence, forge new friendships, and develop skills to become active community members.

The funds raised from this year's Sleep Out will continue to provide essential accommodation, support, advice, and opportunities for those experiencing homelessness and disadvantage in Rochdale, Oldham, and Burnley. Donations are crucial for sustaining these services and making a difference in the lives of vulnerable individuals in the community.

title: Nine-year-old guitar virtuoso Adrian Abraham from Middleton on verge of world record
excerpt: Adrian Abraham, a nine-year-old from Middleton, is set to make his mark in the music world as he approaches a potential world record for his guitar skills, inspired by his father and a passion for heavy metal.
content_html:
Adrian Abraham, a nine-year-old guitar virtuoso from Middleton, is on the verge of setting a world record for his exceptional guitar skills. Having started his musical journey approximately two years ago, Adrian has rapidly developed his talent, showcasing his abilities through performances shared on his Instagram account.

Initially picking up an acoustic guitar, Adrian soon transitioned to electric guitar, where he found his passion for heavy metal music. Inspired by his father, who introduced him to the instrument, Adrian has dedicated himself to mastering various genres, although heavy metal remains his favourite.

As he prepares for his first live performance, Adrian aims to inspire others to take up an instrument, demonstrating that dedication and passion can lead to remarkable achievements at a young age. His journey reflects not only his personal growth but also the potential for young musicians to make an impact in the music industry.

Adrian's story is a testament to the power of inspiration and hard work, and as he approaches this potential world record, the local community is eager to support his musical aspirations.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Nine-year-old guitar virtuoso on verge of setting world record - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Nine-year-old guitar virtuoso on verge of setting world record A nine-year-old rock guitar virtuoso who is on his way into the record books wants to inspire others to pick up an instrument. Adrian Abraham, from Middleton, only started playing the guitar about two years ago. Later this month, he is taking the Trinity College London Grade 8 Rock & Pop electric guitar examination — and could win a Guinness World Record in the process. Adrian loves heavy metal and picked up the guitar after hearing his father, Abraham Joseph, play the acoustic guitar. His favourite band is Iron Maiden and his favourite song to play is Eruption, by Van Halen. His Instagram page features dozens of videos chronicling his journey, including performances of hits by Metallica, Guns ‘n’ Roses, Queen, Deep Purple, Slipknot and System of a Down. The youngster said: “I saw my dad playing the guitar and I thought it really sounded cool, and then I wanted to give it a try. Adrian prepares for his first live performance. Image: adrian_jaams “So then I gave it a shot and I started going through acoustic at first and eventually went to electric.” Abraham added: “I used to play acoustic guitar and he used to sit down and listen. One day he told me he wanted to just hold the guitar to get the feel of it. “He took the guitar and he held a perfect cord. That’s the time I realised the guitar is the instrument for him. “His first guitar was a classic acoustic guitar which he played for about three months before it wasn’t enough for him and we had to upgrade to an electric. He is really progressing well. “I’ve been in choirs and I picked up the acoustic guitar when I was in college. It was just for fun and then I left it, but then when Adrian was born, I had this overwhelming feeling I should play something to him which would sound good. Music brings the out a real person. “But then he reached a point where he discovering grade eight. I can only teach him as much as basics of the guitar but the further grades, he picked it up himself.” With the help of a tutor, Adrian could now become the youngest person to pass the Grade 8 rock and pop guitar exam, setting a world record. He said: “I feel very excited and happy that I could be beating a world record, and I’m very happy that I got this far. If I beat it, I’m gonna be so overjoyed!” READ MORE: New drive to open car wash in town Adrian has been given a Marshall amplifier and Solar guitar by the manufacturers. Image: adrian_jaams While Adrian has to showcase a range of techniques for the exam, playing his favourite song is already a challenge for guitarists. With more than 200 beats per minute, it requires a tapping technique, using fingers from each hand, instead of picking or plucking. Adrian said: “My favourite song would be Eruption from Van Halen, and since I just really like the tapping pod and it just really gets me. It is the most-iconic tapping song in the world and it just sounds absolutely great.” The youngster’s ability has earned global attention, including endorsements from legendary music industry brands Marshall Amplifiers and Solar Guitars, which have supplied him with equipment to help his music journey. Following his exams, the natural outlet for Adrian’s talent would be playing in a band. Abraham said: “When people hear Adrian, a lot of them want him in a band, but by the time they see him, they’re like, he’s too little . . . his guitar is taller than him!” But Adrian is clear that music will be in his future. He said: “My dream would be to be the best guitarist in the world and be playing with famous bands and having fun with them too.” But playing the guitar has other benefits too. He added: “I usually just like it because it sounds good, it comes down my stress and it helps me play it and it helps me to just enjoy relax and play some good songs because usually most of the songs are heavy metal.” By sharing his journey on Instagram, Adrian and Abraham want to inspire others to do the same. Abraham said: “Like Adrian, you don’t have to wait to pick up a guitar. You can do it anytime, and you can’t, if Adrian can do it, so can you.” He joked: “I’ve got a daughter as well now she she’s only four years old, but she’s picked up the guitar because she thinks that’s the only way to get attention in the house!” Adrian and his dad, Abraham. title: Rochdale unemployment claimants increase to 8,775 in September 2026
excerpt: The number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits in Rochdale rose by 270 in September 2026, marking an increase from the previous month and year.
content_html:
The number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits in Rochdale rose by 270 in September 2026, bringing the total to 8,775. This figure represents 6.0% of residents aged 16 to 64, an increase from 5.8% in August 2026.

In September 2025, the claimant count was slightly lower at 8,625, indicating a year-on-year increase in unemployment claims. The latest figures were published by the Office for National Statistics through Nomis, and the September data is provisional and subject to revision.

The rise in claimants may reflect broader economic challenges affecting the local job market, although specific reasons for the increase have not been detailed in the report. The data is crucial for understanding employment trends in the area and may influence local policy decisions.

Residents and local businesses may feel the impact of this increase, as higher unemployment can affect consumer spending and overall economic activity in Rochdale.

title: Inspector rejects garden fence appeal on Town House Road, Littleborough
excerpt: A planning inspector has upheld Rochdale Council's decision to refuse retrospective planning permission for a garden fence at 19 Town House Road, Littleborough, citing its negative impact on the area's character.
content_html:
A planning inspector has ruled against a homeowner's appeal regarding a garden fence at 19 Town House Road, Littleborough. Caterina Buonocore had sought retrospective planning permission for a 1.55-metre high boundary fence, which is approximately twice the height of the original fence. The council had previously rejected her application, leading to the appeal.

In the inspector's decision, it was stated that the main concern was the fence's effect on the character and appearance of the area. The inspector noted that boundary treatments in the locality are typically low-level and visually permeable, contributing to a sense of openness and allowing the greenery in front gardens to be appreciated. The inspector remarked that the existing vegetation helps to soften the street scene, enhancing the area's character.

The inspector further explained that the close-boarded timber fence introduced by the appeal contrasts sharply with the more traditional forms of boundary treatment found in the neighbourhood. Observations made on-site indicated that, due to the prominent corner location, the fence appeared particularly stark and incongruous against the backdrop of traditional stone terraces with lower boundary treatments.

As a result of this ruling, Buonocore may now be required to remove the fence, which could have implications for her property and the surrounding area. The decision underscores the importance of maintaining the character of local neighbourhoods and adhering to planning regulations.

excerpt: Ryan Jackson has departed from Rochdale Hornets to join Keighley Cougars, having served as assistant coach since midway through the 2025 season.
content_html:
Rochdale Hornets have announced that assistant coach Ryan Jackson has left the club to take up a new position with Keighley Cougars. Jackson joined the Hornets midway through the 2025 season, initially in an unofficial capacity, supporting head coach Gary Thornton.

Prior to his time at Rochdale, Jackson spent four-and-a-half years as the assistant coach at Hunslet, where he played a significant role in the club's promotion to the Championship. He departed Hunslet in March 2025 before joining the Hornets.

The club expressed their gratitude to Jackson for his contributions and wished him well in his future endeavours. Jackson's departure marks a change in the coaching staff as the Hornets prepare for the upcoming season.

Fans and players alike will be keen to see how this change impacts the team's dynamics and performance as they look to build on their recent campaigns.

title: Rochdale draw 2-2 with Grimsby after late equaliser from Ian Henderson
excerpt: A late equaliser from Ian Henderson secured a point for Rochdale in a thrilling 2-2 draw against Grimsby Town in League Two on October 20, 2026.
content_html:
Rochdale AFC salvaged a point in a dramatic 2-2 draw against Grimsby Town at the Crown Oil Arena on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. The match saw veteran striker Ian Henderson come off the bench to score an equaliser in the 88th minute, preventing Grimsby from claiming all three points after they had taken the lead in the second half.

The game began with both teams eager to break their recent poor form. Rochdale took the lead in the 38th minute when Dajaune Brown scored following a well-placed cross from Glenn Middleton. However, Grimsby responded strongly after the break, with Kieran Green equalising in the 57th minute after a saved header from Andy Cook. The visitors then took the lead in the 72nd minute through Jamie Walker, who capitalised on a partially cleared corner.

Despite trailing, Rochdale continued to press for a goal. Their persistence paid off when Henderson, who had been introduced as a substitute, headed in a cross from Charlie Tasker to level the score just before full-time. This late goal marked a significant moment for Rochdale, who had recently suffered a defeat against Crewe Alexandra, ending a five-match unbeaten run.

The draw leaves Rochdale in 13th place in League Two with 15 points, while Grimsby Town, who ended a four-match losing streak, sit just behind in 15th with 14 points. Both teams will look to build on this result in their upcoming fixtures as they aim to improve their standings in the league.

excerpt: The lifts at Freehold Tram Stop are currently out of service as replacement works take place, affecting passengers travelling towards Manchester and Rochdale.
content_html:

Passengers are advised to alight at either South Chadderton or Westwood tram stops and use the orange call points located at all stops to request assistance for completing their journeys. For further assistance, customers can contact the helpline at 0161 244 1000, which operates from 7 am to 8 pm on weekdays and from 8 am to 8 pm on weekends and bank holidays.

This service disruption may affect those who rely on the tram for daily commutes or travel to local amenities. It is advisable for passengers to plan their journeys accordingly and consider alternative routes during this period.

Updates regarding the status of the lifts and any further developments will be provided through the Bee Network travel alerts. Passengers are encouraged to check the latest information as the situation evolves.

title: Power outage in Newhey linked to 'Third-Party Interference'
excerpt: Residents in Newhey experienced a power outage lasting approximately three hours following a loud bang linked to third-party interference on the electricity network.
content_html:
Residents in Newhey, Rochdale, were left without power for around three hours following a loud bang associated with an incident on the electricity network. The disruption occurred on the evening of October 18, 2026, and was reported by Electricity North West, who stated that the outage was due to 'third-party interference' on their high-voltage network.

According to a message from Electricity North West, the loud bang was heard at a property on Ogden Lane at the same time the power interruption occurred. While most residents had their power restored by 23:17, one customer remained without supply as further investigations were conducted to ensure safety before restoration could take place.

Electricity North West expressed appreciation for the patience and understanding of the affected residents during the investigation. They confirmed that their teams were working to identify the root cause of the fault and ensure the safety of the network before restoring power to the remaining customer.

Residents are encouraged to stay updated through official channels for any further developments regarding the power supply in their area. For those affected, it is recommended to check the Electricity North West website or contact their customer service for assistance.

title: Rochdale falls to Crewe in 3-2 defeat in League Two
excerpt: Crewe Alexandra secured a 3-2 victory over Rochdale, marking a record-breaking start to their league campaign. Manager Lee Bell praised his team's performance and resilience against a strong Rochdale side.
content_html:
Rochdale AFC faced a disappointing defeat against Crewe Alexandra, losing 3-2 in a League Two match on Saturday, October 17. This defeat marked Rochdale's first loss in six league games, despite a spirited effort in the second half.

Crewe took the lead in the 39th minute when Matus Holicek scored with a powerful strike from outside the box, which goalkeeper Sam Waller managed to get a hand to but could not prevent from going in. Jordan Gibson then added to the scoreline with two goals, one just before half-time and another ten minutes into the second half, putting Crewe ahead 3-0.

Rochdale managed to respond with a goal from Joel Tabiner, who inadvertently diverted a cross from Glenn Middleton into his own net in the 65th minute. Aden Flint then scored a header from a cross by substitute Ed Francis in the closing stages, but it was not enough to secure a comeback for the visitors.

The result leaves Rochdale looking to regroup as they prepare for their next fixture, while Crewe continues their unbeaten run, now boasting three consecutive victories. The match was held at Gresty Road, Crewe, and the defeat will be a point of reflection for Rochdale as they aim to improve in their upcoming matches.

title: Rochdale Council addresses concerns over local pub closures
excerpt: Councillor Richard Jackson has raised concerns about the future of local pubs in Littleborough after the closure of The Wheatsheaf, highlighting restrictive covenants that hinder reopening efforts.
content_html:
The future of local pubs in Littleborough is under scrutiny following the recent closure of The Wheatsheaf. This closure has sparked community outcry and raised concerns about the viability of pubs in the area. Councillor Richard Jackson addressed these issues during a Rochdale council meeting on October 15, highlighting the challenges posed by restrictive covenants that prevent former pubs from being reopened as such.

Councillor Jackson noted that approximately 50 per cent of pubs are owned by breweries or large pub companies, which often include covenants in sales to deter competition. This practice has led to a significant number of closures, with many pubs being sold off for alternative uses. He cited the example of the former Royal Oak pub, which closed in 2015 and was subsequently converted into a vape shop, a change that was later halted by Trading Standards due to regulatory issues.

The council's discussion aims to address the ongoing loss of pubs in the community, with Jackson's motion seeking to reduce the impact of these covenants. He expressed concern over the cycle of tenant attrition that many pubs face, stating, "We have seen this at the former Royal Oak pub. This was sold with an anti-competition covenant."

The implications of this discussion are significant for local residents and pub enthusiasts, as the council considers measures to protect these community assets. The outcome of this motion could influence future policies regarding the sale and repurposing of pubs in Littleborough and beyond.

Is the future of the local pub in danger? That’s the fear in Littleborough where the closure of another pub has sparked outcry. A few months ago The Wheatsheaf closed down in the Rochdalian town. There is strong community interest in reopening the pub as a local asset, but a small loophole means they fear they can’t do that. When breweries or large companies that own and operate pubs sell on the building, they can include a covenant that prevents it from being re-used as a pub. This covenant is inserted into a sale to stop competitors taking the pub on the cheap, the latest town hall meeting was told. Coun Richard Jackson brought forward a motion to Rochdale council to address this very issue to reduce the continued loss of pubs in communities. The Littleborough Lakeside councillor told the chamber on October 15: “The reality is that around 50 per cent of pubs are owned by breweries or large pub companies. They have a history of damaging the industry as a whole. This often leads to tenant attrition. “We are acutely aware of pubs being closed down after numerous tenants have left the building. The point of this motion is to address the churn. “We have seen this at the former Royal Oak pub. This was sold with an anti-competition covenant.” The former Royal Oak pub was closed down in 2015 and then sold off and became a vape shop, which was later shut down by Trading Standards. Coun Jackson called on the council to write to the government to block restrictive covenants on pub sales. He said that this loophole means most pubs get turned into shops or HMOs. His ward colleague Coun Tom Besford shared his annoyance that the future use of a community building can be dictated by the business interests of a brewery or company. The pair also credited Rochdale MP Paul Waugh for his continued work on this issue and raising it in Parliament. Speaking after the motion was passed in Rochdale Town Hall, Mr Waugh said: “This Government has already done the heavy lifting on pubs. Since August, the planning rules make it harder to turn a viable pub into flats or a shop, and the new Community Right to Buy gives people the power to buy their local. But one back door is still wide open. “A pub company can sell up and write into the deeds that the building can never sell another pint, and that ban binds every owner after them. Littleborough lost the Royal Oak that way, and I’m determined that we’re not going to lose the Wheatsheaf too. “The minister has asked for evidence, and with Rochdale council now behind us, I’ll be putting our town’s case to him directly.” It is a tough time for the pub industry nationally, with approximately one pub a day will have closed by the end of 2026, according to the latest figures from the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA).  The trade body estimates that around 360 pubs will permanently shut their doors by the end of the year. excerpt: A Harvest Thanksgiving service will take place in Rochdale on October 17, inviting the community to celebrate and support local foodbanks.

A Harvest Thanksgiving service is scheduled for Sunday, October 17, at 10.30am in Rochdale. The event aims to celebrate the abundance of creation and raise awareness of the need to support those less fortunate in the community.

Led by Rev’d Ben Somervell, the service will include a sermon based on Psalm 126. Attendees are encouraged to bring donations of tinned and dry packaged foods for the local foodbank, highlighting the importance of community support during challenging times.

The service is designed for all ages and will feature performances from the day school choir, who will sing a selection of songs. Following the service, refreshments including coffee and tea will be served in the parish room, providing an opportunity for fellowship and conversation.

Everyone is welcome to attend, regardless of their previous church experience or beliefs. The evening will also include a relaxed prayer meeting, offering a space for reflection and preparation for the week ahead.
