title: Broadfield Park Slopes renovation celebrated at Rochdale Town Hall
excerpt: A special event at Rochdale Town Hall recognised the contributions of volunteers and partners involved in the restoration of Broadfield Park Slopes, highlighting the project's community impact and heritage significance.
content_html:
A celebration was held at Rochdale Town Hall to honour the individuals and groups who contributed to the renovation of Broadfield Park Slopes. This historic site, located between Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Church, has undergone significant restoration, thanks to the efforts of local volunteers and funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund.

The event, organised by Polly Brant, Cultural Engagement Officer for Rochdale Council, brought together volunteers, partners, and community members to acknowledge their roles in the project. Guests were treated to a series of films by local filmmaker Jack Grindrod, showcasing the stories and heritage associated with the park's transformation. The films captured the community involvement that played a crucial role in the renovation process.

The evening featured poetry readings by Alende Amisi, a local poet and former young poet in residence, who shared his personal reflections on Rochdale's heritage. His contributions added a personal touch to the event, which celebrated not only the park's restoration but also the community spirit that drove the project forward.

The renovation has restored the historic Packer Spout Fountain, created a new accessible pathway, improved landscaping, and introduced new heritage interpretation. The lower lawn has been terraced to create a natural amphitheatre, providing a new space for activities and events, enhancing the park's role as a community hub.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Town celebrates the people and stories behind Broadfield Park Slopes renovation - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Town celebrates the people and stories behind Broadfield Park Slopes renovation The people who helped bring Rochdale’s historic Broadfield Park Slopes back to life were celebrated at a special event at Rochdale Town Hall. The celebration, arranged by Polly Brant, Rochdale Council Cultural Engagement officer, brought together volunteers, partners and people who have been involved in the project to recognise what has been achieved and, importantly, the contribution local people have made along the way. Guests watched a series of films created by Rochdale filmmaker Jack Grindrod and Breaking Barriers, capturing the people, stories, heritage and community involvement behind the transformation. The evening also featured poetry readings from Alende Amisi, a poet who grew up in Rochdale and was a young poet in residence during Rochdale’s Town of Culture. Passionate about the town and its heritage, Alende brought a personal perspective to an evening which was as much about Rochdale’s people as its history. A special thank you was also given to the many volunteers who have supported the project, giving their time to archaeological digs, activities and events and helping uncover and share the history of this important part of the town. The Grade II listed Broadfield Park Slopes sit between Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Church and have been restored through a project delivered by Rochdale Development Agency working with Rochdale Borough Council, with funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund. The work has restored the historic Packer Spout Fountain, created a new accessible pathway, improved landscaping, lighting and CCTV, and introduced new heritage interpretation. The lower lawn has also been terraced, creating a natural amphitheatre and new space for activities and events. READ MORE: Customers flock to opening of new Peacocks store Archaeology and community participation have been a major part of the project. Excavations have uncovered the footings of Charles Kershaw’s 19th century Central Corn Mill, cobbled trackways and the former public weigh station, alongside finds including ceramics, clay smoking pipes, animal bones and glass bottles. Four archaeological digs have taken place, with the wider programme involving schoolchildren, students, volunteers and members of the public. It has included 28 work placement students, 12 archaeological volunteers and a two year schools programme involving 715 pupils. Cllr Sue Smith, portfolio holder for Communities and Co-operation at Rochdale Council, said: “This was a wonderful opportunity to celebrate not just the transformation of the Broadfield Park Slopes, but the people who have made this project so special. “Our volunteers deserve a huge thank you. They have given their time, enthusiasm and energy to this project and have helped us uncover and share more of Rochdale’s history. “It was fantastic to see those stories captured in the films created by Jack Grindrod and Breaking Barriers, and to hear from Alende Amisi, whose passion for Rochdale and its heritage really reflects what this project is about. “The Slopes have been part of Rochdale for generations. We have protected an important part of our heritage, opened it back up for people to enjoy and, crucially, involved our communities in doing it.” The Broadfield Park Slopes are now open to the public, creating a restored green space at the heart of Rochdale’s historic town centre. title: Young people inspire £85,000–£100,000 Castleton pump track proposal
excerpt: A site beside the yellow play park on Manchester Road is being explored for a Castleton bike track, with young people helping shape the idea. Funding and approvals remain outstanding.
content_html:
A new pump track costing an estimated £85,000 to £100,000 is being explored for Castleton after local young people asked for somewhere closer to home to ride their bikes.

Councillor Dave Jones said an area beside the yellow play park on Manchester Road had emerged as a promising potential location following discussions with council officers and youth workers.

The proposal remains at an early stage. No funding or final site approval has been announced, and there is no confirmed construction timetable.

In an update shared with Rochdale Daily, Cllr Jones described a positive meeting with Environmental Management, township officer Caroline and Jasmin from the Youth Work Team to discuss the concept.

Several possible locations were considered. According to the councillor, young people suggested the Manchester Road site because it feels safe. Its existing play area and car park could also make it convenient for families with children of different ages.

The idea is for younger children to use the playground while older children and teenagers could enjoy a nearby bike track, bringing different activities together in one central location.

Cllr Jones said those at the meeting supported involving young people in the design process. They also discussed whether contractors could explain how the track is built and explore suitable opportunities for young people to participate.

A bike repair hub was another suggestion. Local young people have spoken about their interest in repairing bicycles and sharing those skills with others. Secure bike storage lockers were also raised during the discussions.

The councillor said some young people currently travel to tracks elsewhere in the borough, including Littleborough, and expressed concern about the busy roads those journeys can involve. He believes a Castleton facility could offer a more convenient option and reassurance for families.

Funding is the main obstacle. Cllr Jones put the initial estimated cost at between £85,000 and £100,000 and said several processes and approvals would need to be completed before any scheme could proceed.

Council officers are now exploring possible funding sources, according to his update. A further meeting is planned to discuss potential designs and ensure any future proposal reflects what local young people want.

Cllr Jones also thanked Keane, the young person who first approached him with the idea, and praised young residents for taking an active role in improving their community.

He cautioned: “It's important to stress that projects like this take time, and there is still a long way to go.”

The potential location, repair hub, storage lockers and construction involvement are all ideas under discussion rather than confirmed features of an approved scheme.

title: Rochdale Council moves forward with Hopwood Hall redevelopment after High Court ruling
excerpt: Following a High Court ruling, Rochdale Council has confirmed plans to redevelop Hopwood Hall, with an emphasis on community use, after ending an exclusivity agreement with Hopwood DePree.
content_html:
Rochdale Council has announced its commitment to the redevelopment of Hopwood Hall following a recent High Court ruling that upheld the council's decision to terminate an exclusivity agreement with American filmmaker Hopwood DePree. The ruling, delivered at Manchester Civil Justice Centre, concluded that the council acted lawfully when it ended the agreement, which had been in place since 2017.

The council leader, Neil Emmott, addressed the future of the historic building during a town hall meeting on October 15, stating that the council is focused on bringing Hopwood Hall back into use for the community. Emmott expressed openness to DePree's involvement, indicating that if he presents a viable plan, the council would consider it. However, he noted that the legal process is not yet concluded, as DePree has the option to appeal the decision by November 18, 2026, with a potential extension to November 28, 2026.

The High Court's decision came after DePree claimed he had a legally binding agreement to purchase the hall for £1, based on a planning approval granted in 2022. However, the court found that this approval did not trigger the option to purchase. The council has already invested over £1.6 million in repairs to the hall, and Emmott assured that any costs awarded to the council, amounting to £114,000, would be reinvested into the project.

As the situation develops, the council remains committed to the restoration and preservation of Hopwood Hall, which is seen as a valuable asset for the local community. Emmott reiterated that the council's focus is on securing the hall's long-term future, and the outcome of any potential appeal will be crucial in determining the next steps.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Download ratings data | title Skip to main content Food Standards Agency - Frontpage Navigation Menu UK food hygiene rating data API The food hygiene rating data published at https://ratings.food.gov.uk are available via an application programming interface (API) in XML and JSON formats. This is a free service and there is no need to register to use it. Terms and conditions apply (see link below), and guidance for developers is available. Terms and conditions Read the terms and conditions of using the data and images. About the data The data provides the food hygiene rating or inspection result given to a business and reflect the standards of food hygiene found on the date of inspection or visit by the local authority. Businesses include restaurants, pubs, cafés, takeaways, hotels and other places consumers eat, as well as supermarkets and other food shops. The data are held on behalf of local authorities participating in either the: national Food Hygiene Rating Scheme (FHRS) in England, Northern Ireland and Wales, or the Food Hygiene Information Scheme (FHIS) in Scotland Data for local authority areas running either of these schemes can be found on the Ratings site: See a list of local authorities running the FHRS or FHIS The scores part of the data is only applicable to scheme type FHRS (not FHIS) and are for hygiene, structure and confidence in management. These scores can be found in part 2 and 3 of Annex 1, A1.1 of the Food Law code of Practice . These scores are then used to calculate the food hygiene rating details of which can be found in the Guidance on implementation and operation of the Food Hygiene Rating Scheme: the Brand Standard and statutory guidance . When a rescore is uploaded by a local authority the scores of hygiene, structure and confidence in management will not be available in the data. Where the establishment is in operation from a private address the address and geocoding data may not be available. The LocalAuthorityBusinessID is provided by the local authority and is unique for that particular local authority data but could also be used by other local authorities. The FHRSID is system-generated and is unique in the data. It is based on the LocalAuthorityBusinessID and the LocalAuthorityCode . Where a new LocalAuthorityBusinessID is uploaded to the system by a local authority, a new FHRSID is generated. If a LocalAuthorityBusinessID is reused, for example for a new registration, the FHRSID will be retained for the establishment. Please note some local authorities use their database as a business database whereas others use an establishment database, therefore some local authorities will recycle the LocalAuthorityBusinessID where others will not. There are circumstances where the LocalAuthorityBusinessID and FHRSID may change, such as local authorities changing databases or where local authorities have merged. Details of where this has occurred can be found on the FHRS status page . Other useful information can be found on this page such as data types for fields. The business types and associated ID's can be found at: api1-ratings.food.gov.uk/business-types/xml Where Awaiting Publication is displayed instead of a rating, this is where the business has appealed their rating, and the local authority is in the process of determining the appeal. NewRatingPending is displayed as true in the data where a local authority has uploaded new data for an establishment which is not yet published as this data is in the notification or appeals period. It will be published after these time periods have elapsed. Where this is displayed as false, no new data is in the workflow to be published. Further information about the scheme can be found at https://www.food.gov.uk/safety-hygiene/food-hygiene-rating-scheme System status Status updates, usage advice and various other pieces of current information can be found at the System Status Page. API guidance for developers The API allows developers access to the underlying food hygiene rating data published at ratings.food.gov.uk . Developers can query XML files to return the geocoded data (longitude and latitude data are provided for food businesses). The XML data are updated daily and can be found below, grouped by local authority. Wales's local authority data can be output in English or Welsh. The API can also be used to query the live system (the data are automatically updated as local authorities upload and publish data) and return data in XML and JSON formats. Examples of how to use the API and information about the API can be found in the guidance document for developers: Read the API V1 guidance for developers (pdf 316KB, updated April 2024) Read the API V2 guidance for developers Images A set of hygiene rating images is available to be used with the API data. The images must only be used in accordance with the FHRS/FHIS Brand Standard and the terms and conditions . Examples of hygiene rating images, and the sizes available, that can be used with the API data: Download new high resolution FHRS badges (ZIP - 1 MB) Legacy online rating images The previous version of the online ratings has now been retired. Please use the images provided above. Score descriptors English language Welsh language Downloading data from the FHRS search results page When you search for hygiene ratings on www.food.gov.uk/ratings , you can download the search results at the bottom of the page. Number of results You can download up to 5,000 results by entering a number between 1 and 5,000 in the 'Number of results' field. If you need to download more than 5,000 results, in the 'Number of results' field enter 5,000, then enter each 'Page number' 1, 2 etc until all results are downloaded. Data formats Data can be downloaded in XML and JSON format. To convert the data into excel format use the following guidance:: Microsoft support page: Open an XML data file to import its data into Excel (Opens in a new tab) To merge multiple Excel files into a single file use the following guidance: Microsoft support page: Import data from a folder with multiple files (Opens in a new tab) Downloadable open data file A complete record of our open food hygiene rating data can be downloaded via the link below. title: Rochdale Council celebrates achievements of over 200 cared-for children at annual awards
excerpt: Rochdale Council hosted its annual awards ceremony at Matthew Moss High School, recognising the achievements of more than 200 cared-for children with medals and a day of entertainment.
content_html:
Rochdale Council held its annual awards ceremony on 16 October at Matthew Moss High School, celebrating the achievements of over 200 cared-for children. The event, known as 'Our Big Day', recognised the resilience and determination of young people in care, with hundreds of medals awarded to honour their individual successes.

The council received 273 nominations from carers, teachers, and social workers, highlighting the inspiring journeys of children up to the age of 12. Awards were given for exceptional progress in education, sporting achievements, acts of kindness, and positive attitudes in the face of adversity. The day included a variety of entertainment, such as trampolines, funfair rides, and face painting, allowing families to create joyful memories together.

Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, expressed her pride in the achievements of the children, stating, "They are all exceptional young people and show phenomenal determination to be their very best. This doesn’t go unnoticed by those around them." The event aimed to provide public recognition for the hard work and accomplishments of these young individuals.

Local businesses sponsored the celebration, contributing to the activities and entertainment provided for families. Notable sponsors included A&T Surfacing Ltd, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, and Rochdale Hornets, among others. This community support helped create a memorable day for the children and their families.

title: St Cuthbert’s evacuated as message reassures parents all children and staff are safe
excerpt: St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust says St Cuthbert’s was evacuated following a possible bomb threat. All children and staff are safe; parents can collect pupils.
content_html:
Latest update — St Teresa of Calcutta trust statement

St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, which oversees St Cuthbert’s RC High School, has released a statement saying staff received a communication detailing a possible bomb threat on Friday morning, 16 October.

The trust says emergency services were called, all school buildings were evacuated as a precaution and Greater Manchester Police attended. All children and staff are safe and accounted for, it says.

Parents and carers can now collect their children or give consent for them to travel home, according to the statement. The trust says specialist security operatives will carry out a full sweep of the building this afternoon. It currently expects the school to reopen as normal on Monday 19 October, subject to further updates.

The trust’s account conflicts with some earlier reports circulating about the incident. In particular, it describes rumours of intruders or weapons on school premises as false. Earlier references to a lockdown should be read alongside this latest statement, which describes a precautionary evacuation following a possible bomb threat.

This remains a developing story. Rochdale Daily will continue to update this article with official information as it is released. The earlier updates below are retained for context; the latest trust statement takes precedence where accounts differ.

Trust statement in full:

Earlier this morning (Friday 16 October 2026), staff at St. Cuthbert's RC High School in Rochdale received a communication detailing a possible bomb threat to the premises.

The emergency services were called and all school buildings were evacuated as a precautionary measure.

All children and staff are safe and accounted for, in line with our established procedures.

Greater Manchester Police attended and parents and carers were notified immediately that their children had been removed to a safe distance and there was no threat or danger to anyone present.

We would like to assure everyone within the St Cuthbert’s School community that the safety and wellbeing of our children remains our absolute priority.

Specialist security operatives will conduct a full sweep of the building this afternoon to confirm if any further actions are required.

Currently, the expectation is that the school will be open as normal on Monday 19 October - but further information will be communicated as needed when received.

Parents and carers can now attend the school to collect their children, or provide consent for their children to travel home.

We’d like to thank parents, carers and colleagues for their understanding and co-operation in this matter.

We’d also urge people to avoid speculation on social media - particularly regarding false rumours, such as any referring to intruders or weapons being present on school premises.

More details will be communicated when appropriate, following consultation with GMP and Rochdale Borough Council.

Source: Statement attributed to St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, supplied to Rochdale Daily on 16 October 2026.

Earlier updates — before the trust statement

Developing update — councillor requests official briefing

Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short has said he is urgently requesting an update from Rochdale Council and Greater Manchester Police following reports of a lockdown at Saint Cuthbert’s High School. In a statement supplied to Rochdale Daily, he said he first learned of the reports through the Manchester Evening News and had not received an official briefing.

His statement does not establish what prompted the incident. The earlier message shared with Rochdale Daily described a precautionary evacuation and said all children and staff were safe and accounted for.

Councillor Tarrant-Short’s statement in full:

I want to address the reports of a lockdown at Saint Cuthbert’s High School.

First and foremost, my thoughts are with the children, their families and the staff. I understand how frightening this situation will be, particularly for parents waiting for information and reassurance.

I want to be clear: I first became aware of this through the Manchester Evening News. I have not received an official briefing.

I am now urgently requesting an update from Rochdale Council and Greater Manchester Police so I can understand what has happened and what support is being provided to those affected.

Having been through a similar situation myself when Newhouse Academy went into lockdown, I know how distressing that uncertainty can feel. Behind every update are children who may be frightened and families desperate to know their loved ones are safe.

I am asking that communication with families is timely, clear and compassionate, and that support is available for anyone left distressed.

Until there is verified information, I will not speculate about the circumstances. Please follow official updates from the school and police, and avoid sharing rumours.

The immediate priority must be the safety and wellbeing of every child and member of staff.

Earlier report

St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale has been evacuated as a precaution, according to a message to parents and carers shared with Rochdale Daily.

The message states: “All children and staff are safe and accounted for.”

It reassures families that pupils’ safety and wellbeing remain the school’s “absolute priority” and says staff are managing the situation in line with established procedures.

Parents and carers have been told they will receive another communication as soon as further information is available.

The message does not explain what prompted the evacuation or give instructions for collecting children.

St Cuthbert’s is on Shaw Road in Rochdale. The school’s website is https://www.stcuthberts.stoccat.org.uk/.

This is a developing story.

title: Rochdale Council plans major investments and heritage restoration
excerpt: Rochdale Council has announced significant investments in heritage restoration and community services, including plans for Hopwood Hall and Middleton's regeneration projects, aimed at boosting local economy and services.
content_html:
Rochdale Council has outlined a series of major investments aimed at revitalising the borough, with a focus on heritage restoration and community services. In a recent column, Councillor Neil Emmott highlighted the council's commitment to enhancing local infrastructure and supporting residents amid ongoing cost-of-living challenges.

A key development is the council's recent victory in the High Court regarding Hopwood Hall, a historic building in Middleton. The ruling provides clarity on the future of the site, which has seen over £1.6 million invested since 2017 by the council and Historic England. Plans for essential repairs and feasibility studies are underway, with the aim of restoring the hall to serve the community and preserve its historical significance.

In addition to Hopwood Hall, the council is advancing its regeneration plans for Middleton. The acquisition of Middleton Old Grammar School is expected to attract a new tenant by the end of the year, while the long-derelict Warwick Mill is also set for redevelopment, potentially including new housing. Furthermore, the transformation of the Middleton Scout Hut into a community venue is in progress, aimed at providing activities and training for young people.

These initiatives are part of a broader strategy to stimulate economic growth and create jobs across the borough. With banking and post office services returning to Middleton town centre in the new year, local leaders are optimistic about the positive impact these developments will have on the community.

title: Court Rules on Ownership Dispute Over Hopwood Hall
excerpt: A High Court ruling has denied Hopwood DePree's claim to ownership of Hopwood Hall, concluding that Rochdale Council acted fairly in its decision to end the exclusivity agreement.
content_html:
A High Court in Manchester has ruled against Hopwood DePree in his bid to gain ownership of Hopwood Hall, a historic manor house in Rochdale. The ruling concluded that Rochdale Council acted fairly when it ended an exclusivity agreement with DePree, who is a descendant of the family that originally built the hall in the 1420s.

The two-day trial, which concluded on 20 October 2026, centred on DePree's claim that the council had reneged on an agreement allowing him to purchase the Grade II-listed property. The council had previously worked with DePree for seven years to facilitate repairs on the dilapidated site, which is now part of Hopwood Hall College. However, in November 2024, the council stated it would explore other options, citing a lack of a commercially viable business model from DePree.

Following the court's decision, DePree expressed disappointment, stating that the ruling was a significant setback for both his family and the community. He indicated that he and his legal team are considering their options moving forward, while also pledging to monitor the council's efforts to restore the hall for public benefit.

Hopwood Hall has a rich history, having been owned by the Hopwood family until 1922, after which it changed hands several times and fell into disrepair. The council acquired the property in the 1980s and has since been responsible for its maintenance.

title: Rochdale fitness group to undertake 100km Arctic challenge for cancer charities
excerpt: Eighteen runners from Resilience gym in Rochdale will embark on a 100km run across the Arctic wilderness on January 29, 2027, to raise funds for cancer charities.
content_html:
A local fitness community in Rochdale is gearing up for a challenging 100-kilometre run across the Arctic wilderness of Swedish Lapland, set to take place on January 29, 2027. The event, known as the Ultra 4 Cancer challenge, will see 18 runners from Resilience gym tackle extreme conditions, including temperatures that may plunge to -30°C, over the course of two days.

The initiative is led by Martin Stapleton, founder and head coach of Resilience gym. Stapleton, a Rochdale-born former Royal Marines Commando and professional MMA fighter, has a history of extreme fundraising efforts, including kayaking the length of the Rochdale Canal and running along the River Thames to support Help for Heroes. Joining him on this expedition are assistant coaches Greg Egan and Oliver Roxburgh, the latter of whom has a personal connection to the cause.

The team aims to raise vital funds for four cancer charities, highlighting the importance of community support in tackling such a significant health issue. The challenge not only tests the physical endurance of the participants but also serves to raise awareness and funds for cancer research and support services.

As the date approaches, the runners will be preparing for the harsh conditions they will face, with training sessions likely to intensify. Community members interested in supporting the cause can follow the team's progress and contribute to their fundraising efforts through the Resilience gym's social media channels.

title: Jolly Josh welcomes Rochdale families with inclusive play, music and activity sessions
excerpt: The Castleton charity is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with weekly sessions and bookable activities.
content_html:
Rochdale charity Jolly Josh is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with a programme of inclusive activities and support.

Based at 2 Ensor Mill in Castleton, Rochdale, OL11 2NU, the centre welcomes children and young adults aged from birth to 19.

The charity says finding activities where a child is welcomed, understood and supported can be difficult, and wants more parents, carers, relatives and professionals to know what is available.

Its programme includes music and signing, themed play sessions, an after-school club, a youth group and activities that families can book directly with the centre.

Weekly sessions

Sing And Sign runs every Wednesday from 10.30am to 12.30pm, bringing together music, songs and signing to make communication fun.

Themed Stay And Play takes place every Tuesday and Saturday from 9.30am to 12.30pm. Sessions offer activities, friendship and a different theme each week.

Sensory Touch And Music runs every Thursday from 10am to noon, offering a relaxing sensory session.

The After School Club takes place every Wednesday from 4pm to 7pm, with inclusive activities and a light tea offered for every child.

The Youth Group meets every Thursday from 5pm to 8pm, giving young people a welcoming space to socialise, take part in activities and build friendships.

Activities available to book

Hydrotherapy sessions can be booked for families or with the centre’s Hydro Lead.

Private sound bath sessions are also available by contacting the centre, offering an opportunity to take time out of a busy schedule.

Rebound Therapy provides supported movement and sensory experiences using a trampoline, with sessions bookable through the centre.

How to get in touch

Parents, carers, family members and professionals supporting a child with complex medical needs are invited to contact Jolly Josh to learn more about its sessions.

Call 01706 399141, email sarah@jollyjosh.co.uk or visit https://jollyjosh.co.uk/

The centre asks anyone planning to visit to contact the team first so an appointment can be arranged.

Families can contact the centre to discuss which sessions suit their child and ask about booking, availability and charges.

The charity is also encouraging people to share its appeal with families who may not yet know about the support available.

title: Fireworks distributor with Rochdale premises fined £40,000 as fire service takes enforcement action
excerpt: GMFRS has announced prosecutions over fireworks storage and licensing breaches, including a £40,000 fine for Boom Fireworks, which operates premises in Rochdale.
content_html:
A national fireworks distributor operating premises in Rochdale has been fined £40,000 following an investigation by Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service.

GMFRS announced prosecutions involving Boom Fireworks Limited and two Greater Manchester retailers after inspectors uncovered fireworks storage and licensing offences.

According to the fire service, Boom Fireworks operates distribution premises in Cheetham Hill and Rochdale. Its director, Hashum Malik, pleaded guilty to storage offences at Manchester Magistrates’ Court on October 6.

Inspectors discovered higher-risk Hazard Type 3 fireworks being stored contrary to licensing requirements. The stock was detained and removed, and the company received a £40,000 fine, alongside a surcharge and prosecution costs.

Separate cases concerned The Vape Store on Hollins Road in Oldham and Wise Buys on Bury Road in Bolton.

The Oldham shopkeeper received a suspended prison sentence after fireworks were stored and sold despite an expired licence. The Bolton shopkeeper received rehabilitation requirements and a curfew after inspectors found fireworks stored and sold without a valid licence. Courts ordered the seized fireworks destroyed.

What this means for late-night fireworks

For Rochdale residents disturbed by repeated late-night fireworks, the announcement highlights enforcement against businesses supplying and storing explosive products.

However, the prosecutions concern storage and licensing offences. Their effect on fireworks nuisance in individual neighbourhoods has not been established.

The existing rules already prohibit setting off fireworks between 11pm and 7am on most nights. The exceptions are:

Bonfire Night: fireworks may be used until midnight.

New Year’s Eve, Diwali and Chinese New Year: the cut-off is 1am.

Midnight is therefore not the usual permitted finishing time: on ordinary nights, the restriction begins an hour earlier.

How to report persistent problems

Greater Manchester Police says irresponsible fireworks use can harm people and animals, damage property and create a serious fire risk.

Residents experiencing an ongoing problem can report fireworks-related antisocial behaviour through GMP: https://www.gmp.police.uk/advice/advice-and-information/asb/asb/antisocial-behaviour/fireworks/

The force also advises reporting retailers selling adult fireworks to under-18s to Trading Standards.

title: Volunteers urgently needed at Hollingworth Lake to help Rochdale Sea Cadets
excerpt: GTAS is appealing for volunteers and a donated skip to help clear an overgrown storage area for Rochdale Sea Cadets on Saturday 24 October, meeting at 10am.
content_html:
GTAS has issued an urgent appeal for volunteers to help clear an overgrown storage area for Rochdale Sea Cadets this Saturday, 24 October.

Anyone able to lend a hand is asked to meet at Hollingworth Lake council car park at 10am. Organisers say help would be welcome for any length of time, whether volunteers can spare an hour or stay for the day.

The group describes the clearance as a big task and is asking people to bring sturdy gardening gloves if they have them. Spades, shovels, loppers, other gardening tools and wheelbarrows would also be useful.

Local businesses are being asked to support the effort too. GTAS is looking for a skip or waste company willing to donate a skip for a few hours to help with the clearance.

The volunteer day is an opportunity for residents and businesses to give practical support to Rochdale Sea Cadets by helping bring the overgrown space back into use.

Anyone who can volunteer or help provide a skip should message GTAS directly through the group’s appeal post.

Could you spare an hour on Saturday, or do you know a business that could help? Share the appeal and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

Source: GTAS community appeal supplied to Rochdale Daily.

title: Safeguarding concerns, community costs and fireworks raised at Rochdale council meeting
excerpt: Farooq Ahmed raised concerns about safeguarding powers, while Jordan Tarrant-Short questioned venue costs, fireworks, foster care and Warwick Mill at full council.
content_html:
Concerns about the potential misuse of safeguarding powers, community venue charges and fireworks nuisance were raised during Rochdale’s full council meeting on Thursday, October 15.

Councillor Farooq Ahmed questioned how the council prevented staff from overstepping their authority, while Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short pressed cabinet members on issues including foster-carer recruitment, Warwick Mill and access to community facilities.

Councillors also rejected a proposal to rescind the council’s climate emergency commitments and backed motions concerning energy costs in new homes, protecting pubs and condemning attacks on places of worship.

Concern over safeguarding powers

Ahmed stressed that protecting vulnerable adults and children must come first, but questioned whether safeguarding procedures could sometimes harm the people they were intended to protect.

He said some officers could overstep their authority, leaving service users and families feeling victimised. He suggested the term safeguarding could be abused and asked how the council ensured staff did not misuse their powers.

Councillor Shah Wazir said safeguarding should protect and support people without causing avoidable distress. He outlined expectations around involving residents in decisions, providing advocacy where required and reviewing complaints and practice.

Responding to Ahmed’s supplementary question, Wazir invited him to provide specific incidents and promised they would be examined. The mayor also encouraged Ahmed to report his concerns.

The exchange raised concerns about potential misuse; it did not establish that misconduct had occurred in any particular case.

Community groups facing venue costs

Tarrant-Short said community organisations had contacted him about hire charges at facilities managed by Your Trust, warning that costs could make their activities financially unsustainable.

He told the meeting that a local dance group had reported being quoted £11,000 for one evening at Heywood Civic Centre. The booking requirements and an explanation of that reported quotation were not established during the exchange.

He asked whether protections, concessions or community pricing policies could prevent voluntary organisations being priced out.

Councillor Sue Smith said reduced rates or room-hire waivers could be available where appropriate, but charges also had to cover staffing, technical support and other operating costs.

She asked him to send details so officers could investigate. Smith said she had helped groups reduce charges, sometimes through changes to booking dates or times, but did not announce a new borough-wide pricing policy.

Fireworks and stronger safeguards

Tarrant-Short raised residents’ concerns about fireworks being used throughout the year, describing distress to families, vulnerable people and pets.

He asked what action the council and partner agencies were taking, then pressed for lobbying for stronger regulation and enforcement powers.

Councillor Tricia Ayrton acknowledged the concerns and said she had been speaking with partner agencies about a coordinated response.

She also said the council’s three community bonfire events would use reduced-noise fireworks, accompanied by music and lights. In response to his request for stronger national action, she encouraged councillors to raise concerns with their MPs.

Recruiting and retaining foster carers

Tarrant-Short asked how the council would increase the number of local foster carers and provide enough family placements for vulnerable children.

Councillor Rachel Massey outlined work through the Greater Manchester fostering recruitment hub, alongside specialist fostering, training and support. She identified particular needs for carers supporting teenagers, sibling groups and children with disabilities.

In a supplementary question, Tarrant-Short congratulated the children’s services team before asking what recruitment targets would replace retiring carers and increase overall capacity.

Massey said recruitment strategies and targets existed, while stressing the importance of finding the right home for each child. She did not give a numerical recruitment target in that exchange.

Warwick Mill and local investment

Tarrant-Short asked whether Warwick Mill would be acquired through compulsory purchase.

Council leader Neil Emmott said the council had negotiated an agreement with the owner and that cabinet had approved exercising an option to purchase following due diligence.

Asked why decisive intervention had taken so long, Emmott pointed to private ownership and previous unsuccessful redevelopment proposals, saying the council was now taking action.

Tarrant-Short also called for more community events in Rochdale South, including his Balderstone and Kirkholt ward.

Later, he asked whether a previously discussed highways review meeting had taken place. Scrutiny chair Councillor Tom Besford said no date had yet been arranged and promised to follow it up with him.

Pub protections and council votes

Tarrant-Short formally moved an amendment to the pub-protection motion, which councillors approved unanimously. The amended motion subsequently passed, supporting action over restrictive covenants that can prevent former pubs reopening.

Councillors unanimously supported motions on reducing energy costs in new homes and condemning attacks on places of worship.

A proposal to rescind the council’s climate emergency commitments was defeated.

title: Future of College Bank towers uncertain as renovation could take over a decade
excerpt: Housing chiefs have stated that renovating the College Bank tower blocks would displace residents for more than ten years, with no decision yet made on their future.
content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) has confirmed that no decision has been made regarding the future of the College Bank tower blocks, known locally as the Seven Sisters. However, housing officials have warned that any renovation of the iconic structures would require residents to vacate their homes for over a decade.

The Seven Sisters, which have stood for 61 years, are in urgent need of modernisation. Residents have been advocating for refurbishment rather than demolition, and recently appealed to Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig for support in their campaign. If the renovation proceeds, RBH has indicated that the buildings would not be habitable until the extensive work is completed.

The discussion around the future of College Bank began in 2017 when RBH expressed concerns about the buildings nearing the end of their lifespan. In response, tenants formed the Save the Seven Sisters campaign, hoping that a partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would lead to restoration. However, in September 2024, it was announced that this partnership would not continue, prompting further calls for assistance from local leaders.

In November 2024, a Mayoral Taskforce was established to explore options for the College Bank estate. Following safety surveys conducted in October 2025, RBH declared that the blocks were unsafe for occupancy, necessitating the relocation of residents. As the situation develops, the community awaits clarity on the next steps for the future of their homes.

title: Heywood and Middleton North MP visits Redwood School’s sixth form at Phoenix Centre
excerpt: Elsie Blundell, MP for Heywood and Middleton North, visited Redwood School’s sixth form at the Phoenix Centre to engage with students and staff about their educational initiatives.
content_html:
Elsie Blundell, the Member of Parliament for Heywood and Middleton North, visited the Redwood School’s sixth form campus located at the Phoenix Centre in Heywood on October 15. During her visit, she interacted with learners and staff to understand their efforts in supporting young people with special educational needs and disabilities.

Ms Blundell praised the teaching team for their role in helping students build essential skills and confidence for education, adult life, and future employment. She expressed her pride in having such a facility within her constituency, stating, "I’m so proud to have this facility - and the learners and parents - in my constituency."

The visit included discussions about various lessons, including the importance of recycling. Ms Blundell also enjoyed a meal of soup during her time at the school, which she described as "delicious." She thanked the staff and students for their warm welcome and the valuable lessons shared during her visit.

In her reflections on the day, Ms Blundell commended the young people, parents, teachers, and support staff for their hard work, writing, "Well done again to the young people, parents, teachers and support staff." This visit highlights the ongoing commitment to enhancing educational opportunities for students with special needs in the Heywood area.

title: Springhill Hospice to host free will information clinic in Heywood
excerpt: Springhill Hospice is offering a free information clinic for those looking to make or update their wills, with expert guidance available.
content_html:
Springhill Hospice will hold a free information clinic aimed at individuals considering making or updating their wills. The event will take place at the hospice, providing an opportunity for attendees to learn about the importance of having a will and to ask questions regarding the process.

David Copeland, a solicitor from Molesworths Solicitors based in Rochdale, will lead the session. Participants will receive a free will template and refreshments will be provided. The clinic is designed for anyone, whether they are making their first will or looking to amend an existing one. Charlotte Mascarenhas, supporter engagement fundraiser at Springhill Hospice, emphasised that the clinic aims to simplify the process of formalising a will, which can often feel daunting for many.

Molesworths Solicitors will waive their usual fees for this service, requesting only a donation to the hospice in return. Springhill Hospice offers care for adults with life-limiting conditions and support for their families across Heywood, Middleton, and Rochdale.

The clinic is open to the public, and there is no obligation to engage further services. Those interested in attending are encouraged to reach out to Springhill Hospice for more details.

title: Plans for 45-home development in Bamford face over 300 objections
excerpt: More than 300 objections have been lodged against plans to demolish a house in Bamford to make way for a new 45-home development, which is recommended for approval by Rochdale Council.
content_html:
Plans to demolish a house in Bamford to facilitate a new 45-home development have sparked significant local opposition, with over 300 objections submitted to Rochdale Council. The proposal, submitted by Wain Homes, involves the demolition of 58 Greenvale, known as Chadwick Farm Barn, to create access to the new housing development planned for land south of the property.

The proposed development includes 39 homes for market sale, comprising 14 three-bedroom, seven four-bedroom, and 18 five-bedroom houses, along with six homes designated for social housing. The council's planning committee is set to review the application on Thursday, following a deferral in August due to concerns regarding the absence of a comprehensive housing masterplan.

Local residents have raised multiple concerns regarding the development, including the premature release of the site, inadequacies in local infrastructure, highway capacity and road safety issues, as well as potential drainage and flooding problems. Additionally, objections highlight the impact on local ecology and landscape, and the effects on the amenity of existing residents.

The planning application comes in the wake of a revised National Planning Policy Framework aimed at boosting housing supply and economic growth. As the council prepares to make a decision, the significant number of objections may influence the outcome of the proposal.

A planning officer’s report states: “Policy S4 of the framework places a very clear presumption in favour of development within settlements, setting out only a single test to determine whether development should be granted planning permission; that they should be approved unless the benefits of doing so would be substantially outweighed by any adverse effects, when assessed against the national decision-making policies in the framework. “As with the previous assessment, it is recognised that the development would deliver significant benefits in the form of housing delivery with particular regard to the delivery of larger, higher-value units and much needed forms of affordable housing. “When assessed against the updated framework and NDMPs, the proposals do not exceed any thresholds which dictate that the development should otherwise be refused, and no harm has been identified that would amount to a material consideration that would substantially outweigh the benefits outlined in respect of housing delivery. “On the basis of the above, despite some harms persisting, it is clear that any harm does not amount to an adverse impact which would substantially outweigh any of the identified benefits of the proposals and therefore it is recommended that planning permission is granted.” Planning officers are recommending approval with conditions that a Section 106 legal agreement includes £150,000 (plus 5% administration fee) towards formal sports within the allocation; £112,727.78 (plus 5% administration fee) towards open space within the vicinity of the site; £22,905 towards highways improvements and public transport infrastructure upgrades within the locality; and securing six dwellings for affordable housing (3 social rent, 3 intermediate rent) in perpetuity. title: Volunteers and council team tackle overgrown areas at Middleton’s Jubilee Park
excerpt: The Friends of Jubilee Park and council staff have joined forces for the second phase of work to manage overgrown shrubs and care for the park’s rhododendrons.
content_html:
Work to open up overgrown shrub areas at Jubilee Park in Middleton has entered its second phase, with volunteers and council staff joining forces to improve the grounds.

The Friends of Jubilee Park have been working alongside Rochdale Borough Council’s Environmental Management team, carrying out maintenance that includes caring for the park’s collection of rhododendrons.

The group says the work will encourage healthy new growth over the next couple of seasons, improve views and sight lines, and help visitors feel safer.

Opening up densely planted areas is intended to create a brighter, more welcoming park while supporting the long-term health of its shrubs.

Visitors may notice that some sections look temporarily untidy as the work progresses. The Friends have asked for patience, explaining that the maintenance is intended to bring lasting improvements.

“These improvements will bring lasting benefits for visitors and help Jubilee Park continue to thrive,” the group said.

The Friends describe Jubilee Park as a Gold Medal-winning Green Flag park and thanked visitors for their understanding while volunteers and staff care for the grounds.

The latest work forms part of an ongoing effort to maintain the much-loved Middleton green space for everyone who uses it.

Source: Friends of Jubilee Park update supplied to Rochdale Daily.

title: Inclusive roundabout and zip line feature in plans for new Falinge Park play area
excerpt: Mayoress Iram Faisal has unveiled plans for new play equipment at Falinge Park, including a wheelchair-accessible roundabout, an inclusive seesaw and a double cableway zip line.
content_html:
Plans for a new play area at Falinge Park have been unveiled, with wheelchair-accessible equipment among the attractions proposed for children and families.

Mayoress Iram Faisal shared details of the project, describing it as a deeply personal undertaking in the park where she played as a child.

The proposed equipment includes a double cableway zip line with ramps; a toddler multi-play unit; toddler and junior swings; an inclusive seesaw; a Crazy Gander springer; and a wheelchair-accessible roundabout.

In her announcement, Mrs Faisal said inclusivity had been central to the vision, with the aim of helping more children enjoy the park together.

“Every child deserves the opportunity to play, explore and enjoy their childhood,” she said.

For the Mayoress, the plans also carry memories of her own upbringing.

“Having lived here and played in this very park myself, to now be in a position to play a part in transforming it for the next generation has been an incredibly emotional journey,” she said.

She thanked councillors Faisal Rana and Amber Nisa, Rochdale Borough Council and its Environmental Management Team, alongside everyone involved in bringing the project forward.

Mrs Faisal said the improvements were about investing in children and creating a space where families could make memories together.

“From playing in Falinge Park as a child to helping shape its future, this really is a full-circle moment,” she added.

The announcement refers to a hoped-for start towards the end of February, with work continuing into March, subject to final arrangements. It does not specify the year or confirm an opening date, so that timetable remains to be clarified.

Residents have been invited to share their views on the proposals.

Source: announcement by Mayoress Iram Faisal, supplied to Rochdale Daily and published on her public Facebook page: https://www.facebook.com/iram.faisal.5095/posts/1764829918060894/

title: Emmerdale star Lisa Riley meets shoppers as Peacocks opens in Rochdale
excerpt: Peacocks opened its new Rochdale Riverside store on Thursday, with Emmerdale star Lisa Riley joining the celebrations and posing for photographs with shoppers.
content_html:
Peacocks opened its new Rochdale Riverside store today, with Emmerdale star Lisa Riley joining the celebrations and posing for photographs with shoppers.

The actress helped officially launch the branch on Thursday 15 October, cutting the ribbon alongside store manager Claire Kershaw and the shop team. Riley also celebrated the visit on her own social media, confirming she had opened the new store.

Her appearance gave shoppers an opportunity to meet a familiar television face while exploring the retailer’s latest addition to Rochdale town centre.

Customers were keen to get through the doors, with the first shopper reportedly arriving at 6.30am. The first ten customers each received a £50 Peacocks gift card.

The new branch stocks clothing for women, men and children, bringing Peacocks back to the town following the closure of its former Wheatsheaf Shopping Centre shop in 2020.

For residents pleased to see the name return, today was a chance to browse the new shop, meet its staff and enjoy a little soap-star glamour alongside their shopping.

title: Rochdale’s Owen Webster ready for fresh start in BKFC featherweight clash
excerpt: Rochdale-born Owen Webster says he is ready to “take over the game” ahead of his featherweight bout against Dan Morel at Glasgow’s OVO Hydro on 7 November.
content_html:
Rochdale-born Owen Webster says he is ready to “take over the game” as he prepares to return to Bare Knuckle Fighting Championship in a new weight class.

Webster is scheduled to face Dan Morel in a featherweight bout at BKFC 96 at Glasgow’s OVO Hydro on Saturday 7 November. The contest is listed on the promotion’s official fight card.

Looking ahead to his return, Webster told supporters: “3 Weeks on Saturday and I make that walk again, totally different fighter whole new weight class but still ready to take over the game.”

His message signals confidence ahead of a change in division, with Webster promising supporters a different version of himself when he steps back into the ring.

For the Rochdale fighter, the Glasgow appearance offers an opportunity to make his mark at featherweight and begin a fresh chapter in his BKFC career.

Morel stands between him and that ambition. BKFC’s official profile lists Morel as a featherweight with a promotional record of no wins, losses or draws ahead of their meeting.

The event marks BKFC’s Scottish debut and is headlined by Conor Cooke defending the UK light heavyweight championship against Sean Weir. Webster’s contest is a featherweight matchup on the card; it is not listed as a title fight.

Supporters can find ticket and viewing information through the official BKFC event page: https://www.bkfc.com/events/bkfc-glasgow

With a new weight class and a determined message to his rivals, Webster will be looking to give his hometown something to celebrate on 7 November.

Sources: Owen Webster’s statement supplied to Rochdale Daily; BKFC’s official event listing and Dan Morel fighter profile; venue event details: https://www.sec.co.uk/events/detail/bare-knuckle-fighting-championship

title: Rochdale social worker Nneamaka Uti shortlisted for national award
excerpt: Nneamaka Uti, who works in Rochdale Council’s adult care service, is a finalist in the Social Worker of the Year Awards, with winners announced on 22 October.
content_html:
A social worker helping adults in Rochdale has been shortlisted for a national award recognising outstanding work in the profession.

Nneamaka Uti, who works in Rochdale Borough Council’s adult care service, is a finalist for Newly Qualified Adult Social Worker of the Year at the 2026 Social Worker of the Year Awards.

The winners will be announced on Thursday 22 October, at an awards reception in London. The organisers have confirmed that the afternoon event will run from 2pm to 5pm.

Councillor Shah Wazir, the council’s cabinet member for adult care, welcomed the recognition.

He said: “This is lovely and deserved recognition for Nneamaka and showcases Rochdale’s caring side at its very best. Following adult care’s good CQC rating this underlines the high-quality care and support the council is delivering for residents across the borough. Best of luck to Nneamaka at the awards ceremony.”

The council’s announcement links Nneamaka’s shortlisting with the adult care service’s good Care Quality Commission rating, highlighting the contribution of staff supporting residents across the borough.

Now marking their 20th anniversary, the Social Worker of the Year Awards recognise achievements across children’s and adult social work in England. This year, the organisers have named 64 finalists across 14 categories.

Nneamaka is one of six finalists in the newly qualified adult social worker category. The shortlist recognises practitioners at the beginning of their careers, giving Rochdale a representative among those in contention for national recognition.

Gold and silver award recipients will be announced at the October reception.

Rochdale Daily wishes Nneamaka the best of luck.

title: Rochdale Council Announces Free Bonfire Night Events for November 2026
excerpt: Rochdale Council will host three free firework displays across the borough in early November, featuring reduced noise fireworks for accessibility.
content_html:
Rochdale Council has confirmed a series of free firework displays to celebrate Bonfire Night in November 2026. The events will take place at three locations across the borough, including Middleton, Heywood, and Syke, with festivities beginning on Monday, November 2.

The first event will be held at Bowlee Community Park, located on Heywood Old Road in Middleton, starting at 6pm. The bonfire will be lit at 7pm, followed by fireworks at 7.30pm. The second display will occur on Tuesday, November 3, at Queen’s Park Road in Heywood, with the same timings. The final council-run event will take place on Wednesday, November 4, at Cronkeyshaw Common in Syke, also starting at 6pm.

In addition to the council events, Milnrow Cricket Club and Lobden Golf Club in Whitworth will host their own firework displays on Saturday, November 7. The Milnrow event will charge £7 for adults and £11.25 for families, while the Lobden Golf Club display will cost £5 for adults and £3 for children.

Rochdale Council has introduced reduced noise fireworks this year to make the displays more accessible for all attendees. The council advises visitors to walk or use public transport due to limited parking at the venues. Alcohol, fireworks, and sparklers are prohibited at all council-run events, and no toilet facilities will be available.

The council confirms the Rochdale display is on Wednesday 4 November 2026: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/481/rochdale-bonfire-and-fireworks-display

title: Rochdale AFC announces community tour of Bowlee

title: Rochdale's Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre set to drive advanced manufacturing
excerpt: The Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre at Kingsway Business Park marks a significant step for Rochdale's advanced manufacturing sector, with operations expected to commence in 2027.
content_html:
A major milestone has been reached with the completion of the base build of the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale. This 30,000 sq. ft facility is poised to become a key player in the UK's advanced materials and manufacturing sector, serving as a gateway for innovation and collaboration within the region.

The SMMC is the first significant development within the Atom Valley Innovation District (AVID), a 25-acre hub designed to foster advanced materials and manufacturing. The centre aims to bring together businesses, researchers, investors, and innovation partners, enhancing Greater Manchester's reputation as a leading centre for advanced manufacturing.

The completion of the building is the result of extensive collaboration among various stakeholders, including the Rochdale Development Agency (RDA), Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), and The University of Manchester. The next phase will involve transitioning from construction to specialist fit-out, with the centre expected to commence operations in 2027.

Since the establishment of the Centre of Expertise in Advanced Materials and Sustainability (CEAMS) in 2023, over 90 companies have engaged with the initiative, benefiting from access to a national network of expertise and support. This development is expected to significantly contribute to the growth of the advanced manufacturing sector in Rochdale and beyond.

title: Cozy Market in Milnrow shut down again for selling illicit tobacco
excerpt: Rochdale Trading Standards has secured a three-month closure order for Cozy Market on Dale Street, Milnrow, following repeated violations involving the sale of illegal tobacco products.
content_html:
Rochdale Trading Standards has successfully obtained a closure order for Cozy Market, located at 79 Dale Street, Milnrow, due to the persistent sale of illicit tobacco products. The order was granted by Manchester Magistrates' Court and will see the shop closed for three months, marking the second time it has faced such action in recent months.

The latest closure comes just weeks after the shop reopened following a previous three-month closure order issued in June. During that period, evidence of illegal tobacco sales was secured by trading standards officers, prompting the court's decision to shut the establishment again.

Rochdale Council announced the closure on its Facebook page, reiterating its commitment to tackling the sale of illegal goods in the area. The law currently allows for a three-month closure for shops found selling illicit products, but there are plans to extend this period to a year, which could further deter such activities.

The repeated closures of Cozy Market highlight ongoing issues with illegal tobacco sales in the region. Local residents and businesses may notice a reduction in illicit goods being sold, contributing to a safer shopping environment. The council's trading standards team continues to monitor the situation closely.

title: Nantwich Town Women defeat Rochdale Women 3-1 in WFA Cup
excerpt: Nantwich Town Women secured a place in the next round of the WFA Cup with a 3-1 victory over Rochdale AFC at the Crown Oil Arena on October 15.
content_html:
Nantwich Town Women advanced to the next round of the Women’s FA Cup following a 3-1 victory against Rochdale AFC at the Crown Oil Arena on October 15. The Dabbers dominated the match, creating numerous chances and controlling possession throughout.

Nantwich goalkeeper Connie was instrumental in the win, making several key saves to keep Rochdale at bay. The visitors took an early lead and maintained pressure on the home side, who struggled to find their rhythm.

Despite a spirited effort from Rochdale, they could only manage one goal in response to Nantwich's three. The defeat means Rochdale will now focus on their league fixtures as they look to bounce back from this cup exit.

The result highlights Nantwich's strong form in the competition and sets them up for a promising next round.

title: Halloween in Rochdale 2026: parties, pumpkins and spooky events across the borough
excerpt: 39 dated Halloween listings across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Milnrow, Littleborough, Norden and Wardle, with prices, times, age suitability, venues and booking links.
content_html:
From free family fun at the Town Hall and Empire to pool parties, pumpkin carving, costume competitions and late-night entertainment, here is our area-by-area guide to the spooky season.

Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October this year, but celebrations stretch across half-term and into Sunday 1 November. There are options for young children, teenagers, families and adults, including events advertised on local Facebook pages.

Find your area below. Listings run in date order within each area; events with several dates appear at their first date. Prices are the published figures available when checked. Where hours, age limits, admission charges or booking details remain unconfirmed, we say so.

This guide brings together the public 2026 announcements we could identify and check. Private groups, unadvertised parties and later announcements mean no guide can guarantee every event. Organisers can send additions to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

Find a plan quickly

Free family events: Town Hall, 26 October–1 November; Empire children’s party, 27 October.

Children’s parties: Rochdale RUFC, Milnrow and Littleborough cricket clubs, BizzyBees and Wardle Club. Check the age policies below.

Older children and teenagers: Younique Talent ages 7–17; Hollingworth Lake activity morning ages 8+; Monsters of Rock for accompanied ages 14+.

A party with a quiet room: Keeley B at Butterworth Hall on 30 October.

Adults: Norden workshops, Royal Toby bingo, Town Hall horror cinema and evening live music. Decadance is separately marked as an adults-only lifestyle venue.

title: East Middleton councillor questions parking charge warning after petrol station breakdown
excerpt: Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned about a parking charge while waiting for the RAC after her car broke down on Oldham Road.
content_html:
Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned she could face a parking charge while waiting for recovery after her car broke down at a petrol station on Oldham Road.

Councillor Jacques, who represents East Middleton on Rochdale Borough Council, described the incident in a public Facebook post, asking whether the business could charge her when her vehicle would not start.

Writing about the breakdown, she said:

“So I’ve broken down in Petrol station on Oldham Road.

“Yes another car that’s absolutely useless ”

She then described a conversation with a member of staff:

“Anyway the guy working there said, I am gunna get charged for parking when his boss comes, as hes saying I can’t stay waiting for RAC!!! I can’t move my car obviously as it won’t start ”

According to her account, the vehicle was beside the station’s tyre inflation equipment. She wrote:

“it’s at the tyre pumper upper so not really blocking anywhere.

“So is this legal does anyone know surly they can’t charge me for breaking down.”

Councillor Jacques said the RAC had given her an estimated arrival window between 9.30pm and 11.30pm.

The screenshot does not establish that a parking charge was subsequently issued, how much was allegedly proposed, or which parking conditions applied. The petrol station is not named in the post, and its account of the conversation is not available.

Could she actually be charged?

A private parking operator can issue a parking charge where it alleges that a driver breached the site’s parking conditions. That is a civil payment demand, rather than a criminal charge. Whether a demand would be enforceable in this particular case cannot be determined from the Facebook post alone. The signage, terms, circumstances of the breakdown and evidence of the recovery arrangements would matter.

However, a breakdown gives a motorist a strong reason to challenge a ticket issued while waiting for repairs or recovery. Citizens Advice specifically identifies being unable to move a broken-down vehicle as grounds for an appeal. That does not guarantee automatic cancellation, but it means a demand should not simply be assumed valid.

Independent parking appeals service POPLA also identifies evidence of a breakdown and a recovery callout as relevant when exceptional circumstances prevented a driver from complying with parking conditions.

Drivers in this situation should retain recovery booking messages, attendance records and photographs of the parking signs. The Competition and Markets Authority advises motorists to preserve evidence when a breakdown occurs and to challenge a disputed charge rather than ignore it.

For now, Councillor Jacques’s post establishes that she reported being warned about a possible charge. It does not establish that she received one or that any payment was legally owed.

Sources: Facebook post attributed to Councillor Georgina Jacques, screenshot supplied to Rochdale Daily; council profile: https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=7226; Citizens Advice: https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/law-and-courts/parking-tickets/when-to-appeal-a-parking-ticket/; POPLA: https://www.popla.co.uk/appeal-guide; CMA: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/parking-charges-cma-takes-action-to-drive-improvements-for-motorists

We hope Councillor Jacques is rescued promptly and back to her council duties in the morning—with her car feeling rather more cooperative.

title: Teenager jailed for fatal crash in Middleton after teaching himself to drive
excerpt: An 18-year-old has been sentenced to nearly seven years in prison after causing the death of a grandfather in Middleton while driving unlicensed and recklessly.
content_html:
A teenager has been sentenced to nearly seven years in prison for causing the death of a grandfather in Middleton while driving unlicensed and recklessly. Ruhul Islam, now 18, taught himself to drive by watching YouTube videos and was behind the wheel of his brother's Nissan Micra when he struck Terence James, 78, on Shawbury Street on September 29, 2024.

During a hearing at Manchester Crown Court on October 13, it was revealed that Islam had borrowed the car to make takeaway deliveries for a local business. Witnesses reported seeing him swerving through traffic, running red lights, and driving aggressively shortly before the crash. Mr James was crossing the road with his 10-year-old granddaughter when he was hit, suffering severe injuries that led to his death the following day after life support was withdrawn.

Judge Kate Cornell described the vehicle as a 'dangerous weapon' in the hands of someone unqualified to drive. She stated that Mr James would likely still be alive had Islam adhered to traffic laws. The court heard that Islam initially attempted to conceal his involvement in the crash, claiming his older brother was driving at the time.

The incident has raised concerns about road safety and the consequences of unlicensed driving. Following the sentencing, it is expected that discussions around stricter enforcement of driving regulations may take place, although no specific measures have been announced yet.
