evidence_sources.captured_text: Unlicensed teen taught himself to drive on YouTube, ran red lights, then killed beloved dad in Middleton horror crash - Manchester Evening News ‌ ‌ Skip to main content Manchester Evening News: Number one for news, opinion, sport & celebrity news Unlicensed teen taught himself to drive on YouTube, ran red lights, then killed beloved dad in Middleton horror crash Ruhul Islam was sentenced to six years and 11 months in prison following the death of Terence James View 4 Images Ruhul Islam had manipulated his brother into allowing him to use his car when Terence James was killed Add to preferred sources News Bethan Finighan Science and Innovation Writer 17:13, 14 Oct 2026 Updated 22:36, 14 Oct 2026 An unlicensed teenager who taught himself to drive by watching YouTube videos swerved through traffic and ran red lights before ploughing his older brother's Nissan Micra into a granddad who was crossing the road with his 10-year-old granddaughter. Terence James , 78, died after being struck by the vehicle on Shawbury Street, Middleton , on September 29, 2024. Yesterday (October 13), Manchester Crown Court heard how Ruhul Islam had borrowed the car to make takeaway deliveries at the time of the offence. The 16-year-old was seen overtaking and undertaking vehicles, running red lights and weaving between lanes in the moments before the crash. Click here to hear the latest from Manchester's courts in our newsletter ‌ Now 18, he has been jailed for nearly seven years. Passing sentence, Judge Kate Cornell said: "The vehicle essentially became a dangerous weapon in the hands of someone unable to use it." View 4 Images Terence Lewis James, 78, who died after being struck by a car in Middleton (Image: Family submit) She said Mr James would still be alive had Islam driven on the correct side of the road, telling him: "That momentary lapse of judgement caused the tragedy that everyone in this room has to deal with for the rest of their lives… None of them will ever be the same again." The court heard Islam initially tried to hide that he had been driving and instead said his older brother was behind the wheel. Investigators later found Islam and his 16-year-old friend had been making deliveries for Chilli Pot takeaway in Middleton - a business owned by family friends - at the time of the offence. ‌ Shortly after 7pm, Islam turned right from Grimshaw Lane into Shawbury Street in Middleton and struck Mr James as he crossed the road. He was on the right carriageway of the road when he was hit, having already crossed the left carriageway. Prosecuting, Philip Hall told the court Islam "cut the corner by a significant margin". Mr James suffered a serious head injury and was rushed to Salford Royal hospital, where his condition deteriorated and he never regained consciousness. His family made the heartbreaking decision to withdraw life support the following evening. A witness who was in a nearby car park on Shawbury Street heard the collision and saw Mr James lying in the road. She gave him first aid and said she was 'surprised the two Asian males were not helping', prosecutors told the court. ‌ Another witness, the court heard, saw two men get out of the Nissan Micra before running away from the car. He said one man later emerged from the nearby takeaway and repeatedly insisted his brother had been driving and was only travelling at 10mph. The court was shown dashcam footage from the vehicle in the hour before the collision, which showed the car swerving between lanes in wet weather , "aggressive" overtaking and undertaking and driving through red lights. View 4 Images Ruhul Islam has been jailed for nearly seven years (Image: Greater Manchester Police) Four minutes before striking Mr James, footage showed Islam overtaking a vehicle into the opposing lane, before undertaking into a cycle lane. Two minutes before the collision, the vehicle made another "completely unnecessary" manoeuvre by contravening a traffic island on the other side of the road, the court heard. ‌ Islam initially failed to come forward as the driver after the fatal collision, with his older brother putting himself forward instead. After an investigation established Islam had been behind the wheel, both brothers were arrested at their home in Chadderton on November 24, 2024. In part of a police interview read to the court, Islam admitted teaching himself to drive by watching videos on YouTube and manipulating his brother, who has autism, to get the keys to his car. In her final remarks, Judge Cornell said: "You now accept that you manipulated and misled him to get his keys. You told him not to tell anyone." ‌ Judge Cornell also questioned how the adults in Islam's life "turned a blind eye" to his driving without a license, given he was just 16 years old and working for a family friend's business. View 4 Images Terence James, 78 (Image: Family submit) Defending, Michael Avery said Islam had no previous convictions or cautions and had received 11 positive character references, including one from Oldham Council Labour councillor Mohon Ali. He said the offence has had a "genuine impact on him and those closest to him", leaving Islam "withdrawn" and "spending more time in his room". The defence also referred to the impact of the offence on his mental health. ‌ Judge Cornell later said she accepted Islam's remorse was genuine and that he had experienced flashbacks and nightmares following the collision. In emotional statements read to the court, Mr James' grandson Harry James described him as a "soft and kind" man who was the "glue of the family". Caroline, one of Mr James's four children, described her father as the "kindest person I knew", saying he "would do anything for anyone and wouldn't hurt a fly". Describing the aftermath of the collision, Caroline rushed to the scene after her daughter, Daisy, returned to the house "hysterical", shouting that "grandad had been knocked down". ‌ She wrote in her statement that she saw her father on the ground as a woman put him in the recovery position. She said a man came out of the takeaway and apologised for what had happened. When she asked if he had been driving, she said he told her: "No, my brother, he's got autism". Addressing Islam, she wrote: "I have never been able to get over how the person in the dock lied to me. You didn't call an ambulance. You could see how upset I was and still came over and lied to my face…But you still tried to blame your brother." Islam pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving after initially pleading not guilty. He also pleaded guilty to causing death while unlicensed and uninsured and perverting the course of justice. ‌ Sentencing, Judge Cornell said Mr James had been "suddenly and heartbreakingly taken from his family". She said Islam's driving had been "clearly unrestrained by the rules of the road that we all have to follow and of course you never properly learned". The judge said there had been an element of "excitement and showing off" in his driving, with footage showing him overtaking and undertaking vehicles, driving in hatched areas and cycle lanes, and twice going through red lights. "Had you driven on the correct side of the road you would not have caused his death and he would be alive today," Judge Cornell said, adding that it was "only good fortune" that Mr James's granddaughter was not also hit or injured. Ruhul Islam, of Little Cot Close, Chadderton, was sentenced to six years and 11 months. He has also been disqualified from driving for eight years after his release. title: A kitchen to be proud of this Christmas: meet Rochdale’s family-run SJF Granite & Quartz
excerpt: With 25 years of experience and a reported 124 five-star reviews, this local family business puts craftsmanship and personal service at the heart of its work.
content_html:
With 25 years of experience and a reported 124 five-star reviews, this local family business puts craftsmanship and personal service at the heart of its work.

Christmas has a way of bringing everyone into the kitchen. From preparing the festive dinner to catching up over a drink, it becomes the busiest—and often happiest—room in the house.

For anyone dreaming of giving that space a beautiful new finish, Rochdale’s SJF Granite & Quartz Ltd offers local expertise with a personal touch.

The family-owned business specialises in bespoke granite and quartz surfaces, serving homes and businesses across Rochdale, Greater Manchester and surrounding areas. Its website highlights 25 years of experience and a commitment to quality, precision and value for money.

Behind every attractive worktop is careful workmanship. SJF describes a process that takes projects from detailed measurement and templating through to cutting, polishing and installation—bringing the individual elements together into a finished surface tailored to the space.

The reported tally of 124 five-star reviews adds an encouraging chapter to this local family-business story. Choosing someone to work in your home is a matter of trust, and recommendations from previous customers can be an important part of that decision.

SJF places personal service at the centre of its approach, alongside carefully crafted stone and competitive pricing. It is a combination with clear appeal for homeowners who want their kitchen to feel special while keeping their budget in mind.

With Christmas approaching, now is a good time to start discussing the kitchen you have been imagining. Choosing a surface, exploring samples and arranging measurements early gives you time to consider the details and ask about installation availability before the festive season.

Whether your plans involve a complete kitchen renovation or replacing existing worktops, a beautifully chosen surface can become the detail that brings the room together.

SJF’s showroom at 47 Church Street, Littleborough, OL15 8AB offers the opportunity to explore samples. Its website also showcases completed projects and provides a free quotation enquiry form.

For inspiration, project enquiries and Christmas availability, visit https://sjfgraniteandquartz.co.uk/ or call 07311 133375.

Your dream kitchen could start with a conversation—and a family business right here in the Rochdale borough.

title: Pacific, Mangos and Empire until morning: remembering Rochdale’s strip
excerpt: Box-dye red hair, Jägerbombs and taxi queues that lasted hours—remembering Rochdale’s strip, its familiar faces and the venues keeping the town alive today.
content_html:
Box-dye red hair, Jägerbombs and taxi queues that lasted hours—Rochdale’s nightlife in the 2000s and early 2010s was a whole chapter of growing up. And places such as Empire are still helping the town make memories.

There was a time when a night out in Rochdale came with its own wardrobe, soundtrack and familiar faces.

Box-dye red hair. Chinos. Ed Hardy. The infamous Rihanna jumper. Outfits that, looking back, were remarkably close to business casual—worn with complete confidence for a night on the strip.

Rihanna and Eminem provided the soundtrack. Ordering a Jägerbomb felt like an event. Pacific, Mangos, Litten Tree and Empire were names woven into the weekend.

Between the bars, the dancefloors and the eventual search for a taxi, Rochdale felt wonderfully alive.

One former glass collector and barmaid remembers an incredible scene: heaving venues, wonderful bouncers and, in her experience, few fights. When the night finally ended, queues for taxis could mean waiting for hours into the early morning.

The people who made the strip

Ask someone about their old nights out and they might start with a club. Before long, they will be talking about a person.

A favourite barmaid. A reassuring face on the door. Someone you always bumped into, whether you had arranged to meet or not.

Among those familiar faces was the man affectionately known to revellers as “the gas man”, remembered sitting at the corner of the strip.

The former bar worker recalls people stopping to hug him and give him money. Despite the difficult circumstances she remembers him facing, he was a beloved presence, recognised and greeted with affection.

His circumstances were his own, and a nickname cannot tell his whole story. But the warmth with which he is remembered belongs in the history of those nights, alongside the music and the venues.

The strip’s character came from its people.

From the glass collector’s side of the dancefloor

Working through those nights meant seeing what customers sometimes missed.

Collecting glasses through a crowded room. Keeping the bar moving. Watching the door team manage another wave of arrivals while friends tried to find one another inside.

The former worker remembers the bouncers warmly. Her account offers a different perspective from the assumption that a busy nightlife scene must have been defined by trouble: what stays with her is how enjoyable it was, how few fights she encountered and how much life filled the town centre.

That is a personal recollection, rather than a claim that every night passed without incident. But it captures something worth preserving—the pleasure of working somewhere everyone wanted to be.

What happened to Pacific, Mangos and Litten Tree?

Pacific, at 8 South Parade, is now listed as closed. An archived council entry records a premises-licence suspension beginning in July 2013 for non-payment of an annual fee or levy. That record does not, by itself, establish the venue’s final trading date or the full reasons it closed.

Sources: https://licensing.rochdale.gov.uk/1/LicensingActPremises/Search/204/Detail?APP_ID=80078 and https://www.pubsgalore.co.uk/areas/rochdale-central/greater-manchester/

Mangos’ connection to a later venue remains visible in the paperwork. The council’s licensing record for Trinity retains conditions referring to the operating plan for Mango Bar at 3 King Street. The familiar address acquired another identity, although the sources reviewed do not establish the complete changeover story.

Source: https://licensing.rochdale.gov.uk/1/LicensingActPremises/Search/203/Detail?LIC_ID=6700

Litten Tree’s premises at 10 Fleece Street subsequently became Yates and are now Courtyard Rochdale. CAMRA records its reopening under the Courtyard name in March 2024. For former regulars, the sign has changed, but the address remains somewhere people can meet for a night out.

Source: https://camra.org.uk/pubs/courtyard-rochdale-rochdale-153361

Empire: the night that kept going

Then there was Empire.

In the former bar worker’s memories, it was the infamous destination where the night could stretch towards 6am. Leaving meant discovering that the early morning had arrived while everyone was still enjoying themselves.

Empire remains part of Rochdale’s nightlife today. Its presently advertised Friday and Saturday hours run until 4am, with live bands and performances central to its programme.

Source: https://empirerochdale.co.uk/

Its contribution extends beyond an ordinary weekend. The council’s 2026 Feel Good Festival programme included performances throughout the day at Empire, followed by a midnight DJ slot.

Source: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/rochdale-feel-good-festival/indoor-venues

That continuing activity deserves recognition. Venues such as Empire give people a reason to come into Rochdale, meet friends, hear music and spend an evening in their own town.

The old strip cannot be recreated exactly. Its customers have grown older; their wardrobes, responsibilities and stamina may have changed.

But the affection remains—for the songs, the people, the staff who looked after everyone and the nights nobody wanted to finish.

Rochdale’s next great night out needs people willing to make it happen. Empire and the town’s other active venues are keeping that possibility alive.

What do you remember about the strip? Pacific or Mangos? Litten Tree before Empire? The Rihanna jumper, the Jägerbombs or the seemingly endless taxi queue? Share your memories—and give a mention to the bar staff, glass collectors and door teams who made those nights special.

title: QTS Group hosts first safety Jamboree in Rochdale with over 350 attendees
excerpt: The QTS Group's inaugural safety Jamboree at Ashworth Valley Scout Camp in Rochdale attracted more than 350 participants, focusing on health, safety, and innovation in the rail industry.
content_html:
National rail contractor QTS Group hosted its first safety-focused Jamboree at Ashworth Valley Scout Camp in Rochdale, bringing together over 350 colleagues, supply chain partners, and activity hosts. The two-day event, which took place recently, was designed to promote health, safety, and innovation within the rail industry through interactive demonstrations and hands-on activities.

Attendees had the opportunity to engage with new technology and best practices from various suppliers and specialists. Jamie Marks, HSQE Manager at QTS Group, stated that the event aimed to foster knowledge sharing and strengthen relationships across the industry. He noted the positive feedback received and expressed enthusiasm for making next year's event even larger and more impactful.

Demonstrations included the Elios 3 drone for aerial mapping, virtual reality experiences simulating drone flights, and a confined space training simulator provided by Eurosafe. Participants also tested their skills on an excavator simulator from Flannery Plant Hire and witnessed mock aerial rescue demonstrations conducted by IRATA-trained teams.

The event not only highlighted the importance of safety in the rail sector but also provided a platform for networking and collaboration among industry professionals. QTS Group plans to build on this success for future events, aiming to further enhance safety practices in the rail industry.

title: Rochdale Council announces new regeneration projects for Middleton
excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has unveiled a series of regeneration projects aimed at revitalising Middleton, including the restoration of Hopwood Hall and the acquisition of Warwick Mill.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced a series of regeneration projects aimed at revitalising Middleton, following a recent High Court judgement in favour of the council regarding Hopwood Hall. This decision brings clarity to the future of the historic building, which has seen over £1.6 million invested since 2017 by the council and Historic England. The council is committed to funding essential repairs and considering options for its long-term future.

In addition to the Hopwood Hall project, the council has made significant strides in Middleton's regeneration ambitions. The acquisition of Middleton Old Grammar School is expected to lead to the announcement of a new tenant before the end of the year. Furthermore, the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be redeveloped for new housing, enhancing the local community.

Plans are also underway to transform the Middleton Scout Hut into a community venue that will provide activities and training opportunities for young people. The council has also confirmed that banking and post office services will return to Middleton town centre in the new year, a move that is anticipated to provide a boost to the local economy.

These initiatives are part of the council's broader commitment to invest in the borough, creating jobs and driving economic growth. The council has also approved a £15 million support package over the next three years to assist residents facing financial difficulties, ensuring that help is available for those in need.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Borough means business as council delivers more pioneering projects | Rochdale Borough Council Search Search View menu Accessibility and translate Borough means business as council delivers more pioneering projects Left to right: Rose Marley and Steve Coogan, with Rochdale Borough Council Leader, Councillor Neil Emmott announcing new Middleton regeneration projects. It's been a busy and productive few weeks across our borough, with positive news, exciting regeneration projects and innovative services making a real difference for residents in Heywood, Middleton, the Pennines, and Rochdale. I want to begin with Hopwood Hall. The council welcomed the recent High Court judgement, which found in our favour and brings much-needed clarity about the future of this important historic building. While it's disappointing that a lengthy and potentially costly legal process was necessary, we are now focused on moving forward. Since 2017, more than £1.6 million has been invested in Hopwood Hall by the council and Historic England, and we remain committed to funding essential repairs. Feasibility studies have been completed and options for its long-term future will be considered in due course. What is certain is that, once restored, Hopwood Hall will serve the wider Middleton community and continue to play an important role in the town's rich heritage. There has also been a significant boost for Middleton's regeneration ambitions, with a series of announcements demonstrating the momentum building behind the town's Mayoral Development Corporation. I'm delighted that Middleton Old Grammar School, recently acquired by the council, is expected to announce a new tenant before the end of the year. This follows news that the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be brought back into productive use, including the potential development of new homes. Meanwhile, plans are progressing to transform Middleton Scout Hut into a vibrant community venue offering activities and training opportunities for young people. There is more good news on the horizon, with banking and post office services set to return to Middleton town centre in the new year. This is something I have long championed and it will provide another welcome boost for the town centre. These projects form part of our wider commitment to invest in every part of the borough, creating jobs, driving economic growth and ensuring our communities thrive. At the recent 'Our Town, Our Future' event, I saw first-hand the passion local residents, businesses and community groups have for Middleton and their determination to shape its future. It is an exciting time for the town, and we are turning ambition into action. Supporting residents through the cost-of-living crisis also remains a key priority. I am proud of the help we have provided through our Helping Hand campaign, which has supported thousands of older and vulnerable residents since 2022. As global economic pressures continue to affect household finances, the council has recently approved a further package of support worth around £15 million over the next three years through the Government's Crisis and Resilience Fund. This will provide emergency financial assistance, help residents keep their homes warm, debt and welfare advice, housing support, access to food provision and free warm spaces. We are committed to standing alongside residents who need support. This package will help reduce inequalities, ease pressure on household budgets and ensure thousands of people receive practical assistance throughout the autumn and winter months. My message is simple: if you need help, please get in touch. Further information is available at www.rochdale.gov.uk/costofliving or by calling 01706 923 685 . Finally, I want to highlight two important events that reflect our borough's strong and enduring support for the Armed Forces community. On Friday 16 October, Rochdale Town Hall will host a Festival of Remembrance featuring military music, marching bands, speeches, reflections and the Act of Remembrance. It promises to be a special evening and everyone is welcome to attend. Then, on Sunday 8 November, communities across the borough will come together for Remembrance Sunday services. It is always a poignant occasion, giving us the opportunity to honour and remember those who made the ultimate sacrifice in service of our country. For details of remembrance events across the borough, visit www.rochdale.gov.uk/events . Lest we forget. title: Temporary closure of Hillcrest Road in Rochdale for roadworks from 26 October 2026
excerpt: Temporary closure of Hillcrest Road will take place from 26 October to 30 October 2026, affecting local traffic and access.

This roadworks initiative is part of ongoing efforts by the council to improve local infrastructure and ensure safer travel for residents and visitors. Local residents and commuters are advised to plan their journeys accordingly and allow for extra travel time during the roadworks. Further updates may be provided as the work progresses, and residents can check the council's website for additional information and maps of the affected areas.

title: Bamford and Norden’s 450-home allocation: housing choice versus pressure on green space
excerpt: The Bamford and Norden allocation envisages around 450 homes alongside improvements to sports and recreation facilities. Its development framework promotes family and affordable housing, but a framework does not establish a completed scheme, a housebuilder’s final layout or an affordable tenancy.
content_html:
The Bamford and Norden allocation envisages around 450 homes alongside improvements to sports and recreation facilities. Its development framework promotes family and affordable housing, but a framework does not establish a completed scheme, a housebuilder’s final layout or an affordable tenancy.

Earlier consultation records document objections about the potential loss of playing fields and pressure on existing sports facilities. Those are recorded community concerns, not evidence that the final scheme necessarily removes those facilities. The council says facilities will be retained and improved through development contributions.

The affordability question remains open. No verified price list, rental schedule or final affordable allocation has been established for a detailed scheme. Describing homes as “high quality” says nothing about whether local households can pay for them.

Infrastructure assessment should address traffic on the surrounding roads, safe walking routes, schools, healthcare and the cumulative effect of other development. The framework’s view that a site is deliverable is not a substitute for funded mitigation attached to a permission.

Until a delivery programme is established, the 450 homes remain potential contributions over time. They should not be represented as homes built this year. A named builder has not been verified, so no builder’s legal history can responsibly be attached to this allocation.

Location: Off Norden Road, Bamford / Norden

Planning stage: Strategic allocation; a current detailed housing permission was not established

Homes: Around 450 allocation homes

Let or for sale: Market and affordable housing envisaged; secured numbers, tenure and prices unknown

Land: Greenfield allocation involving former Green Belt land

Final planning agreement: Strategic allocation: no executed agreement for a current detailed development was established.

Exact rents / prices: No exact future rent, sale price, service charge or estate-charge schedule was established from the council/government material reviewed; no reliable scheme-specific current quotation was identified.

Affordable breakdown: Affordable housing is envisaged in the framework; a secured number and tenure breakdown are not established.

Funded school capacity: No scheme-specific funded additional school places, named capital project and opening date were established from the accessible official records reviewed.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: Framework access and recreation improvements are proposals. A contracted transport package, budget and delivery triggers are not established.

The outstanding details identified above are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. This article will be updated when the information becomes available.

Research checked 14 October 2026. Advertised prices are snapshots, not achieved sale prices.

title: College Bank’s future remains a housing question as residents move from the Seven Sisters
excerpt: College Bank’s future cannot yet be presented as a confirmed number of new homes. RBH’s July 2026 update records that 100 customers had accepted offers of another home and 64 had moved from the high-rise blocks at that point.
content_html:
College Bank’s future cannot yet be presented as a confirmed number of new homes. RBH’s July 2026 update records that 100 customers had accepted offers of another home and 64 had moved from the high-rise blocks at that point.

That is evidence of rehousing progress at a particular date, not evidence that replacement homes have been constructed or that a final demolition or refurbishment programme is approved. Earlier reporting described continuing uncertainty over the solution for the Seven Sisters.

RBH says resident safety drives the move and that it is supporting tenants through the process. A complete account should include the position of residents who wish to stay, the available alternatives and any future right-to-return arrangements.

This is separate from the neighbouring Lower Falinge proposal. Combining the two without checking their boundaries and replacement totals risks overstating supply and obscuring the number of existing affordable homes temporarily or permanently lost.

The January 2026 regulator judgement recognises RBH’s governance improvement but identifies material risks around investment and regeneration. It is not a project approval or an assessment of whether demolition is the best option.

Until the final scheme is evidenced, its contribution to the housing target is unknown. The practical questions are the cost, safety and quality of the eventual homes, and whether existing residents benefit from the change.

Planning stage: Rehousing underway; a verified final replacement or refurbishment scheme not established

Homes: No reliable new-home total established for a final future scheme

Let or for sale: Existing social housing; future tenure and costs require a confirmed scheme

Land: Existing urban residential land

Final planning agreement: No final replacement/refurbishment scheme, permission or executed development agreement was established from the reviewed records.

Exact rents / prices: Exact future rents, service charges and any guaranteed return-tenancy costs cannot be reported without a confirmed scheme and terms. They are not provided in the public update reviewed.

Affordable breakdown: Existing social housing; final retained, demolished and replacement totals, tenure and net gain are not established.

Funded school capacity: No scheme-specific funded capacity established. A final scheme and net household change are needed before assessing additional school demand.

Funded healthcare capacity: No final scheme-specific funded NHS capacity established; rehousing progress does not measure GP capacity.

title: Crimble Mill’s housing plans must balance heritage rescue with the cost to local families
excerpt: Crimble Mill’s detailed scheme is 214 homes: 33 apartments in the mill, 31 houses in the existing complex and 150 houses on neighbouring greenfield land. The broader 250-home allocation is not a second development or the approved detailed count.
content_html:
Crimble Mill’s detailed scheme is 214 homes: 33 apartments in the mill, 31 houses in the existing complex and 150 houses on neighbouring greenfield land. The broader 250-home allocation is not a second development or the approved detailed count.

Urban Green names Redwaters (Crimble) Ltd and Prescot Business Park Ltd as clients. Committee approval was reported in August 2023, but this review did not retrieve the executed legal agreement and formal notice completing the approval process.

Historic England identifies the principal mill complex as Grade II* listed. The restoration’s timing matters as much as the housing total: the recommended obligations tie public benefits to development phasing.

The affordability and infrastructure provisions below are recommendations, rather than verified final payments or funded service expansions. In particular, a mixed-purpose contribution must not be reported as wholly dedicated to affordable housing.

No verified site-specific adverse builder finding was established. The public accountability questions are whether the restoration obligations are enforceable, which benefits the eventual payment buys, and when those benefits reach residents.

Location: Crimble Lane, Heywood

Planning stage: Committee approval reported August 2023; signed deed and formal decision notice not verified

Homes: 214 detailed proposal: 33 mill apartments, 31 complex houses and 150 greenfield houses; distinct from 250 allocation

Let or for sale: No on-site affordable homes in committee viability assessment; final tenure/household prices unverified

Land: Mixed: existing mill/brownfield fabric and neighbouring greenfield land

Final planning agreement: Committee approval was reported in August 2023, subject to further procedural steps and agreement. The complete signed deed, formal notice and variations were not verified. The report recommends restoration/phasing obligations, a viability reappraisal if not started within 18 months, school land and a traffic regulation order.

Exact rents / prices: No exact final apartment/house asking prices, rental offer or household charges established from the reviewed records.

Affordable breakdown: The committee material supports no on-site affordable provision on viability grounds. title: Foundry Fields approval includes only five reported social-rent homes among 199 houses
excerpt: Taylor Wimpey’s Foundry Fields scheme received a reported six-to-four committee vote in favour, with one abstention, in January 2026. The 199-home proposal includes detached, semi-detached and terraced houses, with five reported social-rented properties.
content_html:
Taylor Wimpey’s Foundry Fields scheme received a reported six-to-four committee vote in favour, with one abstention, in January 2026. The 199-home proposal includes detached, semi-detached and terraced houses, with five reported social-rented properties.

Five homes amount to approximately 2.5% of the development. This is the reported on-site social-rent figure, not proof that the scheme has no other affordable obligation. The final Section 106 agreement is needed before a definitive statement about its whole affordable package.

The scheme also includes the first phase of a link road between Smithy Bridge Road and Albert Royds Street. A first section should not be described as the completed relief route. Residents need to know which traffic movements it enables before later sections are delivered.

Around half the site is reported as retained for public or open space. School and healthcare capacity still require evidence, and no verified rent schedule or live sales prices were established here.

Taylor Wimpey agreed CMA undertakings in 2021 to remove historic doubling ground-rent terms. Its separate 2025 information-sharing case ended through commitments without an infringement finding. Neither establishes the same issues at Foundry Fields.

The 199 homes belong to the Roch Valley scheme and must not be added to the council’s approximate 200-home allocation as a second development.

title: Littleborough’s former AkzoNobel site shows how brownfield housing can include discounted ownership
excerpt: The former AkzoNobel site was announced as a 126-home development through Countryside Partnerships and Together Housing. Its original tenure package included 14 shared-ownership homes and five First Homes, with open-market housing sold under the Bovis brand.
content_html:
The former AkzoNobel site was announced as a 126-home development through Countryside Partnerships and Together Housing. Its original tenure package included 14 shared-ownership homes and five First Homes, with open-market housing sold under the Bovis brand.

That package represents 19 affordable ownership homes, approximately 15.1% of the original total. It should not be described as 19 social-rented properties. Shared ownership also requires scrutiny of rent on the unowned share, service charges and the cost of purchasing additional shares.

The scheme occupies previously developed industrial land bought from Homes England. That distinguishes it from Bloor’s neighbouring farmland proposal. The two developments have separate totals and should be examined together for cumulative traffic, school and healthcare effects.

The announcement’s original delivery dates are now historical. A current assessment needs occupied homes, plots still to build and evidence that remediation conditions have been discharged. Prior industrial use justifies checking contamination evidence; it is not proof that completed homes are unsafe.

Vistry joined the CMA’s 2025 commitments settlement, closed without an infringement finding. This does not establish a breach at the local development.

Only remaining future completions belong in a forward housing forecast; houses already occupied cannot be added to the future pipeline again.

title: Hollingworth Road’s 309 homes: the school land promise needs a delivery explanation
excerpt: Bloor’s Hollingworth Road scheme has been reduced from 312 to 309 homes. Council reporting in June 2026 records site preparation. Developer material includes a central green corridor, sustainable drainage, walking and cycling links and land for a primary school.
content_html:
Bloor’s Hollingworth Road scheme has been reduced from 312 to 309 homes. Council reporting in June 2026 records site preparation. Developer material includes a central green corridor, sustainable drainage, walking and cycling links and land for a primary school.

Pre-decision reporting identifies 47 affordable homes, approximately 15.2% of the scheme. However, its quoted breakdown of 12 social-rent and 25 shared-ownership homes totals only 37. The missing ten must be reconciled against the final affordable schedule before a complete tenure split is published.

The school requires careful explanation. Reporting on the planning assessment says population projections did not then justify immediate delivery. Reserving school land is therefore different from promising that a school will open alongside the first houses. The decision must explain funding, demand thresholds and interim provision.

More than 1,000 objections were reported, including concerns about infrastructure. Bloor identifies transport assessments, drainage measures and replacement visitor parking, but the final conditions and funded works determine what will actually be delivered.

Bloor joined the CMA’s 2025 commitments settlement, closed without an infringement finding. This does not establish a breach at the local development.

Location: Hollingworth Road / north of Smithy Bridge, Littleborough

Planning stage: Council June 2026 update records site-preparation work

Homes: 309 revised scheme homes; earlier proposal was 312

Let or for sale: 47 affordable homes reported; social rent/shared ownership envisaged; complete split not reconciled

Land: Farmland / greenfield in an allocated former Green Belt location

Final planning agreement: The executed Section 106 deed, complete schedules, payment triggers and later variations were not verified. This is an evidence gap, not a claim that no agreement exists.

Exact rents / prices: Bloor’s live Hollingworth Rise page advertises plot 271, a three-bedroom Kane, at £334,995; plot 278, a four-bedroom Locke, at £449,995; and plot 267, a four-bedroom Watercroft, at £489,995. These are market asking prices. Exact social rents and shared-ownership shares, rents and charges are not provided in the reviewed records.

Affordable breakdown: 47 affordable homes reported, comprising 26 two-bedroom, 17 three-bedroom and four four-bedroom dwellings. Published tenure reporting gives 12 social-rent plus 25 shared-ownership homes, only 37: the other ten remain unreconciled. Do not silently change the figures.

Funded school capacity: Land for a potential 420-place primary school is identified. The planning assessment reported no immediate need; an allocated plot is not a funded building. A confirmed budget, operator, demand trigger and opening date were not established.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: Drainage, active travel and visitor-parking changes are proposed. Reported contributions exceeding £3 million are not a verified executed item-by-item transport budget, payment record or service-capacity increase.

title: Lower Falinge’s proposed 270 homes would replace 150: what residents gain and lose
excerpt: RBH’s next Lower Falinge phase is reported to envisage 270 affordable-rented homes across two parcels, replacing 150 homes proposed for demolition. If implemented on that basis, the eventual net addition is around 120 homes, not 270.
content_html:
RBH’s next Lower Falinge phase is reported to envisage 270 affordable-rented homes across two parcels, replacing 150 homes proposed for demolition. If implemented on that basis, the eventual net addition is around 120 homes, not 270.

The screening-stage proposal includes houses and apartments. It does not itself grant planning permission for the development. The current reference identified in reporting is OTH/2026/0781; final layouts and consent remain separate steps.

There is a directly relevant legal history. Claimants’ barristers reported that the council conceded a challenge to its earlier demolition prior approval over its EIA reasoning. The later October 2025 decision was reported as a refusal. This concerned the decision-making process and should not be recast as a finding of criminal misconduct by a builder.

RBH says regeneration is intended to create safe, warm family homes and has held resident consultation. Existing residents need clear rehousing commitments, costs and any opportunity to return. A temporary loss of homes before replacement is also important for borough-wide supply.

The regulator’s January 2026 judgement confirmed RBH’s G2 governance and V2 viability grades, recognising improvement while identifying risks. It did not assess consumer standards through that stability check.

The infrastructure test must consider the whole regeneration programme and its phases, including services during demolition and reconstruction, rather than treating every parcel as unrelated.

Planning stage: Regeneration proposals and EIA screening request; full scheme approval not established

Exact rents / prices: Exact new rents, service charges, temporary rehousing costs and return-tenancy terms are not provided in the reviewed council/government records or established from the public proposal.

title: Newhey Quarry’s 250-home allocation needs a clearer account of remediation and affordability
excerpt: Newhey Quarry is allocated for around 250 homes, with additional parking intended to support the nearby tram stop. The council’s land assessment classifies the site as brownfield, but the quarry’s history makes its treatment more complicated than simply describing it as unused land.
content_html:
Newhey Quarry is allocated for around 250 homes, with additional parking intended to support the nearby tram stop. The council’s land assessment classifies the site as brownfield, but the quarry’s history makes its treatment more complicated than simply describing it as unused land.

The allocation topic paper records mineral-working consent extending to 2042 and earlier objections that the proposed housing might not match local affordability needs. Those historic records do not establish current extraction activity or a final permission to build homes.

Restoration obligations, ground stability and the definition of previously developed land need to be checked in the actual application. The existence of a quarry alone is insufficient to settle all those issues.

No verified builder, price list or affordable tenure schedule was established in this review. Residents therefore cannot yet be told how many homes will be socially rented or accessible to first-time buyers.

Tram access is a benefit, but it does not establish capacity in schools, GP services, sewers or the local road network. A phased remediation and infrastructure programme will be needed to show that the allocation can become a safe neighbourhood.

The potential 250 homes contribute to the long-term pipeline. They should not be counted as completed housing, nor allocated to an unverified developer’s legal record.

Northstone’s Hareshill Road phase has moved beyond its earlier promotion for up to 190 homes. The council’s June 2026 development update records planning approval for 186. That distinction matters when residents compare publicity with the scheme that will actually be built.

Russell LDP says Northstone acquired Parcel A in October 2025 and submitted reserved matters in November. The phase forms part of South Heywood’s wider 1,000-home programme, with access associated with Queen Elizabeth II Way.

Public reporting describes a range of housing, open space and landscaping, but the verified material here does not establish affordable numbers, rents, sale prices or estate-management charges. Energy-efficiency claims should be accompanied by actual specifications and predicted running costs.

The larger masterplan promises community facilities. This phase’s contribution to them, and the point at which delivery is required, need to be visible in the approved documents. A contribution is useful only if it results in adequate capacity when residents need it.

Search results for “Northstone” include court cases involving Northstone (NI) and overseas businesses. They have not been attributed to this Peel-associated housebuilder: a similar name is insufficient to establish corporate identity or responsibility.

title: Parkfield House redevelopment brings 20 homes and an 80-bed care home to Middleton
excerpt: Muller Property Group says it has secured approval for 20 townhouses and an 80-bed care home at the former Parkfield House site off Manchester Old Road. The scheme reuses a three-acre brownfield site and involves demolition of the former Chubb Locks headquarters.
content_html:
Muller Property Group says it has secured approval for 20 townhouses and an 80-bed care home at the former Parkfield House site off Manchester Old Road. The scheme reuses a three-acre brownfield site and involves demolition of the former Chubb Locks headquarters.

The building is identified as a non-designated heritage asset. That creates a local heritage issue, but is not the same as demolishing a nationally listed building. The planning decision should explain how the loss was balanced against the public benefits.

The townhouses are described as two- to four-bedroom properties. A secured affordable allocation, sale/rental split and current price list have not been verified. Care accommodation is a different housing product, with fees and support arrangements that should be explained separately.

Eighty care-home beds cannot simply be added to twenty houses and advertised as one hundred ordinary family homes. Any contribution to the housing-delivery measure must use the applicable treatment of communal accommodation.

Access, staff and visitor travel, drainage and the relationship with nearby services are central infrastructure questions. No site-specific capacity assessment was verified here. The developer’s approval statement does not supply that evidence.

No verified adverse builder finding relating to this Middleton scheme was established. A planning dispute elsewhere, or a similarly named company, would not alone establish a problem with this development.

content_html:
A 28-home scheme off Queen’s Drive is reported as approved for Mosscare St Vincent Housing. It comprises 23 one-bedroom apartments and five four-bedroom terraced houses, all intended for social rent.

Social rent is governed by national rent policy; it should not be presented as a guaranteed percentage of every local private rent. A useful affordability assessment needs actual weekly rent, service charges, benefit eligibility and allocation arrangements.

The developer’s reported statement describes reuse of vacant brownfield land. The final plans need to establish accessible routes, parking, drainage and adequate capacity in local services. A small scheme can still have important effects on immediate neighbours.

There is documented landlord-history evidence worth treating fairly. In a separate 2026 Ombudsman determination, MSV was found responsible for maladministration over meal charges at another tenancy and ordered to refund £2,248.47; complaint handling was not found maladministrative. This is not a finding about the proposed Kirkholt homes.

The regulator’s 2026 review also records MSV’s C1 consumer and G1 governance grades, with V2 financial viability. Both the complaint finding and the wider regulatory context matter when assessing how future tenants will be treated.

If delivered as described, all 28 homes would contribute directly to rented affordable supply. The scheme’s exact costs and delivery date still need confirmation.

title: Where Rochdale’s next homes are planned—and who can afford them
excerpt: Our investigation examines 22 housing developments and regeneration plans across Rochdale borough: homes, prices, affordable tenure, land, school places, GP capacity and transport funding.
content_html:
The homes are planned, but will Rochdale get the housing its residents need?

Rochdale’s housing pipeline spans large farmland neighbourhoods, former industrial and retail sites, and replacement of existing social housing. The schemes are at different stages. Allocated land, a committee resolution, a formal permission, a construction start and an occupied home are not interchangeable.

How many homes is Rochdale expected to deliver?

The council’s 2026 housing topic paper uses the adopted Places for Everyone requirement of 10,472 net additional homes in 2022–2039: 568 annually in 2022–2025, 616 in 2025–2030 and 632 in 2030–2039. It records 650 net additions in 2024/25, above that year’s 568 requirement. This is historical performance, not proof of delivery in 2026/27.

Does the pipeline meet the government’s target?

The answer is qualified. The 2025 land assessment identifies sufficient potential supply against the adopted plan benchmark, but availability forecasts do not guarantee completions. National housing need is a separate calculation, using housing stock and affordability. The current national framework was issued in August 2026; older council estimates of the revised need are not interchangeable with a freshly calculated October figure. The latest annual delivery, current standard-method calculation and appropriate land-supply buffer still need confirmation before claiming the borough meets every present national requirement.

Why affordable numbers matter

The May 2026 housing-needs assessment estimates a net annual affordable shortfall of 768 homes under a ten-year backlog-clearance model. That is an assessment of need, not a separate statutory annual building quota, and includes the role of existing stock. Appendix C contains the detailed calculation; its headline gross figures are internally inconsistent, so this series uses the consistent net figure. The distinction is essential: meeting an overall housing target does not automatically meet the needs of households who cannot afford market homes.

What does affordable mean?

Social Rent is set under government rent policy. Other affordable rental products are regulated or discounted against local rents. Shared ownership and discounted sale help eligible purchasers but still involve household costs. For each scheme, actual rent, purchase price, unowned-share rent, service charges, estate fees and eligibility are the useful affordability evidence. A marketing incentive or a claim that a property is cheaper than Manchester does not establish planning-defined affordability.

Green Belt and brownfield are different questions

Green Belt is a planning designation; greenfield and brownfield describe the land and its development history. Agricultural fields can have been removed from the Green Belt while remaining greenfield. Brownfield can also lie within Green Belt. The quarry’s restoration history and the precise development boundary matter. “Brown belt” is not the equivalent planning category.

Do stronger Green Belt affordable rules apply to these schemes?

Current policy GB8 includes affordable provision, infrastructure and accessible green space. Its footnote 43 excludes development on land released through plans adopted before 12 December 2024, and permissions on Green Belt granted before that date. Places for Everyone was adopted in March 2024. It would therefore be misleading to say every listed former Green Belt allocation automatically requires 50% affordable housing. The actual site, date of release, permission and obligations must be checked.

Can infrastructure cope?

The August 2026 infrastructure document is a scoping assessment and coordination framework. It discusses assessment, funding and healthcare planning; it is not proof that every scheme already has funded school places, staffed GP capacity or completed drainage works. The defensible borough-wide conclusion is that support depends on scheme-specific evidence and delivery. This review does not establish that infrastructure either universally supports or universally fails the housing programme.

What evidence would settle the question?

For each scheme, residents need the current decision notice, executed Section 106 agreement, condition-discharge records, affordable tenure schedule and occupation triggers. Infrastructure evidence should cover cumulative traffic, schools including SEND, NHS primary care, drainage and sewer capacity, utilities, public transport, biodiversity and maintenance. A payment or reserved school plot is not the same as an operational service.

Why there is no grand total for these articles

Several entries overlap: Northstone is within South Heywood; Foundry Fields implements the Roch Valley allocation; Barratt’s Stakehill application is within a larger allocation. Lower Falinge replaces existing homes. Completed plots and care-home beds need different treatment. Adding every headline number would produce a misleading total.

Scope and evidence date

Research checked 14 October 2026. This series covers 22 identified major development and regeneration topics across Rochdale borough. It is not a census of every small planning application. Some developments already have occupied homes; asking prices are snapshots. The articles will be updated when outstanding information becomes available.

Secured money, receipts and spending are different

The council’s 2024/25 Infrastructure Funding Statement records £1,522,730 secured through new agreements and £1,629,989 received from agreements across the borough. Of education receipts that year, £619,533 was allocated and none yet spent; separately, £417,976 of older education contributions was spent. It would be false to say no education money was spent. The summary does not identify each development’s payments, school places or occupation triggers. It lists new agreements for Hawks View and Silver Hill, but cannot replace their full signed deeds.

The school forecast is an assessment, not an opening guarantee

The December 2025 primary-school report forecasts Heywood Reception surpluses of 34 in 2026/27, 61 in 2027/28, 29 in 2028/29 and five in 2029/30, with South Heywood housing and school timing to be monitored. For Middleton it forecasts 28 extra places needed in 2026/27, then surpluses of 40, 71 and nine. It discusses additional classes, including use of an existing Hollins classroom; this review does not establish a development-specific approved capital budget or new-school opening from those forecasts. Forecasts are dated planning estimates, not live admissions availability or proof of spare secondary/SEND capacity.

Pennines capacity and the healthcare warning

The school-plan appendix reports, at its assessment date, 75 spare Reception places in North Pennines and 25 in South Pennines, plus 303 spare Key Stage 1 places. Those area figures cannot be treated as guaranteed capacity beside every new estate. For Simister/Bowlee, the NHS’s September 2026 response identifies existing constraints at nearby practices and ongoing assessments, without publishing a funded expansion timetable. Infrastructure support therefore requires more than the existence of nearby schools, surgeries or stations.

Further information and updates

Some final planning agreements, exact rents and prices, affordable-housing breakdowns and infrastructure funding details are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. The relevant articles will be updated when the information becomes available.

title: Rochdale station’s 33 new flats are for private rent: what will tenants actually pay?
excerpt: The Corner Plot scheme near Rochdale station will provide 33 one- and two-bedroom apartments for private rent. Oak Construction Projects is carrying out the build, with Mansell Building Solutions appointed for the specialist frame package.
content_html:
The Corner Plot scheme near Rochdale station will provide 33 one- and two-bedroom apartments for private rent. Oak Construction Projects is carrying out the build, with Mansell Building Solutions appointed for the specialist frame package.

The distinction between private rent and affordable housing matters. A home can cost less than an equivalent Manchester apartment without satisfying the planning definition of affordable housing. No verified monthly rent or service-charge schedule has been established here.

Reporting describes a six-storey development with four commercial units below and net-zero ambitions. Contractor publicity states there are no allocated car-parking spaces and storage for 38 bicycles. The station location supports the transport case, but residents with disabilities, caring commitments or jobs poorly served by public transport need practical arrangements too.

Healthcare capacity and wider neighbourhood services cannot be inferred from railway proximity. The development’s access, tenancy terms, repair responsibilities and actual running costs remain important parts of its offer.

No verified site-specific adverse legal finding against the delivery contractors was established in the sources examined. The construction package should be assessed on its own evidence.

These 33 apartments are separate from Station Gardens’ 81 houses. Both contribute to supply when completed, but neither should be counted twice within broad station-regeneration totals.

title: Silver Hill Manor’s 57 market homes have no affordable provision following viability review
excerpt: Silver Hill Manor is a 57-dwelling scheme associated with David Wilson Homes and Rexel Property Group. It combines new housing with refurbishment of the Grade II-listed Silver Hill Farmhouse.
content_html:
Silver Hill Manor is a 57-dwelling scheme associated with David Wilson Homes and Rexel Property Group. It combines new housing with refurbishment of the Grade II-listed Silver Hill Farmhouse.

David Wilson’s live page advertises three- and four-bedroom homes from £299,995. This is a market asking price observed during research, not an affordable-housing valuation or evidence that all 57 homes cost that amount.

Restoration delivery remains unverified: approval does not mean the work is complete.

The recommended sports and biodiversity payments do not fund affordable homes, schools or NHS services.

Barratt Redrow joined the CMA’s 2025 commitments settlement, closed without an infringement finding. This does not establish a breach at the local development.

The scheme provides homes in an urban growth area, but remaining completions and restoration progress are the measures needed for an up-to-date assessment.

title: Simister and Bowlee’s cross-border plan includes 200 homes in Rochdale, not 1,550
excerpt: Simister and Bowlee’s housing programme crosses the borough boundary. Bury Council identifies 1,550 homes overall, of which 200 would be in Rochdale. Only the Rochdale share belongs in a total of this borough’s new housing.
content_html:
Simister and Bowlee’s housing programme crosses the borough boundary. Bury Council identifies 1,550 homes overall, of which 200 would be in Rochdale. Only the Rochdale share belongs in a total of this borough’s new housing.

The development framework includes a new primary school in the Bury portion, a local centre, a spine road, off-site highway works, active-travel routes, green infrastructure and drainage measures. These are requirements and ambitions for a future neighbourhood, rather than proof that all funding and construction contracts are in place.

Bury’s website cites its own affordable policy rate and an approximate affordable total for the Bury homes. That percentage should not be automatically applied to the Rochdale share. The eventual cross-boundary applications need clear tenure schedules and allocation arrangements.

Residents campaigning against the development raise traffic and drainage concerns. Those are attributed concerns, not verified findings that infrastructure cannot accommodate the plan. The published assessments and conditions must show how risks are addressed.

A specific Rochdale housebuilder and site-specific adverse legal finding have not been verified here. The employment-led Northern Gateway and residential Simister/Bowlee programme should also be kept distinct when explaining approvals.

The core accountability question is whether cross-border delivery provides the services residents actually use, with an enforceable timetable rather than separate promises by different authorities.

Location: Bowlee / Middleton and neighbouring Simister in Bury

Planning stage: Strategic allocation; June 2026 development framework guides later applications

Homes: 1,550 across both boroughs; 200 in Rochdale and 1,350 in Bury

Let or for sale: Affordable housing required; Rochdale-specific number and tenure not established

Land: Largely agricultural land in a former Green Belt allocation

Final planning agreement: Framework/allocation evidence: no executed cross-border development agreement for a detailed housing scheme established.

Exact rents / prices: No exact future rent, sale price, service charge or estate-charge schedule was established from the council/government material reviewed; no reliable scheme-specific current quotation was identified.

Affordable breakdown: 200 of the 1,550 homes are in Rochdale. The Bury affordable percentage must not be applied automatically to those 200; Rochdale-specific signed tenure counts are not established.

Funded school capacity: The framework includes a primary school in Bury. No construction budget, funding agreement, opening date or guaranteed Rochdale pupil access established in the reviewed framework.

Funded healthcare capacity: NHS Greater Manchester’s 1 September 2026 response says it is working with five of six nearby GP practices on estates solutions for existing capacity constraints. NHS Property Services is undertaking capacity assessments. The response provides no funded expansion budget, extra appointment/staffing figures or delivery date.

Funded transport capacity: A spine road, off-site works and active-travel routes are planned. No executed scheme-wide funding/delivery schedule or funded increase in bus capacity established.

title: South Heywood’s 1,000-home masterplan: when will the promised community facilities arrive?
excerpt: South Heywood combines an ambition for 1,000 homes with employment development and new community facilities. Russell LDP’s masterplan describes a primary school, local centre, sports pitches, play areas and a 2.2-kilometre link road. Its original hybrid permission dates from March 2020.
content_html:
South Heywood combines an ambition for 1,000 homes with employment development and new community facilities. Russell LDP’s masterplan describes a primary school, local centre, sports pitches, play areas and a 2.2-kilometre link road. Its original hybrid permission dates from March 2020.

The June 2026 council update records continuing Bellway and Anwyl construction and approval of Northstone’s next phase. The link road has opened, according to the project’s announcement. Older forecasts on the masterplan webpage should not be presented as current construction dates.

For residents, the issue is the sequence of delivery. Roads serving new housing and logistics operations do not by themselves establish that classrooms, bus services or medical appointments will be available when families move in. Those questions require the legal obligations, funding and occupation thresholds for each phase.

The published material reviewed does not establish the total number of secured affordable homes or their rents. Individual phases must therefore be assessed separately. Northstone’s homes are already within the 1,000-home masterplan and cannot be added again.

Bellway joined the CMA’s 2025 commitments settlement, closed without an infringement finding. This does not establish a breach at the local development.

Planning stage: Masterplan consent secured; housing delivered in phases

Homes: Up to 1,000 across the masterplan, including separate builder phases

Let or for sale: Market homes and any agreed affordable provision; masterplan-wide secured breakdown not established

excerpt: Station Gardens is an 81-home development on former Central Retail Park land, delivered through Rochdale Development Agency with Willmott Dixon as contractor. Its announced funding includes £15 million from the Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund, with completion expected in early 2028.
content_html:
Station Gardens is an 81-home development on former Central Retail Park land, delivered through Rochdale Development Agency with Willmott Dixon as contractor. Its announced funding includes £15 million from the Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund, with completion expected in early 2028.

Announcement material describes mixed tenures including social and affordable housing. The public Cabinet record of 23 June 2026 approves housing proposals in principle and delegates final approval; the detailed report is listed as exempt. The final tenure count and household costs therefore cannot be established from that public resolution.

The transport location is one of its principal strengths. Reusing urban land near the station can provide an alternative to greenfield expansion. That advantage still needs accessible routes, adequate services and clarity on any parking restrictions or charges.

Further apartments have appeared in reporting of the wider site. Their capacity and delivery status should be separated from the 81-house construction contract and the 33-apartment Corner Plot project nearby.

No verified site-specific adverse legal finding against the main contractor was established in this review. The funding and environmental claims should be measured against actual completions, energy performance and the costs residents pay.

For the borough’s target, the relevant measure is homes completed in each year. A funded scheme and an announced start provide stronger delivery evidence than an allocation alone, but are not completed housing.

title: Trub Farm’s 158 affordable homes could offer Castleton both rented homes and ownership

content_html:
Trub Farm is intended to deliver 158 affordable homes through MCI Developments and Legal & General Affordable Homes. Reported plans comprise 48 apartments and 110 houses, with homes for social rent and shared ownership.

The distinction between these tenures is crucial. Social rent is a rental product; shared ownership involves buying a share and meeting additional ongoing costs. Until the final schedule is available, the total should not be described as 158 social-rented homes.

The reporting contains a date discrepancy. An August 2025 article records a committee vote in favour, subject to a legal agreement, while an August 2026 deal article describes approval the previous month. The decision notice and agreement are needed to reconcile a committee resolution with formal permission.

The council committee report identifies open grassland within the urban boundary, adjoining Green Belt rather than simply being described as a Green Belt farm. Its consultation responses require mitigation, but do not establish an already funded expansion in school or GP capacity.

The regulator’s 2026 casework review records strong inspection grades for L&G Affordable Homes and oversight of third-party repairs providers. That provides relevant landlord context, rather than a promise about homes not yet occupied. If delivered, Trub Farm would directly expand affordable options, but exact rents, shares and service charges remain essential missing information.

The homes can expand choice for purchasers, but the advertised market offer cannot be counted as low-cost rented provision. For future supply, the 47-home scheme total must be reduced by homes already completed.

title: Rochdale pupils learn about online safety at Milnrow Crucial Crew
excerpt: Year 6 pupils from schools across the Rochdale area have taken part in police-led talks about social media safety and cyberbullying at Milnrow Cricket Club.
content_html:
Year 6 pupils from schools across the Rochdale area have taken part in police-led talks about social media safety and cyberbullying at Milnrow Cricket Club.

PC Hunt, collar number 10683, and PC Eyre, collar number 10811, attended the club last week as part of the annual Crucial Crew event, according to an update supplied by PCSO Tyler Davies.

The officers discussed how children can stay safe on social media and the risks they may encounter online. The sessions also explored cyberbullying, who it can affect and the impact it can have on those targeted.

Pupils were told about ways to help prevent cyberbullying and what to do if they witnessed it, giving them an opportunity to consider how their actions online can affect other people.

PCSO Davies reported that the children were fully engaged and participated throughout the sessions. The police update thanked the pupils for their involvement.

The visit brought pupils from schools around Rochdale together at the Milnrow venue for practical discussions about staying safe online.

What helps your family talk about online safety? Share your experiences in the comments, without naming children or identifying anyone involved in a bullying incident.

title: UK lawmaker threatens visa bans over Rochdale grooming gang ringleader
excerpt: A UK lawmaker has warned Pakistan of potential flight and visa bans if it does not accept the return of a ringleader from the Rochdale grooming gang.
content_html:
A UK lawmaker has threatened to impose flight and visa bans on Pakistan if the country does not accept the return of a ringleader from the Rochdale grooming gang. This warning highlights ongoing tensions regarding the handling of individuals involved in serious crimes abroad.

The comments come amid scrutiny of the UK government's approach to dealing with foreign nationals convicted of crimes in the UK. The ringleader, associated with a notorious grooming gang in Rochdale, has reportedly not been returned to Pakistan despite calls for his extradition.

This situation raises concerns about international relations and the management of criminal justice across borders. Local authorities in Rochdale have emphasised the need for effective measures to ensure accountability for those guilty of such crimes, regardless of nationality.

As developments unfold, it remains to be seen how the UK government will respond to Pakistan's stance on this matter.

title: Rochdale Borough Council publishes Budget Report for 2026/27 to 2028/29
excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has published its Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy, outlining financial plans and priorities for the next three years.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has released its Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy for the financial years 2026/27 to 2028/29. This document outlines the council's financial plans and priorities over the next three years.

The report details expected revenue and expenditure, aiming to ensure financial stability and effective service delivery within the borough. It is a crucial step in planning for the future amid ongoing economic challenges.

Local residents and stakeholders are encouraged to review the report, which is available on the council's official website. This transparency allows for community engagement and feedback on the proposed financial strategies.

The council will continue to assess its financial position and make adjustments as necessary, with further updates expected in future council meetings.

title: Hollingworth Lake to host Wave of Light walk remembering babies and children
excerpt: Families affected by baby or child loss are invited to meet at Hollingworth Lake's beach at 6.30pm on Thursday 15 October for a remembrance walk and 7pm candle-lighting, with bereavement charities and helplines available for support.
content_html:
Families and friends affected by the death of a baby or child are invited to gather at Hollingworth Lake in Littleborough on Thursday 15 October for a candlelit remembrance walk at the end of Baby Loss Awareness Week.

The community invitation asks people to meet at the beach at Hollingworth Lake at 6.30pm. The group plans to walk together around the lake, pausing approximately halfway round at a scenic point to light candles at 7pm as part of the worldwide Wave of Light.

The invitation is open to anyone who has experienced miscarriage, stillbirth, neonatal death, the death of a baby or the loss of a child at any age, as well as relatives, friends, neighbours and others wishing to show their support.

One of the people behind the gathering said that every year they light a candle for the babies they remember. This year, rather than marking the occasion alone, they hope people can come together for a shared moment of remembrance.

Baby Loss Awareness Week takes place each year from 9 to 15 October. At 7pm on 15 October, families around the world take part in the Wave of Light by lighting candles in memory of babies who have died. The Hollingworth Lake walk extends a welcome to those remembering children of all ages.

Those attending can bring a candle or battery-operated light, dress warmly for an October evening and carry a torch for the walk. Please keep a safe distance from the water, take care on paths after dark, never leave flames unattended, and take all candles and materials home rather than leaving them by or in the lake. Details of accessibility arrangements have not been provided in the original invitation.

EVENT DETAILS: Thursday 15 October 2026. Meet at 6.30pm at the beach at Hollingworth Lake, Littleborough, Rochdale, OL15 0AQ. Walk together and stop to light candles at 7pm. This article reports a community invitation; the charities listed below are support resources and are not described as organisers or sponsors of the event.

WHERE TO FIND HELP AFTER BABY OR CHILD LOSS

Grief can affect parents, partners, siblings, grandparents and friends, sometimes long after the death. No one has to attend the walk or speak about a loss to deserve support. The following verified organisations offer specialist information, listening services and, in some cases, counselling or local peer groups.

Sands — confidential help for anyone affected by pregnancy or baby loss, including bereaved relatives and friends. Free national helpline: 0808 164 3332; email: helpline@sands.org.uk; website: https://www.sands.org.uk/support-you/how-we-offer-support/helpline. Telephone hours are Monday to Friday 10am–3pm and Tuesday to Thursday 6pm–9pm, excluding bank holidays.

Child Bereavement UK — support for parents and carers when a baby or child dies, and for bereaved children and young people. Free helpline: 0800 02 888 40, Monday to Friday 8am–8pm, excluding bank holidays. Text or WhatsApp: 07418 341 800 (WhatsApp support for ages 13 and over). Website: https://www.childbereavementuk.org/.

Finding Rainbows — Greater Manchester peer support for families affected by early pregnancy loss or the death of a baby or child. Email: finding.rainbows@outlook.com; website: https://www.findingrainbows.org/.

Tommy's — specialist midwife-led advice on miscarriage, stillbirth, pregnancy after loss and pregnancy-related wellbeing. Free helpline: 0800 0147 800, Monday to Friday 9am–5pm. Email: midwife@tommys.org; website: https://www.tommys.org/. This is a non-urgent advice line.

The Lullaby Trust — specialist bereavement support after the sudden and unexpected death of a baby or young child. Free helpline: 0808 802 6868; website: https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/bereavement-support/find-support/. Phone support is available Monday to Friday 10am–2pm and weekends and public holidays 6pm–10pm.

Antenatal Results and Choices (ARC) — confidential, non-directive support after difficult antenatal test results, fetal diagnosis and pregnancy loss following a decision to end a pregnancy for medical reasons. Helpline: 020 7713 7486, Monday to Friday 10am–5.30pm. Text: 07908 683004; email: info@arc-uk.org; website: https://www.arc-uk.org/.

Miscarriage Association — information and support for anyone affected by miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy or molar pregnancy. Website: https://www.miscarriageassociation.org.uk/.

Petals — specialist counselling for people affected by pregnancy loss, stillbirth or neonatal death, subject to service eligibility and referral arrangements. Website: https://www.petalscharity.org/.

4Louis — bereavement support resources and memory boxes for families following the death of a baby or child. Website: https://www.4louis.co.uk/.

SUDC UK — information, bereavement support and research relating to sudden unexplained death in childhood. Contact: 07880 350942, Monday to Thursday 9am–5pm; email: info@sudc.org.uk; website: https://sudc.org.uk/.

Greater Manchester NHS PETALS Perinatal Trauma and Loss Service — assessment and therapeutic support for people experiencing trauma related to birth, pregnancy or baby loss. A healthcare professional can make a referral. Telephone: 0161 271 0188 (option 4), Monday to Friday 9am–5pm; website: https://www.gmmh.nhs.uk/petals.

If you need somebody to talk to now, Samaritans offers free emotional support day and night on 116 123 (https://www.samaritans.org/). For urgent mental health support in England, contact NHS 111 and select the mental health option. Call 999 if someone is in immediate danger.

Whatever their age, and however much time has passed, every child deserves to be remembered. Those planning to attend are encouraged to offer one another kindness and space during the gathering.
