title: 21 YEARS IN ENGLAND'S BOTTOM 100: Central Rochdale neighbourhood ranked 24th most deprived
excerpt: Government figures show a part of Central Rochdale ranked among England's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods in every index since 2004. Where did regeneration funding go — and what can actually be proved about residents' outcomes?
content_html:
ROCHDALE DAILY INVESTIGATION | 12 OCTOBER 2026

A small part of central Rochdale has been ranked among England's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods in every national assessment since 2004. In the latest official figures it is 24th out of 33,755 areas — and one of just three places in England to have remained in that bottom 100 across all six releases over 21 years.

The finding is not an opposition-party accusation or a campaign slogan. It appears in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government's English Indices of Deprivation 2025. Its code is E01005482, its statistical name Rochdale 010C, and it falls within the wider Central Rochdale and Mandale Park area.

Official sources: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, English Indices of Deprivation 2025 statistical release https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release; Government neighbourhood explorer https://deprivation.communities.gov.uk/about-your-neighbourhood/E01005482; Government research report https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-research-report

2004. 2007. 2010. 2015. 2019. 2025.

The government's researchers identified only three neighbourhoods that were among the 100 most deprived in every one of those six releases: Rochdale 010C, Middlesbrough 003F and Wirral 011C. The government's research report places the Rochdale neighbourhood within the middle-layer area known as Central Rochdale and Mandale Park.

This is not a description of the whole borough and not even of all Central Rochdale. A Lower-layer Super Output Area is a small census-based statistical area, typically home to around 1,500–1,600 people. The boundary of the LSOA matters when discussing local projects and spending. The Department for Education, for example, locates Whitehall Academy on Whitehall Street inside Rochdale 010C, confirming part of the geography, but the area cannot be equated simply with all of Mandale Park or Rochdale town centre.

Source: Department for Education establishment record for Whitehall Academy, LSOA Rochdale 010C https://get-information-schools.service.gov.uk/Establishments/Establishment/Details/151391

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRIVING THE RANKING?

The 2025 government neighbourhood explorer states that employment deprivation is among the area's most severe problems: fewer than 1% of English neighbourhoods rank as more employment deprived. Rochdale 010C also ranks as the most deprived neighbourhood within the borough for income, with higher-than-usual income deprivation affecting children and older people.

The national index measures seven different types of deprivation: income, employment, education, health, crime, barriers to housing and services, and the living environment. Income and employment carry the largest weights at 22.5% each. In other words, the central issue here is not whether a street looks attractive after regeneration; it is the resources and opportunities available to the people who live there.

Source: Government deprivation explorer https://deprivation.communities.gov.uk/about-your-neighbourhood/E01005482; methodology and domain weights https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release

DOES THIS PROVE THAT ROCHDALE HAS BECOME POORER?

No. The government explicitly warns that deprivation rankings describe RELATIVE circumstances. They do not, on their own, measure absolute changes in poverty, wages, health or household income. Boundaries and methods have changed; the 2025 index includes 55 indicators rather than 39 in 2019. Residents could have experienced improvements while their area's national relative position remained extremely poor.

But staying among the 100 most deprived on six separate occasions is nonetheless compelling evidence of persistent relative disadvantage. A serious assessment of whether interventions worked requires more than a new building or investment headline: longitudinal data on earnings, employment, child poverty, housing quality, health and skills, combined with a clear account of which projects actually reached Rochdale 010C.

Source: Government statistical release and guidance https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release

THE REGENERATION MONEY: BIG HEADLINES, BUT WHICH STREETS?

In a 2023 article, Labour council leader Neil Emmott described a £400 million Rochdale town-centre investment programme, including projects such as Riverside, Upperbanks and the restored Town Hall. The council also says the town secured £23.6 million from the government's Towns Fund, intended to support regeneration, skills and connectivity over a wider geographic area. These are genuine funding and development announcements.

Yet neither £400 million nor £23.6 million is an audited total spent exclusively within Rochdale 010C. The figures include a range of projects, investment types, funding sources and locations. Treating either sum as money spent on the approximately 1,600 residents of this one neighbourhood would be misleading.

Sources: Rochdale Council leader's 2023 regeneration statement https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-leaders-blog/investing-future-boroughs-regeneration-continues; council Towns Fund overview https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/business-licensing/towns-fund-money-help-us-improve-rochdale

One more closely relevant entry does appear in Rochdale's formal capital programme: the 2025/26 budget shows £450,000 in external grant funding scheduled for 'Towns Fund – New Homes Central Rochdale', described as land acquisition and remediation before homes are built by Rochdale Boroughwide Housing and private developers. An earlier programme showed £360,000 scheduled in 2023/24 for the similarly named project.

But these are BUDGET entries, not proof that either amount was actually spent. 'Central Rochdale' is also a broader project designation than LSOA Rochdale 010C. The missing link is a project-by-project ledger with actual expenditure, precise sites, housing completions and beneficiary outcomes.

Sources: Rochdale capital programme 2025/26 to 2029/30, 'Towns Fund – New Homes Central Rochdale' https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s112547/Append.%201%20for%20Capital%20Programme%20202526%20to%20202930.pdf; 2023/24 capital programme https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s94502/Append.%205%20for%20Budget%20Report%20202324.pdf

WHAT HAS BEEN DONE ABOUT POVERTY?

The council approved 'The Future We Deserve', its borough-wide 2024–2029 anti-poverty strategy, in March 2024. The authority described rising destitution and inequality as reasons for taking a long-term approach. From April 2026 it also began allocating around £5 million in government-backed Crisis and Resilience Fund support across the borough to assist residents facing emergencies, housing pressures and the cost of essentials.

Those programmes matter. They are also different in purpose from capital investment: emergency food and housing support can reduce immediate hardship, while regeneration may seek longer-term jobs and productivity. Neither a borough-wide budget nor a policy document establishes how many residents of Rochdale 010C received support or whether the area's underlying deprivation indicators improved.

Sources: March 2024 Cabinet decision approving anti-poverty strategy https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieIssueDetails.aspx?IId=55806&Opt=3; council Crisis and Resilience Fund https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/cost-living/crisis-resilience-fund

THE COUNCIL'S OWN RESPONSE TO SOCIAL MOBILITY CONCERNS

In a 2025 response to a social-mobility investigation, Rochdale Council acknowledged significant poverty, deprivation and inequality while pointing to improvements in town centres, education, employment opportunities and transport. It highlighted Rochdale Sixth Form College, Hopwood Hall College, the restored Town Hall and wider development proposals as assets that could improve opportunity.

These represent reasonable arguments for regeneration. But they are evidence of provision and investment, not by themselves proof that low-income residents in Rochdale 010C have entered stable, well-paid work or escaped hardship. This investigation has not obtained an LSOA-specific outcomes evaluation to test that claim.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council response to the Independent Commission on Social Mobility, 2025 https://socialmobility.independent-commission.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Rochdale-Borough-Council-response-to-Deep-dives_-a-local-perspective-on-social-mobility.docx.pdf

WHO SHOULD ANSWER?

Rochdale Council is Labour-controlled, led by Councillor Neil Emmott. The Central Rochdale ward is represented in October 2026 by Councillor Farooq Ahmed (Workers Party of Britain), Councillor Waqar Khan (Workers Party of Britain) and Councillor Sameena Zaheer (Labour and Co-operative), who also holds a Cabinet portfolio for Corporate, Governance and Transformation. The ward is a different boundary from the statistical neighbourhood and its current councillors did not all serve throughout the 21-year period.

These affiliations identify democratic responsibility and representation; the deprivation index does not establish misconduct, negligence or causation by any individual councillor or political party.

Sources: Council councillor directory https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=7214; https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=5385; Workers Party councillor directory https://www.workerspartygb.org/our_councillors; council control https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/councilmeetings

SEVEN QUESTIONS THAT DESERVE DOCUMENTED ANSWERS

1. Which completed, current and planned projects since 2004 have physically overlapped the boundary of LSOA E01005482?

2. For each project, how much public funding was approved, contracted and actually spent — separated from private investment and borough-wide allocations?

3. What proportion of jobs created or safeguarded under those programmes went to residents of this exact neighbourhood, and at what wages?

4. How have child income deprivation, employment deprivation, housing conditions and school attendance changed in absolute terms over time, not merely national rankings?

5. What specific measurable targets did the 2024–2029 Anti-Poverty Strategy set for the most deprived neighbourhoods, and how does Rochdale 010C perform against them?

6. What data will the council use to demonstrate that forthcoming developments are benefiting the people already living in this neighbourhood, rather than simply changing the appearance or population mix of nearby streets?

7. Will the council publish an independently auditable, geographically itemised account of 20 years of spending and outcomes, and allow residents to examine the results?

WHY IT MATTERS

Rochdale's new shops, college provision, housing developments, town-hall restoration and cultural attractions are visible and can produce genuine benefits. The government's latest deprivation statistics show a different and equally important side of local economic life: one neighbourhood has remained among England's most deprived in every national index for more than two decades.

That is not proof that £400 million was wasted. It is proof that the success of regeneration cannot be established from the value of construction projects alone. The ultimate test is whether residents gain lasting opportunities, better homes, improved health and higher disposable incomes.

Rochdale Daily is inviting the council, its regeneration agency, the ward councillors, relevant public bodies and local community organisations to provide a full geographic spending-and-outcomes breakdown and their responses to these findings. Corrections and right of reply can be sent to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

title: BREAKING INVESTIGATION: £50.3m owed by Rochdale Council companies as £19.5m Council Tax shortfall raises scrutiny
excerpt: Rochdale's draft accounts show £50.309m in Upperbanks company loan balances, £2.02m interest added and only £132,000 repaid in 2025/26. We examine the figures, the 2022 decisions and the councillors responsible for oversight.
content_html:
BREAKING INVESTIGATION | ROCHDALE DAILY

Rochdale Borough Council's own draft accounts reveal that three companies behind the Upperbanks development owed it £50.309 million in contractual loans at 31 March 2026. In the preceding financial year, just £132,000 was repaid while £2.020 million in interest accrued, increasing the total balance from £48.262 million.

The figures sit alongside reporting that the borough accumulated a £19.5 million Council Tax collection shortfall over the decade since 2016. These are very different forms of money: Council Tax is revenue for services, while Upperbanks loans finance long-term property assets and are not necessarily due for repayment now. Yet both invite scrutiny of how the authority manages public finances.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council, draft Statement of Accounts 2025/26, note on soft loans, printed page 81: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

Source: Roch Valley Radio, 'Council tax shortfall in Rochdale of almost £20m in 10 years', 12 June 2026: https://www.rochvalleyradio.com/news/local-news/council-tax-shortfall-in-rochdale-of-almost-20m-in-10-years/

WHAT IS UPPERBANKS AND HOW MUCH IS OWED?

The £60 million Upperbanks scheme, beside Rochdale Riverside, comprises 242 rental apartments and a 146-room Hampton by Hilton hotel. The development received more than £17 million from the Future High Streets Fund and over £3 million from Greater Manchester's Brownfield Development Fund. The hotel opened in September 2023.

The council's soft-loan table shows £33.662 million owed by Rochdale BTR Ltd on a property loan and £2.045 million in its working-capital borrowing. Rochdale Hotel Holdings Ltd had a £14.270 million property loan and Rochdale Hotel Ltd owed £332,000 in working capital. Together, these total £50.309 million.

The original loan arrangements included payment-holiday periods under which interest accrued and was added to the loans. The council also confirms the lending was provided below market rates in support of its service priorities. That means a growing balance is not, by itself, proof that any company has missed a scheduled payment. The critical missing information is the agreed repayment profile and actual cash returned to the council.

Source: Council draft accounts, printed page 81: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

Source: Rochdale Development Agency, Upperbanks project details: https://investinrochdale.co.uk/regeneration/projects/upperbanks

THE £2 MILLION INTEREST QUESTION

The 2025/26 loan schedule lists £2.020 million of accrued interest, £159,000 in new advances and £132,000 in repayments. Net contractual loans increased by £2.047 million. The £2.020 million interest recorded is more than fifteen times that year's total repayments.

However, the same page contains an apparent inconsistency. Its narrative says 'no new advances were made', while the adjoining table shows £159,000 of advances to Rochdale BTR Ltd's working-capital loan. The council should reconcile the entries and specify whether the amount was new cash, a transfer or an accounting classification.

The accounts also put the soft loans at a far lower carrying amount, £22.690 million, because below-market loans are discounted for accounting purposes. The council says the concessionary benefit to its subsidiaries is treated as an additional investment; the value of that investment is stated as £27.3 million. The difference is not a £27 million write-off: it reflects accounting treatment of long-term, below-market lending.

WHAT ABOUT THE RISK OF NON-REPAYMENT?

The council's draft accounts record a £472,000 expected-credit-loss allowance across relevant loans at 31 March 2026, of which £267,000 relates to the hotel companies, £189,000 to Rochdale BTR Ltd and £16,000 to other loans. The allowance increased by a net £37,000 during 2025/26. This is a forward-looking credit-risk provision, not proof that a borrower has defaulted or that £472,000 has been lost.

Source: Council draft accounts, printed page 89, impairment table: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

ARE THE APARTMENTS AND HOTEL DELIVERING?

According to Rochdale Development Agency's fourth-quarter delivery plan, 155 of the 242 Upperbanks apartments were occupied on 24 March 2026, with eight more reserved. That left 87 unoccupied at the reporting date, although occupancy had improved from earlier in the year. The agency also reported improving hotel occupancy, average room rates and yields. The public report did not supply a complete profit-and-loss or cash-flow analysis establishing whether the companies were meeting their initial business cases.

Source: Rochdale Development Agency 2025/26 Q4 delivery plan: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s122466/2025-26%20RDA%20Delivery%20Plan%20Q4%20FINAL.pdf

WHICH COUNCILLORS WERE INVOLVED — AND WHICH PARTIES?

The scheme's corporate and funding decisions were considered under a Labour-controlled Rochdale Council led by Councillor Neil Emmott (Labour). Councillor John Blundell (Labour and Co-operative) held the Economy and Regeneration portfolio in 2022, when the Upperbanks proposals came before Cabinet. Councillor Carol Wardle (Labour) held the Finance and Corporate portfolio then and continues as the Finance and Growth portfolio holder in 2026.

Councillor Daniel Meredith (Labour and Co-operative), now the Cabinet Member for Regeneration and Housing, has a different documented voting history: minutes of the 22 November 2022 Cabinet meeting state that he expressly requested his vote AGAINST the Upperbanks loan agreement be recorded. The minutes do not specify why he objected, and he must not be portrayed as having approved that agreement.

The 2022 decision approved a loan agreement while delegating the detail of its terms and structure to officers in consultation with relevant portfolio holders. The politicians' portfolios identify responsibility for decisions and oversight, but do not individually establish blame for any loss or wrongdoing.

Source: Rochdale Council, Cabinet meeting of 22 November 2022, item 19: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieIssueDetails.aspx?IId=51234&Opt=3&PlanId=0

Source: Rochdale Council, May 2026 Cabinet appointments: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieListDocuments.aspx?CId=156&MeetingId=7146

Source: Rochdale Council, Cabinet portfolio responsibilities: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/mgCommitteeDetails.aspx?ID=116

WHY ARE FINANCIAL FORECASTS RESTRICTED?

On 5 February 2026, Cabinet received an Upperbanks trading-company financial update including forecasts compared with the business cases approved in June 2022. The published decision notes that the council is the ultimate parent undertaking and 100% shareholder. But detailed financial enclosures were restricted from public view, leaving the public unable to independently compare the original profitability, occupancy and repayment forecasts with current performance.

Source: Cabinet decision, 5 February 2026: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieDecisionDetails.aspx?AIId=49322

THE COUNCIL TAX COMPARISON — WHAT IT DOES AND DOES NOT SHOW

Roch Valley Radio reported that the £19.5 million figure was a cumulative Council Tax collection shortfall since 2016, drawn from 2024/25 accounts, including about £1.3 million in 2024/25. It is not evidence of a fresh £19.5 million hole in the council's 2026/27 budget, and should not be directly subtracted from or compared with Upperbanks' contractual loan book as though both were immediately available cash.

The comparison does raise a narrower, evidence-based question: how transparent is the council about its own long-term financial commitments, loan repayments and commercial outcomes while it seeks to maximise Council Tax collection?

QUESTIONS REQUIRING ANSWERS

Rochdale Daily is seeking clarity on the contractual repayment timetable, how much loan interest has actually been received in cash, the latest independent valuations of Upperbanks' assets, the trading companies' current profitability, the £159,000 'new advances' discrepancy, and whether a non-confidential comparison with the original 2022 business cases will be released.

Councillor Meredith's recorded vote against the original loan agreement also merits an explanation of his reasons at the time, without assuming those reasons.

Upperbanks has delivered homes and a hotel to the town centre, while published occupancy data show improvement. Neither physical regeneration nor a large outstanding loan balance alone establishes that the scheme has succeeded or failed financially. The public accounts do, however, make a compelling case for clear reporting of when public funds are expected to be repaid and whether the original forecasts are being met.

This investigation is based on the council's DRAFT 2025/26 accounts, which remain subject to audit. Neither the loan balances nor the credit-loss allowances establish unlawful conduct, fraud or improper spending.

Right of reply: Rochdale Borough Council, the named councillors and the Upperbanks companies can send a response, correction or supporting financial evidence to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

title: No Metrolink service between Rochdale Town Centre and Freehold after collision at Westwood
excerpt: A road traffic collision at Westwood stopped Metrolink services between Rochdale Town Centre and Freehold on Monday 12 October, with tram tickets accepted on 17 bus routes.
content_html:
A road traffic collision at Westwood stopped Metrolink services between Rochdale Town Centre and Freehold on the evening of Monday 12 October 2026, according to a Bee Network travel alert.

The section affected covers every tram stop in the borough on the Oldham and Rochdale line, including Rochdale Town Centre, Rochdale Railway Station, Newbold, Kingsway Business Park, Milnrow and Newhey.

While the line was closed, tram tickets were accepted on the 17, 57, 59, 76, 76A, 81, 83, 84, 114, 149, 181, 182, 409, 411, 435, 436 and 471 bus services.

The alert did not give a time for services to resume. Current service information is on the Bee Network travel alerts page: https://tfgm.com/travel-updates/travel-alerts

corrections.note: This story originally said bus services were suspended. The Bee Network alert said there was no service between Rochdale Town Centre and Freehold, which is the Metrolink line, and that tram tickets were accepted on buses. The headline and report have been corrected, and two sentences not supported by the alert have been removed.

title: Rochdale Pioneers Museum hosts archive sessions on local folklore
excerpt: The Rochdale Pioneers Museum will hold free drop-in sessions this weekend, exploring traditional and supernatural tales from the borough's archives, led by Mitch Robinson.
content_html:
The Rochdale Pioneers Museum will host free archive creative drop-in sessions this weekend, focusing on traditional, unusual, and even supernatural tales from the borough's archives. The sessions, led by Mitch Robinson, aim to uncover hidden stories and records, ranging from folklore to magical narratives.

Scheduled for Saturday, October 15, the hour-long sessions will take place at 12.30pm and 2pm, with no prior booking required. Participants will have the opportunity to engage with old books, documents, and letters that often remain stored away, providing a unique insight into the area's history.

title: Why Rochdale says “cruckle”
excerpt: How a tiny local verb — to “cruckle” — links everyday speech in Rochdale to older northern dialects and why linguists care.
summary: How a tiny local verb — to “cruckle” — links everyday speech in Rochdale to older northern dialects and why linguists care.
body:
Anyone from Rochdale who’s ever limped away from a small mishap will recognise the line: “I cruckled my ankle.” For many locals, cruckle means the particular half‑twist or awkward roll of the foot you can often walk off — not a full sprain but a sudden wobble that makes you wince. This usage is recorded in contemporary perceptual descriptions of Greater Manchester speech and has been listed by residents when describing Rochdale’s spoken character. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

The word itself, however, has deeper roots. Historical dialect lexicography gives us a family of related forms — crookle, crukle, cruggle, krukel — all clustered around meanings such as to bend, make crooked, stoop, huddle or hobble. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect sources and Scottish dialect records preserve these cognates, showing the same phonetic shape and similar senses across northern English and Scots varieties. In the Dictionary of the Scots Language you can see cognate entries (kruggle / cruggle / cruckle) used with senses like “to crouch or huddle,” and nineteenth‑century dialect glosses list crookle with senses such as “to make crooked; to bend, twist.” ([dsl.ac.uk](https://dsl.ac.uk/entry/snd00075099))

How did a general sense of bending or crookedness come to mean the small ankle‑roll in Rochdale? Linguists point to ordinary, well‑attested word‑formation processes. A crook/crook‑ family root (suggesting bending, hooking or crookedness) plus a frequentative or diminutive ‑le ending can produce verbs that describe small, repeated, or imitative actions — crook → crookle. Comparable northern and Germanic dialect forms show similar semantic shifts from ‘bend’ or ‘stoop’ toward senses connected with awkward gait or limping; the broader comparative work on Germanic dialect vocabularies helps explain why these forms and meanings sit together. In short, cruckle is linguistically predictable as a local survival and narrowing of an older dialect verb family. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/be/The_semantic_development_of_words_for_%22walk%2C_run%22_in_the_Germanic_languages_%28IA_semanticdevelopm00ihririch%29.pdf))

Is cruckle uniquely Rochdalian? The short answer is: socially, yes — geographically, not absolutely. Perceptual dialect research carried out in Greater Manchester (2024) collected people’s mental maps and comments about local speech; among the keywords used to evoke Rochdale speech were “broad,” “flat,” “guinnel” and “cruckle,” showing that residents and neighbours associate the word particularly with Rochdale. That kind of folk‑linguistic visibility gives a strong local identity to a word even when related forms appear in older records elsewhere. At the same time, historical dictionaries and place‑name evidence show related spellings and senses across northern England and Scotland, so it would be misleading to claim the sound‑type has never occurred outside the area. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

Large projects that collect lived speech and crowd‑sourced dialect entries also help explain how such words persist. When the British Library and other public call‑outs gathered regional words, contributors highlighted locally specific items that researchers had not always recorded in older printed dialect dictionaries; popular reportage of that work singled out “cruckle” as an example of a recognisably local term with onomatopoeic appeal. These crowdsourced attestations, together with formal perceptual surveys, are why small words like cruckle keep turning up in contemporary studies of regional identity. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

What should readers take away? Cruckle matters because it shows how vocabulary anchors place: the word’s form and original sense are old and shared across northern dialects, but memory, everyday use and local attitude have made it feel distinctly Rochdale. Linguists view it as a useful data point — for historical contact between Lancashire and Yorkshire varieties, for small‑scale semantic narrowing, and for how people use language to say where they’re from. If you’ve got family pronunciations, old spellings or written examples from letters, keep them — local archives and dialect projects welcome material that helps trace exactly when and where words like cruckle shifted meaning and stuck to a place.

title: Rochdale Council to implement new planning decision rules from October 31
excerpt: Rochdale Council will shift more planning applications to officers under new rules effective from October 31, aiming to streamline decision-making and focus committees on larger proposals.
content_html:
Rochdale Council is set to implement revised planning decision procedures starting October 31, 2026. The new rules will see a significant shift in how planning applications are processed, with more decisions being made by planning officers rather than elected committees. This change follows the Government's guidance under the Town and Country Planning (Discharge of Local Planning Authority Functions) (England) Regulations 2026.

Under the new system, applications will be categorised into two schedules. Schedule One will include householder applications, minor commercial and residential proposals, lawful development certificates, and technical matters, all of which must be determined by planning officers. Schedule Two will encompass larger developments, listed building consents, advertisement consents, tree preservation orders, and legal agreements with developers, which can be referred to the planning committee but require agreement between a nominated councillor and a nominated officer.

The council's report indicates that the Government aims to provide greater clarity regarding the role of planning committees, allowing them to focus on significant proposals while routine decisions are handled by officers. Councillors will still be able to engage with planning matters, raise residents' concerns, and submit material planning reasons, but a councillor's request alone will not necessitate committee consideration. Additionally, the previous threshold for the number of objections required to trigger committee review will no longer apply.

The council has warned that decisions made by planning committees on applications that should be handled by officers could face legal challenges, potentially leading to judicial reviews. As the new rules come into effect, residents and stakeholders in Rochdale will need to be aware of these changes and their implications for local planning processes.

title: PW Greenhalgh Finishing Limited entering creditors' voluntary liquidation
excerpt: PW Greenhalgh Finishing Limited, based in Newhey, Rochdale, is undergoing a creditors' voluntary liquidation following a resolution passed by its directors.

The joint liquidators appointed to oversee the process are Jason Mark Elliott and Craig Johns, both from Cowgills Limited, whose office is situated at Fourth Floor, Unit 5B, The Parklands, Bolton, BL6 4SD. They will manage the liquidation process in accordance with the Insolvency Act 1986.

For those seeking further information regarding the liquidation, Aniser Hussain can be contacted at Cowgills Limited via telephone at 0161 827 1200 or by email at aniser.hussain@cowgills.co.uk.

This development may impact employees and creditors of PW Greenhalgh Finishing Limited, as the liquidation process will involve settling outstanding debts and determining the future of the company's assets.

title: Rochdale research centre moves closer to opening with £107m economic ambition
excerpt: The Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre at Kingsway Business Park has completed its main building, with specialist fit-out ahead of a planned 2027 opening.
content_html:
A new Rochdale facility designed to help turn scientific discoveries into commercial products has reached a construction milestone, ahead of a planned opening in 2027.

The main building of the Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre, at Kingsway Business Park, is now complete. Specialist equipment and facilities will be installed before it becomes operational.

The centre will support work on advanced materials with potential applications in medicine, electronics and construction, helping researchers test whether ideas developed in laboratories can become practical products.

Scientists and businesses will work with the University of Manchester and specialist innovation partners, connecting research expertise with the facilities needed to develop and manufacture new technologies.

The 30,000 sq ft centre is the first major physical development within the Atom Valley Innovation District, bringing researchers, manufacturers and investors together in Rochdale.

Independent analysis cited by the project’s partners forecasts £107 million in economic value over ten years, alongside opportunities to attract investment, businesses and skilled employment. That figure is a forecast, rather than income already generated.

Professor John Holden, the University of Manchester’s vice-president for civic engagement and innovation, said the next challenge was to connect the building with businesses, research and expertise to create lasting benefits.

For Rochdale, the centre represents a step towards establishing a larger advanced manufacturing sector—although its laboratories are still being prepared for the work ahead.

Sources: University of Manchester project announcement: https://www.manchester.ac.uk/about/news/major-milestone-for-atom-valley-as-sustainable-materials--manufacturing-centre-base-build-completes/ Additional reporting and project details: https://www.themanufacturer.com/articles/sustainable-materials-manufacturing-centre-takes-shape-in-rochdale/

corrections.note: The headline has been corrected to distinguish completion of the main building from the centre’s planned operational opening in 2027. The £107 million economic forecast covers ten years.

title: ‘Really nice’: an editor’s visit to the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road
excerpt: Rochdale Daily's editor visited the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with her little girl and found kind, efficient staff, a fully available menu and a welcome that earned a child's verdict: ‘really nice’.
content_html:
There are plenty of ways to judge a new coffee shop. You can look at the menu, the speed of the service or whether it manages to make a quick stop feel pleasant. But after visiting the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with my little girl, I found that the most telling review came from her.

“Really nice,” she said of the people working there. Two words, and a rather lovely assessment.

As the editor of Rochdale Daily, I spend a great deal of time looking at what opens, closes and changes across the borough. This time, rather than reporting on a launch, I wanted to experience the place as an ordinary customer — and a parent.

What stood out was the staff. They were kind, welcoming and efficient, handling our visit with the sort of ease that makes all the difference when you have a child alongside you. Good service does not need to be theatrical. Often, it is simply being treated warmly while everything runs as it should.

The full menu was available during our visit, too. There were no disappointing discoveries that something we wanted could not be ordered. It is a simple thing, but it matters: choice is only useful when the items are actually available.

The branch, which opened in August near Rochdale Infirmary and Dunelm, provides both indoor seating and a drive-through. For people visiting the hospital, passing along Whitworth Road or simply looking for a coffee stop, those options are convenient. But convenience alone is not what makes a customer want to return.

Children have an uncomplicated way of measuring an experience. They remember whether somebody was kind. They notice when they are made to feel welcome. My little girl did not care about the branding or the opening ceremony; she cared that the people were, in her words, “really nice”.

This was one family visit, not a claim that every visit will be identical. But the team deserve credit for getting the fundamentals right: kindness, efficiency and a menu we could actually order from.

Sometimes a new business makes its best first impression not through a grand announcement but through the people behind the counter. On our visit to Whitworth Road, Starbucks did exactly that.

title: Roadworks on Nowell Road, Thornham Lane, Wallhead Road and Halifax Road from 26 October
excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced roadworks on Nowell Road and Pershore Road in Middleton, set to begin on 26 October 2026, which will temporarily close sections of these roads.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has confirmed that roadworks will commence on Nowell Road and Pershore Road in Middleton on 26 October 2026. The works are part of ongoing infrastructure improvements aimed at enhancing road safety and traffic flow.

During the roadworks, sections of both Nowell Road and Pershore Road will be temporarily closed. Specific details regarding the closures have yet to be fully outlined, but motorists are advised to plan their journeys accordingly and seek alternative routes where possible.

In addition to the works on Nowell Road and Pershore Road, roadworks will also take place on Thornham Lane from 26 October 2026, with closures expected from 9am to 4pm each day until 30 October 2026. The closure will affect part of Thornham Lane starting at the junction with Rochdale Road, extending 23 metres in an easterly direction. Access for emergency vehicles will be maintained where safe to do so.

Furthermore, roadworks will begin on Wallhead Road from midnight on 27 October 2026 until 6am on 28 October 2026, with part of Wallhead Street closed from the junction with Wallhead Road extending 50 metres south. There will be no alternative route for vehicles during this time, but emergency vehicle access will be preserved. Lastly, Halifax Road in Hurstead will also undergo roadworks from midnight on 26 October 2026 until 11.59pm on 1 November 2026, which may affect local traffic patterns.

title: Rochdale Council to consider motion to reassess climate targets amid cost-of-living crisis
excerpt: Rochdale Council will discuss a motion from Cllr John Taylor on 13 October, urging a shift in focus from climate targets to addressing the cost-of-living crisis affecting residents.
content_html:
Rochdale Council is set to discuss a motion on 13 October that calls for a reassessment of its climate emergency targets in light of the ongoing cost-of-living crisis. The motion, proposed by Councillor John Taylor, suggests that the council prioritise immediate support for residents over its commitment to environmental goals.

In 2019, the council declared a climate emergency and pledged to achieve carbon neutrality by 2038. However, Cllr Taylor argues that the local impact on carbon reduction has been minimal and that resources could be better allocated to address pressing economic challenges faced by the community.

The council meeting will also include updates on initiatives such as the expansion of the electric vehicle charging network and the Rochdale Town Centre Heat Network, which aims to utilise heat from sewers to reduce energy costs for buildings. The council has received a £1 million grant from the Government to support this project and will soon begin seeking a development partner.

As the council considers this motion, residents may be interested in how these discussions could influence future policies and support measures during the current economic climate.

When Rochdale’s full council meets on Thursday, it will consider a motion from Cllr John Taylor calling on the authority to rescind its commitment to climate emergency targets. The meeting will also hear updates on expanding the electric vehicle charging network and the Rochdale Town Centre Heat Network which will see heat from sewers beneath Rochdale will be harnessed to cut energy costs and keep buildings warm. The council has received a £1 million commercialisation grant from Government and will begin a tender for a development partner to take the scheme forward and prepare it for construction. Cllr Taylor’s motion reads: “In 2019 this council, in line with national trends, passed a climate emergency motion and committed resources (financial and human) to achieving carbon neutrality. “A key element of the motion was the inclusion of a Carbon Neutral Target which pledged to make both the council’s operations and the wider borough carbon neutral by 2038. “Since 2019 it has become clear that our local impact on carbon reduction is negligible and it does not represent the most efficient use of our resources. READ MORE: Heat from sewers will keep Rochdale warm in future “Consequently, it is appropriate to review our commitment to carbon neutrality and dispense with our 2019 pledge. “This council recognises the direct impact that the cost-of-living crisis and housing emergency have on many residents, and they must be our strategic priorities alongside the efficient and effective delivery of our core services. Future efforts to achieve carbon neutrality must also be cost neutral. “A local repeal will not override national legislation; the UK remains legally bound by the Climate Change Act to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. “This is not a withdrawal from environmental action nor a belief that climate change is not a serious issue. It is a recognition of what is within our capacity to change and a renewed focus on deploying our controllable resources.” By rescinding the commitment to all climate emergency targets, Cllr Taylor hopes the council will direct resources to address the cost-of-living crisis and housing emergency. By reviewing all ongoing climate, carbon-neutrality activity, Cllr Taylor wants to stop any programmes that cannot demonstrate a “clear resident benefit, financial saving or statutory requirement”. title: Rochdale draw 1-1 with Tranmere to extend unbeaten run in League Two
excerpt: Rochdale's unbeaten streak in League Two continues as they secure a 1-1 draw against Tranmere at Prenton Park, with Dajaune Brown equalising after Tom Conlon's opening goal.
content_html:
Rochdale extended their unbeaten League Two run to five games with a 1-1 draw against Tranmere Rovers at Prenton Park on Saturday. The match saw Tom Conlon give the hosts an early lead before Dajaune Brown equalised in the second half, ensuring Dale maintained their impressive form.

Conlon opened the scoring for Tranmere in the 15th minute, capitalising on a defensive error by Rochdale. After the visitors allowed the ball to go out for a throw-in, Conlon struck from 25 yards, finding the top-left corner of the net. Tranmere could have increased their lead before half-time, but Tom Ince missed a close-range opportunity, and Dylan Jones fired wide under pressure from Aden Flint just before the break.

The second half saw Rochdale respond positively, with Brown scoring the equaliser in the 57th minute. He tapped home from close range after connecting with a cross from Charlie Tasker. Tranmere continued to press for a second goal, with Ince's long-range effort hitting the underside of the bar, but Rochdale held firm to secure a point.

This draw leaves Tranmere winless in their last five matches, having recorded six draws this season. Rochdale's next fixture will be crucial as they look to build on their current form and continue their push up the League Two table.

title: New Support Website Launched for Survivors of Child Sexual Abuse in Rochdale
excerpt: A new website, IAmReady.org, offers tailored support for survivors of child sexual abuse and exploitation, providing resources to help them navigate investigations and review closed cases.
content_html:
Survivors of child sexual abuse and exploitation in Rochdale can now access a new support service designed to help them understand their options regarding investigations into their allegations. The website, IAmReady.org, offers tailored advice and guidance based on individual needs, enabling victims to make informed decisions about their cases.

Developed in collaboration with survivors, the website provides trauma-informed information in an accessible format. Users can navigate the site at their own pace, with features that allow them to save their progress and exit quickly for privacy. The platform also includes options for users to request a review of their cases if they were previously closed by the Crown Prosecution Service or local police, particularly under the Victims’ Right to Review (VRR) or the Child Sexual Abuse Review Panel (CSARP).

This initiative is part of Operation Beaconport, which was established in November 2025 following Baroness Casey’s audit of group-based child sexual abuse and exploitation. The operation is currently reviewing hundreds of cases where no further action was taken between January 1, 2010, and March 31, 2025. Victims wishing to submit information about previously closed cases involving group-based offending will have their requests reviewed by specially trained officers from the operation.

The launch of IAmReady.org aims to empower survivors by providing them with the necessary tools and support to navigate their experiences and seek justice. For those affected, this resource may represent a significant step towards healing and accountability.

title: Milnrow woman's appeal against Animal ban rejected by Court
excerpt: A Milnrow woman has had her appeal against a five-year ban on keeping animals dismissed by a judge after her dog was put down due to untreated injuries.
content_html:
A woman from Milnrow has had her appeal against a five-year ban on keeping animals rejected by a judge at Manchester Crown Court. Anne Marie Wood was previously sentenced for causing unnecessary suffering to her dog, Tilly, who had to be euthanised after suffering from a broken leg that went untreated.

The RSPCA received a tip-off in December 2024 regarding Tilly's condition and found the Bichon Frise visibly lame and hesitant to put weight on her front leg. Wood initially refused to cooperate with inspectors but eventually allowed them into her home. She claimed the injury occurred when Tilly fell while being passed through a front window and stated that she could not afford the necessary veterinary treatment, which was estimated to be between £400 and £500.

Despite the RSPCA's offer to take Tilly to their Greater Manchester Animal Hospital for examination, Wood declined. When Tilly was eventually seen by a vet, it was determined that her injuries were severe and that treatment could not restore an acceptable quality of life. The decision was made to put her to sleep to prevent further suffering.

Wood, of St James Street, pleaded guilty at Tameside Magistrates Court on July 31 and received an 18-month prison sentence, suspended for one year, along with a ten-day Rehabilitation Activity Requirement and a nine-month drug rehabilitation programme. Following the rejection of her appeal on September 30, Wood remains banned from keeping animals for five years.

title: High Court rules against filmmaker in Hopwood Hall restoration dispute
excerpt: A recent High Court ruling has concluded a legal battle between American filmmaker Hopwood DePree and Rochdale Council over the future of Hopwood Hall in Middleton.
content_html:
A High Court ruling has determined that American filmmaker Hopwood DePree does not have the right to purchase Hopwood Hall, a Grade-II* listed building in Middleton, following a protracted legal dispute with Rochdale Council. The decision was announced during a hearing at the Manchester Civil Justice Centre last week, marking a significant setback for DePree, who has invested over £750,000 in efforts to restore the historic estate.

The saga began in 2017 when DePree signed an options agreement with the council to lead the redevelopment of Hopwood Hall. His vision included transforming the 1400s stately home into a wedding and hospitality venue, complete with a hotel retreat, gift shop, and guided tours. DePree engaged the local community in his restoration efforts, which included extensive work on the hall's gardens and interior.

Before DePree's involvement, Hopwood Hall had fallen into disrepair, with its last known use being as part of De La Salle College, which closed in 1989. The hall had previously served as a venue for various events, including an underground bar and nightclub during the 1960s and 70s, where notable acts such as Black Sabbath performed.

The ruling concludes a decade-long effort by DePree to revive the hall, which has been under the ownership of Rochdale Council since the college's closure. The future of Hopwood Hall now remains uncertain as the council considers its next steps regarding the estate.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The Hopwood Hall saga | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The Hopwood Hall saga George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 10, 2026 | 8:44 AM Print The Grade-II listed Hopwood Hall in Middleton When an American filmmaker and Rochdale council signed an agreement over a shared ambition to restore Hopwood Hall, no one could have fathomed the furious saga that unfolded. What started as a harmonious relationship between Hopwood DePree and the local authority ended up with them being on opposite sides of a court room. Mr DePree claims ancestral connections to the Grade-II* listed building in Middleton. His dream was to bring the 1400s stately home back to life. He even roped in the local community to help him do it, apparently spending more than £750,000 on the project. On what he described as a ‘sad day’ in Manchester Civil Justice Centre last week, his dream was crushed. The High Court ruled in favour of the council following a legal battle over whether Mr DePree had the right to buy the estate or not. The saga began in 2017 when Hopwood DePree signed an options agreement with town hall bosses to lead the redevelopment of the hall. Since then he has led a decade-long community effort to do exactly that. The Hollywood man’s vision saw the hall transformed into a wedding and hospitality venue, with a hotel ‘retreat’, gift shop and guided tours all part of the package. His team could regularly be seen working on the hall’s gardens and titivating the interior in the years since. Before Mr DePree came along, the hall had fallen into disrepair and irrelevance. Its last known use was as part of the De La Salle College, which shut down in 1989. During the 1960s and 70s it was said to be the setting for an underground bar and nightclub. It is believed that Ozzy Osbourne’s band Black Sabbath and other iconic performers played there. Since the closure of the college, the hall has been in the possession of Rochdale council. The American even created a Youtube series and wrote a book about his journey refurbishing what he affectionately called ‘Downton Shabby’. However, this journey came to an abrupt halt when the council ended the agreement in October 2024 and, without warning, barred Mr DePree and his group from the building. Part of the options agreement allowed the US actor and producer to purchase the historic asset from landowners Rochdale council for a ‘peppercorn fee’ – £1. Mr DePree attempted to exercise that option the day before the council ended the agreement, which was denied by town hall chiefs. Since then, a two-year-long war of words has raged between Mr DePree and Rochdale council. The American threatened legal action for months, but the council never budged. Mr DePree believed the local authority acted unlawfully by denying his ‘legally binding’ option to buy Hopwood Hall. At the time, the council said they ended the agreement because Mr DePree hadn’t made enough progress with the restoration effort. This expulsion from the estate came following a number of extensions to the agreement made by the council. The local authority even granted ‘change of use’ planning permission to Mr DePree for Hopwood Hall in 2022. Until the two sides decided to settle the matter in High Court, it was unclear just how important that planning permission was. Effectively, approved planning permission was the trigger to open up the option for Mr DePree to have the estate transferred to him. The High Court played host to Hopwood Hall Estate Ltd vs Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council this week. In the words of Mr DePree’s barrister, Ashley Bowes, the planning permission was ‘the star of the show’. The court heard details of the dispute over whether Mr DePree had authority to trigger the transfer of the property based on the approved plans. The council’s barrister Geraint Wheatley said the plans did not go far enough in demonstrating a serious commitment to reinstate and refurbish the 1400s building, as required by the options agreement. He described the ‘ruined’ hall as needing far more than some internal works to bring it back to a state of habitation. According to Mr Wheatley the conditions of the options agreement to trigger the purchase of the hall had four elements – authorisation to reinstate and refurbish the building; agreed standard of refurbishment between the parties (fit for habitation); English Heritage approval; and that the property would be reinstated and refurbished in whole, not in part. The defence barrister pointed out that getting permission for events and hospitality space for part of the ground floor doesn’t relate to the building ‘in whole’, as requested in the agreement clause. He also pointed out that the plans wouldn’t have seen the hall be fit for habitation or reinstated and refurbished. “Obtaining a mere ‘change of use’ permission doesn’t show a great deal of commitment,” Mr Wheatley told the court. “Plans of physical work show that commitment.” Mr Wheatley also tried to argue that English Heritage approval wasn’t given. But His Honour Judge Hodge KC believed the organisation’s support for the 2022 plans qualified as their approval. Buoyed by the judge agreeing with one point of the claimant, Dr Bowes said the 2022 application was internal work that would have created an events and hospitality space and enabled future work to be reinstated and refurbished. He said the claimant didn’t think anything more than a change of use application would be necessary to trigger the purchase as it wasn’t specified in the agreement. Dr Bowes said it was ‘wishful thinking’ on the council’s part that a community group would spend huge sums of money drawing up plans for physical works when they didn’t think it would be necessary. After delving into detailed planning legislation; the interpretation of wording in the agreement; and the cross-examinations of both Hopwood DePree and council boss for economy and place, Mark Robinson, the judge ruled in favour of the defendant – Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council. His Honour Judge Hodge KC described how the planning application did not cover the whole of the property or showcase the ability to reinstate and refurbish Hopwood Hall, as required in the options agreement. He added: “I am satisfied, for the reasons I have given, that the planning permission does not satisfy the requirements of the options agreement. I therefore refuse to grant the relief sought by the claimant.” A lengthy saga was ended by a two-day trial. Instead of getting Hopwood Hall for £1, Mr DePree was landed with a £114,000 bill to cover the council’s court costs. However, the American said the fight isn’t over and Hopwood Hall ‘must be saved’. He didn’t confirm whether his team would appeal the judgement, but they have until November 18 to do so. Speaking after the case, Mr DePree said: “Obviously I am incredibly disappointed. Not just me but the community of support around the world and the UK charitable groups as well. “I am already discussing with my legal team about the next steps. In the meantime I hope Rochdale council will be watching over Hopwood Hall because we will be keeping an eye on them. “We are not giving up. Hopwood Hall must be saved. In the two years we have been locked out the gardens have gone into wrack and ruin. I hope they will step up and save the hall. I still think the community group and I are the best people to take this forward. “I am getting messages from around the world with people offering money and support. It is a sad day but we will have to have a look at our options.” The town hall has committed to maintaining the building and have commissioned a feasibility study to look into possible future uses for the historic asset. A Rochdale council spokesperson said: “We are pleased with today’s judgement. It’s a shame that we had to endure a costly court battle to get to this point, as the time and money invested into this process could have been better spent on the hall itself. “We’re now focussed on moving forward. More than £1.6m has been spent on the hall by ourselves and Historic England since 2017 and we will continue to invest in vital repairs to this historic building. Feasibility studies have already been completed and options for Hopwood Hall’s long-term future will be considered in due course. “One thing we are clear on is, whatever the future holds for Hopwood Hall, this building, once restored and refurbished, will be used for the benefit of the wider community of Middleton who rightly cherish it as an important part of Middleton’s rich and varied heritage.” Add Roch Valley Radio as a preferred source on Google News to see more of our local reporting Add as a preferred source on Google Do you have a story for us? title: Rochdale-London train service proposal rejected by regulator
excerpt: The Office of Rail and Road has rejected plans for a direct train service between Rochdale and London Euston, disappointing local MP Paul Waugh and rail operator Lumo.
content_html:
The Office of Rail and Road (ORR) has rejected a proposal for a new train service between Rochdale and London Euston, which aimed to provide four daily return services. The decision has been met with disappointment from Rochdale's MP Paul Waugh and the rail operator Lumo, who had hoped to launch the service by 2028.

The ORR stated that the additional services could increase the risk of delays spreading across the network, ultimately worsening reliability for all passengers. In a statement, Paul Waugh expressed his deep disappointment, highlighting the significance of the service for residents in Rochdale and the surrounding borough. He remains committed to improving transport connections with both Manchester and London.

Waugh noted that there are still reasons for optimism regarding future rail developments. He mentioned the Bee Network, which is set to enhance local rail services across Greater Manchester starting in 2028, and the government's ongoing efforts with Northern Powerhouse Rail, which aims to improve capacity on the West Coast Main Line.

The ORR also rejected similar applications from Wrexham, Shropshire & Midlands Railway Company for Wrexham-London services and Avanti West Coast for additional Blackpool-Euston services. A spokesperson for Lumo indicated that they are considering their next steps following the ORR's decision.

evidence_sources.captured_text: ‘Disappointment’ following Rochdale-London train idea rejected | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch ‘Disappointment’ following Rochdale-London train idea rejected George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 10, 2026 | 8:42 AM Print Land around Rochdale Station The decision to axe the idea for trains between Rochdale and London Euston is ‘disappointing’, says the town’s MP and rail operator. The idea to have four daily return services between Rochdale and London was rejected by the Office of Rail and Road (ORR). The reason given was that the additional services could ‘increase the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers’. Low-cost rail operator Lumo had hoped to start services by 2028, with the plans receiving the backing of Rochdale MP Paul Waugh. Both shared their disappointment following the announcement. Paul Waugh, Rochdale’s MP, said: “I am deeply disappointed that the ORR has rejected the proposal for a direct Rochdale to London service. I know how much this would have meant to people in Rochdale and the wider borough, and I remain committed to improving our connections with both Manchester and London. “There are reasons to be hopeful about the future. The Bee Network is bringing greater integration of local rail services across Greater Manchester from 2028 onwards, while the government is progressing Northern Powerhouse Rail and has set out its long-term intention to develop a new rail connection between Birmingham and Manchester to increase capacity on the West Coast Main Line. “These are important investments in our rail network, and I will continue to make the case for Rochdale to benefit from better and more reliable transport links, including to London.” The ORR explained that gaps in the current timetable provide important space for trains to recover when disruption occurs, minimising delays to passengers. The government body concluded that adding more services into these windows would reduce that resilience and increase risk of disruption. The ORR also rejected the application of Wrexham, Shropshire & Midlands Railway Company (WSMR) for four return Wrexham-London Euston services and Avanti West Coast’s application for additional Blackpool-Euston services. A spokesperson for FirstGroup, who run the Lumo operation, said: “We are disappointed that the ORR has declined our revised application for new Lumo services between London and Rochdale, and we are considering our next steps. “Following the initial decision, we amended our plans in line with feedback and believe the revised proposal demonstrated strong economic benefits for passengers and communities. “It would have delivered the benefits of competition, including greater choice, lower fares and new opportunities for growth across Manchester and the north west. “Open access services have an important role to play in improving connectivity, attracting more people to rail and supporting economic development, all at no cost to the public purse. “We remain convinced that this route offered a compelling case for investment and long-term benefits for communities, businesses and the wider regional economy.” ORR has approved access for Avanti’s weekday 19:29 Chester to Euston service to carry passengers until December 2030. This train already runs as a fully crewed empty service so does not add another train to the route, but will benefit passengers, says the ORR. Stephanie Tobyn, ORR’s director of strategy, policy and reform, said: “New services, destinations and greater choice can bring real benefits for passengers and communities. But the West Coast Main Line is already under significant pressure, with performance reflecting limited resilience on a heavily used part of the rail network. “Our detailed analysis has shown that adding more trains to the current timetable would reduce the ability to recover when disruption occurs, increasing the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers.” Add Roch Valley Radio as a preferred source on Google News to see more of our local reporting Add as a preferred source on Google Do you have a story for us? title: Rochdale's music heritage celebrated in New album 'Kenion Street'
excerpt: The album 'Kenion Street', believed to be the first commercial release by a UK council, showcases local talent and pays tribute to the town's rich musical history.
content_html:
An album titled 'Kenion Street', believed to be the first commercial release by a UK council, has gained significant attention, reaching millions of listeners on national radio and streaming platforms. Launched as part of Rochdale's year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture, the album features local artists performing reimagined versions of classic tracks recorded at the town's iconic studios.

From 1977 to 2001, Rochdale was home to Suite Sixteen and Cargo Studios, located on Kenion Street, where renowned artists such as OMD, The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, Joy Division, and Inspiral Carpets recorded some of their most memorable work. The album includes 11 tracks, featuring PoolEra's rendition of OMD's 'Electricity', Medley's version of New Order's 'Dreams Never End', and Jennifer Read's interpretation of The Fall's 'Totally Wired'.

All tracks were recorded and produced at Voltalab Sound Studios, situated in the original Cargo/Suite Sixteen building, by studio founder Jamie Alsop. The album has received positive reviews and was featured on Radio 6 Music, where Middleton band K-Estate's cover of Gang of Four's 'Damaged Goods' was highlighted as Track of the Day. Other tracks have been played across various stations, including XS Manchester and Mersey Radio, reaching a combined audience of over 3.5 million.

The release of 'Kenion Street' not only showcases local talent but also serves as a reminder of Rochdale's significant contribution to the music industry. The album's success may inspire further initiatives to celebrate and promote the town's rich musical heritage.

Kenion Street has enjoyed glowing reviews after being launched as part of Rochdale’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture. It features local acts performing their version of a classic track originally recorded at iconic studios in the town. From 1977 to 2001, Rochdale was home to both Suite Sixteen and Cargo Studios in Kenion Street, where trailblazing artists including OMD, The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, Joy Division, Inspiral Carpets, Autechre, A Certain Ratio, The Fall and many others recorded some of their most memorable work. The 11 tracks on Kenion Street included PoolEra’s version of Electricity by OMD, Dreams Never End by New Order re-imagined by Medley, and Jennifer Read’s dramatic version of Totally Wired, by The Fall. Micah Stalgic and choir Local Vocals performing Atmosphere by Joy Division, that features on the album All the new tracks were recorded and produced at Voltalab Sound Studios, based in the original Cargo/Suite Sixteen building in Kenion Street, by studio founder Jamie Alsop. Radio 6 Music also featured the album, playing Middleton band’s K-Estate’s version of Gang of Four’s Damaged Goods. It was also made Track of the Day on Radio X with other tracks played across XS Manchester, Mersey Radio, Phoenix FM and many more, with a combined audience of over 3.5 million. One of the album’s singles by Desyfer and Emma Konnanov — a cover of the Happy Mondays anthem Twenty Four Hour Party People — reached 62 in the official UK singles chart and 58 in the official UK singles download chart. Vinyl copies of the album were distributed to record shops nationwide with listening parties held at Rough Trade stores in London, Liverpool, Bristol and Nottingham. READ MORE: Council urged to call time on rules which stop former pubs reopening The album achieved national media coverage with positive reviews from the likes of Louder Than War, The List and many more. Two bands who featured on the album, Metro and K-Estate, were awarded slots on the main stage at this summer’s Rochdale Feel Good Festival, supporting acts including Gabrielle, Ash and Starsailor. Cllr Sue Smith, cabinet member for culture and co-operation at Rochdale Council, said: “Everyone involved should be so proud of creating this lasting record of an important part of our borough’s story. “Thanks to the album, new audiences have discovered the town’s musical past as well as heard some of our talented acts of today. “Music is so important to Rochdale, not just as a part of its history with Gracie Fields in the 1930s and then in the seventies and early eighties but in more recent decades too with the likes of The Courteeners and Lisa Stansfield. PoolEra perform Electricity by OMD, another classic track originally recorded in Rochdale “In the town where these world-famous artists recorded iconic tracks, it’s great to see how ground-breaking music continues to thrive.” Karen Boardman, music development manager at Rochdale Development Agency, added: “I’m incredibly proud of this record which we believe is the UK’s first commercially released album by a council, celebrating a town’s musical history, whilst championing its new talent. It’s been a privilege to work alongside our partners and all the artists to bring the album to life and I’m very excited for the next phase of this project, there’s lots more to come.” The story continued this summer, with synth-pop icons Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark (OMD) returning to where it began when they performed a sold-out show in front of over 5,000 fans at Rochdale Town Hall Square in August, alongside post-punk legends Peter Hook & The Light, and Manchester’s post-punk/funk band – A Certain Ratio. You can listen to the album ‘Kenion Street’ on streaming platforms or pick up a vinyl copy at Rocks Off in Drake Street in Rochdale and other good record stores. Rochdale Music Stories is a collaboration between Voltalab Sound Studios, Stockport Music Story and Rochdale Development Agency, funded by Arts Council England, Rochdale Borough Council and Rochdale Development Agency.
