title: Bev Craig and Rochdale: will Greater Manchester's new mayor deliver beyond the city centre?
excerpt: A detailed examination of Mayor Bev Craig's council voting record, Rochdale's deprivation and earnings, affordable housing and transport pledges, and the financial risks behind Greater Manchester's investment plans.
content_html:
Bev Craig's election as Mayor of Greater Manchester leaves Rochdale with a familiar question: will economic growth across the city-region translate into better-paid jobs, more affordable housing and better transport in the boroughs outside Manchester city centre?

Craig, the former leader of Manchester City Council, succeeded Andy Burnham after the mayoral election on 30 July 2026. The official result gave her 309,525 first- and second-preference votes, on a Greater Manchester turnout of 25.14%. Turnout in Rochdale was 22.95%, and she received 15,927 first-preference votes in the borough.

Her pledges on housing, public transport, high streets and industrial regeneration speak directly to several of Rochdale's needs. But the financial distinction between projects approved, investment proposed and outcomes delivered is essential.

ROCHDALE'S DEEPER ECONOMIC PROBLEMS

ONS figures reported through Nomis put Rochdale's employment rate for people aged 16–64 at 67.1% in the year to March 2026, against 75.5% across Great Britain. Estimated unemployment was 7.2%, compared with 4.5% nationally, although the ONS warns that survey-based local unemployment estimates have small-sample limitations.

In 2025, around 33.5% of working-age residents held a qualification at RQF Level 4 or above, compared with 48.6% nationally. The median weekly earnings of full-time employees resident in Rochdale were £689.50, against £766.60 in Great Britain.

According to the Government's 2025 English Indices of Deprivation, Rochdale's employment deprivation measure was 20.3%, among the highest of England's local authorities. A neighbourhood identified as Rochdale 010C has repeatedly appeared among the country's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods.

These figures expose the limitations of equating economic development with prosperity for existing residents. A growing regional economy does not automatically lift household earnings if local people cannot reach the jobs, lack relevant qualifications or cannot afford the homes built nearby.

A MAYOR WITHOUT A PARLIAMENTARY VOTING RECORD

Craig has never served as a Member of Parliament. Burnham was previously the MP for Leigh and a Cabinet minister. Tony Lloyd, the interim Greater Manchester mayor before Burnham, was also an MP.

Craig entered Manchester City Council in 2011 and became its leader in December 2021. Her record must therefore be examined through council and combined-authority decisions, rather than voting divisions or questions in the House of Commons. Attributing parliamentary votes to her would be incorrect.

This distinction is not unusual among English regional mayors. West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, North East Mayor Kim McGuinness and South Yorkshire Mayor Oliver Coppard had not served as MPs before taking office. The question is what experience of budgets, national negotiations and local delivery each officeholder brings, not whether a Commons career is a qualification for office.

WHAT HER COUNCIL DECISIONS SHOW

While Craig led Manchester City Council, the authority approved a 2026/27 revenue budget exceeding £1 billion and a 4.99% council tax increase, incorporating a 2% adult social care element. The council said this supported existing services, investment in communities, housing and public provision.

At the Greater Manchester Combined Authority meeting on 13 February 2026, the authority endorsed a Band D mayoral general precept of £153.95: £92.20 relating to fire and rescue and £61.75 to other mayoral functions. The decision followed a named unanimous vote. Compared with the previous year, the Band D precept rose £25.

These decisions were collective, and the latter was a proposal originally brought by Burnham, not a unilateral Craig tax policy. Nevertheless, the record is relevant when evaluating promises to reduce household costs and decisions about how services are paid for.

Craig was also a portfolio lead on the Greater Manchester Good Growth Fund and integrated investment pipeline approved in November 2025. The authority reported initial potential investment capacity in excess of £1 billion and approved borrowing of up to £150 million against future retained business rates.

The phrase '£1 billion investment' should not be mistaken for £1 billion in unencumbered grants. Parts of the programme involve repayable finance, borrowing or contributions from other institutions. How much is ultimately invested, and where, is more meaningful than the initial headline figure.

AFFORDABLE HOUSING: WHAT DOES THE PROMISE MEAN FOR ROCHDALE?

Craig has pledged 50,000 council, social and genuinely affordable homes across Greater Manchester by 2039, including 10,000 homes delivered, under construction or in the pipeline by May 2028.

The three categories in that near-term target are not equivalent. A completed home can be occupied. A home under construction may still face delivery risks. A home in the pipeline may lack full financing or planning approval.

Over roughly 13 years, 50,000 homes implies an average of nearly 3,850 annually across the region, although actual delivery is unlikely to be evenly spread. The programme relies on public and private land, delivery partners and capital funding that will vary from scheme to scheme.

Rochdale needs published borough-specific targets, a social-rent breakdown, site-by-site funding and delivery dates. 'Affordable' as a statutory housing designation is not always affordable for a household on below-average wages.

TRANSPORT: AN AREA WHERE THE MAYOR HAS DIRECT SPENDING CHOICES

Burnham's transport legacy includes the Bee Network and bringing local buses under public control. Craig has committed to extending free Bee Network bus travel to young people aged 11–16, building on the existing scheme for those aged 16–18.

Transport for Greater Manchester estimates that nearly 200,000 young people could benefit, saving families up to about £500 per eligible child a year. The proposed start date is January 2027, but detailed eligibility and the formal decision process have yet to be completed. The combined authority's forward plan lists a relevant decision for November 2026.

There is a financial trade-off: cheaper travel can widen access to education and employment, while recurring concessions can create continuing expenditure or foregone fare income. An annual programme budget, estimates of extra journeys and bus capacity would make the policy's cost clearer.

Meanwhile, Rochdale, Heywood and Middleton have longstanding demands for stronger rail and tram links. Early development funding for the Oldham–Rochdale–Heywood–Bury tram-train concept should not be confused with an approved construction budget.

In a September 2026 parliamentary answer to Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell, the Department for Transport confirmed that Greater Manchester is due £2.5 billion in Transport for City Regions funding between 2027/28 and 2031/32, and that scheme prioritisation rests with the mayor. That does not mean all of the money is free for the tram proposal: other regional transport commitments compete for the same settlement.

MIDDLETON AND ATOM VALLEY

Middleton is a practical test of whether investment can extend beyond Manchester's commercial centre.

On 25 September 2026, the GMCA approved the proposed designation of a Middleton mayoral development area, subject to the borough council's consent. Rochdale Council Cabinet endorsed the plans on 29 September. The proposed Middleton Co-operative Mayoral Development Corporation is intended to coordinate land, investment and regeneration.

A development corporation can help assemble and develop sites, but the designation alone creates neither jobs nor homes. Residents will need to know the initial public expenditure, which businesses are being attracted and whether vacant premises are being brought into productive use.

Atom Valley and plans for a Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre offer the possibility of advanced manufacturing employment in Rochdale. Earlier GMCA proposals included an indicative allocation of up to £15 million for the centre. Indicative funding, however, is not evidence that the whole scheme has been built or that local recruitment benefits have been achieved.

Craig's proposed £20 million Good Growth High Streets Fund raises a similar question. Although a simple division across Greater Manchester's ten boroughs would imply £2 million each, that is not the fund's published allocation mechanism. The official forward plan schedules the launch decision for 13 November 2026. Its distribution and final conditions remain important.

IS THE ECONOMIC PROGRAMME FINANCIALLY FEASIBLE?

Three kinds of promise require different financial tests: ongoing services, one-off capital construction and investment meant to generate repayments or returns.

Transport concessions may need continuing annual support. Housing and infrastructure require capital, planning approvals, land and delivery partners. Investment financed by borrowing must produce enough income or wider economic benefit to justify financing costs and risk.

The Good Growth Fund's capacity incorporates future retained business-rates income and borrowing, so its published performance should be judged against debt-service costs, reserves, expected returns and delays. Lower-than-expected project returns could restrict later investment capacity.

There is an economic case for public intervention where contaminated land, weak connectivity or low private returns prevent development. Equally, a funding announcement does not remove the possibility of construction inflation, overruns or weak returns.

None of these observations establishes that Craig's programme is either fully financed or unaffordable. An authoritative judgement requires programme-level budgets that separate committed grants from lending, approved borrowing from available cash, and announced schemes from projects ready to proceed.

HOW OTHER REGIONS ARE APPROACHING THE SAME QUESTIONS

The West Midlands, with a broadly comparable metropolitan scale, has pursued a mix of housing, regeneration and transport investment under Richard Parker. Its announced Futures Fund draws on several funding and investment partners rather than operating simply as a direct grant pot.

In Liverpool City Region, Steve Rotheram has pursued bus franchising and integrated transport, while South Yorkshire's Oliver Coppard has combined transport reform with access to skills and work. Their regions differ in population, devolved powers, infrastructure and financial structure, making simplistic headline spending comparisons unreliable.

For Greater Manchester, much of the institutional machinery was developed under Burnham: bus franchising, devolved transport decisions, investment coordination and city-region policy-making. Craig inherits that machinery rather than beginning from scratch.

WHAT THE BOROUGH SHOULD BE ABLE TO MEASURE

Rochdale residents should be able to see investment figures broken down by borough and funding type; affordable homes completed and their rents; local recruitment and wages on public-backed schemes; transport projects with approved construction budgets; and the proportion of high-street funding that actually reaches each community.

The same applies to Atom Valley and Middleton. How many genuinely new posts are created? How many go to Rochdale residents? How much public borrowing is involved? Which sites have actually begun construction?

Craig has made commitments that address recognisable challenges in Rochdale. Some draw on programmes already in progress; others remain targets or proposals requiring further approval. The economically meaningful comparison with Burnham and mayors elsewhere will be based on achieved outcomes and published finances, not the number of projects announced.

For Rochdale, the fundamental test is whether city-region investment reaches households facing lower wages, weaker employment prospects and inadequate transport connections — and whether the financial costs of delivering it remain transparent.

title: Overnight road closures planned at Sudden Junction, Rochdale from October 12 to 15
excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council will implement overnight road closures around Sudden Junction from October 12 to 15 for resurfacing work, affecting traffic routes and diversions.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that overnight road closures will take place around Sudden Junction from Monday, October 12, to Thursday, October 15. The closures are necessary for resurfacing work, which will include refreshing road markings and renewing traffic signs.

The affected roads will be closed nightly between 8pm and 5am. Manchester Road in Castleton will be closed northbound between Onslow Street and Bolton Road, impacting traffic heading towards Rochdale town centre. Additionally, Silk Street will operate as one-way towards Tesco, preventing drivers from travelling from Tesco towards Manchester Road. Traffic on Bolton Road will also be restricted from turning right onto Manchester Road towards Castleton.

In a statement, the council confirmed that fully signed diversion routes will be in place to guide motorists during the closures. The resurfacing work aims to improve road safety and traffic flow in the area, which has seen increased usage in recent months.

Motorists are advised to plan their journeys accordingly and allow extra time for travel during the closure period. The council will continue to provide updates as the work progresses.

title: Sponsored: Footlights Rochdale runs acting, singing and dance classes for ages 3 to 18
excerpt: Advertisement feature: Footlights Rochdale teaches acting, singing and dance to children aged three to 18 at Wardle Academy, with further classes in Milnrow and Sudden.
content_html:
This is a paid-for advertisement feature.

Footlights Rochdale is a stage school for children and young people aged three to 18, based at Wardle Academy and run by its principal, Aaron Doherty Tubb.

Its Saturday sessions are held in the Watergrove Trust Building at Wardle Academy. Tinies classes for three- to four-year-olds run from 9.30am to 11am and for five- to six-year-olds from 11.20am to 12.50pm, while the Main School for ages seven to 18 runs from 9.45am to 1pm.

The school also runs a Singing Academy for ages five to 18 on Wednesdays from 5.15pm to 6.45pm at Butterworth Hall, New Street, Milnrow, and a Stage School on Fridays from 5.30pm to 8pm at Saint Aidan, Sudden, on Manchester Road.

Footlights says every child takes part in a full-scale show each summer, with a shorter Christmas presentation, and that Arts Award and LAMDA exams are available. It says all staff are DBS checked and a trained first aider is on site at each venue.

The school says children are welcome for a free trial at any time. Prices are not listed on its website.

Contact: Aaron on 07493 622494 or rochdale@footlightstheatre.co.uk.

title: Ofsted releases inspection reports for Greenbank Primary and Meadows schools in Rochdale
excerpt: Ofsted has published new inspection reports for Greenbank Primary School and Meadows School, both located in Rochdale, detailing their findings and ratings.
content_html:
Ofsted has published new inspection reports for Greenbank Primary School and Meadows School, both located in Rochdale, on 9 October 2026. The reports outline the findings from the inspections and any ratings awarded to the schools.

Greenbank Primary School's report indicates the school's performance and areas for improvement, although specific ratings were not detailed in the summary. The inspection process typically occurs every four years unless there are concerns that necessitate an earlier review. Parents and guardians can access the latest data for Greenbank Primary through the Ofsted website and are encouraged to participate in the Ofsted Parent View Survey to share their experiences.

Similarly, Meadows School's report provides insights into its operational standards and educational quality. Ofsted inspects non-association independent schools every three years, with additional inspections conducted when commissioned by the Secretary of State for Education. The report aims to inform parents about the school's performance and help them make informed decisions regarding their children's education.

Both schools are encouraged to use the feedback from these inspections to enhance their educational offerings. Parents interested in the reports can find them on the Ofsted website, where they can also subscribe for alerts regarding future inspections. For any inquiries, parents are advised to contact the schools directly.

title: Did Robin Hood really come to Healey Dell?
excerpt: Local stories tie a lost ring, witches and a 'Fairy Chapel' to Robin Hood — the tales are colourful, but what do the records actually show?
summary: Local stories tie a lost ring, witches and a 'Fairy Chapel' to Robin Hood — the tales are colourful, but what do the records actually show?
body:
There is a pulpit-shaped rock, a narrow pool and a name — the Fairy Chapel — at the base of Healey Dell’s steep gorge. The visitor centre and local heritage guides record a set of vivid stories: a King of the Fairies who turned a coven to stone, a ring lost in the river that cost a would‑be heir his title, and an origin tale that sends “Robert of Huntingdon” on the road to becoming Robin Hood. These versions are the ones you’ll see on site interpretation and in the Heritage Centre’s write‑ups. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

That is folklore, not archival evidence. The most systematic scholarly account of the Dell is an archaeological desk‑based assessment carried out for Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council by the University of Manchester Archaeological Unit in December 2004. It maps the valley’s mills, lodges, railway viaduct and later Victorian and industrial remains; it lists the local archives and printed sources consulted (John Rylands, Lancashire Record Office, Rochdale Local Studies and others) and documents the Dell’s long industrial and landscape history — but it does not produce contemporary medieval records linking a historical Robin Hood or a Robert of Huntingdon to Healey Dell. Put bluntly: the detailed desk‑based study records place, industry and later antiquarian interest, not a medieval outlaw’s itinerary. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

Healey Dell’s real, verifiable past is useful and interesting in itself. The site is a designated local nature reserve and a managed visitor attraction, with a Victorian railway viaduct that is Grade II listed and the valley’s surviving mill archaeology. Rochdale Borough Council describes the reserve, the visitor centre’s pictorial displays and the family‑oriented Fairy Grotto as part of the attraction visitors can find at Dell Road, Healey. The viaduct and the visible industrial remains are the kinds of things that the archaeological assessment and Historic England record in statutory listings. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

How did the Robin Hood story arrive here? Local legends often accrete around striking landscape features; caverns, pools and ravines attract tales of fairies, witches and enchanted tokens across Britain. The Healey Dell accounts appear in local storytelling and modern retellings by the Heritage Centre and local guides: they make no claim to derive from contemporary medieval documents but preserve a late tradition tying a Huntingdon name and a lost ring to the Chapel. Those popular accounts are part of the Dell’s cultural history and of local imaginative life — important for tourism and local identity — but they do not equal documentary proof. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

On the bigger question of Robin Hood’s historicity, mainstream scholarship treats Robin Hood as a legendary figure built from ballads and popular tales rather than a single, verifiable medieval person whose movements can be read off local court rolls. Modern reference works and folklorists stress the ballad tradition and its late medieval and post‑medieval formation; many local Robin Hood claims around England are later inventions, popular attributions or imaginative explanations for landscape oddities rather than recordable events. That does not make the stories worthless — it makes them folklore. ([books.google.com](https://books.google.com/books/about/Oxford_Dictionary_of_English_Folklore.html?hl=en&id=w2BMSAAACAAJ&output=html_text))

So what can a reader reasonably take away? If you mean “is there documentary, contemporary medieval evidence that Robin Hood or Robert of Huntingdon passed through Healey Dell?” the answer is: no such evidence has been produced in the local archival and archaeological surveys cited by the University of Manchester assessment and by the council’s heritage material. If you mean “are there stories that people tell about Robin Hood, witches and a magic ring here?” the answer is yes — they are recorded in local guides and on site interpretation, and they help make the place culturally lively. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

If you want to read more or check sources yourself: the University of Manchester archaeological desk‑based assessment (2004) is the most thorough published study of Healey Dell’s historic fabric; Rochdale Borough Council holds the reserve’s visitor information; the Healey Dell Heritage Centre publishes the Fairy Chapel story used in interpretation. None of these sources substitutes for a named medieval document placing Robin Hood in the Dell — and until such a record appears, the Robin Hood connection belongs to folklore rather than local history. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

title: Mayor Faisal Rana visits Rochdale Sixth Form College to see student support and results
excerpt: Mayor Faisal Rana and the Mayoress visited Rochdale Sixth Form College, highlighting its student support, pastoral provision and recent academic achievements.
content_html: Mayor Faisal Rana and the Mayoress have visited Rochdale Sixth Form College, meeting Principal Karl Smith and touring the college to see its facilities and student support. The visit included the Achievement Centre, which provides additional support for students who may be falling behind or need extra help with their studies. The Mayor and Mayoress also visited the student café and highlighted the college's focus on pastoral support, attendance and punctuality. ### College results and progression Rochdale Sixth Form College says its students achieved strong results in 2026. The college's website describes it as one of the country's strongest sixth form colleges for student progress, while its latest results announcement reported exceptional A-level and BTEC outcomes. The college also says around 80% of its students progress to higher education and that it has retained an Outstanding Ofsted judgement. The college's website currently highlights students progressing to Oxford and Cambridge, including former Oulder Hill student Joseph, who achieved three A*s and an A* in his EPQ before progressing to Cambridge, and former Hollingworth student Summer, who achieved four A*s and an A* in her EPQ before progressing to Oxford. Faisal Rana said the visit was particularly meaningful because four of his children had attended the college and achieved what he described as exceptional results. He said the visit offered a different perspective on the college, beyond that of a parent. He also praised the college's emphasis on supporting students, raising aspirations and creating opportunities for young people in the borough. Principal Karl Smith hosted the visit. Source: Faisal Rana, Mayor of Rochdale; Rochdale Sixth Form College. title: Construction begins on new banking hub at Morrisons in Heywood
excerpt: Construction is under way on a new banking hub at the Morrisons site in Heywood, with Elsie Blundell MP saying the facility is expected to open by the end of October.
content_html: Construction is under way on a new banking hub at the Morrisons site in Heywood, with fencing now in place around the new development. Elsie Blundell MP said she had met with Cash Access UK earlier this year to discuss bringing a banking hub to Heywood and has now welcomed the start of construction. The facility is being delivered as a modular building and is intended to provide banking services from the main banks in a shared location. It will be open to customers generally and will include improved access to cash. ### Expected opening Blundell said she had been told the banking hub should be open by the end of October. The new facility is being built in the car park at Morrisons in Heywood. Rochdale Daily will update this report if further confirmed information about the opening date and services becomes available. title: RBH football team takes part in Housing Association Charity Cup 2026
excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing colleagues took part in the Housing Association Charity Cup 2026 after weeks of training, with the team already looking ahead to next year's tournament.
content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing's football team joined eight other housing providers for the Housing Association Charity Cup 2026 at Goals Manchester.

The tournament followed weeks of preparation from RBH colleagues, who gave up their own time to train every Wednesday at the Soccer Factory in Castleton.

While Team RBH did not bring home the trophy, the organisation said the tournament was a successful opportunity for colleagues to come together and enjoy some friendly competition.

Salix Homes won the 2026 cup, while RBH congratulated everyone who took part and represented the organisation.

### Looking ahead to next year

RBH thanked Chris Hudspith, its Multi Trade Co-ordinator, for arranging the training sessions and encouraging colleagues to get involved.

Hudspith said the football programme had been a positive experience and an opportunity to meet people from other teams and departments while taking part in a shared interest.

Martin Platt, an IT Trainer, said the team came away from the tournament feeling that some close games could have gone differently, adding that they hoped to return next year and win the trophy.

RBH also said it is hoping to have a women's team competing in next year's tournament.

title: Rochdale Golf Club pair crowned Central England Mixed Foursomes champions
excerpt: Rochdale Golf Club's Susan Halpin and Steve Lord have won the Central England Mixed Foursomes Competition at Woodhall Spa after six rounds.
content_html:
Rochdale Golf Club is celebrating a major success after Susan Halpin and Steve Lord were crowned winners of the Central England Mixed Foursomes Competition at Woodhall Spa.

The pair, who served as Rochdale Golf Club's captains in 2024, competed in the competition and emerged victorious after six rounds.

The Central England Mixed Foursomes Competition has been running since 1935, with the winners' names recorded as a board prize in the clubhouse at Woodhall Spa.

Rochdale Golf Club described the achievement as an outstanding result and congratulated both players on their success.

Full competition results are available through Woodhall Spa Golf Club's official competition information.

title: Heywood Army Cadet Detachment opens its doors for National Cadets Week
excerpt: Heywood Army Cadet Detachment is inviting young people and their parents or carers to an open evening on Thursday 8 October to discover what the Army Cadets has to offer.
content_html:
Heywood Army Cadet Detachment is opening its doors as part of National Cadets Week, inviting young people and their parents or carers to come along and find out more about the Army Cadets.

The open evening will take place on Thursday 8 October from 7pm to 8.30pm at Heywood Detachment on Bamford Road, Heywood, OL10 4FT.

Visitors will be able to meet instructors and cadets, look around the detachment and find out more about activities available through the Army Cadets.

The programme can include adventure, fieldcraft, shooting, first aid, sport, the Duke of Edinburgh's Award, camps and leadership opportunities, as well as the chance to make new friends and try something different.

The detachment says no military experience is needed and that the open evening is an opportunity to see what Army Cadets is about and where participation could lead.

Young people and their parents or carers are invited to attend.

title: Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit highlights opportunities for local businesses
excerpt: Businesses and organisations gathered at the Crown Oil Arena for the Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit, with discussions focused on accessing contracts, bidding and local economic growth.
content_html:
Businesses and organisations from across the borough have come together for the Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit, with discussions focused on how local firms can access procurement opportunities and grow their businesses.

The event was organised by the Rochdale Development Agency and held at the newly refurbished Crown Oil Arena, home of Rochdale AFC.

The summit brought together organisations involved in procurement, regeneration and business support, including STAR Procurement, Match My Project, Hopwood Hall College, Willmott Dixon and the Rochdale Development Agency.

Discussions focused on how businesses can get onto the procurement ladder, understand the bidding process and position themselves to compete for contracts and opportunities with larger organisations.

Mayor Faisal Rana, who attended the event, said greater collaboration between local businesses and organisations delivering investment across the borough was important to ensuring local firms can benefit from upcoming opportunities.

He highlighted figures from the Rochdale Development Agency's latest independent economic impact assessment, which it says found that its work had created, supported or safeguarded 765 jobs and supported 699 businesses. The assessment also reported £14.30 in local economic value for every £1 invested.

The mayor also pointed to major investment programmes including Atom Valley, the Rochdale Rail Corridor, town centre regeneration, housing and skills investment as areas where businesses could potentially benefit from future procurement and supply-chain opportunities.

The summit comes as public-sector and regeneration projects continue to create demand for contractors, suppliers and other local businesses across a range of sectors.

The Rochdale Development Agency and organisations involved in procurement are encouraging businesses to understand the opportunities available and build their capacity to bid for work.

The event also underlined the potential economic impact of keeping a greater share of investment within the local economy, through jobs, business growth and local supply chains.

The Rochdale AFC Community Trust was also associated with the event.

title: Syke granted Conservation Area status to protect its historic character
excerpt: Syke has been granted Conservation Area status by Rochdale Borough Council, following a consultation in which 33 of 38 responses supported the designation.
content_html:
Syke has been granted Conservation Area status by Rochdale Borough Council, with the designation intended to protect the area's architectural and historic character from unsympathetic development.

The council confirmed the designation on 17 February 2026, describing Syke as an area with a unique and rich history. It highlighted the area's position on a historic packhorse route and its traditional weavers' cottages, including buildings with distinctive upper-floor windows designed to maximise natural light before electricity became widespread.

The Syke Conservation Area Appraisal provides further historical detail. It identifies Syke Road as part of the historic packhorse route linking Clitheroe with Rochdale and beyond, and records a network of historic paths across the Common, including remnants of the old packhorse trail.

The designated area covers Syke Common, parts of Dewhirst Road and Syke Road, and sections of Buckley Wood. The appraisal also identifies the northern extent of Cronkeyshaw Common and Syke Pond, well-preserved weavers' cottages, evidence of former industry, vernacular buildings and farmsteads, sandstone buildings, dry-stone and flagstone walls, and historic views and paths.

The appraisal includes historic maps from 1851, 1891, 1911 and 1936, alongside sections covering architectural character, historic buildings, key views and vistas, green spaces and the area's overall character. It provides the documented basis for the council's assessment of Syke's special architectural and historic interest.

### Public support for the designation

Rochdale Borough Council said more than 85% of locals backed the proposals. The consultation records 38 responses, of which 33 were positive about Conservation Area status for Syke. That represents approximately 87% of respondents, although the total number of responses was relatively small.

The responses nevertheless provide evidence of strong support among those who took part, as well as an indication that local heritage was an important consideration for respondents.

Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for regeneration, described the designation as a worthy addition to Rochdale's existing Conservation Areas and highlighted local engagement and pride in Syke's heritage.

### What Conservation Area status means

Conservation Areas are designated by local authorities where an area has special architectural or historic interest. Historic England guidance also provides for local authorities to prepare Conservation Area Appraisals setting out an area's character and significance.

The Syke appraisal states that its purpose is to explain the area's significance and identify measures to preserve and enhance its special character. It is intended to guide future development and inform future management plans. The document was prepared following consultation with local residents and draws on site visits, archive material, information from residents and Historic England guidance.

Historic England told Rochdale Daily that it had no involvement in the designation of the new Syke Conservation Area and directed us to its general guidance on Conservation Areas. Council documents show that Historic England guidance and documentation were considered during the process, but the designation itself was determined locally.

### Planning protections and what is not yet established

Conservation Area status introduces additional considerations within the planning process and can make permitted development rights more restrictive. The appraisal identifies circumstances where planning permission may be required, including substantial demolition of buildings or structures and certain works involving walls, gates, fences, extensions and alterations.

Article 4 Directions can remove further permitted development rights, but they are not automatic consequences of Conservation Area designation. The available information does not establish that an Article 4 Direction has been introduced for Syke.

The practical effect on individual properties will therefore depend on the planning controls that apply and any further decisions made by Rochdale Borough Council. The designation provides a framework for protecting Syke's special character, while the appraisal sets out the evidence and management considerations underpinning it.

title: Roadworks scheduled on Well i' th' Lane in Rochdale from 24 October 2026
excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced roadworks on Well i' th' Lane starting 24 October 2026, with alternative routes provided for motorists.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks will commence on Well i' th' Lane from 12 midnight on Saturday, 24 October 2026, continuing until 11.59pm on Sunday, 1 November 2026. During this period, part of the road will be temporarily closed to facilitate the necessary works.

Motorists travelling southbound will be diverted via Queen Victoria Street, Oldham Road, and Queensway. The council advises drivers to plan their journeys accordingly to avoid delays during the roadworks.

In addition to Well i' th' Lane, several other roads in the Rochdale area will also undergo maintenance. Notably, Willbutts Lane and Rooley Street will see roadworks starting on 12 October 2026, with closures expected to last for a maximum of 21 days. Willbutts Lane will be closed at the junction with Edenfield Road, extending 14 metres westward, while Rooley Street will be closed at the same junction, extending 10 metres eastward.

Egerton Street in Heywood will also be closed from 12 midnight on Tuesday, 20 October 2026, until 11.59pm on Sunday, 1 November 2026, with the closure beginning at the junction with Hind Hill Street and extending 165 metres westward. Residents and commuters are encouraged to check the Rochdale Borough Council's website for further details, including maps of the affected areas and updates on the roadworks.

title: Man arrested on suspicion of murder after man found deceased on Curzon Road
excerpt: Greater Manchester Police has arrested a man on suspicion of murder after a man was found deceased at an address on Curzon Road, Rochdale.
content_html:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder following the death of a man at an address on Curzon Road, Rochdale.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said officers received a report of a concern for the welfare of a man at an address on Curzon Road at around 7.55pm on Wednesday 7 October 2026.

Emergency services attended and the man was sadly confirmed deceased at the scene.

A man in his 40s has been arrested on suspicion of murder and remains in police custody for questioning.

GMP said an investigation is underway to establish the circumstances surrounding the death and that detectives are exploring all lines of enquiry.

The man's next of kin have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.

Detective Superintendent Richard Hunt said: “Firstly, our thoughts remain with the family of the man who sadly died, and we have officers assigned to support them through this difficult time.

“An investigation is underway and officers are working at pace to establish the circumstances which led to this man’s death.

“We currently have a man in custody for questioning and ask the public to refrain from speculating at this time. This is a live investigation, and we are currently exploring all avenues of enquiry and keeping an open mind.”

No finding of guilt should be inferred from an arrest or allegation. The arrested man remains under investigation and is presumed innocent unless and until convicted.

Source: Greater Manchester Police.

title: Remembrance and reflection walks offer bereaved service families a place to connect at Denehurst Park
excerpt: Get Together After Serving CIC invites families, partners and loved ones to a gentle weekly remembrance walk at Denehurst Park in Rochdale, with no pressure to talk about loss.
content_html:
A weekly remembrance walk in Rochdale is offering families and loved ones of fallen service personnel a chance to find companionship, fresh air and a little space to reflect.

Organised by Get Together After Serving CIC (G.A.S-CIC), the Remembrance & Reflection Walk takes place every Wednesday at Denehurst Park. Participants are invited to meet outside Denehurst Café at 12.30pm before setting off together.

The gentle walk is expected to last between 30 minutes and an hour, depending on the weather. Dogs are very welcome, although there is no need to bring one to take part.

At the heart of the initiative is the understanding that grief does not always need words. Those attending can share memories of someone they have lost, chat about everyday life, walk quietly or simply enjoy being in the company of people who understand.

The event poster captures that sentiment: “Sometimes you don’t need a meeting or a support group. Sometimes you just need to get outside, walk, talk and spend some time with people who understand.”

After the walk, the group plans to return to Denehurst Café for a warm drink, a slice of cake and more time together for anyone who wishes to stay.

The invitation is aimed at families and loved ones remembering fallen heroes, with partners and friends also welcome. There is no expectation to discuss personal experiences or bereavement, and those who would prefer a quiet walk will be just as welcome as those looking for conversation.

The weekly gathering brings remembrance into the everyday: not only formal ceremonies or anniversaries, but a simple opportunity to come together, one Wednesday at a time.

Walk details: Every Wednesday at 12.30pm. Meeting point: outside Denehurst Café, Denehurst Park, Rochdale. The walk lasts 30 minutes to one hour, weather permitting. Dogs are welcome, but are not required. Participants can return to the café afterwards for optional refreshments and company.

title: Sara Rowbotham: the Rochdale health worker who raised 181 safeguarding alerts
excerpt: Sara Rowbotham repeatedly raised concerns about vulnerable young people while working for Rochdale’s Crisis Intervention Team, later giving evidence to Parliament about the response to child sexual exploitation in the town.
content_html:
Sara Rowbotham became one of the most recognisable figures associated with the response to child sexual exploitation in Rochdale after repeatedly raising concerns about vulnerable young people while working for the town’s NHS Crisis Intervention Team.

Rowbotham worked as the Crisis Intervention Team Co-ordinator and Sexual Health Improvement Specialist. The team was established in 2004 and supported thousands of young people, including those who disclosed concerns about sexual abuse and exploitation.

In evidence to the House of Commons Home Affairs Committee in November 2012, Rowbotham told MPs that, over a period covering the years from 2005 to 2011, her team had identified referrals involving 103 young people.

She also told the committee that she had made 181 alerts to Children’s Social Care about concerns involving young people.

Asked whether she believed police and social services had worked together effectively, Rowbotham said this had happened “very rarely” in the early period and that she had subsequently begun making the Safeguarding Children Unit aware of the referrals so that strategy meetings could be convened.

The committee also heard evidence from other senior officials about the handling of the information. The subsequent Home Affairs Committee report described missed opportunities and examined the response of children's social care and police to child sexual exploitation in Rochdale.

Rowbotham told MPs that she had repeatedly tried to make protective services aware of the vulnerability of young people and that she believed agencies had failed to provide a sufficiently comprehensive and coordinated response.

The evidence came after the prosecution of nine men in Rochdale in 2012 for serious sexual offences against girls. The case prompted wider scrutiny of how authorities had responded to reports of child sexual exploitation.

Rowbotham continued to speak publicly about the response. In 2014, she was made redundant from her role. Contemporary reporting by ITV News and The Guardian documented her concerns about the handling of the case and the impact of losing her position.

Her story later reached a much wider audience when the BBC drama Three Girls was broadcast in May 2017, with Maxine Peake portraying Rowbotham.

A petition calling for Rowbotham to be formally recognised attracted more than 100,000 signatures within days of the programme airing and ultimately exceeded 275,000 signatures, according to contemporary reports.

Rowbotham subsequently entered local politics. She was elected as a councillor for North Middleton in 2015 and went on to serve as Deputy Leader of Rochdale Borough Council and as a cabinet member.

Her public recognition also continued. She received a Special Recognition Award at the NHS Heroes Awards in 2018 and was made an honorary member of the NSPCC Council that year. In 2021, she was appointed MBE for services to young people.

Rowbotham’s evidence to Parliament remains part of the official record of the scrutiny that followed the Rochdale child sexual exploitation cases. Her account of the 181 alerts, and questions about how information held by frontline services was acted upon, formed part of the wider examination of safeguarding failures in the town.

Source: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee evidence and report; contemporary reporting by ITV News and The Guardian; Rochdale Borough Council records.

title: East Lancashire Railway to host first Event, Catering and Retail Volunteer Open Day
excerpt: East Lancashire Railway is inviting prospective volunteers to its first Event, Catering and Retail Volunteer Open Day at Bury Bolton Street Station on Monday 12 October.
content_html:
East Lancashire Railway (ELR) is inviting prospective volunteers to its first Event, Catering and Retail Volunteer Open Day on Monday 12 October 2026.

The railway is looking for volunteers to help support a wide range of experiences, from luxury dining services and Rail Ale Trails to Days Out with Thomas and Santa Specials.

Volunteering opportunities cover events, catering and retail, with roles designed to suit a range of interests and experience. Volunteers could find themselves serving cream tea aboard a first-class carriage or helping to create the atmosphere for the Halloween Ghost Train.

The ELR said it will help match volunteers with roles that suit their interests and experience, with full training provided. No previous experience is needed.

Commercial Manager Lorna Kelly said: “If you’ve ever thought about volunteering at the East Lancashire Railway but felt unsure, or wondered whether you have the right experience, please come along to our Open Day. I’ll be there with some of our lovely volunteers, who can tell you what it’s really like to be part of the ELR.

“You can meet our events, catering and retail teams, hear about the roles available and ask any questions you have. Whether you’re ready to sign up or just curious, we’d love to meet you.”

The Open Day will take place at the Trackside Bar at Bury Bolton Street Station from 10am to 3pm on Monday 12 October.

The railway says prospective volunteers can attend to find out more about the roles available, meet members of the teams and ask questions before deciding whether to get involved.

title: Sculpt & Edit launches wellness clinic after founder builds business from scratch
excerpt: Sculpt & Edit founder Amy has opened a new wellness clinic after finding herself without a job and turning that moment into an opportunity to build her own treatment business, with a focus on lymphatic drainage, post-surgery support and body treatments.
content_html:
A new wellness clinic, Sculpt & Edit, has opened with a focus on treatments designed around body confidence, recovery and wellbeing.

Founder Amy said the clinic is intended to offer an alternative to a traditional beauty salon, bringing together lymphatic drainage and post-surgery support with body contouring and sculpting treatments.

The clinic will also offer more holistic treatments including Reiki and reflexology, alongside a growing focus on skin health and hydration. Amy said vitamin injections and IV wellness treatments will also form part of the clinic's offering.

The launch follows a significant career change for Amy, who found herself without a job at the beginning of 2026 and decided to take the risk of building a business of her own.

Over the following eight months, she has developed Sculpt & Edit from the ground up, initially through her treatment business before moving into a physical wellness clinic.

She described the opening of the clinic as a major milestone after what she said had been a life-changing year, and hopes her experience will encourage other people considering starting their own business.

Sculpt & Edit is now welcoming clients at the new clinic, with further information about treatments and the business available directly from the clinic.

excerpt: Birtle View Nursery has opened at 239 Bury & Rochdale Old Road, with Mayor of Rochdale Councillor Faisal Rana attending the opening.
content_html:
Birtle View Nursery has opened at 239 Bury & Rochdale Old Road in Heywood, with the Mayor of Rochdale, Councillor Faisal Rana, attending the opening.

Mayor Faisal Rana said he was pleased to visit the new nursery and described the transformation of the site as impressive. He said the nursery had created spaces intended to provide children and families with a welcoming, safe and supportive environment.

The mayor also met Councillor Paul Ellison, the councillor for the area, during the visit.

Birtle View Nursery is registered with Ofsted as a childcare setting providing full-day care. Ofsted records show the nursery was registered on 18 September 2026 and is currently listed as open. An inspection report has not yet been published.

The nursery is based at 239 Bury & Rochdale Old Road, Heywood, OL10 4BQ. The site has previously operated as the Bird I' Th' Hand premises.

The nursery's opening comes as new childcare provision is added in the area. Information published by the nursery indicates that it is intended for children aged from birth to five years.

Mayor Rana congratulated the team involved in bringing the nursery into operation and wished the nursery success.

title: Rochdale’s Breaking Barriers secures core funding to expand its cultural work across Greater Manchester
excerpt: Rochdale-based production company Breaking Barriers has secured three years of GMCA core funding to expand cultural programmes, paid opportunities and creative development across Greater Manchester.
content_html:
Rochdale-based multidisciplinary production company Breaking Barriers has secured three years of core funding from the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to strengthen the organisation and expand its cultural programmes across the region.

Over the funding period, Breaking Barriers plans to offer 42 paid placements through its Young Company programme, giving creatives aged 18–25 hands-on experience working on professional arts productions.

It will also provide 328 paid freelance roles and 45 in-kind artist residencies at its Rochdale base at Richard Street Studios.

Young Company participants will gain practical skills in producing, sound design, filmmaking and direction, with a focus on young people from underrepresented backgrounds who have had fewer opportunities to get into the arts.

A producer development programme will also support 36 creative producers a year to develop their own projects, secure resources and build sustainable careers.

Awarded through the Spirit strand of the GMCA Culture Fund, the investment will support Breaking Barriers to continue delivering theatre, film and immersive outdoor artworks, alongside training, mentoring and paid opportunities for emerging creatives.

Parvez Qadir, Artistic Director of Breaking Barriers, said: “Three years of core funding gives us the stability to plan ahead and grow as a company here in Rochdale. There’s so much creative talent locally, and we can now give more young people paid opportunities to work alongside experienced artists on our productions. It also enables us to keep building partnerships across Greater Manchester and develop projects shaped by local people, bringing their stories to life.”

Bev Craig, Mayor of Greater Manchester, said: “Culture has the power to connect communities, inspire creativity and strengthen pride in the places we call home.

“Through the Greater Manchester Culture Fund, we're investing in a diverse range of cultural organisations that help make our city region such a vibrant and inclusive place to live. Breaking Barriers is a fantastic example of a local company creating opportunities for young people to share their stories, develop their creativity and shape cultural experiences on their doorstep.”

Projects are currently planned to span the boroughs of Rochdale, Bury, Salford, Stockport, Manchester, Tameside and Bolton over three years.

Residents and local communities will help create outdoor artworks using sound, projection and light, alongside films and digital storytelling projects reflecting local experiences.

The funding will also help sustain and expand Breaking Barriers’ theatre in education work.

This includes multi-partnership delivery of Crossing the Line, a theatre and workshop programme tackling child criminal exploitation, which has already reached more than 15,000 young people across more than 220 schools.

Blind Side, exploring violence against women and girls, consent and healthy relationships, will continue to tour. Support from the Spirit strand will enable more time and resources to further expand its reach into other boroughs.

title: New Awaab’s Law protections could cover millions more renters and vulnerable households
excerpt: A government consultation will examine extending Awaab’s Law to private renters and other accommodation, with faster legal deadlines for landlords to tackle serious hazards such as damp and mould.
content_html:
Millions more households could receive stronger legal protections against dangerous housing conditions under plans to extend Awaab’s Law beyond social housing.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government has launched a consultation on how the law could be introduced for private renters and whether similar protections should apply to other forms of accommodation.

Awaab’s Law currently provides legal deadlines for social landlords to investigate and address serious hazards, including dangerous damp and mould. The measures were introduced in memory of two-year-old Awaab Ishak, who died in 2020 after prolonged exposure to damp and mould in his home.

The proposed extension could mean around nine million households are covered by new repair timescales, compared with around four million currently covered.

The consultation is considering protections for private rented homes as well as:

temporary accommodation for homeless people and families;

accommodation for young people leaving care; and

supported housing, including accommodation used by older, disabled and other vulnerable people.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook said all renters should be able to expect a safe and decent home, regardless of tenure.

“Awaab’s Law is already helping to drive up standards in the social housing sector. We’re now moving to extend it to private landlords so that England’s 11 million private renters can enjoy the same protections,” he said.

The government says landlords are already required to act when serious hazards are identified. Around one in 10 private rented homes is estimated to contain a Category 1 hazard, the most serious level.

The Renters’ Rights Act has also introduced fines of up to £7,000 where serious dangers are found. Awaab’s Law would add legally defined timescales requiring action on the most serious conditions.

The consultation will help determine how Awaab’s Law should operate in the private rented sector, including the timescales for the new protections to come into force. It closes on 18 December 2026.

Generation Rent welcomed the move. Chief Executive Holly Williamson said too many renters live in homes that can harm their health and wait months for landlords to address problems.

Crisis also backed the proposals, highlighting the conditions faced by people living in temporary accommodation, including hostels and bed and breakfasts.

The Renters’ Reform Coalition said nobody should have to live in a home that makes them ill or puts their life at risk, while Independent Age said older renters can face serious problems including rats and mould and may be afraid to request repairs.

Independent Age said almost 96% of older renters it polled supported Awaab’s Law.

Become, the national charity for children in care and young care leavers, also welcomed the government’s consideration of stronger standards for accommodation used by young people leaving care.

The proposals form part of commitments in the Renters’ Rights Act and the National Plan to End Homelessness.

The government says the changes are intended to ensure dangerous housing conditions are dealt with quickly and that tenants can raise concerns without fear of repercussions.

Source: Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government.

title: From historic chapel to bridal sanctuary: Orla Bridal celebrates its launch in Mytholmroyd
excerpt: A new independent bridal boutique has opened in one of Mytholmroyd’s historic buildings, bringing a new chapter of celebration to The Chapel on Scout Road.
content_html:
A new independent bridal boutique has opened in one of Mytholmroyd’s historic buildings, bringing a fresh chapter of celebration to The Chapel on Scout Road.

Founded by Littleborough businesswomen Jessica Demain and Delphine Gott, Orla Bridal marked its launch on Saturday 3 October with a celebration attended by family, friends and local businesses who helped bring their vision to life.

The pair have created a warm, welcoming bridal sanctuary, combining the building’s character with sparkling chandeliers, thoughtful interiors and a collection of designer gowns from Justin Alexander, Madi Lane and Modeca. Visits are private and by appointment only, giving each bride the space and personal attention to enjoy finding her dress with her closest guests.

Originally built in 1806, the Methodist chapel was extended to accommodate a Sunday school in 1872. Acquired by The Craggs Country Business Parks in 2018, it was sensitively restored and transformed into offices, preserving its heritage for a new generation.

Now, Orla is bringing something of the building’s original spirit back to its rooms: a place to gather, share meaningful moments and celebrate love.

For Jess and Delphine, that sense of occasion and belonging is at the heart of the business. Their vision is for every bride to feel comfortable, celebrated and free to be herself, surrounded by beautiful dresses in a calm and supportive setting.

Saturday’s launch offered guests a first look at the boutique, with flowers, fizz and cakes marking the culmination of weeks of preparation and support from local makers, tradespeople and businesses.

Orla Bridal is now welcoming appointment bookings at The Chapel, Scout Road, Mytholmroyd.

Visit www.orlabridal.com or follow @orla.bridal on Instagram.

title: East Lancashire Railway wins Community Hero Award for its volunteers
excerpt: East Lancashire Railway has been recognised with a Roch Valley Radio Community Hero Award for the contribution of its more than 800 volunteers.
content_html:
East Lancashire Railway has been recognised with a Roch Valley Radio Community Hero Award for the contribution of its more than 800 volunteers.

The awards celebrate people, groups, charities and businesses that go the extra mile to support others and strengthen their communities. The railway said the recognition reflects the commitment of its volunteers and the role the heritage line continues to play across the communities it serves.

The East Lancashire Railway operates heritage trains through the Irwell Valley, connecting communities including Bury, Summerseat, Ramsbottom, Irwell Vale, Rawtenstall and Heywood.

Diesel Driver and Head of the Signalling Department Linda Henderson said the railway could not exist without its volunteers.

"For almost 40 years, the ELR has operated Heritage trains through the heart of the Irwell Valley. Without volunteers, the ELR and Heritage Railways throughout the UK would not exist."

Henderson said the award recognised more than 800 current volunteers as well as those who had previously given their time to the railway.

Chairman Mike Kelly said he was "extremely proud" to accept the award on behalf of the railway and its volunteers, describing their work as generous and unselfish.

Kelly, who is also a volunteer, said the recognition highlighted the commitment and passion volunteers bring to organisations across local communities. He also thanked Roch Valley Radio for recognising volunteers and the contribution they make to charities and community organisations.

The award was collected by a group of volunteers representing several parts of the railway, including train operations, signalling, the guards department, the dining train team and a station café.

The East Lancashire Railway said the award was a recognition of the hard work and continued dedication of all its volunteers.

title: Rochdale Sleepout 2026 returns to raise funds and awareness for people facing homelessness
excerpt: Petrus is calling on Rochdale residents, businesses and community groups to get behind Rochdale Sleepout 2026 and help raise vital funds for local people experiencing homelessness and social exclusion.
content_html:
Petrus Community is calling on people across Rochdale to get behind Rochdale Sleepout 2026, a fundraising and awareness event designed to highlight the realities faced by people experiencing homelessness while raising vital funds for local support services.

The Rochdale-based charity supports people experiencing homelessness, poverty and social exclusion across the borough. The Sleepout challenges participants to spend a night outdoors while learning more about homelessness and the support available locally.

Organisers are keen to stress that the event is not intended to replicate the experience of homelessness. Instead, it aims to encourage conversation, build understanding and raise money to support people accessing Petrus services.

Last year's inaugural Rochdale Sleepout brought supporters together from across the borough and raised £7,875.52 for Rochdale AFC Community Trust and Petrus.

The money raised has already helped launch Changing Lives, a partnership supporting people experiencing homelessness and those living in supported accommodation through football, wellbeing, education and employability opportunities.

According to Petrus, participants involved in the programme are rebuilding confidence, making new friendships, developing new skills and becoming more active members of their communities.

This year's event is also an opportunity for local businesses, community groups and individuals to get involved by taking part, sponsoring participants or making a donation.

Funds raised through the Sleepout will support Petrus' work across Rochdale, including homelessness prevention, housing support, wellbeing services, education and training opportunities, and practical support for some of the borough's most vulnerable residents.

Petrus is encouraging anyone interested in supporting the event to help spread the word and get involved.

title: Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers take on 45-mile charity walk
excerpt: Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers are taking on a 45-mile charity walk on Saturday, 31 October, to raise money for four causes close to their hearts.
content_html:
Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers are swapping the rugby pitch for the road as members of the groups prepare to take on a 45-mile charity walk on Saturday, 31 October.

The challenge is being organised to raise as much money as possible for four causes close to the participants' hearts: Springhill Hospice, the Motor Neurone Disease Association (MND), Rochdale Masters and Rugby League Cares.

Organisers are expecting the walk to be a major physical challenge, but say they want it to become about more than completing 45 miles. They are also appealing to local businesses and members of the community to get behind the fundraising effort.

Businesses are being encouraged to support the challenge through sponsorship, donations, supplies for the day or simply by sharing the fundraiser with customers, colleagues and their wider networks.

The organisers said: "We're not playing rugby for this one… we're putting the boots down and walking 45 miles!"

The group hopes that local support will help raise as much money as possible for the four causes while bringing businesses, sports communities and residents together around the challenge.

Anyone who can help with sponsorship, donations, supplies or promotion is encouraged to get in touch with the organisers.

Mandy from Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers said the group would be happy to provide photographs, route details and further information about the charities involved, as well as speak about the challenge.

title: Castleton night works: Manchester Road’s three traffic phases
excerpt: Overnight restrictions run until 8 November. The council has not published dates for individual phases.
content_html:
Manchester Road drivers face overnight restrictions for Bee Network Phase 2 resurfacing, scheduled from 12 October to 8 November 2026, 8pm–5am. Only one phase operates at a time.

Phase 1 closes Manchester Road between Onslow Street and Bolton Road. Silk Street is westbound-only from Tesco to Manchester Road; right turns from Bolton Road onto Manchester Road are banned.

Phase 2 bans north-eastbound travel on Manchester Road from Bolton Road to Roch Valley Way. There is no left turn from Bolton Road onto Manchester Road. The old Manchester Road section must exit via Roch Valley Way. Manchester Road traffic can only turn left onto Bolton Road. Westbound travel on Silk Street from Tesco to Manchester Road is prohibited.

Phase 3 bans south-westbound travel between Roch Valley Way and Bolton Road. There is no left turn from Edinburgh Way onto Manchester Road, or right turn from Roch Valley Way. Silk Street closes between Manchester Road and Tesco, with no right turn into it from Manchester Road.

Diversions will be signed. Check the current phase before travelling: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/2618/various-roads-roadworks-in-rochdale-from-12-october-2026

title: Boy, 13, stabbed in Rochdale town centre: six arrested, two bailed and stop-and-search powers extended
excerpt: Live story. Six teenage boys have now been arrested after a 13-year-old was stabbed in Rochdale town centre on Saturday night. Two have been released on bail, four remain in custody, and Section 60 stop-and-search powers in the town centre run until 3pm on Tuesday. Updated as Greater Manchester Police confirm developments.
content_html:
Latest, 08:30, Tuesday 1 September: six teenage boys have been arrested in connection with the stabbing of a 13-year-old boy in Rochdale town centre on Saturday night, 29 August. Two were arrested on Sunday and have since been released on bail. Four more were arrested on Monday and remain in custody. All six were held on suspicion of assault and possession of a bladed article, Greater Manchester Police said. The injured boy remains in hospital receiving treatment.

This is Rochdale Daily's single live story on the incident. It is updated in place, newest first, only when Greater Manchester Police or another primary source confirms a development. Earlier separate reports have been folded into this page; see the correction note at the foot.

What we know

The boy was stabbed during a serious assault in the town centre, near the Riverside shopping centre, on the evening of Saturday 29 August. Police described the incident as a serious assault alongside wider disorder in the town centre that night. He was taken to hospital, where he remains.

Monday 31 August: GMP confirmed four further arrests, all teenage boys, on suspicion of assault and possession of a bladed article. The two boys arrested on Sunday were released on bail while enquiries continue. Detective Superintendent Richard Hunt said the force was continuing to make progress on the investigation and that violence on the streets would not be tolerated.

Monday 31 August: the Section 60 order covering Rochdale town centre was extended until 3pm on Tuesday 1 September. Under Section 60 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act, officers can stop and search people in the designated area without needing reasonable suspicion.

Sunday 30 August: GMP announced two arrests and put a 24-hour Section 60 order in place for the town centre from 3pm. Chief Inspector Michael Barton, neighbourhoods lead for GMP's Rochdale district, said detectives were reviewing CCTV, gathering witness statements and analysing intelligence to identify everyone involved.

Saturday 29 August: a 13-year-old boy was stabbed in the town centre. GMP log 2750 of 29/08/2026.

What we do not know

Police have not released the boy's condition beyond confirming he remains in hospital, and have not said what led to the assault. No one has been charged. Rochdale Daily will not name anyone arrested and will not publish speculation about motive or identity while the investigation is live.

How to help the investigation

Anyone who witnessed the incident, was in Rochdale town centre on Saturday evening, or has mobile phone, CCTV or dashcam footage is asked to contact GMP on 101, quoting log 2750 of 29/08/2026, or via the LiveChat function at gmp.police.uk. Information can be given anonymously to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

Story first published 30 August 2026 as "Two arrested following stabbing incident in Rochdale"; consolidated into this live page on 1 September 2026.

title: One in seven Rochdale businesses could be overpaying business rates, research claims
excerpt: More than 1,300 commercial properties in Rochdale could be paying too much in business rates, with potential overpayments worth a combined £2.9 million a year, according to BusinessRateChecker.com.
content_html:
More than 1,300 commercial properties in Rochdale could be paying too much in business rates, with potential overpayments worth a combined £2.9 million a year, according to research from business rates intelligence company BusinessRateChecker.com.

The company's analysis examined 8,607 commercial properties in the borough and flagged 1,308 — 15.2% — as potentially over-assessed.

That was the highest proportion of any English local authority area included in BusinessRateChecker's analysis, ahead of Maidstone at 13.8%, Kirklees at 13.7% and Mid Suffolk at 13.7%.

BusinessRateChecker estimates the affected Rochdale properties could have grounds for reductions worth around £2.9 million collectively each year, equivalent to an average potential saving of approximately £2,217 for each property it identified.

However, the findings do not allege wrongdoing by Rochdale Borough Council.

The underlying rateable value of a commercial property is determined by the Valuation Office Agency. Councils then use the relevant rateable value and multiplier when calculating business rates bills.

Rupert Spiegelberg, CEO of BusinessRateChecker.com, told Rochdale Daily that businesses also have a responsibility to ensure the property information being used is accurate.

He said: “It is actually the responsibility of the property owner to update the VOA with changes in details of floor space, floor usage etc. Different RVs are applied to different spaces in a property. Many don't.”

He said larger companies were generally more likely to scrutinise their valuations because they had the resources to employ professional surveyors, while smaller businesses could be less likely to question what they were being charged.

He added: “Large businesses are usually quite up on this and will have the resources to hire surveyors to help them but for smaller businesses like hairdressers, coffee shops etc they tend not to question the bills as much.”

How Rochdale properties were assessed

BusinessRateChecker says its system compares the rate per square metre and zoning rates of individual properties with comparable nearby premises in the same category and valuation scheme.

It then examines factors including comparable rateable values and floor areas to identify properties whose valuations appear materially different from similar premises.

The company says tolerance bands are included to avoid flagging marginal cases.

Spiegelberg also told Rochdale Daily that the 1,308 figure could be an underestimate because some properties cannot be reliably assessed by its system.

Pubs are one example because valuations can depend partly on trading information which BusinessRateChecker does not have access to.

The company's own Rochdale dataset consequently records some properties as unassessable rather than assuming they are being charged correctly.

BusinessRateChecker currently analyses around 1.9 million commercial properties across England, using the published VOA rating list alongside other data to identify properties which may warrant further investigation.

Businesses can check their own property against comparable premises through the company's online checker.

title: Heywood councillors vote to end Hopwood Triangle road closure trial
excerpt: Heywood Township councillors have voted unanimously to end the Hopwood Triangle traffic trial after sustained opposition from residents, while the Coronation Avenue HGV parking restriction will remain.
content_html:
Common sense has finally prevailed. At an extraordinary Heywood Township meeting last tonight, councillors voted UNANIMOUSLY to bring the Hopwood Triangle trial on Middleton Road and Magdala Street to an end and remove the road closures. The restriction preventing heavy wagons from parking on Coronation Avenue will remain in place, helping to protect local streets.

For residents, this decision has been a long time coming. The consultation results could hardly have been clearer: 86% of the approximately 700 respondents opposed the scheme. Yet despite that overwhelming response, the trial was approved and went ahead. Residents subsequently raised serious concerns about congestion, access, road safety and the effect on local businesses. People living on Manchester Road also felt they had been left out of the original consultation despite subsequently experiencing the impact of displaced traffic. The timing was another major concern. The trial began during the quieter summer holiday period, with residents warning that the true impact would become much more apparent once schools reopened and normal traffic levels returned. Last night, local people turned out in numbers to make sure their voices were heard. More than 50 residents attended the extraordinary meeting, but the size of the room at the old Police Station quickly became an issue. With residents understandably frustrated about access to a public meeting concerning their own streets, tensions rose and the meeting came close to being suspended. At that point, Reform UK Councillor Stuart Crawford intervened constructively. Recognising that many residents had already heard the Highways presentations and wanted councillors to make a decision, Stuart engaged directly with those in attendance, helped calm the situation and pressed for the meeting to move on to the vote rather than risk the evening ending without a decision. The vote was then taken. Every councillor voted to end the trial. That means the temporary road closures will now be removed, while the restriction on heavy wagons parking on Coronation Avenue will remain. And then there is the cost. The figures presented for the scheme are stark: £110,000 to install the temporary measures. That is £110,000 of public money associated with introducing and then removing a trial which had already been rejected by 86% of consultation respondents. The scheme was voted through back in November by Labour councillors Angela Brown, Paul O’Neil, Peter Hodgkinson, Peter Joinson, Susan Emmott and Liam O’Rourke, despite 86% of consultation respondents opposing it. Last night, the decision went the other way. Whatever political arguments follow, one fact should not be forgotten: local residents spoke up, kept speaking up and ultimately got the result they had been asking for. Reform UK will continue to stand with residents when decisions affecting their communities need to be challenged. A huge thank you to everybody who attended, everybody who responded to the original consultation, and everybody who refused to allow their concerns to be ignored. This was people power in action, and people power won.
