title: Rochdale AFC recruiting for five roles across first team, academy and women's side ahead of League Two return
excerpt: Promotion back to the Football League means growth off the pitch too: Dale are hiring a kit assistant, performance analysts, an academy lead coach and a women's first team physio.
content_html:
Rochdale AFC has announced five vacancies across the club as it gears up for life back in the Football League.

The roles span the men's first team, the academy and the women's first team: a kit assistant, two performance analysts, a youth development phase lead coach and a women's first team physiotherapist or sports therapist.

The recruitment drive is a direct consequence of the club's growth. Jim McNulty's side won promotion back to Sky Bet League Two at Wembley in May, ending three seasons in the National League, and a return to the EFL brings bigger demands across every department - from matchday operations to sports science and the academy.

The kit assistant role, focused on the men's first team, is aimed at someone passionate about providing excellent service across the club's teams, with applications closing at 5pm on Friday 14 August. The club is also seeking a men's first team performance analysis work placement student for the 2026/27 season - a role suited to a student taking a sandwich year in an undergraduate degree, though masters students and recent graduates seeking industry experience will be considered.

On the academy side, Rochdale is recruiting a youth development phase lead coach. Applicants must hold a UEFA A Licence and relevant youth coaching qualifications, with previous experience in a professional academy environment an advantage. The club has said academy positions are subject to a Category 3 licence under the Elite Player Performance Plan being awarded this summer - a significant step for an academy that has long punched above its weight in producing first-team players.

The women's first team is recruiting a physiotherapist or sports therapist on a part-time, sessional basis, covering all women's first team fixtures, at least one training session a week, and injury rehabilitation and gym-based work.

The vacancies come with the 2026/27 campaign only just under way. Dale opened their season with a Carabao Cup preliminary round trip to Tranmere Rovers, and the League Two campaign is in its opening days - far too early for the table to tell us anything meaningful about how the newly promoted side will fare. The summer has brought new faces to Sandy Lane, including French midfielder Gomez-Mancini, midfielder Humbles, and Jason Taylor joining the coaching staff.

Full job adverts, including details of how to apply, are available on the club's website at rochdaleafc.co.uk, with any further academy vacancies listed on the EFL's iRecruit platform.

title: Fraudsters who fought over the pensioners they were fleecing jailed - Rochdale woman among victims of £97,000 scam
excerpt: Eight people have been sentenced over a roofing scam that took £97,000 from five elderly victims in three months - including £7,800 from a 77-year-old Rochdale woman. Two victims died before seeing justice.
content_html:
A group of fraudsters who squabbled over the vulnerable pensioners they were ripping off have been jailed - including for a scam that stripped £7,800 from a 77-year-old Rochdale woman.

Eight people have now been sentenced over a ruthless building scam that took around £97,000 from five elderly victims across England in the space of just three months. They pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud and related money laundering offences.

The fraudsters pressured pensioners into handing over cash, making bank transfers and signing large cheques for roof repairs that were never carried out.

The 77-year-old woman from Rochdale was pressured into handing over cash, making transfers and signing cheques totalling £7,800, forced to dip into savings to pay for work that was never done.

Some of the most disturbing details emerged when police examined messages recovered from the offenders' phones. Two rival groups of scammers had independently targeted the same vulnerable man in Ellesmere Port. They regularly took him to local cash machines and made him withdraw money, and also used his bank card to buy themselves food and groceries. As his money ran out, the two rival factions clashed over who had the right to keep defrauding him.

The offending only came to light when the man's regular direct debits started to bounce because his account had been drained, and he turned to a friend for help.

Other victims included an elderly man in Ellesmere Port persuaded to write cheques worth £34,500 for roof work that was never completed, an elderly woman in Coventry whose signed blank cheques were written out for £13,000, and an elderly woman in Corby who had unnecessary roof repairs carried out to a poor standard.

The stolen money was laundered through the bank accounts of several accomplices before being spent on expensive meals and luxury Rolex watches.

Tragically, two of the elderly victims died before the gang finally appeared in court and never saw justice served.

Detective Constable Rob Mackay, of Ellesmere Port CID, who led the investigation, described it as a lengthy and complex inquiry.

The case is a reminder of how doorstep criminals operate: unsolicited callers claiming urgent roof or building problems, pressure to pay immediately in cash or by cheque, and escorted trips to the bank. Trading standards advice is never to agree to work from a cold caller, to seek quotes from traders you approach yourself, and to talk to a trusted friend or family member before parting with money. Anyone who believes an elderly relative or neighbour is being targeted can contact police on 101, or Action Fraud.

title: Hundreds of families join Holiday Hive fun in the parks - and it's back in libraries next week
excerpt: Lawn games, bubble stations and free books drew hundreds of families to the parks this week. The Holiday Hive moves back into libraries next week, starting with a ballerina craft at Spotland.
content_html:
Hundreds of families joined Rochdale Borough Libraries' Holiday Hive in parks across the borough this week, making the most of the sunshine and the borough's green spaces.

The libraries service thanked everyone who came along, with families enjoying lawn games, bubble stations, music stations, parachute play and musical crafts - and well done to everyone who managed to find a free book hidden amongst the activities.

The Holiday Hive returns to library buildings from next week, starting with a ballerina craft at Spotland Library.

There's an extra incentive to keep reading through the summer too. The Holiday Hive will be giving away more free books to any child who completes the Summer Reading Challenge whilst attending a Holiday Hive session - while stocks last, so families are urged not to delay.

The Summer Reading Challenge encourages children to keep reading through the long break, when many pupils' reading otherwise slips back before September. Signing up is free through the borough's libraries.

For venue details and times, families can check Rochdale Borough Libraries' Facebook events page at facebook.com/RochdaleBoroughLibraries/events, or visit the libraries website for the full summer programme.

title: Got a Uniform For All order waiting? Balderstone Library needs the shelf space
excerpt: The school uniform reuse scheme says its collection point is 'busier than Amazon's warehouse' - and is asking families with ready-to-collect orders to pick them up to make room for new deliveries.
content_html:
Families with a school uniform order waiting at Balderstone Library are being asked to collect it as soon as possible - because the shelves are full and new deliveries are arriving fast.

Uniform For All, the borough scheme that gives pre-loved school uniform a second life, says anyone who has received an order-ready-to-pick-up email from www.uniformforall.co.uk should call in and collect it promptly to make space. "It's busier than Amazon's warehouse at the Uniform For All office right now," the scheme said.

What is Uniform For All?

Uniform For All collects donated school uniform - the coats, jumpers, polo shirts, trousers and PE kit that children outgrow long before they wear out - checks and sorts it, and passes it on to families across the borough. Orders are placed through the website and collected locally, with Balderstone Library serving as a collection and donation point.

The idea is simple but the impact is real. Kitting a child out for September can cost families well over a hundred pounds per child, and for households already stretched by rent, bills and food, uniform costs land at exactly the wrong time of year. A reuse scheme means good clothing goes to a child who needs it instead of landfill, families keep money in their pockets, and children start term dressed the same as everyone else.

With the summer holidays in full swing and the new school year only weeks away, demand is at its annual peak - hence the plea for prompt collections.

How to donate

If you have school uniform your children have outgrown, you can drop it off at Balderstone Library too. Clean, wearable items are what the scheme needs most. And if your child needs uniform for September, orders can be placed at www.uniformforall.co.uk.

title: Rainbow Health Group invites residents to open day at new clinic after 17 years on Hornby Street
excerpt: The health and wellbeing clinic is moving to a new home after 17 years, and is welcoming the community to an open day this Saturday - with the Mayor and Mayoress performing the official opening at 1pm.
content_html:
A local health and wellbeing clinic is inviting Milnrow and Newhey residents - and anyone else who fancies a look around - to celebrate the start of a new chapter this weekend.

After 17 years at its Hornby Street clinic, Rainbow Health Group is moving to a brand-new home, and is holding an open day on Saturday 8 August from 11am to 3pm to welcome the community through the doors.

The clinic offers a range of treatments including sports massage, clinical massage, acupuncture, K-Laser therapy, podiatry and rehabilitation, helping people recover from injuries, manage pain and improve their overall wellbeing.

Its new address is Unit 9A, Southgate Industrial Park, Green Lane, Heywood, OL10 1ND.

Visitors on the day can explore the new clinic, meet the team, and learn more about the treatments and services on offer, with complimentary light refreshments provided. There will also be a charity raffle in aid of Help 4 All, and the Mayor and Mayoress will officially open the clinic at 1pm.

"Whether you've been visiting us for years or have never heard of Rainbow Health Group before, everyone is welcome," the clinic said. "We'd love to see you there and celebrate this exciting new chapter with our local community."

title: New grassroots club Heywood Hurricanes FC appeals for raffle prizes to keep football free for every child
excerpt: A brand-new junior football club with one simple goal - making the game accessible to every child regardless of family finances - is asking local businesses to donate raffle prizes.
content_html:
A brand-new grassroots football club in Heywood is appealing to local businesses for raffle prizes as it works to keep the game affordable for every child who wants to play.

Heywood Hurricanes FC has been set up with what it calls one simple goal: to make football accessible for every child. The club says every young player deserves the opportunity to enjoy football, make friends, build confidence and be part of a team - regardless of their family's financial circumstances.

Rather than leaning on sponsorship from the outset, the club is trying to raise funds itself. "As a brand-new club, we're under no illusion that sponsorships are easy to come by," the Hurricanes said. "We know local businesses receive lots of requests, and we completely understand that not everyone is in a position to help financially."

Over the coming weeks the club will hold a raffle to help ease the financial burden on its families and keep costs as low as possible for players. It is asking whether any local businesses would be willing to donate a prize - a voucher, gift hamper, experience, service, or anything else. Every donation, big or small, the club says, will make a genuine difference.

The appeal comes at a time when many families are struggling with the cost of children's sport. Subs, kit, boots and travel add up quickly, and money is increasingly the reason children drop out of the game. By fundraising to keep its own costs down, the Hurricanes hope no child in Heywood is priced off the pitch.

"Your generosity will help us provide opportunities for children to play the game they love without additional financial pressure on their parents, especially at a time when many families are finding things incredibly tough," the club said.

Anyone who would like to support Heywood Hurricanes, or who knows someone who might be able to help, can get in touch by messaging the club's Facebook page.

title: RBH warns tenants over cold-calling 'claims farmers' offering compensation for repairs
excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing says customers are being cold-called by firms offering 'no win, no fee' solicitors for repair claims - a warning that lands against the backdrop of the Awaab Ishak tragedy and the reforms that followed.
content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing has warned tenants to be on their guard after a number of customers reported being cold-called by a firm asking about property repairs.

The landlord says the callers offered to provide a solicitor to work on tenants' behalf so they could claim compensation. Firms operating this way - sometimes called claims management companies or "claims farmers" - typically describe themselves as offering "no win, no fee" services.

"Be careful - if something sounds too good to be true, it probably is," RBH said, urging anyone with a concern about their home to talk to the landlord directly so it can be sorted. Repairs can be reported via the MyRBH portal at www.myrbh.org.uk, by calling Freephone 0800 027 7769, or by emailing rbh.repairs@rbh.org.uk. RBH says it aims to get things right first time, and tenants who feel it has fallen short can find details of how to complain at www.rbh.org.uk/feedback.

Why this matters in Rochdale

No warning about housing disrepair in this borough can be read in isolation from what happened to Awaab Ishak.

Awaab was two years old when he died in December 2020. In November 2022, a coroner concluded that his death was caused by prolonged exposure to mould in his family's RBH flat on the Freehold estate - mould his parents had repeatedly reported. The case caused national outrage, cost RBH its chief executive, and led directly to Awaab's Law, which sets legal time limits for social landlords in England to investigate and fix damp, mould and other hazards, with the first phase of those duties coming into force in October 2025.

That history cuts two ways. It explains why RBH is now at pains to encourage tenants to report repairs directly and to demonstrate that reports will be acted on - rebuilding confidence that was badly damaged. And it also explains why claims firms see RBH tenants as a market worth cold-calling: disrepair claims against social landlords have grown sharply across the country, and a landlord with RBH's recent history is an obvious target for firms seeking clients.

Tenants are entitled to seek independent legal advice about genuine disrepair, and nothing prevents them doing so. But consumer bodies have long warned that some claims firms take large cuts of any compensation, sign tenants up to agreements with exit fees, or pursue claims that leave tenants worse off than simply having the repair done. A tenant's first and simplest route remains reporting the problem to the landlord - and, if it is not fixed, escalating through the complaints process and then to the Housing Ombudsman, which is free.

The test for RBH is the one Awaab's case set: whether reports of damp, mould and disrepair are fixed properly and fast, first time. If they are, the cold-callers will find little to farm.
legal_disclaimer: RBH's warning is reported as published by the landlord. References to the death of Awaab Ishak reflect the coroner's findings of November 2022. No specific claims management firm is identified in this article and no allegation of unlawful conduct is made against any firm; tenants remain entitled to seek independent legal advice.

title: Shoppers donate 368 kilos of food at Rochdale Foodbank's Morrisons Kingsway drive
excerpt: Generous shoppers added extra items to their trolleys over two days at Morrisons Kingsway, donating 368kg of food. How the foodbank works, how to get help - and how to give it.
content_html:
Shoppers at Morrisons Kingsway have donated a remarkable 368 kilos of food to Rochdale Foodbank after a two-day food drive at the store last Thursday and Friday.

The foodbank thanked all the generous shoppers who added extra items to their shopping, saying donations came in all shapes and sizes and included many of its most needed items. The charity also paid special tribute to the volunteers who staffed the collection and made the event a success, adding that every single item received will make a big difference to its clients.

Rochdale Foodbank has been part of life in the town for more than a decade. Registered as a charity in its own right in 2017, it operates as part of the Trussell network of food banks and is run almost entirely by volunteers - around 70 of them - who sort, date-check and pack donated food into emergency parcels at its base off Newgate in the town centre.

How the foodbank works

The foodbank operates on a referral system. Care professionals - including GPs, health visitors, social workers, Citizens Advice staff, welfare officers, the police and probation services - identify people in crisis and issue them with a foodbank voucher. That voucher can then be exchanged at a foodbank session for an emergency parcel containing at least three days of nutritionally balanced food. Volunteers meet clients over a cup of tea and can signpost them to agencies able to help with the longer-term problem, from debt advice to benefits support.

Alongside its main sessions, the foodbank has expanded in recent years. A Saturday morning session runs at Branches Christian Fellowship in Smallbridge, where clients can collect parcels between 10am and 12pm, and the charity has also opened Rochdale Central Pantry in the Rochdale Exchange Shopping Centre - a membership pantry for people who have recently needed foodbank support and could use a little extra help each week.

If you need help, you can call the foodbank on 0300 102 1646 or visit rochdale.foodbank.org.uk, which lists the organisations able to issue vouchers.

How to donate

More than nine in ten items given out by Trussell network food banks are donated by the public, which is why collections like the Morrisons drive matter so much. There are permanent donation points in Rochdale's larger supermarkets, including Tesco, Asda and Morrisons, intended for food purchased in-store. Larger donations can be dropped off at the foodbank's warehouse via the Newgate service area - ring ahead on 0300 102 1646 for big deliveries - and the foodbank publishes a shopping list of the items it most urgently needs on its website. Money donations, which help cover running costs and fill gaps in donated stock, can also be made through the website.

As the foodbank itself puts it: even if it's just one tin every week, every tin helps.

title: Loombrook Meadows: 302 new homes coming to Castleton - what we know so far
excerpt: Barratt Homes has broken ground on a 302-home development at Cowm Top Lane, with two, three and four bedroom houses expected to go on sale from autumn. What's being built, who it's for, and the affordability question.
content_html:
A brand new development of two, three and four bedroom homes is coming to Castleton - and buyers are already being invited to register their interest.

Loombrook Meadows, being built by Barratt Homes on Cowm Top Lane, will deliver 302 new homes on the southern edge of the borough. Construction began in early June, and the developer expects the first properties to be available to reserve from autumn 2026.

Barratt says the homes will be built with a stone effect intended to match the character of the local area, using modern construction methods designed to make them more energy efficient and cheaper to run. The development is expected to support around 604 jobs during construction.

The developer is pitching the site at young professionals, first-time buyers and growing families, pointing to Castleton railway station, the M62 and local schools and shops on the doorstep. Rhys Nicholson, managing director at Barratt Homes Manchester, said the scheme had already seen strong interest from those groups and encouraged anyone interested to register for updates on the homes available later this year.

How affordable will they be?

Prices for Loombrook Meadows have not yet been released. As a guide, Barratt's other current developments in the wider area list two to four bedroom homes from around £198,000 up to £459,000, and the company promotes schemes such as reduced-rate mortgage products and assisted moves for buyers with a home to sell. Until the first releases are priced, it is impossible to say where Loombrook Meadows will sit within that range, or how many of the 302 homes will be classed as affordable housing - a figure usually settled through the planning process. Rochdale Daily has asked for details of the affordable housing provision and will update this article when they are confirmed.

The bigger picture

The development lands in the middle of a familiar local argument. Rochdale, like most of Greater Manchester, does not have enough homes: demand for social housing far outstrips supply, private rents have climbed steeply, and many working households find themselves priced out of buying altogether. New building on this scale is one of the few levers that can ease that pressure.

At the same time, large housing schemes in and around Castleton routinely draw concern from existing residents about traffic on already busy roads, pressure on GP surgeries and school places, and the loss of open land. Those arguments were aired when the Cowm Top site went through planning, and they will not disappear now the diggers have arrived.

What is not in dispute is the need. A borough of around 220,000 people cannot house its next generation in its existing stock, and every credible plan for Rochdale's future involves building substantially more homes. The test for Loombrook Meadows will be whether the homes that emerge are ones ordinary Rochdale families can actually afford - and whether the infrastructure around them keeps pace.

Buyers can register their interest through the Barratt Homes website.

title: Comment: Government changes to local planning risk shutting residents out
excerpt: From October 2026, most planning applications will be decided by officers with no route to a public committee hearing. Castleton councillor David Jones argues the reforms trade local democracy for speed.
content_html:
This is a comment article by Councillor David Jones (Reform UK, Castleton), a member of Rochdale Borough Council's Planning Committee. The views expressed are his own.

As a member of Rochdale Council's Planning Committee, I want to make residents aware of significant changes being introduced by the Labour Government to the way planning applications are decided.

From 31 October 2026, a new national system will divide planning applications into two schedules.

Schedule 1 applications must be decided by planning officers, with no option for them to be brought before the Planning Committee. This will include householder applications, minor commercial developments and some residential developments of up to nine homes. Regardless of the level of local concern, these applications will not receive a public decision by elected members.

For Schedule 2 applications, the starting assumption will also be that they are decided by officers. They will only come before the Planning Committee if they meet a test relating to significant local or planning issues, and both a nominated senior planning officer and the chair of the Planning Committee agree that committee consideration is warranted. If they cannot agree, the application will remain with officers.

Perhaps most concerningly, ward councillors will lose the ability to call a planning application before the committee. Councils will also be unable to guarantee committee consideration simply because an application has attracted a large number of objections.

Residents will still be able to submit comments and objections, and relevant planning concerns must still be considered. However, making an objection is not the same as having the application examined and debated publicly by elected councillors.

HMOs are a major concern for many Castleton residents. Where an HMO proposal requires planning permission, residents may submit objections, but neither they nor their ward councillor will be able to guarantee that it receives a public committee hearing. Instead, that decision will rest with a senior officer and the committee chair.

The Government says these changes will provide greater consistency and allow committees to concentrate on the most significant developments.

I understand the need for an efficient planning system, but I do not believe efficiency should come at the expense of local democracy.

A planning application that appears "minor" on paper can have a major impact on the people living beside it. Local circumstances cannot always be understood through a national classification or an officer's written report.

In my view, removing councillors' call-in powers takes away an important democratic safeguard. It weakens the ability of elected representatives to ensure that residents' legitimate concerns are heard and debated publicly.

This is not about councillors ignoring planning law or blocking development without proper grounds. It is about retaining openness, accountability and meaningful local representation in decisions that can permanently affect our neighbourhoods.

I will continue to speak up for Castleton residents and raise my concerns about any change that further distances local people from decisions affecting where they live.

Greater consistency should not mean less democracy, and faster decisions should not mean residents having less of a say.

Details of the national scheme of delegation are as described by the author and readers should consult official government guidance for the definitive position.

title: Reform UK councillors explain vote against 74-bed Sparth House care home
excerpt: All three Reform UK members of Rochdale's Planning Committee voted against the revised 74-bed care home at Sparth House, saying concerns over scale, trees and parking had not been resolved.
content_html:
All three Reform UK councillors serving on Rochdale Borough Council's Planning Committee voted against the proposed 74-bed care home development at Sparth House, Manchester Road, when the application returned to the Committee.

The application had previously been deferred after members raised concerns regarding the scale and massing of the proposed building, its impact on neighbouring residents, the loss of mature trees, parking provision and whether the development represented an appropriate use of the site.

In a statement setting out their reasons, the Reform UK group said that when the revised application returned to Committee, its councillors remained of the view that those concerns had not been adequately addressed. Whilst amendments had been made to the application, the group said it did not believe they sufficiently overcame the fundamental planning issues that had led to the original deferral.

"Let us be absolutely clear," the statement said. "Reform UK fully supports investment in high-quality care facilities. We recognise the growing need for dementia and nursing care across Rochdale Borough, particularly as our population ages. However, supporting better care does not mean supporting every planning application regardless of its merits."

The group said every development must be judged on whether it is appropriate for its location, whether it protects neighbouring residents, whether it provides suitable living conditions for future occupants and whether local infrastructure is capable of supporting it.

In this case, the Reform UK councillors concluded that the proposed four-storey building represented an overdevelopment of a constrained site, arguing that its overall scale, height and massing would create an overbearing presence, harm the character of the surrounding area and adversely affect neighbouring residential amenity.

The councillors also said they were concerned by the environmental impact of the proposal, including the loss of mature trees, together with what they considered to be limited meaningful outdoor space for a development accommodating 74 vulnerable residents.

Parking provision remained another significant concern for the group. With 13 parking spaces proposed for staff, visitors, healthcare professionals and servicing vehicles, the councillors considered there to be a real risk of additional parking pressure on surrounding residential streets.

Whilst not a material planning consideration and ultimately a matter governed by Building Regulations, the group said members also noted concerns raised during the planning process regarding the practical challenges of evacuating a four-storey building occupied by elderly and vulnerable residents, including people living with dementia, in the event of an emergency. Although these matters fall outside the planning system, the councillors said they nevertheless formed part of the wider public concerns expressed during the application process.

The statement also criticised the local MP, Elsie Blundell, who the group said had commented critically on the decision on social media rather than engaging with the planning concerns debated by the Committee. "Planning decisions should be based on planning merits, evidence and policy, not reduced to political point scoring," the group said. Ms Blundell has been invited to respond, and any reply will be added to this article.

The Reform UK councillors said their responsibility as Planning Committee members is not to approve applications simply because they provide a particular type of development, but to consider every application impartially against planning policy, the evidence before them and the impact on both existing and future residents.

"Had this application demonstrated an appropriate scale, adequate infrastructure, sufficient parking, suitable landscaping and a design compatible with its surroundings, Reform UK would have had no hesitation in supporting it," the statement concluded. "Good care homes deserve good planning. Residents deserve developments that are both needed and appropriate. We will continue to stand up for both."

Planning applications refused by the Committee can be appealed by the applicant to the Planning Inspectorate.

title: 60 police officer misconduct cases in a single year. To protect and serve?
excerpt: A Rochdale Daily analysis of Greater Manchester Police's own published misconduct reports found 60 officer misconduct case entries in 2025 - with 41 ending in dismissal or a finding that dismissal would have followed.
content_html:
The words "To Protect & Serve" represent one of the most recognisable ideals of modern policing. The overwhelming majority of police officers go to work every day to protect the public with professionalism and integrity.

But Greater Manchester Police's own published misconduct records reveal another side of policing that deserves public scrutiny.

An analysis by Rochdale Daily of GMP's published quarterly misconduct outcome reports found 60 police officer misconduct case entries during 2025.

Those cases involved allegations ranging from criminal convictions and violence to discriminatory behaviour, misuse of confidential police systems and failures to investigate serious offences.

Among the allegations recorded by GMP were: assault occasioning actual bodily harm; drink-driving convictions; positive drug tests, including cocaine; sexual assault; domestic abuse and coercive control allegations considered through misconduct proceedings; criminal damage; misuse of police computer systems; racist, misogynistic, homophobic and discriminatory messages; sexual harassment of colleagues; inappropriate contact with vulnerable members of the public; failures to investigate allegations of rape; and breaches of police business interest regulations.

The outcomes were equally striking.

Of the 60 officer misconduct case entries reviewed, 19 resulted in dismissal without notice. A further 22 resulted in findings that the officer would have been dismissed had they still been serving with Greater Manchester Police. Six resulted in final written warnings, five in written warnings, and two allegations were not proven. The remaining cases resulted in other disciplinary outcomes, including practice improvement or findings below the threshold for gross misconduct.

In other words, 41 of the 60 cases resulted in either dismissal or a finding that dismissal would have been the outcome had the officer remained in service.

Every misconduct case has its own facts and circumstances, and misconduct proceedings are separate from criminal court proceedings. Some officers had already resigned or retired before their hearings concluded, which is why some outcomes are recorded as "would have been dismissed."

It is also important to recognise that Greater Manchester Police employs thousands of officers. The misconduct cases published during 2025 represent a small proportion of the overall workforce, and the published reports do not suggest that misconduct is typical of policing within the force.

Nevertheless, policing relies on public confidence. Every misconduct finding, particularly those involving violence, dishonesty, discrimination, abuse of authority or failures to investigate serious crime, has the potential to undermine that trust.

Transparency matters.

That is why Rochdale Daily has launched Police Watch, an ongoing series examining police accountability using official records, misconduct decisions, court judgments, Freedom of Information responses and reports from independent oversight bodies.

This investigation is not about attacking policing. It is about ensuring that the public can see how misconduct is identified, investigated and dealt with when officers fall below the standards expected of them.

Methodology: This analysis is based on Greater Manchester Police's published quarterly misconduct outcome reports covering January to December 2025. The figure of 60 refers to police officer misconduct case entries published by GMP. Police staff cases were excluded from the analysis. Because some published cases are anonymised, the reports do not always allow confirmation that every entry relates to a different individual, and therefore the figure should be understood as the number of recorded officer misconduct cases rather than confirmed unique officers.

Sources: Greater Manchester Police's official published misconduct outcome reports - GMP Misconduct Outcomes, January to March 2025; April to June 2025; July to September 2025; and October to December 2025.

title: Lord-Lieutenant's visit, a surprise inspection passed and a packed cafe: quite a week for Whitworth's Stronger Together
excerpt: The Whitworth carers' group welcomed the King's representative in Lancashire, retained its 5-star hygiene rating in a surprise inspection, and saw its Community Cafe overflow into the main hall — all in one week.
content_html:
A remarkable week for Whitworth carers' group Stronger Together began with a royal representative at the door and ended with a cafe so busy it spilled into the main hall.

On Monday the group welcomed the Lord-Lieutenant of Lancashire, Amanda Parker, and her husband Robert. Mrs Parker is His Majesty The King's personal representative in Lancashire and the first woman to hold the role in the county in almost five hundred years, and her visit is a mark of how far the volunteer-run group has come.

The same day brought a test of a different kind: an unannounced visit from environmental health officers just before lunch service. The inspectors found everything in order and the group retained its food hygiene rating of 5, the top score, which it has held since Rossendale Borough Council first awarded it in December 2024.

By Tuesday the group's Community Cafe was packed, with every table full and half of the main hall pressed into service to seat everyone.

Stronger Together was founded in 2023 by Angela Forster and Kathleen Proctor, both unpaid carers themselves, after they found there was nowhere locally for carers to turn for support. What began as a weekly coffee morning has grown into something much bigger, now based at The Ashcroft on Market Street, where volunteers serve more than 70 fresh, home-cooked meals every week alongside cakes and unlimited drinks, all free of charge with donation pots for those who wish to give.

The group describes itself as a warm, safe space offering advice and emotional and practical support, with activities including prize bingo, crafts and quizzes, and it runs entirely on fundraising, raffles, donations and grants. A crowdfunded project launched last year added gentle exercise sessions with a qualified trainer, healthy eating advice and a singing group open to all ages and abilities.

Recognition has followed. The founders received a Mayor's Special Award at the Whitworth Business and Community Awards in 2023, with the then Mayor of Whitworth describing the pair as truly inspirational to the community. The group went on to win the Not-for-Profit category at the Rossendale Business Awards, and this summer it was shortlisted for Community Group of the Year at the Pride of Rossendale Awards.

Reflecting on the week, the founders thanked the group's volunteers and supporters, saying the group is truly blessed in the people around it.

Anyone who would like to support Stronger Together, volunteer or find out about its sessions can contact the group through its Facebook page.

Families across the borough are being invited to a full day of free activities next week as Creativity for All takes over Rochdale town centre, part of Touchstones' Side-by-Side festival.

The event runs on Thursday 13 August from 10.45am to 4pm across the town centre and Temporary Touchstones, and everything on the programme is free.

Highlights include 100 free ice creams from 12pm, handed out on a first come, first served basis, so families are advised to arrive early. Throughout the day there will be artist-inspired workshops where children and adults can make their own creations and take them home, alongside Make Your Mark activities suitable for all ages.

A pop-up play area will offer giant games, chalks and marble runs, while Movers, Shakers and Storymakers sessions are aimed at the youngest visitors, ages 0 to 4.

Between 11am and 4pm, visitors can also drop into a one-day-only art experience staged in partnership with ARTIST ROOMS.

Organisers say the day is designed so there is something for everyone, whether that is keeping the kids entertained over the summer holidays, getting creative together or simply enjoying a day out in the town centre.

title: Elderly lady found after incredible community effort
excerpt: A woman in her 70s who went missing in Newhey has been found after hundreds of residents joined Greater Manchester Police in an extraordinary community search.
content_html:
An elderly woman who went missing in Newhey has been found following an extraordinary community effort involving hundreds of local residents.

Christine, who is in her 70s, was reported missing earlier in the evening, prompting an urgent response from Greater Manchester Police and a huge mobilisation across Newhey and the surrounding area.

As concern grew, residents left their homes to help officers search on the ground. People walked streets, paths and open spaces, checked nearby areas and shared information rapidly across community groups in an effort to bring Christine home.

The response was remarkable. Hundreds of people are understood to have assisted either directly with searches or by sharing appeals and helping coordinate information alongside GMP.

At around 11pm, local woman Charlotte Rigby found Christine. In a touching detail after hours of worry, Christine was found clutching a bunch of flowers.

News that she had been located was met with enormous relief across the community, bringing a frightening evening to the best possible conclusion.

Tonight demonstrated Newhey and the wider Rochdale borough at its very best. Residents did not simply share a post and hope for good news. They put on their shoes, went outside and actively helped search for someone who needed them.

Credit must also go to Greater Manchester Police and everyone who supported the search, but special recognition is due to the countless members of the public who gave their time and refused to give up.

The borough should be very proud tonight. This was community spirit in its purest form, and the outcome is the great news everyone had been hoping for.

Out of respect for Christine and her family, no further personal or medical details should be shared unless released through official channels.

title: Shabir Ahmed barred from Rochdale under strict licence conditions as government pushes to deport him
excerpt: The Rochdale grooming gang ringleader is excluded from the borough under his licence conditions, is living under 24-hour supervision at an undisclosed location outside the area, and faces active government efforts to deport him.
content_html:
Shabir Ahmed, the ringleader of the Rochdale grooming gang jailed in 2012, was released from prison on licence on 2 July after serving 14 years of a 22-year sentence for multiple rape and sexual offences against young girls. Rochdale Daily can confirm, based on conditions set out by the Home Office and Ministry of Justice, that he is not living in Rochdale and is barred from entering the borough.

His licence conditions include an exclusion zone covering Rochdale and Oldham, electronic GPS tagging to monitor his movements, a requirement to live in approved accommodation staffed 24 hours a day, and a ban from his last known address in Oldham. The Ministry of Justice has said he is subject to the toughest supervision possible and would be returned to prison immediately if any condition were breached.

Ahmed, 73, was initially placed in approved premises in Accrington, Lancashire. After that address was shared on social media, prompting protests in the town and calls from the local MP for his removal, he was moved. The government has not confirmed his current location, and Rochdale Daily will not publish unverified claims about his whereabouts. Speculation of that kind has already forced one relocation and puts bystanders at the shared addresses at risk.

The question survivors and residents have pressed hardest is why he remains in the country at all. Ahmed was stripped of his British citizenship after his conviction, and victims had been led to believe he would be deported on release. It has since emerged that a provision of the Immigration Act 1971 prevents the removal of Commonwealth citizens who arrived in the United Kingdom before 1973, as Ahmed did as a teenager in 1967.

The government says it is exploring every option to remove him. Downing Street has confirmed talks with Pakistan, and a Home Office minister told the Commons that “all options are on the table”, saying the government would not give up its efforts given the nature of his crimes. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has set out plans to amend the 1971 Act so that people convicted of the most serious offences, including child sexual exploitation, can no longer rely on its protections, and ministers have indicated emergency legislation could be considered.

Pakistan, however, has publicly rejected the request. Officials in Islamabad have said responsibility for Ahmed lies with Britain, where he was brought up, and he is reported to have renounced his Pakistani citizenship, which complicates removal further even if the British law changes. The Prime Minister's spokesman has declined to comment on specific proposals while the talks continue.

The pressure on ministers is cross-party. The Conservatives have proposed amending the government's immigration legislation to close the loophole, with their leader urging ministers to adopt the change and the shadow home secretary suggesting visa sanctions or cuts to aid if Pakistan continues to refuse. Greater Manchester's mayor is among those who have called publicly for deportation, and the MP for Hyndburn, where Ahmed was first housed, has demanded he be barred from the North West entirely.

Campaigners including former Greater Manchester Police detective Maggie Oliver have criticised the handling of the release, saying victims learned of it through social media and continue to live with fear that the authorities have not taken seriously.

Rochdale Daily will update this article as official information is released. Readers should treat any claim about Ahmed's location that does not come from the Home Office, the Ministry of Justice, Greater Manchester Police or the courts as unverified.

title: Every GP practice in Rochdale ranked by patients in the 2026 survey
excerpt: The latest GP Patient Survey shows a wide gap in reported patient experience between practices across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough and Milnrow.
content_html:
Patients have rated their experiences at GP practices across Rochdale borough in the latest national survey, revealing a wide difference between the highest and lowest results recorded on one key measure.

Rochdale Daily compared practices using the percentage of respondents who described their overall experience of their GP practice as good in the 2026 GP Patient Survey.

Dr GWD Bhima recorded the highest result among the borough practices included in the comparison, with 96.2 per cent of respondents reporting a good overall experience. Milnrow Village Practice followed on 95.4 per cent, with The Village Medical Centre in Littleborough on 94 per cent.

At the other end of the comparison, Croft Shifa Health Centre recorded 44.9 per cent. The difference between the highest and lowest results was therefore 51.3 percentage points.

The England figure was 76.7 per cent.

WHAT THE FIGURES SHOW

The results show substantial variation both across the borough and within individual townships. Heywood practices ranged from 91.8 per cent at Birtle View Medical Practice to 66.7 per cent at Heywood Health.

In Middleton, The Hive Health Centre recorded 88.9 per cent, compared with 71.9 per cent at Woodside Medical Centre.

The four Littleborough practices included in the comparison all recorded results above 87 per cent, with The Village Medical Centre leading the township on 94 per cent.

WHAT THE COMPARISON DOES NOT MEAN

The table compares practices on one patient-experience measure only. It is not a clinical-safety rating and does not assess diagnostic accuracy, prescribing, treatment outcomes or the performance of individual doctors.

The GP Patient Survey is based on a sample of registered patients, rather than every patient at each practice. Results are weighted, but smaller samples carry greater statistical uncertainty and practices serve populations with different needs and circumstances.

NHS England and Ipsos advise that the survey was not designed to create a definitive league table of GP practices. The ordering above is therefore a straightforward comparison of the published overall-experience percentage, not a declaration that one practice provides objectively better clinical care than another.

The 2026 survey was conducted between 2 January and 13 April and published on 9 July. Practices may have introduced changes since patients completed their questionnaires.

Rochdale Daily will invite practices to comment on their results and explain any improvements introduced since the survey period.

title: Heywood singer-songwriter releases heartfelt debut single 'Rewind'
excerpt: Twenty-year-old Heywood singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson has achieved a lifelong ambition with the release of her debut single, Rewind, a soulful pop track inspired by heartbreak, hope and moving forward.
content_html:
A young musician from Heywood has realised a lifelong dream with the release of her debut single.

Twenty-year-old singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson released her first original song, Rewind, on 31 July. The soulful pop track draws on her own experience of heartbreak and the realisation that someone she believed was 'the one' ultimately was not the right person after all.

Music has always played a central role in Rhiannon's life, and releasing her own song is something she says she has dreamed about since childhood.

"Having my own song has always been my biggest dream, so finally releasing Rewind is such an emotional and proud moment for me," she said.

Rhiannon worked alongside her friend, songwriter and producer Jack Carroll, who helped write and produce the track in his studio. She cites Sienna Spiro as one of her biggest musical inspirations.

The response to Rewind has already been overwhelming.

"Seeing people say they love my song means everything to me. I hope when people hear it, they remember there is always a light at the end of the tunnel and that things do get better with time."

Looking ahead, Rhiannon hopes to release an EP and continue sharing her music with the world.

"One of my biggest dreams is to hear my music played on the radio. If people enjoy Rewind, I would be so grateful if they could share it and help more people discover my music."

She added: "Thank you to everyone who has supported me so far. I appreciate every listen, every comment and every share — it truly means the world to me."

Rewind is available now on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. Rhiannon can also be followed on Facebook, Instagram at rhiannon_t05 and TikTok at @rhiannonthompsonxx.

title: Are Facebook Groups Becoming the Gatekeepers of Local News?
excerpt: Large community Facebook groups now play a major role in determining which local stories residents see, raising questions about moderation, access to information and the influence of digital gatekeepers.
content_html:
Recent posts from independent local news publishers have, at times, remained pending approval or failed to appear in large community Facebook groups. The reasons are not always clear and may range from routine moderation and administrative delays to editorial decisions made by group administrators.

Whatever the explanation, the situation raises a wider question about how much influence large local Facebook groups have over the news and viewpoints residents are exposed to.

Many of these groups have memberships larger than the circulation of traditional local newspapers. For thousands of people, they have become the primary place where local news, events and community discussion are discovered. Decisions about which posts are approved can therefore have a significant impact on what information reaches the public.

Independent journalism exists to report what is happening within a community, regardless of whether those stories are politically convenient or uncomfortable. It should not matter whether a story reflects positively or negatively on any political party, campaign group or public body. The role of journalism is to inform readers, not to tell them what to think.

Equally, moderation is an important part of running any online community. Administrators are entitled to remove unlawful material, spam, abuse, hate speech or defamatory content. However, where lawful reporting is prevented from reaching large community audiences, it is reasonable to ask whether local people are receiving a balanced picture of events.

Too often, debate can become centred on labels rather than evidence. Terms such as 'misinformation', 'divisive' or 'harmful' should only be used where they can be supported by facts. If reporting is inaccurate, it should be corrected. If facts are disputed, they should be challenged with evidence. Robust debate is healthier than silent suppression.

Independent local journalism has become increasingly important as traditional local newsrooms have shrunk. Smaller publishers often report stories that might otherwise receive little attention, giving residents access to a broader range of information and perspectives.

Ultimately, Facebook groups have become powerful gatekeepers of local information. That influence brings responsibility. While moderators are free to manage their communities as they see fit, readers should also recognise that what appears in a Facebook feed is not necessarily the full picture of what is happening across Rochdale borough.

A healthy democracy depends on people having access to a range of lawful reporting and being trusted to reach their own conclusions.

title: Rochdale's biggest event returns this Saturday as Feel Good Festival takes over the town centre
excerpt: Thousands of people are expected to descend on Rochdale town centre this Saturday as the borough's biggest annual event returns with headline performances from Gabrielle, Ash and Starsailor alongside a packed programme of live music, street food and family entertainment.
content_html:
Rochdale's biggest and most attended annual event returns on Saturday 8 August as the Feel Good Festival once again transforms the town centre into one of Greater Manchester's largest free celebrations of live music, food and entertainment.

Thousands of visitors are expected to flock to Rochdale throughout the day, with the stunning backdrop of the newly restored Rochdale Town Hall providing the setting for a packed programme of performances, street food and family activities.

Headlining this year's main stage in Town Hall Square is BRIT Award-winning singer Gabrielle, whose career has produced chart-topping hits including Dreams, Rise and Out of Reach. She will be joined by legendary Northern Irish rock band Ash and indie favourites Starsailor, alongside performances from The Allergies, Alex Spencer, K-STATE, Metro and Dave Sweetmore.

Away from the main stage, live music will continue throughout the day inside venues across Rochdale town centre, with pubs, bars and independent venues hosting local artists and emerging talent, creating a festival atmosphere across the borough.

The festival officially opens at 11:30am, with entertainment continuing throughout the afternoon and evening before the headline performances conclude at approximately 10:45pm.

One of the festival's biggest attractions remains its popular Food and Drink Village, where visitors can enjoy everything from gourmet burgers and pizzas to international street food, loaded fries, desserts, artisan coffee, ice cream, licensed bars and locally produced drinks. Independent traders from across the region will once again showcase a wide variety of food and beverages throughout the day.

Visitors travelling by car are encouraged to use Rochdale town centre's public car parks, including those at Number One Riverside, Rochdale Exchange Shopping Centre and nearby council-operated facilities. Due to the popularity of the event and temporary road closures, organisers recommend arriving early or making use of public transport wherever possible. Rochdale Railway Station, Rochdale Interchange and the Bee Network Metrolink stop are all within a short walking distance of the festival site.

The event has been designed to be accessible for everyone. Step-free routes are available throughout the main festival site, accessible toilets are provided, designated accessible viewing areas will be available near the main stage and British Sign Language interpretation will accompany selected performances. Festival stewards will also be on hand throughout the day to assist visitors requiring additional support.

Since launching in 2008, the Feel Good Festival has welcomed internationally renowned artists to Rochdale and has become one of the North West's premier town-centre music festivals. Beyond the entertainment, it provides a significant boost to the local economy, with restaurants, cafés, bars, shops and hotels all benefiting from the influx of visitors.

Whether you're heading into town to sing along with Gabrielle, relive the guitar anthems of Ash, enjoy Starsailor's iconic hits or simply spend the day sampling fantastic food while supporting local businesses, the Feel Good Festival promises another unforgettable celebration of everything Rochdale has to offer.

title: Interactive Pumpkin Patch and Autumn Festival heading to Castleton this autumn
excerpt: Families looking for an autumn day out won't have far to travel as The Patchworks Interactive Pumpkin Patch and Autumn Festival returns to nearby Castleton with pumpkin picking, games, food and seasonal entertainment.
content_html:
Autumn is just around the corner and one of the Peak District's newest family attractions is preparing to welcome visitors from across Greater Manchester.

The Patchworks Interactive Pumpkin Patch and Autumn Festival will return to Castleton throughout October, offering a traditional pumpkin-picking experience alongside interactive games, seasonal activities, marshmallow toasting, food, drinks and plenty of opportunities for those all-important autumn photographs. The attraction is expected to operate across selected dates from early October until Halloween.

Located at the foot of Winnats Pass near Castleton, the attraction is less than an hour's drive from Rochdale, making it an ideal day trip for families during weekends and the October half-term holidays.

Visitors will be able to choose their own pumpkins directly from the patch before enjoying a range of family-friendly activities designed for children and adults alike. Organisers are also promising refreshments, hot drinks, sweet treats and seasonal food throughout the event. Advance online booking is available and is recommended for the busiest dates.

Pumpkin patches have become one of Britain's fastest-growing seasonal attractions, offering an alternative to traditional Halloween events while encouraging families to spend time outdoors together. Combined with the spectacular scenery surrounding Castleton and Winnats Pass, organisers are hoping visitors will enjoy a full day out in the Peak District.

For many Rochdale families, destinations such as Castleton have become popular autumn escapes thanks to their close proximity and beautiful countryside setting. The combination of pumpkin picking, interactive entertainment and locally prepared food makes The Patchworks another welcome addition to the region's growing calendar of family-friendly seasonal events.

The event is expected to conclude at the end of October, with Halloween marking the final days of this year's Pumpkin Patch and Autumn Festival.

title: Veterans invited to weekly breakfast club as Rochdale continues to support Armed Forces community
excerpt: Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being encouraged to attend a free weekly breakfast club in Heywood, offering friendship, support and an opportunity to reconnect with fellow servicemen and women.
content_html:
Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being invited to attend a weekly Armed Forces Breakfast Club held every Thursday morning at The Flying Horse Hotel in Heywood.

Supported by Rochdale Borough Council, the breakfast club has become a welcoming meeting place for former members of the Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force. Breakfast is served between 9am and 10am every Thursday, with organisers reporting that thousands of breakfasts have now been served since the initiative began.

While the event offers a free breakfast, its real purpose is bringing veterans together. Leaving military service can often mean leaving behind the camaraderie and close friendships built over years of service. The breakfast club provides an opportunity to reconnect with fellow veterans, share experiences and offer informal peer support in a relaxed environment.

Rochdale has a proud military heritage stretching back generations. The borough has long been associated with the Lancashire Fusiliers and today remains home to a significant Armed Forces community, including serving personnel, reservists, veterans and military families. Many continue serving their communities long after leaving the military through volunteering, public service and local charities.

Research has consistently shown that social connection can play a vital role in improving wellbeing, particularly among veterans who may experience loneliness or find the transition to civilian life challenging. Community initiatives such as breakfast clubs provide an important opportunity to maintain friendships, reduce isolation and ensure no veteran feels forgotten.

The club is open to any military veteran, regardless of how long they served or when they left the Armed Forces. Whether someone completed a full career or served for only a short period, organisers say everyone who has worn the uniform is welcome.

The Armed Forces Breakfast Club takes place every Thursday between 9am and 10am at The Flying Horse Hotel, Heywood.

Rochdale has always been a borough that values those who have served. While remembrance services rightly honour military sacrifice each November, supporting veterans throughout the year is equally important. Initiatives such as the Heywood Breakfast Club demonstrate how something as simple as sharing breakfast can strengthen friendships, improve wellbeing and remind those who have served that their contribution continues to be appreciated by the community.

title: Fresh complaints over persistent landfill odour as Heywood residents report 'sewer' stench and fly infestation
excerpt: Residents across Heywood have once again reported a strong foul odour and increasing numbers of flies, prompting renewed questions over the long-running issues surrounding the Pilsworth South landfill site.
content_html:
Residents across Heywood have once again reported a strong unpleasant smell drifting across parts of the town, with many describing an odour resembling sewage, rotting waste or landfill gas. The latest complaints have reignited concerns over the long-running issues surrounding the nearby Pilsworth South landfill site.

Several residents also reported unusually high numbers of flies, a problem which campaigners have previously associated with the landfill during earlier periods of odour complaints.

Rebecca Hodkinson wrote: "Yep... Unfortunately. And the amount of flies is something else this year."

Billy Casper added: "It stunk rotten like sewers when I was walking up Heywood past Iceland at 5.30 this evening. I don't think it was the landfill though."

Jeanette Noble commented: "I've been smelling it on Darnhill for a few months and the amount of flies is terrible."

Although some residents believe the smell may have originated elsewhere, the recurrence of similar complaints has led many to question whether problems linked to the landfill have returned.

The issue first gained widespread public attention during 2024 when thousands of complaints were submitted to the Environment Agency by residents across Heywood, Middleton, Bury and Rochdale. The smell became one of the borough's most significant environmental concerns, leading to regulatory investigations into landfill gas management and odour control measures at the site.

Under environmental law, landfill sites are permitted to operate only under an Environmental Permit issued by the Environment Agency. Operators are legally required to use Best Available Techniques (BAT) to prevent or minimise pollution, including offensive odours. Persistent smells escaping beyond the site boundary are not automatically unlawful, but they can lead to regulatory enforcement where permit conditions are breached. The Environment Agency has powers to require operational improvements, vary permit conditions, or take enforcement action where appropriate.

The issue has also attracted political attention. West Heywood councillor Angela Brown has repeatedly encouraged residents to report every odour incident directly to the Environment Agency, stressing that detailed reports help investigators establish patterns and build evidence. Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has likewise raised concerns publicly and in Parliament regarding the impact of the landfill on surrounding communities.

Controversy has continued following approval for further landfill operations despite ongoing complaints from nearby residents. Campaigners argue that expansion should not proceed until odour problems have been fully resolved, while regulators maintain that environmental permits require operators to comply with strict controls.

Residents experiencing offensive odours are encouraged to report incidents directly to the Environment Agency, recording the date, time, location, weather conditions and a description of the smell. Multiple reports from different locations can assist investigators in determining whether a wider environmental incident is occurring.

For many residents, the recurring nature of the complaints is becoming increasingly frustrating. While only a full investigation can determine the source of any individual odour event, the persistence of reports over recent years demonstrates that confidence among the local community has yet to be restored.

title: Late-night fireworks return to Shawclough and Healey as residents' frustration grows
excerpt: Residents in Shawclough and Healey have reported a second consecutive evening of fireworks after 11pm, with growing frustration over disrupted sleep, distressed pets and concerns for wildlife near Healey Dell Nature Reserve.
content_html:
Residents across Shawclough and Healey have once again reported being disturbed by late-night fireworks, with explosions heard at approximately 11.21pm on Sunday evening. The latest incident marks the second consecutive night of reports, leaving many residents questioning when meaningful action will be taken to tackle the ongoing nuisance.

For many households, the issue extends far beyond a brief display. Parents have described children being woken after bedtime, pet owners report anxious and distressed animals, and residents working early shifts say repeated interruptions to their sleep are becoming increasingly difficult to tolerate.

The repeated use of fireworks late at night has also prompted renewed concerns for local wildlife. Healey Dell Nature Reserve, together with the surrounding woodland, provides important habitat for nesting birds, bats and other protected species. Wildlife organisations have long warned that unexpected loud explosions can disturb feeding, nesting and breeding behaviour, particularly during sensitive periods of the year.

Residents have increasingly questioned whether existing legislation is sufficient to prevent repeated anti-social use of fireworks. While fireworks can be legally purchased and used subject to restrictions, businesses selling them must comply with licensing and storage regulations. However, any decision to suspend or revoke a retailer's licence would require evidence that they had breached those legal requirements. Simply because fireworks are being misused by individuals does not automatically mean a retailer has acted unlawfully.

Enforcement remains difficult, particularly when fireworks are discharged from private property under the cover of darkness. Identifying those responsible often relies on witness evidence, CCTV or reports made at the time of the incident.

Nevertheless, residents say patience is wearing thin. After another evening of disrupted sleep, many are calling for stronger enforcement, tighter controls on sales and greater action against those repeatedly using fireworks in residential neighbourhoods late at night.

Fireworks remain an important part of many cultural and community celebrations when used responsibly. However, repeated displays after 11pm in quiet residential areas are a very different matter. Communities should not have to endure nightly disruption, frightened pets, exhausted children and unnecessary disturbance to local wildlife. As complaints continue to mount, many residents are asking a simple question: when will enough finally be enough?

title: Reform UK councillors reject proposed allowance increase
excerpt: The Reform UK councillor group on Rochdale Borough Council has formally rejected a proposed increase in councillor allowances, with every group member notifying the council’s governance team that they will not accept any additional payout.
content_html:
The Reform UK councillor group on Rochdale Borough Council has formally rejected a proposed increase in councillor allowances, with every group member notifying the council’s governance team that they will not accept any additional payout.

The controversial increase was rubber-stamped by Labour councillors present at the full council meeting on Thursday 16 July, with every single Labour member in attendance voting in favour. In contrast, Reform UK councillors voted unanimously against the motion, while other political groups on the council either abstained or voted against. At a time when local residents continue to face significant cost-of-living pressures and squeezed household budgets, the Reform UK group believes it is entirely wrong to increase politician payouts funded by the taxpayer. Each Reform UK councillor has now individually written to council officers to officially opt out of the increase, ensuring the extra funds remain in the public purse.

Speaking on behalf of the Reform UK group, Group Leader Councillor John Taylor said: "Hard-working families across Rochdale are having to make tough financial decisions every single day. The idea that local politicians should push through an increase in their own allowances—as Labour did at the full council meeting on 16 July—is completely out of touch with reality. We were elected to serve our community, not to line our own pockets. Reform UK voted against this increase in the chamber, and every single member of our group has now formally instructed council governance that we will refuse to take a single extra penny. We urge councillors from other parties to do the right thing and follow our lead." Reform UK remains committed to promoting financial responsibility, cutting waste in local government, and ensuring council resources are spent directly on frontline public services for the people of Rochdale.
