title: Young bowlers invited to take part in Syke Bowling Club fun day
excerpt: Syke Bowling Club is inviting young people from across Greater Manchester to a free Junior Fun Day featuring crown green bowling, prizes, refreshments and activities aimed at introducing more children to the sport.
content_html:
Young people from across Greater Manchester are being invited to try crown green bowling at a free junior fun day taking place at Syke Bowling Club this weekend. The event is designed to introduce children and teenagers to the sport in a relaxed and welcoming environment, with food, drinks, prizes and coaching all included.

The Junior Fun Day will take place on Sunday, 2 August, at Syke Bowling Club on Dewhirst Road, Rochdale, with activities beginning at 11am. Organisers say the event is open to all juniors aged 18 and under, whether they have played crown green bowling before or are trying it for the first time.

Throughout the day, young participants will have the opportunity to take part in friendly bowling activities, meet other players and develop new skills under the guidance of club members. Organisers hope the event will encourage more young people to become involved in a sport that has a long history across Rochdale and the wider North West.

Prizes will be awarded during the event, including cash prizes, sweets and chocolate, while every junior attending will receive complimentary food, drinks and snacks. The organisers say the emphasis is on having fun, making new friends and giving children the confidence to have a go in an informal setting.

The event is also being used to appeal for local businesses and organisations to support junior bowling. Syke Bowling Club is seeking sponsors to help fund prizes and refreshments, saying contributions of any size would be welcomed to help expand opportunities for young players and support future events.

Grassroots sports clubs play an important role in communities by providing affordable activities, encouraging exercise and helping young people build confidence and friendships. Crown green bowling, while often associated with older generations, has seen clubs across the region working to attract younger players in an effort to secure the sport's long-term future.

Anyone interested in attending or finding out more can contact Lisa on 07900 493969. Organisers are encouraging families to come along, support the event and discover a sport that can be enjoyed by people of all ages.

With free refreshments, prizes and a welcoming atmosphere on offer, Syke Bowling Club hopes the Junior Fun Day will inspire the next generation of bowlers while showcasing one of Rochdale's long-established community sports clubs.

title: Reform's strongest showing yet reshapes Greater Manchester politics
excerpt: Labour retained the Greater Manchester mayoralty, but Reform UK's strongest regional performance to date has reshaped the political landscape and established the party as the city's principal opposition force.
content_html:
Greater Manchester has elected a new mayor, with Labour's Bev Craig succeeding Andy Burnham after winning the mayoral by-election. While Labour retained the office, one of the election's defining stories was the emergence of Reform UK as the city's principal opposition force, with Sian Astley delivering the party's strongest performance in a Greater Manchester-wide contest to date.

Craig secured 309,525 votes in the final round, representing 66.3 per cent of the vote, while Reform UK's Sian Astley received 157,178 votes, or 33.7 per cent. The result followed a second-round count after no candidate achieved an outright majority of first-preference votes.

Astley's campaign marked a significant moment for Reform UK in Greater Manchester. Standing on a platform centred on neighbourhood policing, transparency in regional government, public spending and directing more investment towards towns across all ten boroughs, she introduced the party's message to hundreds of thousands of voters and established Reform as Labour's most significant electoral challenger in the city-region.

The first-preference vote illustrated that shift. Astley secured 111,928 votes, comfortably finishing ahead of every other opposition candidate. While Labour maintained its lead, Reform's result demonstrated that many voters are now looking beyond the traditional political parties, reflecting wider political changes seen across England over recent years.

The election also highlighted the scale of the challenge facing every political party in reconnecting with the electorate. Turnout was 25.14 per cent, the lowest since the Greater Manchester mayoralty was introduced in 2017. More than three quarters of eligible voters chose not to cast a ballot despite the mayor holding responsibility for transport, policing, housing, regeneration, adult education funding and significant economic investment across the region.

For many observers, that figure raises important questions about public engagement with devolved government. The office of Mayor of Greater Manchester has become one of the most influential elected positions outside Westminster, yet millions of residents continue to feel disconnected from regional politics. Whether the low turnout reflected election fatigue, limited awareness of the mayor's powers or wider political dissatisfaction will no doubt be debated in the months ahead.

Astley's campaign also carried wider historical significance. Had she been elected, she would have become the first woman to serve as the directly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester since the office was created in 2017. Although that milestone was not reached, her candidacy demonstrated the increasing diversity of those seeking senior political office within the city-region.

The campaign itself was notable for the issues it placed at the centre of debate. Reform UK argued for greater scrutiny of Combined Authority spending, more visible neighbourhood policing, improved road maintenance and stronger accountability within regional government. Labour focused on continuing the Bee Network, delivering new housing and building on the devolution settlement developed under Andy Burnham. Voters were therefore presented with two distinctly different visions for Greater Manchester's future.

For Rochdale residents, the outcome will have practical consequences regardless of political preference. The mayor oversees Greater Manchester Police through the Police and Crime Commissioner powers, shapes strategic transport investment including the Bee Network, influences regeneration funding and represents the region in negotiations with central government. Decisions taken over the next four years will directly affect communities throughout Rochdale borough.

Although Labour retains control of the mayoralty, the election demonstrated that Greater Manchester's political landscape is becoming increasingly competitive. Reform UK's performance suggests future elections may no longer be defined by a straightforward Labour contest, with Astley's campaign establishing the party as a credible challenger across much of the city-region.

Attention now turns from campaigning to governing. Bev Craig inherits responsibility for one of England's largest devolved administrations at a time of financial pressure, growing demands on public services and continuing debate over transport, policing and housing. At the same time, Reform UK leaves the campaign with increased visibility, a larger regional profile and the opportunity to build on its strongest Greater Manchester result to date ahead of future elections.

title: Labour Wins GM Election: a narrow mandate, a continuity platform, and a borough still waiting
excerpt: Bev Craig is Mayor of Greater Manchester, elected on the lowest turnout the office has seen and taken to a second round by Reform.
content_html:
Bev Craig takes office as Mayor of Greater Manchester having won 309,525 votes to Sian Astley's 157,178, a second-round margin of 66.3 per cent to 33.7. She inherits transport, policing, housing and skills powers assembled over nine years, and a budget running to billions.

Turnout was 25.14 per cent, the lowest since the office was created. Craig's total amounts to roughly one in seven of those entitled to vote. That is not a criticism of her — she did not choose the date, and no candidate can compel people to the polls. But it could set the stage for what follows. A mayor with powers of this scale and a base of active consent this narrow should expect close questioning, and would be wise to welcome it.

The contest was also tighter on first preferences than the final figure implies. Neither candidate reached 50 per cent outright, which is why a second count was needed. Reform UK finished second across all ten boroughs at its first serious attempt at this office. Labour has held the mayoralty since it was created; it has now been taken to a second round in its strongest English region.

The substantive disagreement is about continuity. Craig campaigned on carrying forward the programme she inherits — the Bee Network, housing delivery, neighbourhood policing, further devolution talks with government. For Manchester that is a reasonable prospectus. For Rochdale it is the least attractive offer available, because the arrangement now being continued has not worked here. The borough sits at the end of a Metrolink line, with a rail service that has been unreliable for years, contributing to a city-region strategy whose most visible results are concentrated closer to the centre.

There is a fair answer to that, and it deserves stating. Craig's supporters argue that a Labour mayor working with a Labour government is better placed to win further devolved powers and the money attached to them, and that Rochdale gains more from that than from opposition. It is a serious argument. It is also a testable one, and the test is whether the borough's share of transport and housing investment rises over the next four years or stays where it is.

On policing, the mayor holds the powers of a Police and Crime Commissioner, which makes this the area where the office touches residents most directly. Our measure will be simple and public: response times, charge rates, and whether people who report a crime in this borough hear back. Those figures are published. We intend to use them.

The by-election itself carried a cost — the 2024 mayoral contest cost taxpayers £4.7 million, and this one is expected to run to millions again. That is a consequence of a sitting mayor leaving mid-term for Westminster, not of anything the new mayor did. But it is money spent on an election in which three quarters of the electorate did not participate, and it is reasonable to ask what the region got for it.

Craig begins with substantial powers and a quiet electorate. We will report what she does with them, and judge her on what changes in this borough rather than on what is announced in Manchester.

title: Residents in Shawclough and Healey call for action over late-night fireworks
excerpt: Residents in Shawclough and Healey are calling for stronger action after repeated late-night fireworks disrupted neighbourhoods, with concerns over sleep, vulnerable people, wildlife and the difficulty of identifying those responsible.
content_html:
Residents in Shawclough and Healey are calling for stronger action after repeated late-night fireworks disturbed neighbourhoods, with many saying explosions after 11pm are affecting sleep, frightening children and causing distress to vulnerable people. While organised displays remain an important part of celebrations throughout the year, many residents say fireworks are increasingly being let off on ordinary evenings with little regard for those living nearby.

The latest complaints prompted a strong response on social media. Local resident Nick Simpson wrote: "Absolutely outrageous. These people need to be locked up and fined," reflecting frustration shared by others who say the disturbances have become an unwelcome feature of late evenings.

Councillor Shah Wazir also urged residents to report incidents wherever possible. Responding to complaints, he said: "Please report this to police and if you know the address then it will certainly help. Firework at night is totally unacceptable, no matter what occasion."

Fireworks are already regulated by law. In most circumstances they cannot legally be set off between 11pm and 7am, with later cut-off times applying only on Bonfire Night, New Year's Eve, Diwali and Chinese New Year. Retailers can only sell fireworks all year if they hold the appropriate licence, while most other retailers are restricted to seasonal sales.

Despite those laws, many residents believe enforcement remains one of the biggest challenges. Fireworks are usually set off after dark from private gardens, alleyways or open spaces, making it difficult for neighbours to identify exactly where they have come from. By the time officers could arrive, the noise has often stopped and those responsible may have left the area.

Many people are also understandably reluctant to confront those responsible themselves. Approaching unknown individuals late at night carries obvious risks, particularly where alcohol or antisocial behaviour may already be involved. Residents say they often feel they have little practical option beyond reporting incidents after they have happened, despite recognising that successful enforcement depends on accurate information.

The disruption extends far beyond a few loud bangs. Parents describe young children being startled awake and struggling to settle again, while elderly residents and people recovering from illness can lose valuable sleep. Mental health charities have also highlighted the impact unexpected fireworks can have on people living with anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder and other conditions where sudden loud noises may trigger distress.

Wildlife is also affected. Conservation organisations have warned that repeated fireworks can disturb nesting birds and protected species such as bats, while many pet owners report dogs, cats and other animals becoming frightened by sudden explosions. Unlike organised displays, fireworks used without warning leave residents with little opportunity to prepare vulnerable family members or animals.

The issue has prompted wider debate over whether existing laws go far enough or whether stronger enforcement is needed. While legislation already restricts when fireworks can be used, many residents argue the difficulty lies in identifying those responsible quickly enough for police to take effective action.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing the illegal use of fireworks or persistent antisocial behaviour to report it, particularly where an address or precise location can be provided. As concerns continue to emerge from Shawclough, Healey and other parts of the borough, many residents hope greater awareness, responsible use and more effective enforcement will help restore quieter evenings to Rochdale's neighbourhoods.

title: Could Greater Manchester elect its first woman mayor?
excerpt: As the Greater Manchester mayoral count continues, Sian Astley could become the first woman to hold the office if elected, marking a historic milestone for the city-region's devolved government.
content_html:
As Greater Manchester awaits the declaration of its mayoral by-election, one potential milestone has emerged alongside the political contest. If Reform UK candidate Sian Astley is elected, she would become the first woman to serve as the directly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester since the office was established in 2017.

The mayoralty has grown into one of the most influential elected positions outside Westminster. The successful candidate will oversee transport through the Bee Network, hold the powers of the Police and Crime Commissioner, help shape housing and regeneration policy, manage elements of adult education funding and represent Greater Manchester in discussions with central government over future devolution.

Astley entered politics after a career in business and property development before winning election as a councillor in Manchester. Her mayoral campaign has focused on transparency in regional government, neighbourhood policing, public spending and directing investment across all ten Greater Manchester boroughs. She has argued that communities outside Manchester city centre should receive a greater share of future funding and infrastructure projects.

If elected, Astley would follow Tony Lloyd and Andy Burnham, both of whom held the office before her. While women have led councils and held senior public roles across Greater Manchester, the directly elected mayoralty has so far only been occupied by men.

The possibility of the city-region electing its first female mayor has attracted attention beyond party politics. Supporters describe it as an opportunity to broaden representation in one of England's most significant devolved offices, while political opponents have continued to debate her policies rather than the historical significance of her candidacy.

The election itself follows Andy Burnham's departure after almost a decade in office. During that time, the role expanded considerably through devolution agreements, making the mayor responsible for decisions that affect millions of residents across Rochdale, Manchester, Salford, Bolton, Bury, Oldham, Stockport, Tameside, Trafford and Wigan.

Whatever the outcome, the by-election represents a significant moment for Greater Manchester. Voters are choosing not only who will lead the combined authority but also who will inherit responsibility for some of the region's most important public services. If the result confirms Astley's election, it would also mark the first time a woman has held the office, adding a new chapter to the history of Greater Manchester's devolved government.

The official declaration is expected once counting has concluded. Until then, the result remains subject to the completion of the count and formal confirmation by the returning officer.

title: Everything You Need to Know Before Rochdale Feel Good Festival 2026
excerpt: From headliners and ticket prices to travel, parking, accessibility and the latest weather forecast, here's everything you need to know before Rochdale Feel Good Festival returns next weekend.
content_html:
Rochdale's biggest annual music event returns next weekend, with thousands of visitors expected to descend on the town centre for the 2026 Feel Good Festival. Headlined by BRIT Award-winning singer Gabrielle, alongside indie favourites Ash and Starsailor, the festival promises a full day of live music, street entertainment, food, drink and family activities, continuing a tradition that has become one of Greater Manchester's most successful free town centre festivals.

Now celebrating its 15th edition, the Feel Good Festival has grown from a small local music event into one of the highlights of the borough's cultural calendar. Previous festivals have welcomed acts including Ocean Colour Scene, Razorlight, Feeder, The Coral, Scouting For Girls, The Fratellis, Heather Small, Cast, Toploader, Badly Drawn Boy, The Feeling, The Lightning Seeds and The Beat, attracting visitors from across the North West and providing a welcome boost to Rochdale's hospitality and retail sectors.

This year's main stage takes place in the stunning surroundings of the newly restored Rochdale Town Hall Square on Saturday, 8 August. Headlining the evening is Gabrielle, whose catalogue includes classics such as Dreams, Rise and Out of Reach. She is joined by Ash, Starsailor, funk and soul outfit The Allergies and Manchester indie rising star Alex Spencer, with additional performances throughout the day and live entertainment continuing across numerous indoor venues around the town centre. Most indoor performances remain completely free, with only the main stage requiring a ticket.

Festival organisers have continued their commitment to making the event affordable. Early bird tickets sold out quickly at £15 before subsequent release phases increased to £25, £30, £35 and the final allocation at £45 plus booking fees. VIP upgrades remain available for those wanting premium viewing areas and additional hospitality. Every ticket includes a reusable festival cup as part of the organisers' ongoing efforts to reduce single-use plastics.

Entertainment begins from 11.30am and continues until approximately 10.45pm, with the main stage located in Rochdale Town Hall Square. Festival organisers recommend arriving early to collect wristbands, avoid queues and enjoy the wide variety of free entertainment taking place throughout the town centre before the headline performances begin.

Getting to the festival is expected to be straightforward thanks to Rochdale's excellent public transport links. Organisers are encouraging visitors to use public transport where possible, with Metrolink trams running directly into Rochdale town centre and Northern train services providing regular connections from Manchester Victoria, Leeds, Halifax and Blackburn. Numerous Bee Network bus services also stop within a short walk of the festival site, while taxi ranks will operate throughout the day and into the evening to assist those travelling home after the headline acts.

Drivers are advised to allow extra time, as town centre car parks are expected to fill quickly. Public parking is available at several locations including The Esplanade, Riverside, Baillie Street and other nearby council-operated car parks, although temporary road closures around the Town Hall may affect access during the festival. Visitors are encouraged to check council travel advice before setting off.

Accessibility continues to be a major focus for organisers. A dedicated accessible viewing platform will be available within the main stage arena for wheelchair users and those with mobility issues, while British Sign Language interpreters will be present during main stage performances. Accessible toilets are provided both within the outdoor festival site and nearby indoor venues. Essential companion tickets are available free of charge for eligible visitors, assistance dogs are welcome and a quiet space will also be available for anyone requiring time away from the crowds.

Toilets will be located throughout the festival site, including accessible facilities, with additional public conveniences available inside participating venues. Festival stewards will be on hand throughout the day to assist visitors and provide directions around the event.

Food has become almost as popular as the music in recent years, with dozens of traders expected to serve everything from gourmet burgers and wood-fired pizzas to Asian street food, desserts and locally produced refreshments. Although organisers have not published official bar prices, visitors should expect festival-standard pricing broadly comparable with similar outdoor events across Greater Manchester. Outside alcohol is not permitted inside the main stage arena, although sealed soft drinks and water may be allowed subject to festival rules. Visitors are encouraged to support local independent food and drink traders operating throughout the event.

The weather currently looks favourable for festival-goers, with forecasts suggesting a mostly sunny day, light winds and temperatures reaching around 19°C. While conditions can always change, current forecasts indicate comfortable weather for spending the day outdoors, although organisers still recommend bringing sunscreen, drinking plenty of water and packing a light waterproof just in case the British summer has other ideas.

Beyond the music, the Feel Good Festival has become an important economic event for Rochdale. Thousands of visitors pass through the town centre every year, providing a significant boost to local restaurants, pubs, cafés, hotels and independent retailers. The festival also showcases Rochdale's cultural offer following the restoration of the Grade I-listed Town Hall and supports the borough's wider ambitions to attract more visitors and investment.

The festival is organised on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council with support from Rochdale Development Agency, ticket sales and sponsorship from local businesses and community partners. Over the years, numerous organisations have supported the event, helping to ensure it remains one of the North West's best-value music festivals while continuing to celebrate local talent alongside nationally recognised artists.

For anyone planning to attend, organisers recommend arriving early, using public transport where possible, checking travel updates before setting off and allowing extra time to move between venues. Whether you're there to see Gabrielle, discover new artists, enjoy the food village or simply soak up the atmosphere in Rochdale town centre, this year's Feel Good Festival looks set to continue one of the borough's proudest summer traditions.

title: Who is Sian Astley? The businesswoman hoping to reshape Greater Manchester politics
excerpt: Businesswoman, councillor and Reform UK's Greater Manchester mayoral candidate, Sian Astley has rapidly become one of the region's most talked-about political figures. Here's a closer look at her background, campaign and policies.
content_html:
Until recently, Sian Astley was better known for property development and television appearances than frontline politics. Today, the Reform UK councillor is one of the party's most recognisable figures in Greater Manchester, having been selected to contest the mayoral by-election following Andy Burnham's departure from the role.

Astley's political rise has been rapid. Earlier this year she won the Baguley ward on Manchester City Council, ending more than half a century of Labour representation in the area. She now leads Reform UK's group on the council, giving the party a significantly higher profile in one of Labour's traditional strongholds.

Away from politics, Astley runs a design and property business and has appeared on national television discussing housing, renovation and landlord issues. A graduate of the University of Manchester, she has frequently argued that politics benefits from representatives with experience outside Westminster and local government. Speaking after her selection, she said she wanted 'real people with real life experience' making decisions that affect local communities.

Her campaign centred on a message that Greater Manchester has become too heavily dominated by a single political party. Astley argued that decades of Labour control across many parts of the city-region had reduced scrutiny and accountability, claiming residents deserved greater transparency over how public money is spent. Reform UK's campaign presented itself as offering robust opposition rather than continuity.

One of Astley's headline pledges was to review major contracts and spending decisions taken during Andy Burnham's time as mayor. She proposed examining combined authority spending on development projects, reviewing expenditure connected to the abandoned Clean Air Zone proposals and increasing public access to information about regional decision-making. Reform UK argued that taxpayers should have greater visibility over how devolved budgets are allocated.

Crime and community safety formed another central pillar of her campaign. Reform UK proposed increasing police visibility, taking a tougher approach to knife crime, expanding the use of stop-and-search powers, tackling shoplifting and antisocial behaviour, and prioritising neighbourhood policing. The party argued that public confidence in policing had declined and that stronger enforcement was needed to improve safety across Greater Manchester.

Transport policy also featured prominently. Astley criticised spending on what she described as underused cycling infrastructure and opposed introducing additional charges on motorists. She argued that investment should be distributed more evenly across Greater Manchester rather than concentrating predominantly on Manchester city centre, saying outer boroughs such as Rochdale, Bolton and Wigan deserved a larger share of future transport and regeneration funding.

Economic development was another recurring theme. Reform UK's manifesto called for greater support for high streets, road maintenance and local businesses, alongside efforts to reduce what the party described as unnecessary expenditure within the Greater Manchester Combined Authority. Astley argued that improving everyday infrastructure would deliver more visible benefits to residents than prestige projects concentrated in the regional centre.

Immigration also featured in Reform UK's regional campaign, although many aspects remain matters for national government rather than the Mayor of Greater Manchester. The party proposed greater transparency around asylum accommodation, opposition to the use of hotels for asylum seekers and stronger cooperation with councils on community impacts. Supporters argued these proposals reflected public concerns, while critics questioned how much influence a metro mayor could realistically exercise over national immigration policy.

Like every candidate in the contest, Astley also faced criticism during the campaign. Political opponents challenged the practicality of some of Reform UK's proposals, particularly where powers rest with Westminster rather than the combined authority. There was also discussion after Astley withdrew from one mayoral hustings organised by The Mill, with Astley stating she objected to the exclusion of independent candidate Marcus Farmer, while organisers maintained their own position on participation.

Whatever the election result, few would dispute that Astley has helped establish Reform UK as a more visible force in Greater Manchester politics. Her victory in Baguley demonstrated the party's ability to make gains in areas long considered Labour strongholds, and her mayoral campaign brought Reform's message before voters across all ten boroughs.

The longer-term question is whether that momentum can be sustained. Metro mayoral elections often provide smaller parties with greater exposure than they receive during local elections, but converting visibility into long-term electoral success is a more difficult task. Reform UK will likely judge Astley's campaign not solely by the final vote share but by whether it has expanded the party's organisation, profile and support across Greater Manchester.

As Greater Manchester enters a post-Burnham political era, Astley's campaign reflects wider changes taking place in British politics. Voters are increasingly presented with alternatives beyond the traditional two-party contest, while regional elections are becoming an important testing ground for emerging political movements. Whether Reform UK can translate growing national support into sustained regional influence remains to be seen, but Sian Astley's campaign has undoubtedly ensured the party is now part of that conversation.

title: After Burnham: What the Next Mayor Inherits
excerpt: The next Mayor of Greater Manchester will inherit far more than Andy Burnham's office, taking responsibility for one of England's most powerful devolved administrations at a time of political and financial change.
content_html:
Whoever becomes the next Mayor of Greater Manchester will inherit one of the most powerful devolved political offices in England at a pivotal moment for both the city-region and national politics. Andy Burnham's departure after almost nine years in office marks the end of an era that saw the mayoralty evolve from a relatively new experiment in devolution into a position with significant influence over transport, policing, regeneration, housing and economic development.

Burnham's resignation to return to Westminster has inevitably altered the political landscape. During his time as mayor he became synonymous with Greater Manchester's devolution agenda, frequently acting as the public face of the region during negotiations with successive governments. Whether residents agreed with his policies or not, few would dispute that he raised the national profile of Greater Manchester and demonstrated how influential a metro mayor could become.

The incoming mayor therefore faces a different challenge from Burnham in 2017. Rather than creating the office's identity from scratch, the next incumbent must decide whether to build on Burnham's approach or chart a new direction. Expectations are considerably higher than they were nine years ago because the public now expects the mayor to deliver visible improvements rather than simply establish the role.

Transport remains the most obvious priority. The Bee Network has become one of the flagship achievements of Greater Manchester's devolution settlement, bringing buses back under public control and integrating services with trams and active travel. While supporters argue that the network is beginning to create a genuinely joined-up public transport system, critics continue to raise concerns about reliability, congestion, funding and the pace of implementation. The next mayor will inherit both the opportunities and the political scrutiny that accompany such an ambitious programme.

Policing is another area where expectations remain high. The Mayor of Greater Manchester also exercises the powers of the Police and Crime Commissioner, giving the office direct responsibility for setting policing priorities, overseeing budgets and holding Greater Manchester Police to account. Crime, antisocial behaviour and neighbourhood policing featured prominently throughout the by-election campaign, with candidates from across the political spectrum promising safer communities, stronger visible policing and better support for victims.

Housing and regeneration are likely to remain central themes throughout the next mayoral term. Greater Manchester continues to experience significant demand for affordable housing while balancing pressures for economic growth, environmental protection and infrastructure investment. Large regeneration schemes are transforming parts of Manchester city centre, Salford and several surrounding boroughs, but many communities continue to ask whether the benefits of that growth are being shared equally across the region.

For Rochdale, those questions are particularly important. Investment decisions made by the combined authority influence transport links, skills funding, brownfield regeneration, town centre renewal and wider economic development. Although individual councils retain many planning responsibilities, the mayor plays a significant strategic role in shaping investment priorities across Greater Manchester.

The constitutional picture is also changing. Devolution has steadily expanded over the past decade, with successive governments transferring additional responsibilities from Whitehall to regional authorities. Greater Manchester has often been used as the model for further devolution elsewhere in England, meaning decisions taken by its mayor frequently attract national attention. The incoming mayor is therefore likely to spend as much time negotiating with ministers as delivering local policy.

The by-election campaigns reflected differing views about how those powers should be exercised. Labour argued for continuity, seeking to build on existing transport and regeneration programmes. Reform UK focused on reducing public spending, increasing accountability and prioritising crime and community safety. Restore Britain centred its campaign on transparency, democratic reform and greater public involvement in local decision-making. The Conservatives promoted business growth and improved public services, while the Green Party emphasised sustainability and environmental investment. Liberal Democrats highlighted local accountability and public service reform. Although their policies differed considerably, almost every candidate accepted that the mayoralty has become one of the region's most influential political offices.

Another challenge awaiting the successful candidate is rebuilding public engagement. The record-low turnout has inevitably raised questions about democratic participation. While the mayor's powers have expanded significantly since 2017, public awareness has not always kept pace. Many residents still struggle to distinguish between the responsibilities of local councils, Parliament and the combined authority. Improving understanding of what the mayor actually does may become almost as important as delivering new policies.

Financial pressures will also shape the next administration. Like councils across England, Greater Manchester faces difficult decisions over public spending. Rising demand for public services, inflationary pressures and competing investment priorities mean every major project will come under close scrutiny. The next mayor will need to balance long-term ambitions with short-term financial realities while maintaining public confidence.

Perhaps the greatest test, however, will be leadership. Andy Burnham's tenure demonstrated that a metro mayor can become a nationally recognised political figure capable of influencing debates far beyond the boundaries of Greater Manchester. His successor now inherits not only extensive powers but also heightened expectations. Residents will judge the next mayor not simply by campaign promises but by whether transport improves, neighbourhoods feel safer, regeneration reaches towns beyond Manchester city centre and economic growth benefits communities across all ten boroughs.

The constitutional significance of this transition should not be underestimated. For the first time since the office was created, Greater Manchester is entering a post-Burnham era. Whether that represents continuity or a fresh chapter will depend not only on the election result but on how effectively the next mayor uses one of the most powerful devolved mandates in the country. The office has matured; now its next occupant must prove that devolution itself can continue to deliver meaningful change for the people it was designed to serve.

title: Veterans charity says demand for support is growing after emotional day for volunteers
excerpt: A Rochdale organisation supporting military veterans and disadvantaged young people has issued an emotional appeal for greater support after a recent case reminded volunteers why their work remains so important.
content_html:
A Rochdale-based community organisation supporting military veterans and disadvantaged young people has issued an emotional appeal for greater public support after what it described as one of the most challenging days in its history.

Get Together After Serving CIC (GTAS) said a recent case involving people it was assisting left members of its leadership team deeply affected, highlighting the growing pressures facing both former servicemen and women and vulnerable children within the community. While the organisation has not released details of the case in order to protect those involved, it says the experience reinforced the urgent need for the support services it provides every day.

In a heartfelt statement shared with supporters, GTAS explained that one of its directors, Wayne, was left visibly emotional after witnessing the circumstances surrounding the latest referral. According to the organisation, despite a lifetime of experience dealing with trauma, military service and personal hardship, the situation served as a powerful reminder that many people continue to struggle in silence.

The organisation says these moments rarely become public. Instead, staff and volunteers often work quietly behind the scenes, providing practical assistance, emotional support and signposting to those who find themselves in crisis. GTAS says much of its work takes place away from social media and public attention, with the focus remaining firmly on helping individuals rather than seeking recognition.

Founded to support former members of the Armed Forces while also creating opportunities for disadvantaged children and young people, Get Together After Serving CIC has steadily expanded its role within the local community. Alongside offering companionship and welfare support for veterans, the organisation works to reduce social isolation, improve wellbeing and create positive opportunities for young people who may otherwise feel overlooked.

Veterans' charities across the UK have repeatedly highlighted the complex challenges many former service personnel face after leaving the Armed Forces. Although the transition to civilian life is smooth for many, others experience difficulties relating to housing, employment, mental health, financial hardship or adjusting to life outside military service. Community organisations often play an important role by offering early intervention before problems escalate.

At the same time, many charities supporting children and young people have reported increasing demand for services as families continue to face financial pressures and wider social challenges. Community groups such as GTAS frequently rely on volunteers, donations and fundraising to continue delivering projects that might otherwise be unavailable to those who need them.

GTAS says its work demonstrates how relatively small organisations can have a significant impact despite operating with limited resources. Its latest appeal emphasises that a dedicated team of volunteers continues to provide support every day because they believe nobody should have to face hardship alone.

In its statement, the organisation said the latest events reinforced its belief that its work is not simply beneficial but, in some cases, life-changing. It described helping veterans find safety and dignity while giving disadvantaged young people opportunities, stability and a place where they feel valued.

The charity is now encouraging local residents, businesses and community organisations to become involved, whether by volunteering, making donations, fundraising or simply helping raise awareness of its work. It believes that increasing community support will allow it to reach more people before problems become crises.

Like many community interest companies, GTAS operates in an increasingly challenging funding environment. Demand for grassroots support services has grown while competition for grants and charitable funding has become more intense. As a result, many organisations rely heavily on local goodwill to sustain their work.

The latest appeal serves as a reminder that behind every public fundraising campaign or social media post are real people facing difficult circumstances, often away from public view. For the volunteers involved, success is not measured by headlines or recognition but by the number of people who receive help when they need it most.

Anyone wishing to learn more about Get Together After Serving CIC, volunteer their time or support its work can find further information through the organisation's social media channels. GTAS says every contribution, no matter how small, helps strengthen its ability to support veterans and young people across the Rochdale area.

title: One in Four: Why Greater Manchester Stayed Home
excerpt: A record-low turnout of around 25.14 per cent has become one of the defining stories of Greater Manchester's mayoral by-election, raising fresh questions about voter engagement and the future of devolution.
content_html:
The biggest story to emerge from Greater Manchester's mayoral by-election may not be who won, but who did not vote. With turnout reported at around 25.14 per cent, almost three quarters of eligible voters chose not to cast a ballot in an election that will determine who oversees policing, transport, housing, regeneration, skills funding and billions of pounds of public investment across the city-region.

The result represents the lowest turnout recorded since the office of Mayor of Greater Manchester was created in 2017. The inaugural mayoral election attracted around 28.9 per cent of eligible voters, participation increased to approximately 34.7 per cent in 2021 before easing to just over 32 per cent in 2024. Even allowing for the fact that by-elections traditionally attract fewer voters than scheduled elections, the latest figure has reignited debate about whether the region's devolved political system is truly engaging the public.

It is a striking contradiction. Over the past nine years the mayoralty has become significantly more powerful. The office now controls Transport for Greater Manchester, the Bee Network, policing through Police and Crime Commissioner powers, the Fire and Rescue Service, adult education funding, strategic planning and large parts of the region's regeneration programme. The mayor also acts as Greater Manchester's principal representative in negotiations with Westminster over devolution and investment.

Despite those responsibilities, many residents appear to remain unclear about exactly what the mayor does. Throughout the campaign, local news outlets, community groups and social media users encountered comments from voters asking whether the mayor controlled local councils, council tax or national government policy. That confusion suggests there remains a considerable gap between the powers exercised by the office and public understanding of those powers.

Several factors are likely to have contributed to the record-low turnout. First, this was a by-election rather than a scheduled mayoral contest. By-elections almost always produce lower participation because they lack the wider publicity generated by a general election or a full round of local elections. Without national party leaders dominating television debates and newspaper headlines, many casual voters simply pay less attention.

Timing may also have played a part. Polling took place during the school summer holidays, when many families were travelling or focused on other priorities. While postal voting allows people to participate away from home, elections held during holiday periods have historically struggled to match turnout achieved during spring or autumn campaigns.

Political fatigue is another possible explanation. Since 2024, voters have been asked to participate in multiple elections at different levels of government. Some political scientists argue that frequent elections can reduce participation over time, particularly where people feel they are repeatedly being asked to vote without seeing immediate improvements in their daily lives.

The departure of Andy Burnham also changed the character of the election. During his nine years as mayor, Burnham became one of the country's best-known regional politicians, often appearing on national television while leading campaigns on transport, homelessness, devolution and Greater Manchester's response to the Covid-19 pandemic. Whether voters agreed with him or not, his public profile undoubtedly helped define the office. This by-election was the first opportunity for voters to choose a successor rather than simply judge Burnham's record.

Campaign visibility became another talking point. While candidates visited communities across the ten Greater Manchester boroughs, many residents commented online that they had seen little evidence of campaigning compared with previous elections. Others said they only became aware of polling day shortly before voting opened. Those comments are anecdotal and should not be taken as representative of the wider electorate, but they echo criticism that metro mayoral elections still struggle to capture public attention despite the growing importance of the role.

The campaign itself was also unusually fragmented. Seven candidates contested the election, offering markedly different visions for Greater Manchester. Labour sought to build on Andy Burnham's legacy of transport integration and devolution. Reform UK focused heavily on crime, public spending and accountability. Restore Britain campaigned on transparency and local democracy, while the Conservatives, Greens, Liberal Democrats and independent candidate each promoted distinct policy priorities. Yet despite this broad choice, turnout remained stubbornly low.

For Rochdale residents, the result matters regardless of party politics. The mayor will influence transport investment affecting the borough, oversee policing priorities through Greater Manchester Police, support regeneration funding, negotiate future devolution settlements and help shape long-term economic strategy. Decisions made by the combined authority often have direct consequences for local services and infrastructure.

Some observers have argued that the low turnout should serve as a warning rather than simply another election statistic. Devolution was designed to bring political decision-making closer to local communities. If only one in four voters participates in choosing the person leading that process, questions inevitably arise about democratic legitimacy and public engagement.

There are no easy answers. Better civic education, clearer communication about the mayor's responsibilities, greater local media coverage and more visible campaigning have all been suggested as ways of increasing participation in future elections. Others believe turnout will naturally recover once the new mayor establishes a public profile and begins making decisions that directly affect residents across the region.

Whatever the explanation, one conclusion appears difficult to avoid. Greater Manchester now possesses one of the most powerful devolved political offices in England, yet public participation has moved in the opposite direction. Whoever occupies the mayor's office over the coming years faces a challenge extending beyond transport, housing or policing: rebuilding public confidence in local democracy itself.
